News.title: Ballon d'Or 2026 LIVE: Updates as full list of nominated players to be confirmed
News.content:
The nominated list for the 2026 Ballon d'Or is set to be released this morning with Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham expected to be among those in the running

The nominees for the 2026 Ballon d'Or will be released this morning.

England forward Harry Kane is the bookmakers' favourite to win the prestigious award following a prolific season for Bayern Munich. However, history suggests that football's biggest individual prize rarely gets decided by goals alone.

After the Ballon d'Or was first awarded in 1956, performances in the biggest competitions have shaped the outcome. World Cup years, in particular, have followed a clear pattern and it has been shown just how difficult it is to win the award without lifting a major continental or global tournament.

With that in mind, Spain are expected to have several players feature among the 30 nominees after they triumphed at the World Cup in North America. Argentina ran them close, while England and France both reached the semi-final, and those three nations are poised to nave a number of players in there, too.

Stay tuned here on Mirror Football for the latest on the Ballon d'Or nominees...

News.title: These everyday habits mean young adults use more water than any other age group
News.content:
These everyday habits mean young adults use more water than any other age group

New research shows younger generations are more likely to have higher water use than older generations - as expert says 'small changes can make a real difference'

View 2 Images Younger generations use more water than anybody else (Image: Getty Images)

Younger generations use more water than older adults, either by taking longer showers or using the washing machine for smaller loads. A recent survey by Let’s Save Water campaign, which wants people to reduce the amount of water they use each day, found millennials were most likely to take baths instead of showers (26%) and rinse dishes before putting them in the dishwasher (30%).

‌



The poll of 2,000 adults in England and Wales also found Gen Z were most likely to take showers longer than 10 minutes (44%) and use the washing machine for very small loads (24%). But 45% of Baby Boomers still report letting the tap run while waiting for water to get hot or cold, making them more likely to do so than adults under 29 (37%).

‌



View 2 Images Millennials love to take a bath (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Environmental behaviour psychologist Ian Walker said: “People underestimate just how much water is used through everyday habits, but the good news is that small changes can make a real difference.

“Whether it’s spending a little less time in the shower, only putting on full loads of washing, or turning the tap off when it’s not needed, there are lots of simple ways to cut back without disrupting your routine.

“By making a few mindful choices each day, households across England and Wales can help save thousands of litres of water over the course of a year."

‌



The study found turning the tap off while brushing their teeth (43%) and waiting until the washing machine is full before running it (37%) were among the simple changes respondents would be willing to make.

But 44% think taking a two-minute shorter shower and using a washing-up bowl instead of leaving the tap running (41%) were among the water-saving habits that could make the biggest difference.

‌



According to the campaign, saving 28 litres (about a kitchen sink full) in England or 38 litres (3 buckets) in Wales per person, per day will ensure there's enough water for generations to come - something 97% of respondents didn't know.

Separate research of 3,330 adults in England and Wales found 66% of those in England feel a personal responsibility to help reduce water consumption - while only 33% of those in Wales feel the same.

A spokesperson for Let’s Save Water added: “It's encouraging that most people already want to do their bit to save water. The reality is that we all use water differently, which means we all have opportunities to make a difference.

Article continues below

“Small changes at home can add up to a significant impact when millions of people make them together.”

News.title: RNLI fundraiser for 'Flying Farage' hovercraft jumps £5,000 after far-right thugs attack hero volunteers
News.content:
RNLI fundraiser for 'Flying Farage' hovercraft jumps £5,000 after far-right thugs attack hero volunteers

EXCLUSIVE: After a far-right group confronted RNLI crews on Sunday night in Portsmouth, a wave of good-hearted Brits poured money into the charity once again, to counteract their attacks

View 5 Images Donations have soared for the Flying Farage fundraiser (AI image) (Image: GoFundMe)

A satirical fundraiser for an RNLI 'Flying Farage' hovercraft has jumped by more than £5,000 in just two days, after far-right attacks on volunteers sparked a furious backlash.

‌



The GoFundMe campaign, launched by Simon Harris - known as ManBehavingDadly on social media - has raised a staggering £336,000 for the Royal National Lifeboat Institute (RNLI) since 2021. He started the fundraiser years ago, after Reform UK leader Nigel Farage brazenly branded the RNLI a "taxi service for illegal immigration".

‌



It's been running for five years now, and donations suddenly spiked in the aftermath of vile attacks on volunteers. After a far-right group confronted RNLI crews on Sunday night in Portsmouth, a wave of good-hearted Brits poured money into the charity once again, to counteract their attacks. The total amount raised subsequently jumped from £331,000 on Sunday, to more than £336,000.

‌



The crews, who were based on the Isle of Wight, helped a 'mega dinghy' carrying about 120 people which was stranded in the Channel. It came into UK waters from Cherbourg, near the ferry crossing for Portsmouth, rather than using the usual route from Calais into Dover, Kent. They were saved by lifeboat rescuers, who returned back to shore to find a group of balaclava-clad men in a boat shouting: “How do you feel bringing illegal migrants into this country?”

You can donate to the GoFundMe here

View 5 Images The GoFundMe fundraiser has topped £336,000 (Image: GoFundMe)

‌



A volunteer in a yellow life jacket told them: “I don’t know; I haven’t brought any in.” The protestors replied: "Look at these guys. Absolute traitors to this country. Look at the state of you.” Other footage posted also showed people shouting abuse at an RNLI crew on their boat. There were again calls of 'traitors' and 'Yellow jackets, yellowbellies'. Another protestor described the lifesaving crews as 'scum'.

Police launched a hunt for the masked thugs, who injured officers and damaged vehicles during anti-migrant protests in Portsmouth. They were investigating potential assaults and criminal damage, after black-clad activists attempted to block migrants being driven away overnight on Sunday.

Meanwhile, Mr Farage also previously criticised the RNLI, claiming it was encouraging more unsafe crossings in small boats, as it was working as a "taxi service". The RNLI later responded by declaring its obligation to help anyone in distress on coastal waters, under international maritime law.

‌



View 5 Images The RNLI has responded saying they will rescue people 'without judgement or preference' as the service has done for more than 200 years

Mr Harris said his opinion of the Reform leader was low, and it gets lower every time he attacks the RNLI.

He told the Mirror: "It's like the NHS. RNLI volunteers are risking their lives - they're not being paid for it. It should be almost like a sacred cow."

‌



The campaign has quietly been raising hundreds of thousands of pounds over a number of years, with the ultimate goal of reaching £500,000. All money was donated directly to the RNLI, and the decision whether to buy a 'Flying Farage' was at the charity's discretion.

But, all donations have been ring-fenced for running costs at RNLI stations in the south-east of England. Mr Harris wrote on the GoFundMe: "This means that there’s always a very good chance that donations will go towards helping the very people that Farage and many other ruddy-faced gammons love screaming at in The Channel."

View 5 Images RNLI rescuers returned from helping the stranded migrants to find a group of men shouting abuse

‌



Mr Farage was the inspiration behind the fundraiser, but right-wing criticism of the charity has been continuing for a number of years, meaning donations have continued to rise.

Mr Harris said: "We're trying to make sure that for every dipstick who pulls his direct debit to the RNLI, there are another five or six people who are ready to step in and speak up on their behalf and help them out.

"In the last few days, it's taken a really sinister turn . Now we've got RNLI volunteers being photographed and named, and addresses flying around and getting doxxed. I've had quite a few messages from people who have got relatives who are serving lifeboat volunteers, and they're absolutely worried sick - especially after what happened in Portsmouth the other night."

‌



View 5 Images RNLI volunteers were targeted by far-right protesters in Portsmouth after helping rescue stranded migrants (Image: Barry Williams/PA Wire)

Just 5.7% of people who crossed the Channel in small boats in 2015 were rescued by RNLI volunteers. The overwhelming majority of people were rescued by other agencies, including the Border Force.

The charity wrote on its website: "Lifeboat crews don’t pick who they rescue. They will answer the call for help whenever it comes. Whatever the situation, they will always do what they can to save every one they can."

Article continues below

News.title: New fruit in Tesco and M&S improves high cholesterol, blood pressure and sugar
News.content:
New fruit in Tesco and M&S improves high cholesterol, blood pressure and sugar

According to research, the fruit can improve blood flow and reduce 'bad' cholesterol

View 3 Images Shoppers will find the fruit in Tesco and M&S stores (Image: Getty)

A new fruit that has landed in Tesco, M&S and Ocado for a limited time could help people trying to manage their high cholesterol and blood pressure levels. Known as Boombites, these new red berry grapes are being praised by health specialists not only for their vibrant flavour, but also for what's inside.

‌



It comes as a new research review has been published in Nutrients Journal titled Polyphenols and Cardiovascular Health: Emerging Relevance for Blueberries, Grapes and Red-Fleshed Table Grapes. The study found that compounds in naturally red-fleshed grapes, known as red berry grapes, could help support heart health alongside a healthy diet and an active lifestyle.

‌



Dr Emma Derbyshire, public health nutritionist and co-author of the new paper, said: "A daily diet of five fruit and vegetables including the colourful addition to your five-a-day, red berry grapes, as well as being active, can potentially help to improve blood flow and lower levels of bad cholesterol, which all help support our heart health."

‌



She added: "And if you were after a snack that delivers on both taste and nutrition, red bed grapes, including those marketing under the Boombites brands, do just that." Boombites Red Berry grapes are now being stocked by UK retailers, after a successful trial pilot last year.

The grapes are said to be the first in the world to have a deep red, skin-to-centre colour throughout the whole grape. The fruit will be on sale in M&S and Tesco stores, and Ocado online, for a limited time only - until October 2026.

View 3 Images The red berry grapes will be on sale in-store for a limited season only (Image: M&S)

‌



How can eating red berry grapes be good for you?

The research published in the journal analyses various grapes and blueberries, but it seems that red-berry grapes have taken centre stage. Research shows they generally have higher levels of beneficial natural plant compounds, including anthocyanins (a type of polyphenol), other polyphenols, and resveratrol.

Red berry grapes contain resveratrol and antioxidant compounds, just like blueberries. However, what makes red berry grapes so unique is that they have six times more anthocyanins than a traditional black-skinned table grape.

Dr Emma Derbyshire said: "Vibrant red berry grapes are rich in colour from the inside-out including the skin, thanks to the anthocyanins, and unlike many grapes, their pigments are present throughout the fruit. The review brings together research examining how polyphenol-rich fruits and their naturally occurring compounds may influence cardiovascular risk markers. It also identifies red-fleshed table grapes as an emerging area of interest."

‌



Dr Roy Jogiya, Chief Medical Advisor from Heart Research UK, a charity at the forefront of the detection and treatment of heart diseases, said: "Heart disease remains one of the leading causes of death in the UK. Many cases of cardiovascular disease can be prevented or delayed through healthy lifestyle choices, including a balanced diet, regular physical activity, avoiding smoking, and managing blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes.

"Eating the rainbow is a simple way to increase the variety of beneficial plant compounds in your diet and support long-term heart health. However, the greatest benefits come not from a single dietary nutrient, but from consistently eating a varied, plant-rich diet alongside other healthy lifestyle habits. Red berry grapes are one example of many fruits that provide beneficial polyphenols and can form part of a colourful, balanced diet."

View 3 Images Experts say the superfruit is giving blueberries a run for their money (Image: Boombites)

‌



How good are red grapes for cholesterol, blood pressure and blood sugar?

An 80g handful of delicious Boombites red berry grapes counts towards one of your five-a-day. Each 125g serving contains less than 100 calories. The grapes also contain fibre, vitamin C, vitamin E, thiamine, vitamin B6, folate, potassium, magnesium, phosphorus, iron and zinc.

Dr Emma Derbyshire added: "Some of the studies within the Nutrients review paper reported reductions in total cholesterol and LDL ‘bad’ cholesterol. For example, in an eight-week study, participants with high cholesterol who consumed 500g of red grapes daily, experienced reductions in total and LDL cholesterol, helping to support good heart health."

Co-author, Professor José Abellán-Alemán a prominent Professor of medicine, Director of the Cardiovascular Risk Chair at the Catholic University of Murcia (UCAM) and with a specialist in Medicine and Cardiovascular Risk, said: "Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance which at times is essential for your body to function. But too much of the wrong kind can build up on the walls of your arteries, narrowing your blood vessels and this is bad news for our heart health. This latest research paper in Nutrients journal, discovered that several studies found improvements in blood pressure - vital for good, vascular health."

‌



According to research, a diet rich in polyphenols can potentially help to reduce the risk of developing cardiovascular disease by 46%, while resveratrol is known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, which can help manage blood pressure. As a result, polyphenols, resveratrol, and anthocyanins are thought to contribute to various wellness benefits, including vascular health.

Research from the Spanish tech centre AINIA shows that the unique combination of polyphenols in these red-fleshed grapes alters how sugars are absorbed in the gut, resulting in reduced glucose absorption even though they taste sweet. These grapes are packed with fibre and beneficial plant compounds like anthocyanins and resveratrol, which support insulin response and help manage blood sugar levels. Experts point out that they offer a lower-glycemic-index (GI) option for snacks compared to regular high-sugar fruits, but it's still important to watch portion sizes.

Article continues below

How were the new red grapes created?

Dr Nisa Aslam, GP and co-author of the new paper, says: "Red berry grapes have been found to be abundant in resveratrol and antioxidants, just like blueberries, which help support your body’s cells from damage caused by everyday stress, diet and environmental factors such as the sun.

"It took thousands of different combinations of small and soft, red-fleshed wine grapes with large, sweet, and crunchy seedless table grapes to come up with the new red berry grapes. This new category has the beautiful visual impact of a berry, combined with the sweetness, crunch and convenience of a premium seedless table grape."

News.title: UK sanctions illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank Q&A - why it's happening, vile response, key maps
News.content:
UK sanctions illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank Q&A - why it's happening, vile response, key maps

The UK government has announced sanctions in response to a controversial new Israeli settlement in the West Bank - there are around 700,000 Israeli settlers in the occupied territory

View 10 Images Ed Miliband said the E1 settlement plans were 'illegal under international law' (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

The UK government announced a new set of restrictions and sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

‌



Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband today announced an import ban on goods from illegal settlements and sanctions on companies and people who "provide services" for settlement expansion. This comes as Andy Burnham's government sets out a tougher stance on Israel.

‌



Prime Minister Burnham in particular has voiced his concerns about the E1 settlement, where Israel has given final approval for a controversial project that would effectively separate the occupied West Bank from East Jerusalem.

‌



Heartbreak as Gaza children gather to watch The Lion King around rubble and destruction READ MORE :

View 10 Images Israeli far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich holds a map of the proposed E1 land corridor (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Mr Miliband, speaking to the Common on Tuesday, said the Israeli government has "turned a blind eye" to the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in the West Bank. He said: "The British Government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists. And all too often, the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this."

While the government's current stance has drawn strong opposition from Israel and even several US officials, the controversy surrounding Israeli settlements in the West Bank has ensued for years.

‌



What is the West Bank?

The West Bank is the larger of the two Palestinian territories occupied by Israel. The landlocked territory, which borders Jordan, is home to around three million Palestinians and around 700,000 Israeli settlers living illegally in the region.

The West Bank was occupied by Israel following the 1967 Middle East war, marking the longest military occupation in modern history. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) declared Israel's settlements in the West Bank were "illegal". Israel however has consistently disputed the courts outcome.

View 10 Images Map of the West Bank and Gaza (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Mr Miliband today revealed the UK government has change its position in line with the ICJ. He said: "The official view of the British Government is that the occupation is unlawful, because of Israel’s entrenchment of its control, its intention to extend permanent sovereignty, and its expansionist agenda via illegal settlements."

The West Bank and Gaza Strip, the second Palestinian territory which is also Occupied by Tel Aviv, are not connected and are instead separated by Israeli land.

Why are Israeli settlements being set up?

Israel has built around 160 settlements inside the West Bank and East Jerusalem since the 1967 war. Israel claims is has a religious and historic right to the West Bank as part of the ancestral land of Jewish people.

‌



Benjamin Netanyahu, the far-right president of Israel, has long pushed for more settlements in the occupied area. More than 50 new West Bank settlements were approved in 2025 alone.

View 10 Images Number of Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank in 1967 (Image: AP)

Netanyahu signed an expanded settlement plan, in September 2025, and told a crowd at the settlement of Maale Adumim - east of Jerusalem - that there would be "no Palestinian state". He said: "We are going to fulfil our promise that there will be no Palestinian state. This place belongs to us. We are going to double the city's population."

‌



Foreign Secretary Miliband. on Tuesday, told the Commons: "More settlements have been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years."

View 10 Images Huge rise in the number of Israeli settlement in the West Bank (Image: AP)

Has settler violence been an issue?

At least 81 Palestinians have been killed by settlers or Israeli forces in the West Bank since the start of 2026, according to the UN. Data also showed that 242 Palestinians were killed in the territory in 2025.

‌



107 Palestinian communities have been displaced following settler Israeli attacks since January 2023, according to Human Rights Watch. Some other crimes committed by settlers have included sexual violence and property theft, according to the UN.

Mr Miliband told the Commons that 65 Palestinian communities had been completely expelled since 2023 and over 4,000 evicted from homes "due to settler violence and state actions". He added: "On top of official state policy, settler terrorism is rampant. The UN reports an average of six violent settler attacks against Palestinians per day this year, per day, the highest on record."

Israel’s High Court of Justice, on Sunday, ruled that the police, IDF, and government had not done enough to tackle the rise in settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.

‌



View 10 Images Israeli forces restrict Palestinians' movement in Hebron, West Bank (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

What does the law say?

The occupation of the West Bank and Israeli settlements are considered illegal under international law. It defies article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, which states: "Individual or mass forcible transfers, as well as deportations of protected persons from occupied territory to the territory of the Occupying Power or to that of any other country, occupied or not, are prohibited, regardless of their motive."

The article also says: "The Occupying Power shall not deport or transfer parts of its own civilian population into the territory it occupies."

‌



View 10 Images Israeli flags in a new Jewish settler outpost on land belonging to Palestinians, near Nablus in the West Bank (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Why is the E1 settlement so controversial?

The area known as E1 is between the Eastern edge of Jerusalem and through the desert to another Israeli settlement. If approved, this land would create a continuous Israeli settlement corridor from East Jerusalem straight across the West Bank.

View 10 Images Benjamin Netanyahu's government has approved plans for a controversial settlement (Image: Ronen Zvulun/UPI/Shutterstock)

‌



The proposal includes building 1,200 new homes, but has previously held off on these plans for decades due to international scrutiny. Israel now has given final approval for the project that would effectively separate the occupied West Bank from East Jerusalem, and could disrupt the movement of Palestinians moving from the north to the south of the territory.

In joint statement, from August 20, the leaders of 22 countries and the European Commission slammed the proposal and said Tel Aviv's decision to publish construction tenders for the E1 settlement was "unacceptable".

The statement, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham was also past of, said: "The international community has long opposed this settlement expansion, and has voiced their grave concerns privately and publicly. The E1 settlement will undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank and harming the territorial contiguity of the Palestinian Territories."

‌



Mr Miliband said the approval E1 plans were the "crossing of a longstanding red line" and told the Commons he visited a community in the E1 area in 2014. The Foreign Secretary said they had lived on the land for generations but added: "E1 proposals would evict them and place settlements directly between East Jerusalem and the West Bank, cutting through the heart of Palestine."

View 10 Images Smoke rising after the demolition of a Palestinian home by the Israeli army, in the settler village of Tell (Image: Nasser ishatyeh/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

What has the UK government said?

Mr Miliband, speaking in his first address to Parliament as foreign secretary last week, said the E1 settlement plans were "illegal under international law", and called them "the crossing of a red line, as it cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable".

‌



Dame Emily Thornberry, the head of the foreign affairs select committee, said: "They're about to cut the whole of the West Bank in half. There is also a level of settler violence which is just the worst we've ever seen, so the tens of thousands of Palestinians are being displaced, either by the Israeli army or by settler violence."

The Dame also urged the government last month to introduce a ban on goods from the occupied West Bank. She also said British money should not be funding settler expansion in the area.

View 10 Images Ed Miliband speaking in the Commons on Tuesday (Image: House of Commons/UK Parliament/PA Wire)

Article continues below

What has the response to the UK's proposed sanctions been?

The UK is facing a backlash from the US and Israel over plans for sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called it an "irrational action". Speaking on the BBC's Today programme on Tuesday, he said: "I feel like it's discrimination against the Israeli government. It's a discrimination against the Jewish people."

Israeli president Isaac Herzog said UK sanctions "would be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation" as the country prepares to go to the polls next month. He said: "If this happens – and other nations may join – I believe it will prove to be a grave miscalculation, a decision that will fall on the wrong side of history."

News.title: 'My brother died distraught, desolate and in despair - now MPs must back assisted dying'
News.content:
'My brother died distraught, desolate and in despair - now MPs must back assisted dying'

EXCLUSIVE: Former police officer Jane Brown is speaking out for the first time as MPs prepare to take part in a 'make-or-break' vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill

View 3 Images Jane Brown with her 'big, clever, quirky' brother before he suffered a terrible death

A former police officer is urging MPs to back assisted dying after her brother died “distraught and in despair.”

‌



Jane Brown, 63, says the excellent care her brother Colin received could not prevent the suffering and loss of control he experienced before his death from cancer.

‌



Now, days before MPs vote on assisted dying, she is asking them to give other terminally ill people the choice he did not have. Jane from Maidstone was by the side of her 65-year-old brother Colin Mutimer, in the weeks before he died from cancer on June 24th 2025.

‌



Jane believes her older brother's experience also shows why improving palliative and end-of-life care, while vital, cannot be a reason to delay assisted dying. Colin had access to specialist care which he and Jane valued enormously, but there remained suffering that medicine could not undo.

She said: "Colin wanted the choice to decide when he had had enough. He should have had that choice.” Having spent decades in the police, Jane was no stranger to difficult situations and death, but watching someone she loved become increasingly distressed and lose his independence as his illness progressed has had a profound effect on her.

She is speaking publicly ahead of the assisted dying vote in Parliament on Friday 11 September because she believes terminally ill people should have a choice over how and when they die.

‌



View 3 Images Jane says her brother Colin was a sociable, independent and creative person

Six in 10 people support return of assisting dying bill to Parliament ahead of MPs' vote READ MORE :

The private members bill proposes allowing mentally competent adults with a terminal illness and six months or less to live to request an assisted death, subject to strict medical and independent panel approvals.

Earlier this year it went to the House of Lords after being passed by MPs. But a small handful of Peers made 1,000 plus amendments to it, making it run out of time. This Friday it is going back to the Commons for a second time.

‌



Opponents of the plan have warned that legalising assisted dying could put pressure on vulnerable people to end their lives prematurely.

Kerry Hogan, Campaign Communications Manager at My Death, My Decision, said: “Friday's vote is make-or-break. If this Bill is voted down in the Commons, it is gone, and reform could be pushed back for years, potentially a decade. If it gets through, there is a very real chance assisted dying will finally become law.

“The House of Commons has already backed this legislation once. Now MPs need to show up, vote and finish the job they started. If this fails because supportive MPs stay away, dying people and families like Jane’s will be left paying the price.”

‌



Jane says her brother Colin was fiercely independent, sociable and creative, playing percussion in a band for 40 years. He loved to tap dance, had published a book of poetry and transformed a derelict allotment into a place where friends would gather.

As late as January 2025, just five months before his death, he was still swimming with Jane and could swim 25 metres underwater. But Colin had lived with cancer for many years after being diagnosed with Non-Hodgkin lymphoma in 2000. Eighteen years later he had a cancerous kidney removed but then the cancer began to spread.

In 2023, after extensive research and conversations with specialists, he decided against immunotherapy because of the impact it would have on his quality of life.

‌



Jane said: “Colin’s decision not to have further treatment had given him much angst. It was not, and I stress not, a decision taken lightly.

"I remember him asking, ‘Will it make me stronger than I am today?’ The answer was 'no, just longer'. He always maintained to me that he wanted quality over longevity and I always told him I would support whatever he decided.”

By March 2025 Colin was experiencing severe pain and was admitted to the Royal Marsden, where Jane says he received exemplary care and remained extremely grateful to those treating him. But his cancer had spread aggressively.

‌



On May 12th he was told he had less than six months to live and three days later, that prognosis was revised to weeks. Then on May 18th his arm broke because of cancer in his bones and nothing could be done to repair it.

By then Colin could no longer feed himself, walk, go to the toilet independently or use his phone. A man who had always been intensely sociable stopped seeing almost everyone apart from Jane, her husband and one close friend.

“He was so distraught,” Jane said. “He was in despair. Once he was told he’d only got a few weeks to live he refused all visitors and family. Only me and my husband went to see him. It could have been so different.

‌



“He shut down everything, even the cards had to be put away and the radio turned off because he was so distraught.”

His final days were marked by "agitation, fear and anxiety" and constant discomfort. Jane stayed with him, sometimes able to do little more than hold his hand. At one point Colin told her: “I’m in despair. I want the day to come.” Jane asked whether he meant the day he would die. He said ‘yes’.

A few weeks before his death, Jane told Colin she was going to a demonstration outside Parliament in support of assisted dying. By then he was unable to speak, but gave her a thumbs up. Jane believes her brother would have wanted the option of an assisted death in his final days.

‌



“He just wanted to live life while he could. I miss our daily chats about life and I just miss my big, clever, quirky brother every day. He had strength, tenacity and resilience in abundance. It is so, so sad that it had to end the way it did."

View 3 Images My Death My Decision are urging MPs to vote through the historic bill

Dave Sowry, Chair of My Death, My Decision, said: “Jane should not have to relive the worst weeks of her brother’s life and campaign for change. She should be allowed to grieve him.

Article continues below

“Colin knew what mattered to him. He had thought deeply about the choices he faced, he received excellent care, and still he ended his life frightened, in pain and asking for the end to come.

“It is deeply frustrating that families are still being put through this. MPs have the power to change that. Next week, they need to use it.”

News.title: 7 in 10 carers say loved one’s chronic illness has impacted their mental health
News.content:
7 in 10 carers say loved one’s chronic illness has impacted their mental health

Seven in 10 adults supporting a loved one with a chronic health condition say the role has had an impact on their own mental health.

The hidden impact of chronic illness

Seven in 10 adults with a loved one living with a chronic health condition say it has taken a toll on their own mental health. Research by Curaleaf Clinic found those in caregiving roles are often left feeling isolated and anxious, yet have never spoken to their loved one about how the condition affects them.

‌



The study found 73% of people with a friend or family member suffering from chronic health issues feel guilty watching them struggle. Of the 1,000 adults surveyed, 62% said they would take on their loved one’s pain and symptoms 'in a heartbeat' to spare them.

‌



View 2 Images Three quarters feel guilty watching their loved ones suffer (Image: Getty Images)

‌



However, many also admitted their support role has affected their own wellbeing. Two in five (40%) said they have experienced anxiety, while 16% reported feelings of isolation.

Nearly half (46%) said supporting their loved one has eaten into their personal time. Others said it has impacted their sleep (41%) and social life (37%). What’s more, 19% admitted the pressure of providing daily support has put a strain on their relationships.

The research found emotional support is the single biggest thing caregivers provide (64%). However, many also take on the shopping (57%), household chores (53%) and driving to appointments (50%).

‌



On average, this adds up to nearly eight hours a week, rising to 11 and a half for those aged 55-64. Meanwhile, 19% spend 24 hours or more a week offering some form of support.

Dr Simon Erridge, director of research at Curaleaf Clinic, said: "Chronic illness rarely stays within the boundaries of a single diagnosis. The people around a patient - partners, parents, friends - often carry a significant emotional and practical burden that isn’t widely recognised."

He added: "That burden often pushes families to keep searching long after conventional treatments have been exhausted. But it’s often loved ones who often end up helping a patient find their way to a specialist clinic."

‌



View 2 Images Finding treatment if often part of the role of a caregiver (Image: Getty Images)

For 16%, searching for new treatment options is part of their role as a caregiver. More than half (51%) say they have researched or discovered a treatment option through their own efforts, rather than through a formal referral.

As a result, 64% said their loved one has tried two or more treatments, but 70% of those haven’t yet found something that adequately manages their condition.

‌



However, despite spending time searching for alternative treatments, the research carried out via OnePoll, found, many were unaware medical cannabis is a legal medication in the UK. This is something 43-year-old Mat Booth says has helped his wife, Sancharie, manage her symptoms.

Sancharie Booth, 39, suffers from spasms at night and in the morning which leave her in severe pain. She also experiences 'incredibly intense' and 'overwhelming' womb pain several times a month.

Mat said that watching his wife live in pain — and struggle to rest — left him feeling helpless. "There’s not much you can do to fix it," he said.

Article continues below

Sancharie started using medical cannabis to help relieve her symptoms and is now a Curaleaf Clinic patient. Since starting treatment, she said she is sleeping better and has more energy, adding it has given her a "great deal of relief".

Mat added: "It’s a real relief to see some of her key symptoms subside and to see her able to relax more."

News.title: Harry and Meghan 'surprised' by King's letter making clear they remain non-working royals
News.content:
A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex says the couple were surprised to see a letter sent on behalf of King Charles clarifying that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.

The spokesperson said the couple, who have recently moved back to the UK, "were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance".

But royal sources say Prince Harry and Meghan were made aware of the letter, sent on Monday afternoon, before it was made public.

It is also understood a security committee, which includes Home Office representatives, is meeting this week to look at the level of taxpayer-funded security that should be given to the Sussexes who are now resident in the UK.

The Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - decides security for royals and public figures and Prince Harry has previously complained about a lack of adequate police protection in the UK.

The Home Office does not comment on such decision making - and would be unlikely to reveal the outcome of such a meeting.

"The UK government's protective security system is rigorous and proportionate. It is our long-standing policy not to provide detailed information on those arrangements, as doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals' security," said a Home Office spokesperson.

In terms of Prince Harry and Meghan being "surprised" by the King's message on Monday - it's understood that reflects the lack of time given to them to respond.

They were believed to have had only had sight of the letter about an hour before it was shared with the media. By the time his team had made contact with Prince Harry it's understood the letter was almost published.

News.title: Nottingham attacks victim's death 'potentially preventable'
News.content:
Langdale added: "Although Sir Rob was talking generally about bereaved families, his words could have been written as a description of the bereaved families and their legal team in this inquiry. Indeed, without their efforts there would not have been a public inquiry at all."

"The evidence we have obtained has revealed one failure after another.

"There is a suggestion in some submissions that further oral evidence should be called. We submit that there's no need for further oral evidence from any source.

"Barney, Grace and Ian should be alive. And the survivors - uninjured."

These further updates will be followed by closing statements - the final oral submissions to the chair, retired senior judge Deborah Taylor KC.

On Tuesday, Taylor said it was "disappointing" that over the break, evidence had emerged which "ought to have been identified" and disclosed earlier.

She directed core participants to provide any corrections to errors or omissions by no later than 31 December.

The evidence - which was not disclosed during public hearings - included a holdall bag discovered at Calocane's former address in Burford Road in Nottingham.

Calocane was evicted from the address on 11 June 2023 and travelled to London, before returning via to Nottingham shortly before midnight on 12 June, a day before his killings.

The inquiry was told detailed examination of the holdall bag was not prioritised because efforts were focused on finding a bag which Calocane had with him on the evening of the attacks.

The notebooks were not disclosed to the inquiry until June this year, which was described as an "oversight by Nottinghamshire Police".

In those notebooks, Calocane had written that he had died, that he was god and made references to police having "mind-reading software".

Tim Moloney KC - representing the bereaved families - said in his closing statement that the notebooks revealed "relevant information including what we say was a deep-seated misogyny".

In documents found at the Burford Road address, Calocane had also listed explosives and made reference to a number of public venues.

The inquiry heard further violent assaults by Calocane on colleagues at warehouses in Nottinghamshire were also not disclosed to the inquiry team until after the public hearings took place.

This included an assault on a colleague in a warehouse in Eastwood in 2021 and another in Normanton in February 2023.

Footage of the February 2023 attack, described by Moloney as "sustained attack with punches thrown", was shown to the hearing on Tuesday.

News.title: Monty Don to leave Gardeners' World after more than 20 years
News.content:
Monty Don is to step down as the host of Gardeners' World after more than 20 years, the BBC has announced.

The 71-year-old, who is the programme's longest-serving head gardener, will leave at the end of the current series.

In a statement, Don said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience," but added: "Now is the right time for a change."

The BBC said Don had "inspired and guided millions of viewers with his warmth, wisdom and passion for gardening" since joining the programme in 2003.

Don began presenting the programme at Berryfields, a rented garden in Stratford-upon-Avon, before it moved in 2011 to his own garden, Longmeadow in Herefordshire.

"Throughout that time - and around 700 programmes - I have had the privilege of sharing my own abiding passion for gardens and gardening with an equally passionate, and often equally knowledgeable audience," he said.

"That connection with millions, not just in Britain but across the world, who share a love of gardens, plants and the natural world is something I have always treasured and which I increasingly believe to be at the heart of a life well lived."

Don added he had "always relished the craft of programme making" and paid tribute to the "superlative BBC team" he worked with over the years.

"I look forward to continuing to work with and for the BBC on other projects, as well as following new avenues," he concluded. "And of course, I will still be gardening, dog by side, here at Longmeadow."

News.title: Prince George begins first day at a rainy Eton College
News.content:
Prince George arrived on a rainy morning for his first day at Eton College, accompanied by his father and mother, the Prince and Princess of Wales.

Prince William and Catherine carried umbrellas as they brought George, wearing a jacket and tie, to be welcomed by the head teacher, Simon Henderson, and provost Sir Nicholas Coleridge.

"Welcome, good luck and enjoy," said the head teacher, shaking hands with Prince George.

They made small talk about the bad weather before the new pupil, parents and staff disappeared inside the historic school, where 13-year-old George will be a boarder.

George, who had travelled the short journey from his home at Forest Lodge in Windsor, was seen with his parents arriving at Eton's school yard, overlooked by the school's Tudor landmark of Lupton's Tower.

He was later photographed wearing the school's uniform, with black tailcoat, waistcoat and a stiff white collar.

The future king follows in the footsteps of his father in attending the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around Â£65,000 a year.

News.title: English pupils ahead of rest of UK in international school tests
News.content:
Pupils in England have outperformed those in Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales in international tests sat by hundreds of thousands of teenagers around the world.

England ranked above the other home nations in the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) across all of reading, science and maths.

However the latest Pisa report, which is published every three years, also warned of a worldwide decline in teenagers' reading skills.

Teenagers were losing the skills that "matter most in the age of AI", such as being able to critically evaluate information from different sources, it said.

The share of "hasty readers", who rush through texts to give quick, incorrect answers, has almost doubled between 2018 and 2025. The report warned the fall was greatest in those from "relatively well off" families.

The Pisa tests, run by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), assess teenagers on their ability to solve problems, think critically and communicate, before asking them a wider range of questions about their education in a questionnaire.

Although the UK performed well overall, the rankings varied significantly again, with results showing England, where the curriculum is significantly different, pulling consistently ahead of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

England's schools minister, Georgia Gould, said the government wanted to "build on" the positive results and "go further so all young people leave school with strong literacy and numeracy".

News.title: Borrowers expecting mortgage rates to drop have hopes dashed
News.content:
Nearly all the major mortgage lenders in the UK have announced increases in the cost of home loans in recent days.

Analysts are uncertain over whether there are more to come, but are urging people who need to find a new deal to act now.

Someone whose five-year deal is coming to an end faces paying more than Â£5,000 more a year on their next deal under a typical rate, if they borrow the same amount of money.

Many lenders allow people to lock in a new deal six months before their current one comes to an end, with an opportunity to switch if the costs come down before it kicks in.

"Borrowers expecting mortgage rates to drop in the coming weeks have had their hopes dashed," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts.

"It is still essential borrowers do not delay seeking advice to navigate the mortgage maze."

News.title: UK's third-biggest taxpayer to leave for Greece
News.content:
Dan Neidle, the founder of the think tank Tax Policy Associates, told the BBC's Today programme that the Â£330m in tax revenue the UK could lose was "quite a lot of money".

"It is enough to fund 4,500 teachers... we have entire taxes that raise less than Â£330m."

"He will probably pay almost nothing in Greece, and we can't compete with that," he added.

Despite the potential loss, Neidle said there are "no easy answers and no good statistics" on the issue of ultra-wealthy taxpayers leaving the UK.

He said the Treasury has some estimates on the number of wealthy people leaving, but otherwise there are few facts about the true scale of the revenue loss.

"We have lots of anecdotes... what we don't really have is data," he said.

He said the government needed to "give certainty" to ultra-wealthy people living in the UK, arguing that lots of changes to the non-dom regime in a short space of time and reports of a possible wealth tax don't help.

"Stop rumours, stop tinkering," he said.

Rokos's decision comes ahead of UK Chancellor John Healey's first Budget on 28 October.

In an interview with the BBC on Monday, Healey did not rule out tax increases in the Budget, with a recent increase in government borrowing costs piling pressure on the public finances.

He refused to comment on any decisions about tax, promising only to "balance the books" and "control public spending".

In March, Cambridge University said the money from Rokos would be "the largest single donation made to a British university in modern times".

It will be used to create a school of government in Cambridge named after him with the aim of training leaders of the future. It is set to open this autumn.

Despite his generosity to Cambridge, Rokos is an Oxford graduate, having studied mathematics at Pembroke College.

He attended a state primary school before winning a scholarship to Eton College.

News.title: Charli XCX says bye to Brat and Liam Gallagher's tambourine grin - Music Photography Awards 2026 shortlist
News.content:
Striking images of Oasis's reunion tour and Charli XCX bringing Brat to Glastonbury Festival are among the nominees at this year's Abbey Road Music Photography Awards.

The awards, which this year considered works by more than 24,500 submissions from 42 different countries, released a shortlist of 40 finalists across eight categories on Tuesday.

The likes of Kendrick Lamar, Fontaines DC, Tame Impala and Sombr also feature in the shots, while other images of stars including FKA Twigs have been selected - out of competition - for judges' awards.

All of the finalist photographs will go on display in the LED tunnel at entertainment complex Outernet London from 8 to 14 September.

These will include the five pieces picked out for consideration in the fan-voted music moment of the year award.

Voting is available online via the official website, external, and in person at the exhibition.

The winners will be announced at a ceremony at the London studios - made famous by the 1969 Beatles album of the same name - on 24 September.

News.title: Shetland spaceport project secures £30m of UK government investment
News.content:
Two German companies have signed launch agreements with the spaceport.

Rocket Factory Augsburg (RFA) is working towards its first vertical orbital test flight from UK soil. In August, SaxaVord paused plans for a test launch after RFA said it had "encountered an issue".

A five-week "launch window" had been due to begin, with temporary traffic restrictions introduced in the event of a flight attempt.

A second company, HyImpulse Technologies GmbH (HyImpulse), plans the second flight of its SR75 suborbital launch vehicle from Shetland this year.

The German firm recently secured investment of more than â¬50m (Â£43m).

Derek Harris, head of programmes at Space Scotland, said he was not concerned about the timescale of the launch, adding that the Â£30m investment was a "good starter".

"The technology is difficult to master but you would prefer it to be there and be reliable so if the timescale slips into next year, I do not see that as a failure," he told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast.

"I see that as a very well-maintained programme to make sure health and safety and reliability are at the forefront."

Harris said rain and storms could also impact the process and it was important to remain open minded.

He added: "It will take time and a lot of money but once it launches, the benefits it unlocks for Scotland and the UK will be amazing."

News.title: I was fired from The Voice - I didn't want to leave, says Sir Tom Jones
News.content:
Sir Tom Jones has said he did not want to leave The Voice, saying he "loves the show" and ITV made the decision to "fire" him from the judging panel.

The Welsh singer, 86, has appeared as an on-off coach on the singing competition since it premiered in 2012.

Following rumours that he may not return to the panel for the upcoming series, Sir Tom said the broadcaster decided a while ago and "I was told recently".

ITV has been asked to comment, but the Press Association reported that a source at the show was "hopeful" the singer would return for its upcoming series.

In a social media post, the star said: "The reason given is because of a financial difficulty with insurance.

"They now say in the press they wanted to 'refresh' the show, and with a new coaching line-up there wouldn't be a chair for me.

"They are offering a much-reduced role where I would make an appearance but without being actually involved from the start, and I'm not thrilled about that.

"So the only thing I know right now, is that there's never a good time to fire an 86-year-old who's still pretty good at his job."

The programme's 2027 series was due to begin production soon.

The Press Association reported that a show insider said: "ITV absolutely loves working with Sir Tom.

"They are in talks with him and are hopeful he will return to the series."

In the most recent series of The Voice UK Sir Tom features as a coach alongside McFly stars Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones, as well as US rapper Will.i.am and Destiny's Child singer Kelly Rowland.

Sir Tom has featured alongside many coaches during his tenure on the show, including singers Jessie J, Olly Murs, Kylie Minogue and Rita Ora.

He has also mentored three winners on the programme: Leanne Mitchell in series one, Ruti Olajugbagbe in series seven and Anthonia Edwards in series 11.

News.title: Pensioner with 'largest hoard' of child abuse images found in Scotland jailed
News.content:
A pensioner who amassed what is thought to be the largest collection of child sexual abuse material ever seized by police in Scotland has been jailed for four years.

Alan MacPherson, 83, from Stenhousemuir, was found to have more than two million images on various electronic devices after his home was raided in 2025.

More than 805,000 were identified as depicting child sexual abuse - much of it in the most serious category - while the overwhelming scale of his collection meant much of material was not checked and categorised.

MacPherson was told by Sheriff Mayram Labaki that the scale of his crime was "exceptional".

The sheriff said: "The quantity [of images] was so great that a substantial proportion could not be examined and categorised by forensic examiners.

"Every image records the abuse or exploitation of a child. The possession and circulation of such material perpetuates that abuse."

MacPherson will also be supervised for three years following his release from jail and placed on the sex offenders register for life.

He previously admitted downloading the material over a 14-year period.

Sheriff Labaki added: "Your views towards your offending and your victims are unconscionable.

"I refer specifically to the passages in the [social work] report where you state that not only were the children consenting, but they were willing participants.

"Your attitude is unremorseful".

News.title: World-first surgery for baby's rare skull condition
News.content:
A "happy and cheeky" baby boy with a rare skull condition is doing well a year after becoming the first in the world to be given a new type of treatment.

One-year-old Rory Potter, from Chesterfield in Derbyshire, was diagnosed with severe sagittal craniosynostosis, external - a condition where the skull fuses before birth - shortly after he was born in April last year.

He underwent surgery in September to have "super elastic" springs inserted, which gradually reshaped his skull before being removed.

His mother Jo Potter said: "You wouldn't know what he's been through."

News.title: Some veterans to be called up to test UK's war resilience
News.content:
Some veterans will be mobilised as part of a major exercise next year testing the UK's resilience for war.

The government exercise will challenge the Ministry of Defence (MoD) "on a scale that we haven't seen for a very long time" on its reaction in the event of a conflict, armed forces minister Louise Sandher-Jones said.

The drill will involve an as-yet unspecified number of the British military's strategic reserve, which has an estimated 95,000 retired regular and reserve officers.

It forms part of a plan by the MoD for a "real step change" to use the strategic reserve more, following warnings of a workforce retention crisis.

Sandher-Jones is herself part of the strategic reserve, having previously served in the British Army as an intelligence officer before becoming an MP.

"Certainly when I left the Army and found out I was in the strategic reserve, I just filed it away and never thought about it again," she told the House of Lords national resilience committee on Monday.

"We are definitely no longer in that space - the strategic reserve is a real commitment for those who are in it, and they will be exercised as part of our exercise programme next year."

The exercise in 2027 will "go through measures to call out, to use and equip" procedures to mobilise retired troops at scale should it ever be needed, she added.

It comes after the chief of the defence staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, warned in January there was not an effective system of engaging them.

Earlier this year, ministers raised the age limit for the strategic reserve - which includes the Army, Navy and Royal Air Force - from 55 to 65 and lowered the threshold for them being called into service.

News.title: Drought and hosepipe bans remain despite wettest week since early February
News.content:
In the last few days of August and start of September, more rain fell than any other week since early February, according to the Environment Agency.

Despite the change to more unsettled and wetter conditions, all of Wales and most of England remains in drought.

And water companies are reminding customers that temporary hosepipe bans are still in force despite the rainfall and decreased demand with the cooler weather.

More rain is in the forecast this week and while that will be welcome, sustained rainfall is needed to reverse drought conditions.

While we had a brief return of summer heat over the weekend for some, the weather since the start of September - and meteorological autumn - has been more unsettled.

According to figures from the Environment Agency (EA), in the week from 28 August to 3 September, rainfall totals ranged from 26mm in south-east England to 48mm in central England.

However, the National Drought Group said that water storage "continued to decline at most reservoirs".

There has been no change to the EA drought status or the temporary use bans in force across ten water company areas.

While there has been less demand for water due to the cooler and wetter weather, "further significant rainfall is needed" to return to normal conditions the EA suggests.

News.title: What we know about the journey of the Portsmouth migrant boat
News.content:
Protests in Portsmouth broke out after the arrival of migrants who had come from France on a small boat - after a much longer journey than usual.

BBC Verify has been using ship-tracking websites to monitor activity in the English Channel at the time the migrant boat made its crossing on 6 September. BBC Verify correspondent Merlyn Thomas reports.

Produced by Sophie Bott and Jenna Abaatouk. Graphics by Sally Nicholls. Verification by Barbara Metzler.

News.title: What we know about anti-migrant protests and organiser Danny Thomas
News.content:
Hundreds of demonstrators gathered in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend in protests against small boat crossings.

But what is the connection between the two protests?

The answer is one man - Danny Thomas, more often known as Danny Tommo.

UK correspondent Daniel Sandford looks into the background of Danny Tommo and how he has galvanised these protests through social media and local support.

Matchroom Boxing’s CEO has highlighted a problem in the ongoing talks between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury, with their super-fight at risk of collapsing.

This year, British heavyweights Joshua and Fury signed to fight each other at long last, five years after they previously signed a deal that fell through. Once again, however, a problem has arisen.

Joshua’s contract is for a clash in the UK, while Fury’s contract is flexible on location. Fury and certain key figures are pushing for a 20 November showdown in New York City, while “AJ” is digging in his heels in hopes of boxing at Wembley Stadium.

open image in gallery Anthony Joshua (left) with Kristian Prenga after beating the Albanian ( Getty )

And Matchroom’s Frank Smith has pointed to an issue with the “narrative” around the negotiations, while speaking to Playbook Boxing – powered by Betway.

“I’ve always been open: I think it would be disappointing if this fight doesn’t take place in the UK,” Smith said. “I’m not going to sit here and say that if it does take place in the US... ultimately you can never win.

“Because if it doesn’t happen, people go, ‘Joshua’s pulling out,’ and the narrative, the spin [from Fury] will be: ‘AJ doesn’t want to fight me.’ Now, that’s the truth [of what Fury will say], isn’t it?

“But let’s be honest: if it happens in New York, people will be like, ‘[Joshua and his team] just gave up.’ It’s like, well, which one do you want? Because he can’t win, really, can he?

“We will fight tooth and nail to get the fight in the UK, but ultimately, everyone wants to see the fight. AJ wants the fight, hence why he signed up for the fight.

“So, it’s going to be a case of: you’re never going to keep everyone happy. But I’m hopeful we can get there with it [...] If it doesn’t happen, all I can say is it’s not down to Anthony Joshua, because Anthony Joshua is ready and willing to fight.

“If two parties enter into a contract, both sides have got an obligation to deliver upon it, so Anthony Joshua has an obligation to turn up to a venue in the UK to fight Tyson Fury this year – by the end of December.

“It won’t be Anthony Joshua’s fault if the fight doesn’t happen. I’m not going to say whose fault it will be. I can’t be bothered to get myself in any trouble or cause any more issues.”

A hedge fund billionaire and Britain’s third-biggest taxpayer is set to leave the UK for Greece – marking the latest exit among the country’s billionaires, according to reports.

Chris Rokos, the founder of Rokos Capital Management, is preparing to switch his residency and will open an office in Athens as part of the move, according to Bloomberg News.

Mr Rokos is the UK’s third-biggest taxpayer having paid an estimated £330 million in the latest tax year, according to the Sunday Times Tax List.

He has an estimated wealth of £3 billion, according to the Sunday Times Rich List, and earlier this year pledged to donate £190 million to the University of Cambridge, believed to be the biggest individual donation to a British university in modern times.

Rokos Capital Management has grown to manage around 20 billion US dollars (£14.8 billion) in assets, and has offices in London, New York, Abu Dhabi and Singapore, according to its website.

A spokeswoman for the company declined to comment on the reports.

The latest research for the Rich List revealed an ongoing exodus of wealth from the UK following the Government’s non-dom crackdown and inheritance tax changes.

Robert Watts, compiler of the Sunday Times Rich List, previously said there had been a “sharp rise in the number of British nationals now resident in Dubai, Switzerland and Monaco”.

Becoming a resident in a different country does not automatically mean people stop paying tax in the UK, but it throws into question how much the Treasury can continue to collect from those who relocate.

Greece has introduced rules which mean that some individuals who transfer their residency to Greece can pay a lump-sum of 100,000 euros (£86,000) per tax year, regardless of the amount of income earned abroad, for as much as 15 years.

Other high-profile figures to have reportedly exited the UK include British hedge fund manager Michael Platt, who co-founded BlueCrest Capital Management and switched his residency to Switzerland, and Richard Gnodde, a Goldman Sachs executive who moved to Italy.

A new documentary about Elon Musk uses an Artificial Intelligence avatar to simulate an interview with the SpaceX and Tesla CEO using things he’s really said in interviews. The choice, filmmaker Alex Gibney said Tuesday in Venice before the film's world premiere, was intentionally ironic.

It both references Musk’s proposition that we’re all living in a simulation and pokes at his somewhat paradoxical and shifting views of the technology. Gibney said it is to convey the “reality of what he’s done and unreality of his narrative.”

The filmmakers consulted lawyers before going too far down the road and got the sign-off to use the Musk avatar.

The Oscar-winning filmmaker was joined at the Venice Film Festival by Ashley St. Clair, once a conservative influencer, who shares a child with Musk and who appears in the film. She talks about their relationship, his character and the nondisclosure agreement she was asked, and refused, to sign to guarantee paternity support.

“I was offered the opportunity not to speak for $40 million,” she said.

St. Clair earlier this year also sued Musk's AI company, saying its Grok chatbot allowed users to generate sexually exploitive deepfake images of her that have caused her humiliation and emotional distress.

The film goes into Musk's takeover of X and what Gibney says is the manipulation of the algorithm.

“One thing that I didn't properly understand when I started the film was how Musk tweaked algorithms at Twitter to, in fact, prioritize vitriol and hate over, you know, the town square,” Gibney said.

“Wired” reporter Zoë Schiffer, who also appears in the film, added that “he has tweaked the algorithm, both to suppress mainstream journalism and then to augment some of the more inflammatory comments and voices on that platform.”

St. Clair said she believes he’s stoking fires and “causing deliberate division that could be catastrophic if it’s not regulated or contained.”

With a runtime of nearly four hours, “Musk” delves into his traumatic childhood, including an interview with his father, Errol Musk, and traces his early days in Silicon Valley through his DOGE work with the second Donald Trump administration and involvement in right-wing politics internationally. It was, Gibney said, going to be a much shorter film before Musk wrapped himself in Trump's campaign.

Those interviewed include Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard, his first wife Justine Musk, neurologist Sam Harris, tech reporter Kara Swisher and former USAID Administrator Samantha Power.

Gibney said he thinks Musk is “extremely” dangerous to democracy. The film, which will be released in theaters in October, raises alarms about the information the “DOGE boys” gathered on U.S. citizens with their unfettered access to so many government agencies.

The foreign secretary has accused Israel of “turning a blind eye” to the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians living in the West Bank, who are increasingly under pressure to relocate from settlers.

"The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank - perpetrated by settler terrorists.

"And all too often, the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians," Ed Miliband said.

In what is the UK’s strongest intervention yet, the foreign secretary said it was for the courts to determine if Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

He added that he was a “proud British Jew” and insisted the UK had “unshakeable bonds” with the people of Israel, before announcing sanctions on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories.

The Israeli president Isaac Herzog has called the British plan to ban trade goods from West Bank settlements a “grave miscalculation”.

The US ambassador to Israel has also condemned the UK sanctions, describing them as “an irrational action” and “discrimination against the Jewish people”.

Tensions in the West Bank have flared in recent months, with Israeli settlers involved in violent disputes with Palestinians.

Alexis Mac Allister revealed Liverpool made him sad when they told him they were not in a position to offer him a new deal and said he had options to leave Anfield in the summer.

The Argentina midfielder, a £35m signing from Brighton in 2023, has entered the last two years of his current contract.

But whereas Liverpool spent over £200m on new signings Bradley Barcola, Jeremy Jacquet and Victor Munoz and gave his fellow midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai a new five-year deal, they informed Mac Allister there was no offer to him.

Mac Allister was a target for other clubs in the transfer window, including Wednesday’s opponents Atletico Madrid, and admitted he might have gone. “There was a chance,” he said.

“I received the news that the club was not in a position to offer me a new contract, which of course makes me very, very sad. I think I give 100 per cent for this football club every single day in training, games.

Alexis Mac Allister puts in a sliding tackle on Nottingham Forest midfielder James McAtee ( PA )

“Of course I can have very good games, bad games, like everyone, but I always give my best. I see Dominik and Ryan [Gravenberch] renewing their contracts and that makes me very happy because they deserve it but at the same time it makes me a little bit sad I didn’t get mine.

“Of course, there is still time, the fans don’t need to worry because I will give 100 per cent until the last day I am here. We will see what happens. There were options to leave this summer but I think right now I am in the right club and I have the right mindset to give my 100 per cent to the club.”

Liverpool did not give Mac Allister an explanation as to why there was no contract offer. He added: “There wasn’t any direct conversation with me, it was with my agent and I don’t want to say things that they never said but what I got from my agent was that they were not in the position to renew me. It’s really sad because we won the Premier League together, we went through difficult times as well together and I always give my best. We will see what happens but, of course, it makes me a little bit sad.”

The World Cup winner hopes he can earn a new deal, saying: “Maybe, it is going to depend on how I perform during these years, like every football player, and they are right to make the decision. The fans don’t need to worry as I will give 100 per cent and maybe they change their minds.”

Mac Allister explained why he wanted to stay at Anfield and insisted he had never taken it for granted.

“Because this is the right club,” he added. “I love being here, this is something special. If. I love this club, love being here and love the fans and as a player it sometimes happens you are at a club for a long time and don’t realise where you are, but that doesn’t happen to me, I love being here.”

Diplomatic tensions flared on Monday when Iceland summoned the U.S. ambassador after President Donald Trump posted an uncaptioned social media image showing the island alongside several other countries under the American flag.

The graphic, shared on his Truth Social platform without explanation, depicted a map encompassing the United States, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean, with the entire combined landmass explicitly labeled "United States of America". The post immediately raised concerns in international diplomatic circles and prompted a swift response from officials in Reykjavík.

Iceland's Foreign Minister, Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir, officially called in Billy Long, the U.S. ambassador to Iceland, to discuss the matter. Long, who formally assumed his diplomatic post in the capital only last month, was informed directly of the government's strong disapproval regarding the graphic.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump confused Greenland and Iceland so much that Reykjavík hired a lobbyist in Washington, D.C., for advice, as reported in February ( Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images )

In a statement to local broadcaster RUV, the foreign ministry said, "The position was clearly expressed that the post was completely inappropriate." Following the summons, official diplomatic channels remained largely silent, with neither the U.S. State Department nor European embassies immediately replying to requests for comment.

The online posting comes after years of persistent assertions by President Donald Trump regarding the strategic necessity of the U.S. acquiring Greenland, a semi-autonomous territory belonging to Denmark. These statements have repeatedly generated diplomatic friction between Washington and Copenhagen—both NATO founding member states—while raising broader concerns among European nations about U.S. foreign policy in the region.

In Iceland, the surrounding geopolitical debate has also touched upon domestic policy decisions. Just last month, Icelandic voters participated in a referendum in which they voted against reopening talks for accession to the European Union.

open image in gallery Trump posted the image on his ​Truth Social platform without explanation ( Truth Social )

Throughout that campaign, Trump's publicized plans for neighboring Greenland often served as a significant political backdrop. While some advocates for European integration pointed to concerns over U.S. reliability as a reason to consider closer EU ties, analysts noted that voters were ultimately guided primarily by domestic economic concerns at the ballot box.

Furthermore, Trump's social media post was published only hours after European leaders reaffirmed their commitment to the region. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Greenland to formally announce a major €200 million ($232.50 million) investment initiative to support local development.

Speaking to news agency Ritzau in Nuuk, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen emphasized that local leaders and citizens have remained consistent: "The Greenlandic government and the Greenlandic people have said again and again that they do not want to be American."

open image in gallery William “Billy” Long is the U.S. Ambassador to Iceland. He previously served as the 51st Commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service from June to August 2025 ( US Embassy of Iceland )

The diplomatic friction follows persistent confusion within the White House about the distinct identities of Greenland and Iceland. Reports revealed that Trump previously mixed up the two Atlantic territories during a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. In response, officials in Reykjavík hired Washington lobbying firm Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck on a $25,000 monthly retainer to advise on navigating interactions with the U.S. government.

Observer accounts noted the curious timing of the lobbying agreement, which came shortly after Trump's Davos speech and subsequent floor jokes by U.S. Ambassador Billy Long—who had previously quipped to former House colleagues that Iceland would become America’s 52nd state with himself as governor. Long later apologized, clarifying the remarks were a joke, but the incident has underscored the heightened sensitivity surrounding North Atlantic territorial sovereignty.

News.title: Dark website owner who encouraged ‘swatting’ and hoax bomb calls loses sentence bid
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A man who encouraged a hoax call claiming there were nail bombs and hostages at a Cardiff hotel, leading to “widespread panic and disruption”, has lost a challenge against his jail sentence at the Court of Appeal.

Callum Dare was sentenced to two years and three months at Cardiff Crown Court after admitting in June to encouraging and boasting about “swatting” incidents.

The 26-year-old ran a dark website between 2018 and 2019, when he was aged between 18 and 19, where he shared links related to swatting.

This included sharing information about a 2016 hoax call made to police in Los Angeles in the United States that claimed there were bombs under chairs at the University of California, which led to the site being evacuated.

Another false call was made to a journalist in Cardiff claiming that there were nail bombs and hostages at a hotel in the city centre, which led to the area being sealed off.

Dare, of Talbot Green, South Wales, later admitted encouraging or assisting the commission of malicious communications and possession of articles for use in frauds, and was sentenced in July.

open image in gallery Callum Dare was sentenced to two years and three months at Cardiff Crown Court after admitting in June to encouraging and boasting about ‘swatting’ incidents ( PA )

He sought to challenge his jail term at the Court of Appeal, with his barrister telling a hearing on Tuesday that it should have been suspended rather than one of immediate custody.

But three senior judges dismissed the appeal bid, ruling that the sentence handed down by Judge Tracey Lloyd-Clarke was “entirely open to her”.

Mr Justice Linden, sitting with Lord Justice Popplewell and Mrs Justice Hill, said: “It is abundantly clear that she took into account all of the factors of the case.

“The conclusion that she reached was well within the scope of her discretion.”

Dare, who watched proceedings from HMP Parc, was arrested after being identified by a joint investigation by the FBI and Canadian authorities, with information handed to South Wales Police.

The Crown Prosecution Service said in July that when Dare was arrested, police found files containing “sophisticated phishing fraud” on his devices which were “designed to obtain personal or payment details of dark web users for use by fraudsters”.

open image in gallery Dare, of Talbot Green, South Wales, later admitted encouraging or assisting the commission of malicious communications and possession of articles for use in frauds, and was sentenced in July ( Getty Images )

Sentencing him, Judge Lloyd-Clarke said that she was “satisfied that this offending is so serious that the appropriate punishment can only be achieved by immediate custody”.

But barrister Peter Donnison, for Dare, told the Court of Appeal on Tuesday that the judge “fell into error by treating deterrence as a trump card” and that the “factors weigh in favour of suspending the sentence”.

He continued that there was “strong personal mitigation”, including the fact that Dare had no previous convictions, had pleaded guilty before a trial, and has autism and ADHD.

Mr Donnison also said: “It is not offending that is prevalent… and therefore there was not a requirement for a deterrent sentence.

“An immediate custodial sentence was not justified on the ground of deterrence, in the view of Mr Dare’s age, in the view of the significant amount of time that there had been since the offending, (and) the prospect of rehabilitation.”

But Mr Justice Linden said in relation to the hoax in the United States that although prosecutors did not allege that Dare had made the call, he “appeared to be seeking to take credit” online.

He continued that the hoax in Cardiff caused “widespread panic and disruption”.

He added: “The offending in this case was also akin to any encouragement to waste police time… where any deterrence is fully warranted.”

News.content:
