Standard Chartered had a window of exclusivity to renew that expired last year. Liverpool’s sleeve sponsorship deal, presently with Expedia for between £9m and £12m a season, is also up for renewal.

Sports.title: Champions League is fertile ground for new managers – but knowhow could be key later on
Sports.content:
A delve into the history of the Champions League shows that managers can and do win in their first season at a club, but also that experience matters. Which makes it interesting, given that tenures for the 2026‑27 crop range from newly appointed coaches to one with almost 15 years in charge. Some have managed more than 100 matches in the competition, others none.

It gets under way on Tuesday with 14 of the 36 clubs led by managers who have been in the role for less than a year. It cannot match the turnover of the Premier League, in which 11 of 20 managers were appointed in 2026, but the tenures of the head coaches involved this season break down neatly.

There are also 14 managers who have been in charge for at least two years. This leaves eight in the middle, who qualified for the Champions League in their first full season at their club and now get to show what they can do.

Being new to a team is no barrier to winning. Many who have led sides to the ultimate European club glory did so in their first campaign. Both Chelsea’s Champions League triumphs were secured by managers who got the job the same year. Carlo Ancelotti began both of his stints at Real Madrid by helping them to become champions of Europe in his year one, and in between Zinedine Zidane won three Champions League trophies on the bounce when he first managed the club.

Pep Guardiola and Luis Enrique also won the competition with Madrid’s great rivals, Barcelona, at the earliest opportunity. Barcelona’s current manager, Hansi Flick, ended his first season at Bayern with a treble. Liverpool fans will hope Andoni Iraola can emulate his countryman Rafael Benítez by winning the Champions League immediately after settling into the Anfield hot seat.

Despite these examples making a decent case for new managers winning the competition this season, betting markets are favouring the more established coaches.

And predictably enough, Paris Saint-Germain are the favourites with bookmakers, but it has nothing to do with this being Luis Enrique’s fourth season at the helm. The two‑time defending champions have a deep squad and face nothing like the domestic demands of their rivals in other top leagues.

Barcelona, Arsenal and Bayern Munich make up the top four in the betting, with their managers also among the 13 longest-serving as the league phase begins. This contrasts with the next quartet of likeliest champions, all of whom have managers who took charge this year.

But do not assume freshness in the role automatically equates to inexperience. Real Madrid’s new manager, José Mourinho, has recorded 160 matches in the competition, the fifth most in history. Ancelotti leads on 218 Champions League games, ahead of three of the Premier League’s five “big beasts” of management: Alex Ferguson (206), Guardiola and Arsène Wenger (both 191). Mourinho and Jürgen Klopp (102 matches, seventh most) are the other members of modern English football’s most heralded managerial quintet.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Only Mourinho is involved in the Champions League this season and he will savour being the new kid on the block who is also the old hand. Mourinho will be confident of going past the last 16 for the first time since 2014 given the talent at his disposal.

The eight managers he will face in the league phase have collectively managed fewer Champions League games than he has. Indeed, the combined total of the 24 least experienced managers in the competition adds up to fewer than Mourinho will bring to Madrid. These relative rookies are not only managing outsider, either. Inter’s Cristian Chivu has 10 Champions League games under his belt, which is more than the managers of Manchester City (six), Manchester United (one) and Liverpool (none).

As the competition gets under way, the key number is 16. That tally of points in the league phase has proven enough to secure an automatic spot in the last 16. Whatever a manager’s level of experience, the first target is to finish above the playoff places. After that, Champions League knowhow could prove vital.

Sports.title: ‘Girl’s day’ controversy reignites debate over how women are treated in South Korean football
Sports.content:
It was a comment allegedly made by a referee during a WK League match that became one of the biggest controversies in South Korean women’s football. What began as an on-field dispute involving South Korea’s all-time top goalscorer, Ji So-yun, has since developed into a wider debate, prompting a response from the Korea Football Association and raising questions about the treatment of female players, the structural set-up of women’s football in Korea and accountability within its governing bodies.

It was around the 31st minute of the Suwon FC Women v Seoul City Hall game on 28 August when the incident happened. Suwon’s former Chelsea midfielder Ji appealed for a foul after what she felt were repeated rough tackles by the opposition. The female referee, Bae Sun-young, is then alleged to have made, over the officials’ radio system, a remark interpreted as referring to menstruation after describing Ji as “sensitive from the start”. Ji says she overheard the comment and footage from the game shows Ji visibly upset as she talks to the referee. Ji was shown a yellow card after confronting the official. In frustration Ji threw a water bottle as she approached the Suwon bench. Bae walked towards Ji, appearing to reach for a red card before deciding against issuing one, showing a yellow instead.

After the match Bae denied making the remark, saying later that it had been a private conversation between match officials. The KFA’s refereeing department has said that the word “period” was not used and that the comments were not directed at Ji, but there have been reports that the term “girl’s day” was used instead.

View image in fullscreen Ji So-yun was shown a yellow card after confronting Bae Sun-young. Photograph: KWFF

After the match Suwon asked the Korea Women’s Football Federation and the KFA to look further into the matter. The KFA has now begun disciplinary proceedings and said: “Considering the seriousness of the matter, we decided to refer the case to the fair play committee in accordance with referee regulations.” The KFA’s fair play committee will listen to explanations from those involved and will review the incident. It will then determine disciplinary action based on the outcome.

The KFA further announced that it will use this incident as an opportunity to prevent similar events and strengthen education to create a culture of respect for players, referees, and participants in the WK League.

The Korea Pro-Footballers Association said it does not see this as a mere dispute on the pitch, but a serious human rights violation and abuse of refereeing power. The organisation called for Bae’s expulsion and a complete overhaul of the refereeing system, characterising the alleged remark as sexual harassment.

The controversy has revived scrutiny of the KFA’s previous treatment of women’s football. Last year, the women’s national team threatened to boycott the 2026 Women’s Asian Cup over what the players described as discriminatory treatment. Players said they faced long journeys, were forced to stay in “inadequate” accommodation far from training grounds and felt their conditions were evidence of discrimination compared to those of their male counterparts. In a statement the team said they would suspend all training related to the tournament if the KFA did not respond to their letter. The KFA said in February the matter had been “resolved”.

With the investigation still under way it may be some time before the fair play committee reaches a final decision. Yet the incident has become about far more than Ji’s confrontation with a referee and has brought back into focus long-running concerns about the treatment of female players, and renewed questions about the KFA’s accountability. And that is no bad thing.

Sports.title: Maresca eyes rest for busy dad Haaland as Manchester City prepare for Porto
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca believes Erling Haaland has become “complete” as his priorities have changed after the birth of the Manchester City No 9’s son two years ago.

Haaland has again started the campaign in prolific form, scoring three goals in City’s opening three Premier League victories. In three of the 26‑year‑old’s four previous seasons at City he has won the Premier League golden boot. Maresca pointed to how the birth of his son in 2024 changed the Norwegian’s motivation.

The manager said: “He’s a man now. He’s a dad. When he arrived here [in summer 2022] he was not a dad and now he’s a dad and life completely changes because the priority becomes his son. I’m happy for him because he was already top as a player and as a boy but now you can see that he is complete. He is a family man, he is still scoring goals so I’m very happy for him.”

City are at Porto in the opening league‑phase game of the Champions League on Tuesday. Haaland has played every competitive minute of the campaign so far, and Maresca said he will be rested at some point, particularly as as the striker was part of the Norway team that reached the World Cup quarter-finals.

The Italian said: “It’s not easy for Erling or for any of the players that play for club and international teams. I think it is normal that you [may] see these players start to be tired. So, it’s correct to give them some rest. It can be one game out or one week away.

“It depends on which moment we are in but the priority is to allow the players to be good and happy. When you see them tired the risk of injury increases, and we need players who are 100%.”

While Maresca’s options if Haaland is rested against Porto would be selecting Antoine Semenyo at centre-forward, or fielding Phil Foden or Rayan Cherki as a false 9, he pointed to the in-game control the two latter players can give City when required.

View image in fullscreen Nico O’Reilly pulled up with an injury before the Coventry match but will ‘probably’ be available to face Porto. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

“There is always a gameplan and Rayan can drop a little bit to manage the tempo and the game,” the 46-year-old said.

“We [also] need Rayan in the position to be dangerous – the last game against Coventry [a 1-0 win] we made contact with him five or six times between the lines and created chances.

“It depends on the game. Against Coventry, it was good for him to drop a little bit and manage the tempo and not always be a reference for the other team. We need him in the right position because he gives us the quality. Phil can also do that – and the last pass between the lines is very good so we are lucky that we have two very good players that can do this.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In his first campaign as head coach, Francesco Farioli led Porto to their 31st title, and they have a maximum 15 points from their opening five Primeira Liga games.

Maresca was asked if City will be favourites at the Estádio do Dragão. “We are here to do our best,” he said. “The game will dictate the favourite. This is a hard place to come. This season they started very good. In the last 14, 15 games in Europe they just lost one so we are going to try our best and try to win the game.

“I know that Porto is very good in set pieces. I think it has become part of the game now so we need to do our best, defend in the right way, score goals as much as we can from set pieces because it’s part of the game and you need to be perfect because all teams are prepared for that.”

Maresca said Nico O’Reilly would “probably” be available after missing the Coventry game with a late fitness problem, but the manager said he was “not sure” about Jérémy Doku’s availability after injury.

Sports.title: Emery ready to ignite Aston Villa’s season at Club Brugge after familiar slow start
Sports.content:
Unai Emery is not panicking. He may kick every ball on the touchline but, behind closed doors, Aston Villa’s players are used to him being the calmest person in the room, routinely more demanding after victory than defeat. John McGinn tells a story in which the Villa manager, early in his now almost four-year tenure, broke character and lost his cool during a half-time interval not owing to a lukewarm performance but because he witnessed his captain tearing into teammates. In Emery’s eyes, it was McGinn expending unnecessary energy rather than seeking solutions.

Emery, McGinn and Villa have been here before. Just last season, in fact; at this point, they were pointless in the Premier Leagueand still another 157 minutes from registering their first goal. So in one sense Villa, who shook off a slow start to qualify for the Champions League for the second time in three seasons, are ahead of schedule. Villa’s goalless draw at Hull on Saturday was not the most absorbing display but there were enough green shoots to trust Emery when he says he is confident they can again exceed expectations.

It is hard to disbelieve a man with Emery’s record, having overseen the most successful era in the club’s recent history. “When we started the project here, the ambition we had, it was [not even] in our highest expectations to be in Europe four years in a row,” the Villa manager says. “It was very difficult when we started working together but it was the ambition of the owner. We set our standards high with the players to be there and we are. Now is the moment to remember how we got here and the way we did. Now it is a different moment and chapter.”

In these moments, Emery tends to double down on his methods. Last season they did not taste victory until their seventh game of the season in all competitions, McGinn scoring the only goal in a Europa League win against Bologna. Before that game, players assembled around 11.30am for the kind of opposition analysis meeting to which they have grown accustomed, so much so McGinn says they now walk in like robots.

Emery lasers in on players’ positioning and tactical details. Jhon Durán, now on loan at Benfica from Al-Nassr after spells at Fenerbahce and Zenit St Petersburg, is famously the only player to have requested to leave mid-meeting.

Villa face Club Brugge on Tuesday for the fourth time in the past two years, hoping Europe will again ignite their season.

After that victory against Bologna last September, Villa embarked on an extraordinary run of 17 wins in 19 matches. Half of the 14 players involved in that game have departed but one of those who did feature, Emiliano Buendía, is hopeful that Emery’s new-look squad can put together a similar run. “It has not been the start we wanted, but we are trying to take the positive things from every match,” said the Argentinian, who has started all four Villa games this season. “We will try to change this momentum in terms of results and try to get our confidence back to perform well and [achieve] the results we want.”

View image in fullscreen Unai Emery is remaining calm despite Aston Villa’s slow start to the season. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Stewart Kendall/Apl/Sportsphoto

Another Champions League campaign should not be taken for granted and returning to this stage, after winning the Europa League last season, is arguably Emery’s greatest feat. The strides made under Emery will surely occupy the minds of supporters as they wander the cobbled streets of Bruges and when they explore Barcelona in November, too.

Crucially, Emery is energised by the challenge, helped by the odd siesta at Villa’s Bodymoor Heath base. “Sometimes I need a good nap, after intensive work in the morning,” he said with a smile last week.

For now, George Hemmings’s 13th‑minute shot against Hull represents Villa’s sole effort on target this campaign. In the same game it was the 19-year-old, who joined from Nottingham Forest aged 16, who supplied Buendía for a golden chance. It is easy to focus on the shortcomings but it would also be remiss to overlook Villa’s encouraging performance in the Super Cup against, in Emery’s view, the best team on the planet; defeat against Paris Saint-Germain was less than a month ago and Villa have only strengthened since.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

One of the most exciting of their 11 summer arrivals, the 18-year-old Ibrahim Mbaye, was an unused substitute for PSG in Salzburg. Another talent signed this summer, Johan Manzambi, continues to step up his fitness after a knee injury and could feature as early as Saturday against Nottingham Forest.

Only two of Villa’s new arrivals – Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson – started at Hull last time out. Matteo Ruggeri, Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho arrived from the bench. Taylor Harwood-Bellis, a £25m buy omitted from Villa’s Champions League squad, had a watching brief in Yorkshire. João Gomes was sent off on debut. Leon Goretzka, who joined on a free after leaving Bayern Munich, will not feature until at least October after a knee injury setback.

Quick Guide Play our football trivia game, On the ball Show The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues? Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Emery often takes time to integrate signings. Youri Tielemans had to wait four months for his first Villa start before embedding himself as one of Emery’s undroppables. He demands a lot of his players and even more of himself. “In football, if you are expecting transition, maybe you are not in the right way,” he said last month.

“We have to rebuild the team as fast as possible. I don’t know if we need time or not. We are progressing – still not enough because we are not getting good results – but tomorrow is a new test in Europe.”

Sports.title: Newcastle admit they started planning for Eddie Howe’s exit at start of year
Sports.content:
Newcastle’s sporting director, Ross Wilson, has revealed he began planning at the start of this year for Eddie Howe’s departure. Howe stepped down as manager in late July and the club turned to Matthias Jaissle, who had been identified as the preferred successor.

Wilson, who arrived on Tyneside from Nottingham Forest, said: “Eddie leaving didn’t feel chaotic and it didn’t feel painful. Eddie would be the first to tell you that. I came here 10 or 11 months ago and I’ve been planning in the background for a managerial change over eight or nine of those months. That doesn’t mean we were always going to go to Matthias, but he was always part of our planning.”

When Wilson began making contingency plans, Howe seemed more likely to be poached than to resign or be dismissed. Yet Newcastle’s 12th-placed finish last season raised questions about his future and, after the sales of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali, Howe decided he wanted out.

“Big respect to Eddie for the job he did for us over a long period of time,” Wilson said. “He did a wonderful job bringing that trophy [the 2025 Carabao Cup]. He’s a club legend, for sure.”

No one had envisaged parting with Howe three weeks before the season. “Clearly the timing wasn’t planned,” Wilson said. “But the reason we could move so quickly was because we’d been preparing for a number of months.

“Eddie’s an exceptionally talented coach and that meant he was probably going to do something else at some point. We had to be prepared for that.”

With Newcastle having entered a settlement agreement with Uefa after breaching European spending rules last season, selling Gordon and Tonali for almost £170m proved essential but Wilson admitted that offloading Bruno Guimarães to Arsenal for £75m was one sale he never wanted to complete.

“There’s no point pretending otherwise: we did not want to lose Bruno Guimarães. That was really disappointing. But everything else that happened during the window was planned. That doesn’t mean every single player [who signed] was the No 1 name on our list. Clearly we were disappointed a couple of times but that’s normal. No club reaches the end of a window getting every target they wanted.”

View image in fullscreen Bruno Guimarães’s move to Arsenal was ‘really disappointing’ for Newcastle, Ross Wilson has admitted. Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA

Wilson has presided over the acquisition of eight players aged 24 and younger this summer including Guimarães’s replacement, the £52m midfielder Nico González, signed from Manchester City. They have in common a suitability for the high-intensity pressing game choreographed, in different forms, by Howe and Jaissle.

“I cannot imagine Newcastle United playing a style of football that isn’t aggressive, vertical and attacking,” Wilson said. “For this club to be successful we have to play an attacking, high-press, proactive style and we had to find a coach to do that.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Ultimately all roads led to Jaissle, for whom Newcastle paid £10m to Al-Ahli. “We used our [data] models to identify those coaches who played the type of football we wanted,” Wilson said. “Matthias was the No 1 choice. It was really, really clear.”

Cue what Wilson described as a “busy” summer. “We had the situation with the manager which we dealt with in complete secrecy for two weeks as well as trying to run a transfer window. So it was really, really busy. But good fun as well.”

Until this summer Newcastle had resisted selling established players but that stance has changed. “If you want to be successful in the Premier League you have to trade players,” Wilson said. “If you don’t trade you’re going to get stuck.”

Although Jaissle has not been set targets this season, Newcastle’s chief executive, David Hopkinson, remains confident they can disrupt the dominance of the traditional “big six” by 2030.

“We’re going to be consistently and credibly competing for those top prizes,” Hopkinson said. “If we’re compliant with the regulatory regime [spending rules] we can compete consistently.”

Sports.title: Joey Barton to remain in custody until trial after bail application turned down
Sports.content:
The former footballer Joey Barton will remain in custody until his trial next year after a bail application was refused.

The 44-year-old had been due to stand trial at Liverpool crown court last week accused of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to Kevin Lynch, 51, at Fairway, Huyton, on 8 March. But on Wednesday the case was adjourned and put back to March next year.

Barton, wearing a grey zip-up fleece, appeared over video link from HMP Liverpool at a hearing on Monday, when the judge David Potter refused a renewed bail application. Barton nodded as the judge remanded him in custody in advance of a pre-trial hearing on 11 December.

His trial will take place exactly a year after the alleged assault, meaning the defendant, who was arrested shortly after the incident, will have spent 12 months on remand.

Barton is accused of carrying out the attack on Lynch after they had been drinking together at Huyton and Prescot golf club. Lynch, a former non-league football manager and founder of the special education school NexGen Academy, was said to have sustained serious injuries to an eye.

Barton, the former Manchester City and QPR midfielder, of Widnes, Cheshire, won one England cap and also played for Newcastle, Rangers, Burnley and Marseille. After stopping playing he moved into coaching and had managerial spells at Fleetwood and Bristol Rovers.

Sports.title: The return of Man United, how will Jose Mourinho fare back at Real Madrid, the underdog to look out for and the major challenge facing Arsenal... SIX things to be excited about as the Champions League returns
Sports.content:
The return of Man United, how will Jose Mourinho fare back at Real Madrid, the underdog to look out for and the major challenge facing Arsenal... SIX things to be excited about as the Champions League returns

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

It seems an age since Gabriel Magalhaes' penalty flew over the bar in Budapest, breaking Arsenal hearts as PSG were crowned Champions League winners for the second season in a row.

But, just over three months on Europe's premier club competition is back, with the league phase starting on Tuesday. That kicks off eight gameweeks across the next four-and-a-half months before the knockout rounds take centre stage.

The drama will run all the way to June 5, with the final at Atletico Madrid's Metropolitano.

So, ahead of the action getting under way, Daily Mail Sport has picked out six reasons to be excited about the return of the Champions League....

The Champions League returns tonight, just over three months since PSG won the competition for the second year in a row

Can underdogs stun Europe again?

Bodo/Glimt won the hearts of many fans last year as they managed to reach the round of 16 after a magical run.

The team massively surpassed expectations and even beat the likes of Manchester City, Inter Milan and Atletico Madrid.

They were the undisputed dark horses of the competition, and they will be hoping to once again cause upsets this time around.

The Norwegian champions had a quiet transfer window i terms of signings but more importantly were able to retain most of their squad, with only striker Kasper Hogh departing to Celtic.

Or maybe we will see a new underdog emerge? One potential option is Austrian side LASK, who are making their Champions League debut.

Another is Azerbaijan champions Sabah, who were founded just eight years ago and battled through four qualifying rounds to reach this stage. First up? A trip to Manchester United.

Bodo/Glimt will hope to back up last year's fairytale Champions League run this season

How will Jose Mourinho fare back in Spain?

Real Madrid have had a big summer, with several new players joining the team including Yan Diomande, Bernardo Silva, Marc Cucurella, Ibrahima Konate and Denzel Dumfries.

But there has also been change in the dugout with Jose Mourinho returning for a second spell as manager, 13 years after he left the club.

The Special One is looking to bring glory back to Real by winning their 16th Champions League title, after two quarter-final exits in a row.

The Portuguese manager has a squad full of world-class talents like Vinicius Junior, Kylian Mbappe and Jude Bellingham, yet his biggest challenge may be in controlling the dressing room, after the squad faced several disciplinary problems last season.

They kick off their campaign on Tuesday night as they welcome Inter Milan to the Bernabeu.

Jose Mourinho is back at Real Madrid and will have his eyes set on another trophy with the club

Man United are back!

Manchester United return to the Champions League for the first time since 2023-24 after an impressive league campaign where they finished third under Michael Carrick.

The Red Devils will look to try to compete once again, and they will no doubt be leaning on the quality of Bruno Fernandes, who had a remarkable season last year as he broke the assist record in the Premier League.

Despite being widely regarded as one of the continent's top stars, Fernandes has spent just two of his five full seasons at United playing in Europe's elite competition - and they've never passed the round of 16 in that time. This is his big chance to help them mark their mark.

There are warning signs, admittedly. United have had a mixed start to the Premier League, picking up just four points from their first three games, and although it is exciting to be back in Europe, the increase in fixtures will test the depth of Michael Carrick's squad.

Michael Carrick helped Man United return to the competition after he replaced Ruben Amorim

Can PSG do the three-peat?

This season gives PSG the opportunity to be just the second team in the modern Champions League era to win three titles in a row after Real Madrid achieved the feat between 2016 and 2018.

Their squad remains as strong as ever despite the loss of Bradley Barcola, Goncalo Ramos and Ibrahim Mbaye.

As well as retaining key stars like Ousmane Dembele, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Desire Doue, and their Portuguese midfield duo of Joao Neves and Vitinha, they have been active in the market, bringing in players such as Lucas Digne, Ferran Torres and Maghnes Akliouche.

PSG have started their league campaign poorly, with Luis Enrique's side taking just two points from three games, giving them some early questions to answer.

Luis Enrique's PSG side are hoping to win their third successive Champions League title

Can Mbappe secure elusive title?

Kylian Mbappe has achieved nearly all you can as a footballer. He was the Champions League Golden Boot winner last season and also won that award at the World Cup.

He has also won the domestic title with PSG, the Super Cup with Real Madrid and in 2018 the World Cup with France.

These achievements establish him as one of the greatest players in the modern era , yet he is still chasing one trophy - the Champions League.

Mbappe is yet to conquer European football, failing to win the competition at PSG, Monaco and Real Madrid.

This year feels like one of the best chances for the Frenchman to fulfill his dreams after Real reshaped their squad significantly in the summer after a difficult 2025-26 season.

Kylian Mbappe is still yet to win the Champions League despite his glittering career so far

Arsenal's tough run

Arsenal are kicking off their Champions League campaign against Napoli, looking to kick on from their heartbreaking defeat in the final by PSG last season.

The Gunners have started the season superbly, with three Premier League wins in a row, including a brilliant performance against Chelsea on Sunday.

Having finally won the Premier League last season, the next frontier for Mikel Arteta's side is the Champions League.

However, it won't be easy, with Arsenal set to take on Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and Borussia Dortmund in the league phase.

This season's European campaign promises to be an intriguing test for the Gunners, yet they will fancy their chances of going all the way this time.

Sports.title: England cricket legend Andrew Flintoff puts stunning Cheshire mansion on the market for £6.75million - complete with its own cinema, swimming pool and games room - four years after his Top Gear car crash
Sports.content:
England cricket legend Andrew Flintoff puts stunning Cheshire mansion on the market for £6.75million - complete with its own cinema, swimming pool and games room - four years after his Top Gear car crash

Do YOU have a story? Email tips@dailymail.co.uk

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

England cricket legend Andrew Flintoff has put his Cheshire mansion on the market - and it is listed for sale at £6.75million.

The 48-year-old, better known to fans as Freddie, played 79 Test matches for England and after retiring from playing went on to become a successful TV presenter, fronting shows including Top Gear and Freddie Flintoff's Field of Dreams.

He bought the mansion in 2021 from former Manchester United star Phil Neville, who moved to the US to coach Inter Miami, the MLS team owned by David Beckham.

The property, which covers 10,000 square feet and boasts six bedrooms and six bathrooms, is described on Rightmove as a 'stunning detached family home arranged over four floors'.

The listing in Cheshire goes on to mention the house's three main reception areas and stylish kitchen, as well as a leisure suite including swimming pool, gym, games room and cinema.

It also points to a 'comprehensive monitored CCTV & security system'.

'Designed with both entertaining and family living in mind, Longwood combines clean contemporary architecture and luxurious modern finishes with a distinctive sense of character throughout.

Andrew Flintoff's mansion is listed for sale on Rightmove at £6.75million

The cinema room forms part of the extensive leisure suit in the four-floor mansion

The listing includes a description of the leisure suite including a swimming pool and gym

'The principal living accommodation is exceptionally well proportioned, with three impressive reception rooms complemented by a magnificent open-plan kitchen and family room.

'The kitchen is fitted with an extensive range of bespoke cabinetry and integrated appliances, creating a superb central hub for everyday family life and entertaining.'

It also mentions a passenger lift serving all floors, 'providing effortless access throughout the house and adding considerably to its practicality and accessibility'.

Flintoff and his wife Rachael have four children - Holly, Corey, Rocky and Preston.

Corey and Rocky have both followed in his cricketing footsteps, with 20-year-old Corey an all-rounder for Kent and Rocky, 18, playing for his father's former county Lancashire.

In 2022 Flintoff suffered life-changing facial and rib injuries during a crash while filming Top Gear.

It also mentions the games room, which has football and cricket memorabilia on the walls

Flintoff went on to coach England Lions before leaving the role last month

Flintoff and his wife Rachael, pictured in 2019

'Afterwards, obviously, there's the physical scars that I've got. But then the mental side of it,' he said. 'I didn't leave the house for probably six or eight months. The only times I was leaving the house was for medical appointments and surgeries.'

Flintoff expanded on the incident in the Sunday Times, saying: 'Suddenly the car was rolling and the world was all slow-motion chaos. I knew, somehow, exactly what was coming. I knew the options: If I stuck my arm out, I’d lose it. If I didn’t brace, I’d snap my neck.

'So I made the call. I shut my eyes and flung up my left arm, with the thinking being that as a right-hander, I was prepared to lose my left.

'The car dragged me underneath for 50 metres, face skidding, body flipping. Minus two degrees, busted face, but alive — because in that instant, my mind, honed on cricket’s demands, made the right call. A split-second decision. One that saved my life, and changed it.'

Flintoff stepped down as head coach of England Lions in August after nearly two years to focus on his new role at Australia’s Sydney Thunder franchise in the Big Bash League, which starts later this year.

Sports.title: Liverpool agree one of the most lucrative sponsorship deals in Premier League history with Turkish Airlines paying Reds £60MILLION-A-YEAR to front their shirts from next season
Sports.content:
Liverpool agree one of the most lucrative sponsorship deals in Premier League history with Turkish Airlines paying Reds £60MILLION-A-YEAR to front their shirts from next season

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Liverpool have signed a £300million deal with Turkish Airlines, who will become their main sponsor from next year.

It represents the end of an era after 17 years with Standard Chartered, with the branding on the kits of the men’s, women’s and academy teams changing from the start of next season.

The deal is thought to be worth in excess of £60m a year and the club believe it is among the most lucrative front-of-shirt agreements in Premier League history, in line with Manchester United and Manchester City.

Turkish Airlines flies to more airports in the world than any of its competitors and will invest big money into the football club.

Liverpool famously won the Champions League in the country in 2005, coming from 3-0 down to beat AC Milan on penalties in what became known as 'the Miracle of Istanbul'.

Chief commercial officer Ben Latty said: 'This is a milestone announcement for us and we are delighted to welcome Turkish Airlines as our main club partner from June 2027.

The new deal with Turkish Airlines brings to an end a 17-year deal with Standard Chartered

'The front of the Liverpool shirt holds a special place in the history of our club. Turkish Airlines is a globally recognised organisation with an extensive international network, and we look forward to beginning our partnership and building a strong relationship together, with already strong foundations built from those special memories back in 2005.'

Their most recent deal with Standard Chartered was understood to have been worth around £50m a year, making this a significant upgrade.

Liverpool believe one of their shirts is sold every 20 seconds around the world and they have more standalone retail stores than any club – they have recently just opened a branch on London's Oxford Street.

Standard Chartered will remain as a global partner when Turkish Airlines becomes the club's principal partner.

It will be just the third new sponsor in 35 years after Carlsberg were on the front of shirts from 1992-2010.

Sports.title: Paul Scholes hints at World Cup fallout between England duo Declan Rice and Morgan Rogers as possible reason pair were involved in furious incident during Arsenal's win vs Chelsea
Sports.content:
Paul Scholes has suggested there may be some history between Declan Rice and Morgan Rogers after the England team-mates clashed at the Emirates on Sunday.

Arsenal's Rice infuriated the Chelsea man during the closing stages of Sunday's pulsating London derby, which Arsenal won 2-1.

Rogers, a £117million summer signing from Aston Villa, was looking to get up to support Cole Palmer as Chelsea pushed to get back into the game. But a cynical trip from Rice put an end to that, with Rogers tumbling to the ground.

The 24-year-old was incandescent with rage and confronted Rice, jabbing his finger at him before the players were separated by referee Chris Kavanagh.

It left onlookers shocked given the two midfielders were key components in England's run to the semi-finals of the World Cup over the summer.

'Do you think there's a little bit of something between Morgan Rogers and Declan Rice?' Scholes asked his former Manchester United team-mate Nicky Butt on their The Good, The Bad & The Football podcast.

Morgan Rogers was trying to get up in support of Cole Palmer when Declan Rice tripped him

A melee ensued after Rogers had reacted and attempted to confront the Arsenal man

Rogers jabbed his finger in the face of his opponent before referee Chris Kavanagh intervened

'Do you think there might have been a little bit of something during the summer? What Declan Rice did to him was the most annoying thing in the world.

'When people just leg you up when you're running. He snapped, Morgan Rogers, and rightly so.'

Rogers had opened the scoring against the champions in the second minute with a volley after the Gunners failed to clear Reece James' free-kick. That was cancelled out by Kai Havertz midway through the first half, before Martin Odegaard netted the winner for the Gunners.

So annoyed was playmaker Rogers that he refused Rice's olive branch after the final whistle and also showed little interest in former Villa team-mate Ezri Konsa's offer of a handshake.

Rogers had been linked with a move to Arsenal before Chelsea moved in to make him the most expensive-ever British player, just surpassing the fee Manchester City paid for another England midfielder, Elliot Anderson, earlier in the window.

Konsa said afterwards: 'I love duels. As a defender, I think these are things you have to cherish.

'For me personally, I love a challenge. I love being in duels. I had a few today and I'm glad I came out on top.

'Rogers is a good friend of mine, but on the pitch, it's a different story. I saw the opportunity to go in and make the tackle and it came off.'

Sports.title: Champions League supercomputer: PSG are FIFTH favourites for a third consecutive crown and Man United are given almost the same chance of winning as Real Madrid - but which of Arsenal and Man City top the list?
Sports.content:
Champions League supercomputer: PSG are FIFTH favourites for a third consecutive crown and Man United are given almost the same chance of winning as Real Madrid - but which of Arsenal and Man City top the list?

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Two-time defending champions Paris Saint-Germain have been deemed fifth favourites to win this year's tournament, with a supercomputer viewing Arsenal as the team to beat.

PSG became just the second team after Real Madrid to go back-to-back in the tournament in the Champions League era when the French giants overcame Arsenal in May.

Luis Enrique's side overcame the Gunners in a penalty shoot-out in Budapest following a 1-1 draw.

Ahead of the league phase of this season's competition beginning on Tuesday, Opta's supercomputer has deemed PSG have just a 7.1 per cent chance of clinching a third successive title.

It follows PSG having endured their worst start to a season in 19 years after losing to Lens in the French Super Cup, as well as drawing against Rennes and Lille in Ligue 1 before a 2-1 loss to Monaco on the weekend.

PSG are ranked behind Arsenal, Bayern Munich, Man City and Barcelona in the supercomputers list of favourites.

Two-time reigning champions PSG are deemed by Opta to be the fifth favourites to win this season's Champions League

Arsenal are backed as favourites as they bid to bounce back from losing last season's final to win the tournament for the first time

The favourites have been devised after the supercomputer ran 10,000 simulations of the Champions League season.

Arsenal have come out on top following the simulations, with Mikel Arteta's side backed to win Europe's elite club competition for the first time.

The reigning Premier League champions finished as runners-up in the Champions League for the second time last season, having also made the final back in 2006.

Arsenal have been given a 20.9 per cent chance of glory.

The Gunners are seen as having a 50 per cent chance of reaching the semi-finals and are 34.8 per cent to make the final.

Bayern Munich are narrowly behind Arsenal, with the German champions given a 19.4 per cent chance to win the Champions League for the first time since 2020.

Man City follow at 12.3 per cent in their first season under Enzo Maresca, while Barcelona are fourth at 8.2 per cent.

The Spanish giants last reached the Champions League final back in 2015, when they were crowned winners for the fifth time.

Barcelona's best showings since have been two semi-finals, achieved in 2019 and 2025.

Liverpool are ranked as sixth favourites at 6.1 per cent, with Andoni Iraola set to experience his first Champions League campaign in charge of the Reds.

Record champions Real Madrid are ranked down in seventh place, with Jose Mourinho's side given just a 4.4 per cent chance.

Their prospects are only marginally better off than Manchester United, who are given an outsiders chance at 3.8 per cent on their return to the competition.

The top ten is completed by 2025 runners-up Inter Milan and Europa League winners Aston Villa.

Sports.title: 'A line has been crossed': Furious Man United fans will protest over controversial 'ticket tout' clampdown before Old Trafford derby on Sunday
Sports.content:
'A line has been crossed': Furious Man United fans will protest over controversial 'ticket tout' clampdown before Old Trafford derby on Sunday

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Manchester United fans will protest before Sunday’s Old Trafford derby over the club’s controversial clampdown on ticket touts.

United have been accused of targeting innocent supporters and issuing bans without providing clear evidence, and protest group The 1958 say ‘a line has been crossed’.

They have urged fans to take part in a peaceful protest before Sunday’s game against Manchester City, gathering outside The Bishop Blaize pub near Old Trafford in a show of unity from 3pm.

A statement from the group read: ‘Manchester United supporter groups are being called upon to all stand together following reports of bans and season ticket sanctions without clear and compelling evidence always being presented.

‘For generations, match-going Reds have given their time, money and loyalty to Manchester United, home and away. That loyalty deserves to be treated with respect.

‘This is not about one group or one individual. It is about how Manchester United treats its match-going supporters. It may not affect you today, it may not next time but that day is coming for all of us.

‘All Reds. All groups. One voice. Show the evidence. Lift the bans.

Manchester United fans' group The 1958

‘Supporters are now facing serious sanctions which can remove their right to attend matches. We believe nobody should face such action without being told clearly what they are accused of and being shown the evidence used to justify it.

‘This goes beyond individual supporters or supporter groups. If this approach is allowed to stand, it should concern every match-going Red.

‘Whatever differences have existed between supporter groups in the past, this is a time to put them aside.

'A call has gone out for Manchester United supporter groups, fans’ forum representatives, supporters’ clubs and independent fan organisations to stand together on a simple principle: if there is clear, substantive evidence of serious wrongdoing or organised ticket touting, show it.

'No loyal supporter should be treated as guilty without being given a fair opportunity to understand and challenge the case against them.’

Sports.title: 'I let my country down. People are going to be on our case for a while and rightly so': BEN DUCKETT on England's drinking scandals, how he's making up for it under new captain Joe Root and why he prioritised Test cricket over the IPL
Sports.content:
'I let my country down. People are going to be on our case for a while and rightly so': BEN DUCKETT on England's drinking scandals, how he's making up for it under new captain Joe Root and why he prioritised Test cricket over the IPL

It’s possible that no English summer has generated as many uses of the phrase ‘the penny has dropped’ than 2026 – but for Ben Duckett it feels like more than a cliche.

When Joe Root spoke to the dressing room about player behaviour two days before the first Test against Pakistan at Lord’s, and two days after Brydon Carse found himself in handcuffs outside a Derby nightclub, Duckett decided to follow his captain by saying a few words himself.

In some ways, this was a natural progression: of the team who will take the field at Edgbaston on Wednesday, Duckett trails only Root in terms of age (he turns 32 next month) and caps (48). He is now, officially, a senior statesman.

But his own role in England’s tapestry of misadventure – the late-night wanderings in Noosa during the Ashes tour, captured on video for posterity by a member of the public – persuaded him to back up his captain’s words. Has the penny dropped? You bet it has.

‘In those situations, anyone can talk,’ Duckett tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘But from someone who’s been in situations like that, who’s let the group down, let the country down, it felt important for me.

‘Rooty can’t speak on behalf of everyone all the time. He’s England captain right now and he’s taking a lot of stick in the media on behalf of England cricket. It’s up to me, Brooky and a few of the other guys to take some of that off his plate and help lead as much as we can.’

It’s possible that no English summer has generated as many uses of the phrase ‘the penny has dropped’ than 2026 – but for Ben Duckett it feels like more than a cliche

'Joe’s taking a lot of stick in the media on behalf of England cricket. It’s up to me, Brooky and a few of the other guys to take some of that off his plate and help lead as much as we can'

What exactly did Duckett say to his team-mates in the Lord’s dressing room? 'Don’t do what I did in Noosa'?

He laughs: ‘No, not at all. You know, I didn’t actually break any rules. It was more that this was the moment where we just need to move forward. It’s about showing what it means for us to play for England.’

If it seems strange after the events of the winter that Root even needed to remind the players of their wider responsibilities, Duckett concedes it was ‘probably necessary’.

But he adds: ‘All this stuff off the field only concerns probably five per cent of the group. It’s the team, the management, everyone involved, who get all the stick, but it’s only been a few different people who have put us in these situations, and I spoke about being one of them.

‘I think we have moved past it. The fans want to see us winning games and series, and that’s the easiest thing to put right. The rest of it’s going to come in time, and people are probably going to be on our case for a little while. Rightly so: we’ve made that very easy for them.’

Duckett believes he confirmed his dedication to the cause by turning down a £200,000 deal with Delhi Capitals in the IPL in March, and committing himself to his red-ball game after a difficult Ashes. His reward was a superb century against New Zealand at Trent Bridge in a summer where everyone has found runs hard to come by.

‘I could very easily have gone to the IPL, earned a bit more money, come back to England pretty tired and not scored that Test hundred,’ he says.

Duckett turned down a £200,000 deal with Delhi Capitals in March to work on his red-ball game and was rewarded with a century against New Zealand at Trent Bridge in June

'My biggest advice for Emilio Gay (right) is don't try to be anyone else. He’s been picked for a reason: the way he bats, the time he bats, the hundreds he scores'

‘Ultimately, those decisions should show people how much it means to play for England. I’ve got zero regrets. I want to play as many games as I can for England, and that’s my priority.’

Duckett should win his 50th cap against South Africa at the Wanderers in Johannesburg on December 17, but the question is whether his opening partner will still be Emilio Gay, whose first five Tests this summer have brought him two gutsy half-centuries but an average of just 23.

‘It’s tough,’ says Duckett, ‘because I certainly wouldn’t want to come in at the start of my career and bat on the pitches we have done this summer.’

Speaking from a seat in Edgbaston’s Hollies Stand, he gestures out to the middle, where groundstaff are putting together the finishing touches on a pitch that is browner than the grassy surfaces which helped England bulldoze Pakistan at Headingley and Lord’s.

‘This could be a big week to go and put a big score on the board and showcase what he can do. My biggest advice for Emilio is don't try to be anyone else. He’s been picked for a reason: the way he bats, the time he bats, the hundreds he scores. So I said to him: “Just play the exact way you got into this team.”’

Duckett says his age and experience have helped him deal with the challenge of forming a new opening relationship after three years with Zak Crawley – just as they helped him move on from the disappointment of an Ashes series in which he averaged only 20 with a top score of 42.

‘I’m batting at the top of the order against the best bowlers every time I go out there,’ he says. ‘Maybe the Ashes would have affected me more if I were younger. I’d have probably lost belief.

‘But I walked out there and faced Mitchell Starc bowling 93mph from the first Test to the last, and if you looked through most of my innings, I was in good positions and I was hitting the ball well. I just didn’t go on to get a big score.’

Duckett was speaking to Daily Mail Sport at a Tyrrells event at Edgbaston. Tyrrells are the official snack partner of the England men's and women's Test teams

The 31-year-old isn’t going to change the methods that have brought him nearly 3,500 Test runs at a tick under 39 and at a strike rate of 86

Above all, he isn’t going to change the methods that have brought him nearly 3,500 Test runs at a tick under 39 and at a strike rate of 86.

‘If I tried to be someone else in… let’s call it a new era, then I don’t think I’d perform as well. I know at the age I am how I’m going to get the best out of myself.’

Ben Duckett was speaking at a Tyrrells event at Edgbaston. Tyrrells Crisps are proud to be Official Snacks Partner of England Cricket. Visit tyrrellscrisps.co.uk.

Sports.title: INSIDE NEWCASTLE 2.0: Ross Wilson and the men running the show reveal the truth about summer of upheaval - from secret Eddie Howe succession plan to Bruno Guimaraes shock and the deal that had to happen to sign Matias Fernandez-Pardo
Sports.content:
INSIDE NEWCASTLE 2.0: Ross Wilson and the men running the show reveal the truth about summer of upheaval - from secret Eddie Howe succession plan to Bruno Guimaraes shock and the deal that had to happen to sign Matias Fernandez-Pardo

For much of this summer, Newcastle’s transfer window was viewed from the outside as one of chaos and crisis.

Eddie Howe left, Bruno Guimaraes, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali were sold and early deals for the likes of Victor Munoz and Johan Manzambi were hijacked by Premier League rivals.

But now, in a revealing sit-down with sporting director Ross Wilson, chief executive David Hopkinson and chief financial officer Simon Capper, they lift the lid on how the club emerged from that summer in a stronger position than many had anticipated – in the dugout, and on the pitch and balance sheet.

Our chief football reporter, Craig Hope, was in the room on Newcastle's Quayside as the hierarchy explained the thinking behind Newcastle 2.0, why trading stars will remain part of their model and the truth of Howe’s succession plan…

In a revealing sit-down with Ross Wilson (left), David Hopkinson (right) and Simon Capper, they lift the lid on how the club emerged from the summer in a stronger position than many thought

Newcastle are unbeaten to start the season and have been hugely entertaining going forward

‘IT NEVER FELT CHAOTIC… BUT LOSING BRUNO WAS NOT PART OF THE PLAN!’

Q: And breathe… the window is closed! But from the outside, it looked like there were moments when it was chaotic and stressful?

WILSON: 'Genuinely, no. It never felt chaotic on the inside. We did not want to lose Bruno Guimaraes and that was not part of our plan. It was really disappointing that we did, albeit we were happy with the numbers (a £75million sale to Arsenal). But everything else that happened during the window was part of the plan. That does not mean every single player (who signed) was the No1 name on our list, but that is never the case. Clearly, we were disappointed a couple of times. But that’s normal.'

Q: So, how do you reflect on the transfer window on the whole?

WILSON: ‘It was almost like running two transfer windows, because we also had the situation with the manager to deal with. We dealt with that with complete secrecy for just under two weeks, as well as trying to run a transfer window for players at the same time.

‘I had a clear idea, identity-wise, of what I wanted Newcastle United to look like, which we (points to Hopkinson) absolutely shared and our ownership share. The key for us was getting to the end of the window, not to the start or halfway through it, and really feeling that identity. That doesn't mean it's perfect, it doesn't mean that we are over the moon with it, but we're happy where we've got to.

‘We're not patting ourselves on the back or saying any more than that. We have to move forward bravely and strongly with our new coach, with our new players and with the players that were here before. There’s lots of work still to be done to get the whole club to where we want to get it to.’

CRAIG HOPE'S VERDICT: To be in a position to praise the work Newcastle have done did not feel likely as recently as three weeks ago. Since then, the new manager, Matthias Jaissle, has made a very good first impression, while the last three signings – Amar Dedic, Nico Gonzalez and Matias Fernandez-Pardo – have added strength, pedigree and excitement.

It’s early days, but I think it’s fair to say Newcastle have managed to salvage their summer. Saying that, I also think it was fair to look at the situation in early August and believe they were teetering on crisis. The work since has avoided such a scenario, and credit must go to those involved.

Amar Dedic has made an excellent start to life on Tyneside after joining for £30m from Benfica

Nico Gonzalez, brought in for £50m from Manchester City, has also been a huge boost

‘WE HAD BEEN PLANNING FOR A MANAGERIAL CHANGE FOR EIGHT OR NINE MONTHS’

Q: Did losing Eddie Howe create any chaos or pain?

WILSON: ‘It didn’t feel chaotic and it didn’t feel painful. Eddie would be the first person to tell you – I came to the club 11 months ago, and I’ve been planning in the background for a managerial change for eight or nine of those months. We knew which direction we were going to go.

‘Again, that does not mean we were always going to go to Matthias, but he was always part of our planning.

'Part of our responsibility as leaders of the club is to be prepared. Eddie is an exceptionally talented coach and at some point that meant he was probably going to do something else, and we had to be prepared for that. Clearly the timing was not one we had planned for, but we had a plan in place which is why we could execute it as quickly as we did.

‘There is big respect to Eddie for the job he did for us over a long period of time. He did a wonderful job and is a legend of the club.’

Q: Was Jaissle the only manager that you spoke to?

WILSON: ‘No. He was the No1 choice. We knew the type of coach and the type of football we wanted to play. We had to use our models to identify who those coaches might be. So it was really clear that Matthias was someone who would be really interesting to us.

‘I spoke to him on the phone and it was a really good conversation. Then I met him and when I was on the phone he (Hopkinson) said, “You sound really excited about this one”. I said, “You’re probably right!”.’

CRAIG HOPE'S VERDICT: The timing of Howe’s departure was a shock, but him going was less of a surprise. It should have happened at the end of last season, when he had doubts about carrying on. Nonetheless, Newcastle have, it appears, found a replacement that shares many of the same principles when it comes to playing style and intensity, but crucially Jaissle brings a fresh energy.

I think they’ve appointed a very good coach who will be around the Premier League for many years, even if this season could yet be one of transition and ups and downs for Newcastle.

The timing of Eddie Howe’s departure was a shock, but him going was less of a surprise

Newcastle have, it appears, found a replacement that shares many of the same principles when it comes to playing style and intensity, but crucially Jaissle brings a fresh energy

‘AGGRESSIVE, VERTICAL AND ATTACKING’ – THE NEWCASTLE IDENTITY

Q: When Howe went, did you have to change the profile of player you were targeting, or did you keep the same idea?

WILSON: ’I cannot imagine, in the short term, Newcastle United playing a style of football that isn’t aggressive, vertical and attacking. For this club to be successful, we have to play an attacking, high press, high engaging, proactive, vertical style of football – and we had to find a coach to do that for us.’

Q: Has Jaissle got a specific target?

WILSON: ‘No. He's here for four years, I hope. If he is, that’s us all doing well.’

Q: Can you feel the rise in expectation (on the back of an unbeaten start and some big signings)?

WILSON: ‘We want Newcastle United to be a club with anticipation and excitement. Because if we’re not, it probably means we’re doing it wrong. We want to feel excitement and ambition and a rise in anticipation. Of course we have to manage that and be balanced. But we want to be a club that’s got excitement around it.’

CRAIG HOPE'S VERDICT: On the playing style… while I agree with Wilson’s assessment of the fundamental principles of an aggressive and attacking team, I also believe there needs to be an evolution into control.

We saw on Saturday, during the 2-2 draw with Bournemouth, that Newcastle still struggle to take charge of a football match when it comes to keeping possession and dictating where and how the game is played. When fully fit, Gonzalez and Lewis Miley in midfield need to have a big impact on this improvement. Cohesion must complement the chaos.

When fully fit, Gonzalez and Lewis Miley (right) in midfield need to have a big impact on Newcastle's ability to control games

‘WE HAD TO DO A DEAL LIKE ANTHONY GORDON… AND BRUNO MEANT MORE SIGNINGS!’

Q: What is the club's position now with Squad Cost Ratio rules?

WILSON: ‘It (our SCR position) wasn’t hanging over the whole window, but where the club were previously, strategically and financially, led to the sale of Elliot Anderson (to Nottingham Forest) and Yankuba Minteh (to Brighton) and a UEFA sanction (£5m fine).

‘That's the facts, that's the reality. Nobody wanted to be there again. Going into this transfer window, we had to do a deal like Anthony Gordon (sold to Barcelona for £70m). It might have been another player, but it had to be a deal like that.

‘The window started with a new contract for Lewis Miley, which was a big signal for us in terms of identity and what we wanted to look like. A young player with an unbelievably high ceiling.

‘But until we had certainty over that transaction (sale of Gordon), we had uncertainty. Now, we’re very clear that we're in a positive place.’

CAPPER: ‘Every top-level football club in Europe is managing their budget on every transfer. Sometimes, you have to link transactions together, “So we can do this if that player comes in or goes out”. For example, we were able to sign more players because Bruno left. That gave us more headroom to be able to invest.

‘That's the other point. The club has managed to utilise as much of our headroom as we can strategically afford to lose. You can't use 100 per cent on day one, because there's more than just the squad cost moving. If you finish two places lower, that's £7m off your revenue, for example. So you need to have a bit of a margin of error in your planning, because lots of things can change.’

Anthony Gordon has hit the ground running at Barcelona after his £70m move, providing four assists in his first four LaLiga matches

‘FERNANDEZ-PARDO WAS ONLY POSSIBLE BECAUSE OF WOLTEMADE LOAN’

WILSON: 'Because we try to link things together, the ultimate deal for Matias Fernandez-Pardo was only possible because we did the Nick Woltemade loan to Juventus. That (Pardo) was the ultimate deal. Now, if we didn't do the Woltemade deal, we might have done another, but that's what we mean by linking things together.

CAPPER: ‘So the conversation we were having internally was, “If you want to do that, you're going to have to give me something back, otherwise we'll be in a position we're not comfortable with”. We managed to get that.

‘We have come out of this transfer window, I wouldn't say in an absolutely comfortable place, we have some risk around all of our Financial Fair Play measures, but it's an acceptable amount of risk at this point.

‘Our forecasts are all compliant as of today and we can afford a few little things to go wrong and remain compliant. As an organisation, that's the right place to be. We're not going with £100m headroom, just in case. I'm not going to say what the headroom is, but it's not that.’

WILSON: ‘But there is headroom, and that's the key point.’

CRAIG HOPE'S VERDICT: Former sporting director Paul Mitchell had some fair ideas when it came to changing Newcastle’s transfer strategy. It was an approach to diplomacy akin to a bull in a china shop that meant it was never going to work.

Wilson has arrived with far more footballing statecraft and, primarily because of the sales of Gordon and Tonali (£100m to Tottenham), he has got the club on a sound footing from an SCR perspective. Internally, they’re calling it ‘ripping off the sticking plaster’, and I get that. It’s better to do the big sales at once as opposed to drip feed over several windows, and it serves to redraw the reality of where the club is at.

I’m still not sure about one or two of the younger players brought in at big fees this summer – they will clearly need time – but the evolution of the model was necessary and has been overseen in a relatively short period. With that, they’ve signed some top players who look ready to impact immediately.

'The ultimate deal for Matias Fernandez-Pardo was only possible because we did the Nick Woltemade loan to Juventus'

‘IF YOU DON'T TRADE PLAYERS, YOU'RE GOING TO GET STUCK’

Q: Do the players you’ve signed fit into the 2030 Vision (of being among the top clubs in the world)?

WILSON: ‘We hope they’re with us on our journey to 2030, but we’ve got a player trading model as well. I’m sure there will be players in the 2030 squad that aren’t in the 2026-27 squad – I hope there are anyway! We want to have players here who are on a journey with us, but equally if some of those players’ journeys go at a rapid speed, they might go somewhere else. That’s part of football.’

Q: Does that (SCR headroom) allow you to spend in further windows, if you’re not so close to the limit?

WILSON: ‘Of course, but we built a squad for the season. That doesn’t mean we might not make further alterations to it in January. If you want to be a successful club in the Premier League, you have to trade players. If you don’t, the chances are you won’t be a successful club, particularly when the revenues of this club are in a phase where David and his team are making those really, really grow. But without that, if you don’t trade players, you are going to get stuck.’

HOPKINSON: ‘We’ve been consistent the whole way through – we are going to be consistently and credibly competing for those top prizes. Part of consistently competing means we’ve got to be compliant with the regulatory regime.

‘We know what our revenues are going to be projected, we can figure that part out. At the end of last season, and we did not have a strong finish, we ended up in 12th. When we started our pre-planning for the window – with each match we lost it got worse, because it meant our ultimate envelope would be smaller. So we came into this window knowing how much we would have to work with and a strong recognition that we have to be compliant.’

THE £60-70MILLION CHAMPIONS LEAGUE QUESTION

Q: Does the financial forecasting mean that you need to get in Europe this season?

CAPPER: ‘We forecast all (the scenarios), and basically we're good for this season now. While we've got different scenarios, the answer is the number is quite different depending on where we are. If we're in the Champions League, we've got a much bigger number to spend next summer than if we're not in Europe at all.

‘The revenue difference is so big. We're talking £60-70million minimum for the Champions League. Probably £30-40million for the Europa League and £20million minimum for the Conference League. So even the Conference League is material.

‘Once you get to the Champions League, it ends up being potentially 20 per cent of your revenue. So of course that affects our budgets. Again, we spend what we've got.’

'If we're in the Champions League, we've got a much bigger number to spend next summer than if we're not in Europe at all'

WILSON: ‘But these are the conversations that every club's got to have. So this isn't a choice. And if you don't do it (trade players), then you just keep the squad you've got and they'll grow old and achieve less and leave for nothing.’

CRAIG HOPE'S VERDICT: I left the room with a clear sense of the direction Newcastle 2.0 will be taking. The thinking behind it is sound – and necessary – and I believe those leading that reboot are well intended.

What I’m less certain of is the likelihood of delivering the 2030 Vision the club has as its stated ambition. For that, there needs to be a big upturn in revenue and, probably, a new stadium for that to be possible. Also, the trading model they talk about cannot afford too many misses, not when margins are so tight. Manchester City can get a couple wrong, the chasing pack cannot.

But this, because of SCR and the like, is how a club outside the established top order must operate now. As is the way at Newcastle, it will never be dull seeing how it all plays out.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
