World.title: ‘Limit overshoot, peak, decline’: A new global goal for climate change?
World.content:
The world agreed to limit temperature rises in 2015. Now, that goal is proving impossible. Is it time for a course correction?

The signing of the Paris Agreement by 200 countries in 2015 was a rare moment of global unity, and the euphoria was real.

To cheers and tears, the international climate treaty was approved by nearly every country in the world. Fundamental to the agreement was a commitment to keeping temperatures from rising beyond 1.5C (2.7F) above the pre-industrial levels of the mid 19th-century.

But 11 years on, it is evident that the Earth is soon going to exceed that threshold because of the continued record burning of fossil fuels.

A report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) in Nairobi, Kenya – called Limiting Overshoot – has found that even under the most optimistic scenario, the Earth will heat up by 1.8C (3.2F) above pre-industrial levels. It adds that the best hope for the planet is an “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway.

That would mean it is still possible, and essential, to bring temperatures down and achieve the Paris goals, but a course correction is required to get there.

The UNEP report envisions that the global temperature rise will pass the 1.5C threshold “within the next few years”, continue to increase, then gradually cool to below the 1.5-mark, hopefully by the end of the century.

Limiting the shock

The report makes it clear that the impact of rising temperatures will intensify with every year spent above the 1.5C threshold. Extreme weather will get more extreme; the danger of small island states and coastal cities being submerged will be more likely, while biodiversity loss will accelerate.



That means disasters such as the recent catastrophic Nepal flash floods – in which more than 1,300 people have died and thousands are still missing – which were caused by melting glaciers, could become more frequent.

Tom Rivett-Carnac, who helped shape the architecture of the Paris Agreement, told Al Jazeera that this overshoot looks increasingly locked in.

“Overshooting is extremely dangerous and raises the risks of runaway tipping points,” Rivett-Carnac told Al Jazeera. “If it has to happen, our task is to make it as small and as short as possible.”

But to ensure the temperature rise threshold returns to 1.5C in the future, the world needs to act now, the report warns, with sustained cuts to greenhouse gas emissions.

Mohammed Adow of the think tank Power Shift Africa told Al Jazeera that every fraction of a degree above 1.5C means more lives lost, more crops failing and more damage to economies.

“If exceeding 1.5C can no longer be avoided then of course we must keep that overshoot in check and bring temperatures back down as soon as possible,” he said. “Giving up because 1.5C is temporarily breached would be a catastrophic, unforgivable mistake.”

‘We need political courage’

Despite the extraordinary momentum the Paris Agreement prompted, as it reduced the scale of projected warming and supercharged clean energy growth, the political will to see it through has failed to emerge, Rivett-Carnac said.

“Temperature projections have fallen from 3-3.5C in 2015 to roughly 2.3-2.5C now, so the progress from Paris has been real,” he said.

“However, the 2015 assumption was that politics would follow economics, that falling costs in renewable energy would pull political ambition with them. That has not proved to be constantly the case.”

Most notably, the United States has proved entirely inconsistent. Under both presidencies of Donald Trump, it has withdrawn from the Paris Agreement altogether while the Trump administration remains heavily invested in touting US – and now Venezuelan – oil to international consumers.

Since 2015, global fossil fuel consumption has only increased. According to the International Energy Agency, carbon dioxide emissions rose by about 145 million tonnes in 2025, reaching a new record high of 38.4 billion tonnes, 5 percent above 2019 levels.

This is happening despite extraordinary declines in the cost of producing renewable energy. According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), solar power is now 90 percent cheaper than it was in 2010.



Furthermore, renewables surpass fossil fuels as the most cost-competitive source of new electricity generation, the agency says. More than 90 percent of utility-scale projects commissioned in 2025 delivered power below the cost of the cheapest new fossil fuel plant built in their market.

“The tragedy is our technological progress has outrun our political progress,” said Mohammed Adow. “What we lack is governments willing to deploy renewable technology at the necessary speed, to phase out fossil fuels and to provide developing countries with the finance to make that transition.

“The route out of this crisis is clearer than it was in 2015. We now need the political courage to take it.”

Climate rollbacks and AI data centres

US climate policy rollbacks under President Trump and his withdrawal from the Paris Agreement have undoubtedly slowed the momentum for change at the level of global governance. Global energy demands, particularly from artificial intelligence, continue to rise.

In 2024, AI data centres were estimated to have consumed approximately 1.5 percent of global electricity. That consumption is projected to double by 2030.

Many believe it is incumbent upon Big Tech like Apple and Meta to make use of new technologies to reverse the direction of travel with AI emissions.

“The demand for data centres is rising sharply,” Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford, told Al Jazeera. “And too many being built are powered by fossil fuels. Tech companies need to do the right thing.”

Rosenow pointed to the use of circular energy systems as one means of reducing emissions. “The waste heat from data centres can and should be recovered – this is something that has been happening in Sweden for years.”

The explosive demand for electricity to power AI means Big Tech is struggling to meet its climate pledges. In July this year, British daily The Guardian reported that Microsoft, Amazon and Google’s collective carbon emissions have increased by nearly 20 percent in a year, an increase equivalent to about one-third of the CO2 emissions of France.

In its annual sustainability report, Amazon said: “We recognise the path to being a more sustainable company is not a straight line. Though our emissions increased in 2025, we remain steadfast in our commitment to sustainability.”

The AI-fuelled demand in the US, in particular, is increasingly being met by fossil fuels. The Environmental Integrity Project reports that there are plans for at least 74 gas-fired power plants to cater for data centres, which could emit upwards of 660 million tonnes of greenhouse gas per year, equivalent to Australia’s pollution annually.

Removing carbon

To help bring the world back to its 1.5C threshold course, the UNEP report points to the need for the implementation of large-scale carbon dioxide removal (CDR) projects.

These include conventional methods, such as planting trees and restoring ecosystems, and more controversial ones such as carbon capture and storage, where emissions are collected, cleaned and stored deep underground, a technology hard to implement at scale.



Rosenow said carbon removal technologies have their place but not as a primary route to decarbonisation.

“Why? Because it is far cheaper to avoid emitting in the first place,” he said.

World.title: What to watch in the US’s New Hampshire and Rhode Island primary elections
World.content:
Some of the US midterm election’s biggest themes will play out in these New England states’ most notable races.

Share What to watch in the US’s New Hampshire and Rhode Island primary elections on social media

Voters in two US states — New Hampshire and Rhode Island — will head to the polls this week to select Democratic and Republican candidates for this November’s United States midterm elections.

In what’s been a campaign season full of unexpected twists and turns, from the continued growth of the Democrats’ progressive arm to mixed results for President Donald Trump-endorsed Republican candidates, the contests mark some of the last primaries before the US makes a final determination on which party will control both chambers of the US Congress.

Before that happens, candidates in some of these New England states’ most notable races will have to contend with some of this midterm’s biggest themes: How much Republicans should align with Trump, and whether a Democratic incumbent can fight off a primary challenger.

Here are the races to watch:

In New Hampshire, a battle to replace a retiring senator

When does voting in New Hampshire start? Opening times for polling locations vary across the state, but all polls must open on Tuesday, September 8 by 11am (15:00 GMT).

Opening times for polling locations vary across the state, but all polls must open on Tuesday, September 8 by 11am (15:00 GMT). When does voting in New Hampshire end? Closing times also vary, but state law stipulates polls cannot close earlier than 7pm (23:00 GMT).

The most notable race in New Hampshire will determine the two candidates who will face off to replace outgoing Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen.



US Representative Chris Pappas has emerged as the frontrunner to win the Democratic nomination. On the Republican side, John Sununu holds the benefit of strong name recognition from being a part of the state’s most prominent political dynasty.

Democrats have hoped to retain this seat, a critical must-keep as they look to take back the US Senate currently controlled by Republicans. But recent polling of likely voters conducted by Senate Republicans’ campaign arm shows Sununu leading Pappas by one point. The survey, conducted in the final days of August, found nearly one in four voters are undecided.

However, both candidates, if they win their primaries on Tuesday, may have to confront actions by their party’s top figures, who could complicate their campaigns.

In the Democratic primary, Pappas remains the favourite, but his lead has dropped by double digits, according to some polls.

Pappas’s closest opponent is democratic socialist Karishma Manzur, who has picked up support, in part, over her calls to “end US complicity in the genocide of Palestinians”. While Pappas has stressed the importance of the current US-Israel relationship, the congressman has also said he supports a two-state solution and “increasing” aid to Gaza.

Manzur has criticised Pappas for connections to political donors, including those connected to Israel.

Former US Vice President Kamala Harris endorsed Pappas last week. Harris’s support, which Pappas said he was “proud” to receive, could help him across the finish line in the state’s Democratic primary, where most of the party’s voters lean more moderate. Pappas has served in the US House since 2019 and has held elected office almost continuously since graduating from college in 2002. He defeated Karoline Leavitt in his 2022 reelection bid before her stint as Trump’s White House press secretary.

In the Republican primary, Sununu is running to recapture the Senate seat he once held before being defeated by Shaheen in 2008. He faces Scott Brown, also a former senator who once held Massachusetts US Senator Elizabeth Warren’s seat, along with seven other opponents.

Sununu has been trying to put distance between himself and Trump. Trump is, however, backing Sununu over Brown in the primary, despite an ongoing war of words he’s had with Sununu’s family over the years — Sununu’s father and brother have both served as governor, and all have been critical of Trump.

Brown won a special election in Massachusetts after the death of Senator Ted Kennedy in 2009, lost his seat three years later, and unsuccessfully challenged Shaheen in 2014. In Trump’s first administration, Brown served as the US Ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa.

In Rhode Island, can an unpopular sitting Democratic governor fight off a challenge?



When does voting in Rhode Island start? With the exception of one town, voting starts on Wednesday, September 9 at 7am (11:00 GMT).

With the exception of one town, voting starts on Wednesday, September 9 at 7am (11:00 GMT). When does voting in Rhode Island end? Polls close at 8pm on Wednesday (00:00 GMT on Thursday).

Unlike other states this election cycle, the biggest race in Rhode Island is for governor, not for seats in the US Congress.

Vulnerable Democratic Governor Dan McKee is fighting off a strong primary challenge from pharmacy executive Helena Foulkes.

The highly unpopular incumbent has trailed Foulkes, whose grandfather and uncle were both lawmakers in the neighbouring US state of Connecticut, by as much as 38 points, according to a recent poll. Foulkes has also outraised McKee.

This race is a rematch of a bitter, hard-fought primary four years ago, when McKee, who had been elevated to governor when his predecessor became former US President Joe Biden’s commerce secretary, narrowly beat Foulkes in a crowded race.

While most of this year’s competitive midterm primaries have centred on ideological or generational differences, the outcome of this race could come down to complaints about a freeway bridge in Providence, the state’s largest city, that was partially closed in 2023 due to safety issues.

The resulting congestion and economic fallout caused by the closure have fuelled strong voter resentment towards McKee, one of the most endangered elected Democrats this cycle. Should McKee be unsuccessful in warding off Foulkes, he would become the first sitting US governor to lose a primary in eight years.

In the Republican primary, Aaron Guckian and Elaine Pelino are vying for the nomination. Guckian is a state trade association executive and was the nominee for lieutenant governor in 2022. He won the two-way primary that year with about 68 percent of the vote. Pelino is a former actress and first-time candidate. The state’s Republican Party has endorsed Guckian.

It’s been 20 years since Rhode Island elected a Republican governor.

World.title: Canada braces for prolonged trade war as counter-tariffs on US take effect
World.content:
Canada's retaliatory tariffs on a range of US goods came into effect on Tuesday, with no sign of a trade deal on the horizon.

The counter-tariffs will apply to nearly C$28bn ($20bn; Â£15bn) worth of American products, from steel to furniture to cotton T-shirts, and will be as high as 50%.

Fresh fish and lobster were also on the list, but Canada later omitted them after pushback from its seafood industry - a sign of the tricky balance it has to strike as it retaliates against its largest trading partner.

Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a deal, but no movement has been made to resume talks after they collapsed in late August.

Speaking to reporters last week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada is still in search of a deal with the US that is "durable" and in the best interests of both countries.

"We're ready to sit down and strike that deal when the Americans are ready," Carney said.

US trade representative Jamieson Greer said on Thursday the ball is in Canada's court.

"We offered them the best deal, they looked at it square in the face and turned around," Greer said in an interview with Fox News, adding that there has been sparse communication with the Canadians since talks collapsed.

In a separate interview with Canadian broadcaster CBC, Greer cautioned against retaliation and suggested the US might hit back by banning the import of some Canadian products.

President Donald Trump threatened on Monday to halt all US business with Canada-based airplane maker Bombardier unless it moved its manufacturing south.

The aerospace giant is one of the largest in the country, contributing over C$7bn to Canada's annual GDP in 2024, according to a report by accounting firm PwC.

World.title: At least two people dead after Russian strikes on Kyiv
World.content:
At least two people have been killed after Russia resumed airstrikes on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv early on Tuesday, officials said.

The attack came after both countries agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while US Donald Trump's top envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday he expected the war to continue into the winter, following talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - their first visit to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion.

Air raid alerts warned civilians to seek shelter as Russian forces launched drone strikes on Kyiv early on Tuesday, authorities said.

A series of explosions across Ukraine's capital overnight killed two people and injured ten others, the city's state emergency service said on Telegram.

Residential buildings were hit, according to authorities, including a five-storey apartment block in the Solomianskyi district, while vehicles caught fire in the Podilskyi district.

People sought shelter inside a metro station in Kyiv during the overnight missile attack, something that is routine for residents protecting themselves during the ongoing war.

In Russia, buildings were struck in the city of Saratov during a Ukrainian drone attack, its regional governor Roman Busargin said on Telegram early Tuesday.

The talks with Trump's top envoys on Sunday in Ukraine, which lasted several hours behind closed doors, finished without any major breakthroughs.

Zelensky told reporters they had agreed that officials from Ukraine, Europe and America would meet in the near future to continue discussions. He also called for a trilateral meeting with Russia and the US.

According to a BBC Verify analysis, Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's invasion in 2022.

World.title: Investigation after female staff at Eiffel Tower replaced by men for religious visit
World.content:
An investigation has been launched in France after female staff at the Eiffel Tower were replaced by male colleagues for the visit of a Hindu religious group.

A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the iconic landmark in Paris on Saturday.

"Women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated", staff union representative Diane Davoine said. The tower closed on Monday as staff went on strike to show their outrage.

BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances.

Ariel Weil, who is the president of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower, blamed its managers for being "a bit overzealous" in complying with the request without considering whether it was "inappropriate".

Weil, who is also mayor of Paris Centre, told French broadcaster Franceinfo on Tuesday that the incident was "totally shocking and unacceptable".

An internal investigation will determine who was responsible for putting the conditions in place, Weil said, and ensure it "never happens again".

In a statement reported by AFP news agency, staff at the monument said that during Saturday's visit, female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present".

"Tensions mounted over the weekend, so [on Monday morning], the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again," Davoine said.

SociÃ©tÃ© d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), which runs the Eiffel Tower, had previously said the conditions imposed on female staff were not in line with its values "nor with the principles of equality between men and women".

World.title: Highest paid world leader to get salary increase of $1 million
World.content:
Singapore's government says it will raise the annual salaries of its ministers and other office holders, including its prime minister who is the highest paid political leader in the world.

Lawrence Wong will see an increase of 1.4 million Singapore dollars ($1.1m; Â£818,000) in his annual pay package. He has said he will donate this pay increase to charity over the next five years.

Wong said that raising the pay of ministers was necessary to attract better talent. The government has previously argued that paying ministers high salaries deters corruption.

But the move has attracted criticism in Singapore where there is deep concern about job security and the rising cost of living.

Even before his pay raise kicks in, Wong is still by far the highest paid world leader.

He currently receives an annual salary of S$2.2m and will now see his pay go up by more than 60% to S$3.6m ($2.8m).

Next is Hong Kong chief executive John Lee, who earns about $719,000, followed by Switzerland's president Guy Parmelin with $606,000.

US president Donald Trump earns $400,000 a year, while British PM Andy Burnham takes in $230,000.

On Tuesday, Wong acknowledged that Singapore ministers' salaries have attracted scrutiny given that they were much more than what most citizens earn. The median monthly income in the country is S$5,775.

But he argued that he has faced difficulty convincing business leaders and top civil servants to run for political office.

While the government cannot match what some of these people earn, "we do not make the financial hurdle unnecessarily high" for them to give up their careers and join politics, he said.

"Overall, I believe this will give me and future prime ministers a better chance of persuading capable Singaporeans to step forward, and of building the strongest possible team for Singapore," he said.

Currently, the base pay package of ministers is about S$1.1m. With the new pay scheme, that will increase to around S$1.2m.

But Wong said he expects most of these ministers to receive even more than that - around S$1.35m - by the end of the current term of government, as pay will increase based on performance.

Part of their pay package is determined by whether the country reaches certain targets for unemployment rate, income growth, and GDP growth.

The topic of high salaries for Singapore's ministers has long been a lightning rod of criticism for the ruling People's Action Party (PAP), which has led the country since independence.

In a landmark general election in 2011 the PAP saw its lowest vote share in decades, fuelled partly by voters' unhappiness over ministers' pay as well as immigration policies. The following year, the government slashed ministers' salaries.

Wong's predecessor, Lee Hsien Loong, had also pledged to donate his salary increase to charity for several years back in 2007.

The government has for years pointed to its lack of corruption - Singapore consistently ranks near the top of Transparency International's annual Corruption Perceptions Index - as proof that the ministerial pay system works, arguing that it reduces the temptation for ministers to accept bribes.

But in a country where the average income is far below such sums, the issue continues to rankle and the latest announcement is no exception.

On Tuesday many online posted comments critical of the pay raise, saying it was "tone deaf" given current concerns about retrenchments, jobs for fresh graduates and inflation.

Retrenchments in Singapore hit their highest level in more than five years in the last quarter, according to government figures.

But there were a few who agreed with the move, saying it was necessary to have "the best of the best" running the country.

World.title: Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands
World.content:
The Argentine government has said that it would file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Islands.

The move came just days after Argentine President Javier Milei said he would sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean.

Sovereignty of the archipelago remains disputed between the UK and Argentina more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982.

The simmering dispute heated up last week, when Milei said in a speech to the nation that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the Falklands.

Milei has, in the past, been criticised by Argentine veterans of the 1982 conflict for being "too soft" on the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas.

In his speech on Thursday evening local time, Milei restated his government's position on the territory, saying "the Malvinas are Argentine, historically and legally... there's no debate about that."

The president described drilling for oil in the archipelago as a "clear and urgent danger" to Argentine sovereignty.

He also dismissed the result of a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands' residents voted in favour of the Falklands remaining a British oversees territory.

Milei argued that they were living on land which had been "usurped" by the British and therefore "have no legitimate right to self-determination".

World.title: Five killed in Miami plane crash were in two vehicles on ground, investigators say
World.content:
The five people killed and five injured when an Amazon cargo plane crashed on landing at Miami International Airport were in two vehicles on the ground, investigators said.

The Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air, overshot the runway on Sunday and hit an airline cleaning van holding seven people before breaking the perimeter fence and striking a Toyota SUV with three inside.

Jennifer Homendy, chairwoman of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), called the crash scene "utter devastation" and said it was too early to identify a cause.

Investigators have recovered the flight recorders and will look at flight systems, crew experience and weather as potential factors, say aviation experts.

Speaking at a press conference at Miami International Airport on Monday, Homendy said the aircraft had two crew members on board and was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on its third flight of the day.

The plane struck navigational aids and equipment after overrunning the runway, before hitting a white Ford van owned by a contract cleaning company.

It then travelled through a perimeter fence and collided with a Toyota Corolla, coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.

It was not clear from the NTSB's updates how many people died in each vehicle on the ground, or the condition of the two crew on board the plane.

World.title: Trial over killing of Australian surfer brothers and US friend starts in Mexico
World.content:
Three men have gone on trial in Mexico for the alleged murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in 2024.

The bodies of Callum Robinson, his younger brother Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad from California - all in their early 30s - were found at the bottom of a well with gunshot wounds to their heads, days after they went missing during a surf trip in Baja California.

Prosecutors are seeking jail sentences of more than 200 years for the defendants, who also face charges of violent robbery and auto theft.

The parents of the brothers were in court on Tuesday in the coastal town of Ensenada, telling the media that it was "incredibly important and overwhelmingly difficult".

"We want the men accused of murdering our sons to see, in person, the human consequences of what happened," Martin and Debra Robinson said in a statement, according to Australia's national broadcaster, the ABC.

"Callum and Jake were not simply victims in a case file - they were our sons, deeply loved by their family and friends, with lives, dreams and futures that were brutally taken away."

On the opening day, the accused - JesÃºs "El Kekas" Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ãngel JesÃºs - were moved to a smaller courtroom amid accusations that some witnesses had been intimidated by people associated with the defendants.

Dozens of witnesses are expected to give evidence during the four-week, judge-only trial.

The 2024 alleged killings of the Robinson brothers and their US friend shocked Australians as well as many residents of the normally peaceful town of Ensenada.

Despite high levels of cartel violence in the northern Mexican border states, tourists are rarely targeted for such violent attacks in Baja California's surf towns.

The ex-girlfriend of one of the accused, Ari Gisell, became the first person to be convicted over the tourists' killings last year and was sentenced to 20 years in prison for her role in their murders.

Mexican prosecutors are pursuing jail sentences of more than 200 years for each of the defendants, as well as an additional 168-year sentence for the alleged ringleader.

Prosecutors say the victims were killed due to a bungled robbery, while the defence argued there was not enough evidence to prove that theory.

Callum Robinson was a member of Australia's national lacrosse team and lived in San Diego where he was a professional lacrosse player.

His younger brother Jake had travelled from Australia for the surf trip and was due to start a job as a doctor when he returned while their friend Rhoad was killed a few months before his wedding.

World.title: Nepal cracks down on online abuse of flood survivors
World.content:
Nepal is cracking down on online abuse directed at survivors of last month's deadly floods, with Prime Minister Balendra Shah warning that authorities will "show no leniency" to people who "belittle" those who are suffering.

Some have taken to social media to appeal for information about their loved ones and to urge officials to step up search efforts, only to be hit by hostile comments.

"People who make unnecessary remarks, belittle those in pain or seek to cause them further suffering at this sensitive time are criminals," Shah wrote in a Facebook post.

Nepali police say they are looking into where these comments have originated from to identify addresses and phone numbers.

A woman, whose brother has been missing since the floods hit two weeks ago, had earlier told the BBC that search and rescue operations were too slow.

"If the government had mobilised experts and equipment for rescue in time, would we have known the condition of our family members sooner?

"We still hope we can find him alive."

Days later, she wrote back saying she had "received many nasty comments" in response to her criticism of the search efforts.

"We are already suffering so much and this has only added to our pain," she said.

In a separate case, a young woman had expressed her anger at what she perceived as authorities' "lack of urgency" in searching for her husband.

"My husband is missing now, if the government cannot find him, can it at least show me his body?" she said in a video clip that has gone viral online â and attracted its fair share of insults.

One comment, for instance, urged her to "jump into the river" and help with the search, while another read, "not everything happens just by you putting the blame on the government".

But others have called out the insensitive remarks. "The victim should be consoled at this time, not cursed," one of them read.

Nepali police say they have convened a 10-member committee to look into these online comments.

Under the country's Electronic Transactions Act, those who use social media to defame or harass others could be jailed for up to five years and fined up to 100,000 rupees ($662; Â£490), or both.

Dovan Rai, the executive director of Body & Data, a Nepal-based non-profit organisation that advocates for a safe digital space, says some of the insensitive comments could have come from social media users who engage in "rage baiting" â that is, those who produce negative content as a "bait" to trigger outrage, or force people to click on or share their posts.

They could also have come from "staunch supporters of the government".

"There is also extremism that is very sympathetic to the government and condemns those who question it. That has further polarized the dialogue on social media," she told the BBC.

World.title: FIFA U-20 WWC: Aduku promises improved Falconets display after Spain defeat
World.content:
Nigeria’s Falconets were beaten 2-0 by Spain in their opening Group F match at the 2026 FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup, leaving head coach Moses Aduku admitting that his side failed to turn up for the encounter.

The 2022 champions made a strong start to their campaign against the seven-time African champions, with Nigeria struggling to impose themselves as Spain controlled the contest and eventually secured all three points.

Spain broke the deadlock through forward Marisa Garcia, who finished after clever work from Noe Bejarano opened up the Nigerian defence.

The Falconets then faced an even tougher task in the second half when Spain introduced Alba Cerrato from the bench.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Cerrato needed just seven minutes to make an impact, producing a neat left-footed strike to double Spain’s advantage and effectively put the game beyond Nigeria’s reach.

The goal was another notable moment for Cerrato, who was part of the Spain side that finished runners-up at the 2024 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in the Dominican Republic.

Nigeria struggled to create clear-cut opportunities throughout the encounter, with their best chance arriving seven minutes from full time.

Precious Oscar found herself with an opportunity from 10 yards but saw her effort narrowly miss the target as the Falconets were unable to find a way back into the game.

Spain coach David Aznar praised his players for overcoming what he expected to be a physically demanding Nigerian side.

“We are very pleased. Winning the first match at a tournament of this level is always positive because it means that your destiny remains in your own hands going into the following games. It was a very difficult match. We knew Nigeria would make things extremely difficult for us because they have tremendous physical potential, and we knew it was going to be demanding. I think we made an enormous effort and deserved to win.”

For Nigeria, Aduku speaking to FIFA media, did not hide his disappointment with his team’s performance, but insisted that the defeat would not derail their campaign.

“We did not come to the party today, we did not play. But all the same we have two more games to play, we will get it right. Of course, we are going to go through [to the knockout rounds]. I am confident. We did not play today.”

“Although my girls tried their best but, that’s football. We’ll get it right the next game.”

The result leaves the Falconets with work to do in their remaining Group F fixtures, but Aduku remains confident that Nigeria can recover and progress to the knockout stages.

The Nigerian side will now have to respond strongly in their next two group matches against China and New Caledonia, with the coach insisting that the team can still get their campaign back on track.

For the Falconets, the challenge is now to put the disappointing performance against Spain behind them and deliver the response Aduku believes they are capable of producing.

World.title: “Colours of My Mind”: A citizen’s chronicle of Nigeria in real time
World.content:
Colours of My Mind is…a record of how an engaged Nigerian citizen thought through his country in real time, from the particular vantage point of the Niger Delta. Its value lies less in the comprehensiveness of its political analysis than in the immediacy of its observations, the force of its convictions and its willingness to turn the critical gaze upon the author’s own community.

In the foreword to Colours of My Mind, Professor Godini G. Darah places Austin Emaduku within a distinguished lineage of Nigerian public intellectuals, from Nnamdi Azikiwe and Anthony Enahoro to Dele Giwa and Tunji Dare, who used the written word to interrogate power and hold public authority to account.

It is an ambitious comparison for this collection of 69 commentaries. But the ambition is not entirely misplaced.

Colours of My Mind is something perhaps more modest, but in some respects more interesting: a record of how an engaged Nigerian citizen thought through his country in real time, from the particular vantage point of the Niger Delta. Its value lies less in the comprehensiveness of its political analysis than in the immediacy of its observations, the force of its convictions and its willingness to turn the critical gaze upon the author’s own community.

The pieces, written predominantly between 2016 and 2017, with some extending to 2023, cover politics, governance, religion, ethnicity, culture, social values and local affairs. They originated largely as social media commentaries, and the book retains much of the immediacy of that form.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This is not a conventional work of political philosophy. It is part political commentary, part local history, part moral argument and, above all, an archive.

What Kind of Book Is This?

Emaduku himself provides the key to understanding the collection. In his introduction, he explains that “a bulk of these articles were written between 2016 and 2017, a trying period in my life that turned out to be my most productive and creative years thus far.” He says he put the collection together “to record my thoughts for posterity.”

Fair enough. That is an important declaration of intent.

The reader should therefore resist the temptation to judge every piece as though it were written as part of a single, carefully constructed political thesis. These are interventions made at particular moments, responding to particular events and controversies. Some are angry. Some are reflective. Some are deliberately provocative. Some are much stronger than others.

Taken together, however, they create a portrait of a Nigerian citizen trying to make sense of his country during a difficult period.

That is the book’s real organising principle.

The Niger Delta Vantage Point

Emaduku’s most distinctive contribution is his rootedness.

He writes from Udu Kingdom in Delta State, from a region that produces a substantial portion of Nigeria’s wealth while bearing many of the environmental, economic and social consequences of oil extraction. His commentary, therefore, comes with a perspective that is often missing from national political writing.

In a keynote address on youth restiveness and militancy delivered in October 2016, he recalls the Warri of his youth:

“I can recall the mid-80s to the early 90s when Warri, the economic hub of Delta State was home to hundreds of oil companies. Oil production was at its peak and many of our young men and women were engaged in one form of employment or the other. Technicians, fitters, welders, caterers, security guards, etc.”

The passage is valuable because it is not simply nostalgia. It becomes an indictment of what happened afterwards. Emaduku writes:

“We created the state of insecurity that chased away the companies that would have provided employment for our teeming unemployed youths.”

The significance lies partly in where the criticism is directed. He acknowledges the failures of government and the injustices suffered by the Niger Delta, but he is equally prepared to confront destructive choices made within the region itself.

That willingness to look inward recurs throughout the book.

His description of the social consequences of the collapse of the local economy, including the uncomfortable account of “club girls” who once rejected African customers because of their lack of “dollar power”, is hardly polished sociological analysis. But it is vivid social observation, recording the mentality that developed around oil wealth, foreign workers, local deprivation and the distorted expectations created by a boom economy.

He does not merely describe the Niger Delta as a victim. He tries to understand how victimhood, grievance, opportunism, militancy and communal responsibility became entangled.

The Community Intellectual

The book also introduces us to Emaduku as a community intellectual.

His interventions in Udu politics, the affairs of the Union of Udu Communities, the BEDC electricity crisis and the Aladja-Ogbe-Ijoh conflict may appear specifically local to readers outside Delta State. Yet they reveal something important about citizenship.

For Emaduku, politics is not an abstraction taking place in Abuja. It is electricity that does not reach communities, institutions that fail, traditional authorities that are contested, neighbours who become enemies and local leaders whose conduct affects ordinary people.

His letter to the Aladja and Ogbe-Ijoh communities in August 2017 is particularly striking because it draws upon memory as a form of moral argument. Recalling a period when the two communities enjoyed close relations, he writes:

“I recall with clarity and fond memories the peaceful brotherly relationship that existed between your two communities. I recall my first visit as a student of Aladja Grammar School to the then sleepy community of Ogbe-Ijoh.”

Then comes the question:

“What or who brought this calamity upon you?”

It is a simple question, but its force comes from the person asking it. This is not an outsider offering an editorial judgement on an unfamiliar communal conflict. It is someone invoking a shared past to challenge a present he regards as intolerable.

In passages such as this, Colours of My Mind becomes something more than political commentary. It becomes journalism of memory.

The Courage to Criticise One’s Own

Perhaps the most admirable quality in the collection is Emaduku’s willingness to criticise his own side.

He challenges Niger Delta militancy, questions aspects of Urhobo political culture and takes issue with Igbo nationalism. His targets include governments, political parties, ethnic communities, religious institutions and ordinary citizens.

His critique of Niger Delta militancy is particularly uncompromising:

“You are like the mad man who in an attempt to solve the problem of rats in his house, set the house on fire only to sleep out in the rain.”

He then goes further, arguing that militants are in an even worse moral position than Boko Haram because, unlike the latter’s distorted religious justification, the militants have no theological escape from the consequences of their actions.

The language is severe. But its significance lies in its direction. Emaduku is not simply denouncing a distant enemy. He is speaking to his own community.

The same tendency appears in his criticism of Urhobo social media activists. Reacting to the celebration of the Olu of Warri’s English-language coronation speech alongside criticism of another Urhobo leader for speaking English, he asks:

“‘You well?’ ‘Them, do you?’”

The humour is unmistakably Nigerian, but the underlying point is serious. Emaduku is attacking what he sees as the selective application of standards according to ethnic and political convenience.

That willingness to apply uncomfortable standards to one’s own community gives the book much of its moral credibility.

Interesting Contradictions

Emaduku’s arguments also contain tensions that the book does not always resolve.

In “Where Did Our Values Go?”, he criticises Pentecostal Christianity for having “demonised those traditional beliefs that helped maintain the right values in our communities”. At one point he declares:

“Christianity is our greatest problem.”

Yet elsewhere his writing is unmistakably shaped by Christian moral convictions, and he criticises the failures of Christian institutions from within a recognisably Christian worldview.

There is a fascinating argument waiting to be developed here: whether Christianity itself is the problem, or whether the problem lies in the way Christianity has been institutionalised and practised.

The same applies to restructuring. Emaduku advocates greater autonomy while criticising state and local political actors for misappropriating resources and failing their communities.

To be fair, these are not necessarily irreconcilable positions. Greater decentralisation can coexist with stronger accountability. But the argument requires more careful institutional reasoning than the book provides.

The contradictions should therefore not simply be condemned. They should have been explored.

The Missing Conversation with His Former Self

Perhaps the greatest missed opportunity in the book is the absence of retrospective reflection.

Emaduku tells us that these writings were gathered “to record my thoughts for posterity.” Posterity, however, has arrived with questions.

What does he now think of his earlier positions? Which predictions came true? Which political figures surprised him? Did subsequent events alter his understanding of restructuring, ethnic politics, militancy, religion or protest? What does he now make of the Buhari years from the vantage point of their aftermath?

A concluding essay would have transformed the book. It would have allowed the author to sit across the table from his younger self and ask whether he was right, where he was wrong and what subsequent events taught him.

That would have turned an archive of opinion into a record of intellectual development.

The Audience Problem

The book also has an audience problem.

Its local material is potentially fascinating to readers from Delta State and the Urhobo community but can be opaque to outsiders. Its national essays, meanwhile, sometimes do not quite reach the depth required to distinguish them from the large body of Nigerian political commentary already available.

The answer is not to remove the local material but to contextualise it. A glossary of local institutions and terms, brief explanatory notes and perhaps a short introduction to the political history of Udu and the wider Urhobo area would help national readers understand why these local disputes matter.

The local can become national when properly framed.

Indeed, one of the book’s most important contributions could be precisely this movement from the particular to the general: showing how the Nigerian state is experienced not in constitutional abstractions but through electricity supply, traditional institutions, communal conflict, employment, political representation and the conduct of local leaders.

A Book Worth Preserving

Colours of My Mind is a worthwhile book.

Its value lies in the fact that Emaduku has preserved something that disappears easily in the digital age: the record of sustained civic engagement.

Social media is full of opinions. Far fewer people preserve those opinions systematically enough for others to examine them years later. Emaduku has done so.

His collection allows us to see what Nigeria looked like from the mind of one engaged citizen at particular moments in its recent history. It captures anger, disappointment, humour, moral conviction, ethnic anxiety, community pride and the persistent desire to make sense of a difficult country.

Emaduku belongs to the democratic tradition of citizens who believe that public affairs are too important to be left entirely to politicians. He is also a community intellectual and citizen commentator who decided to put his thoughts on record.

That is valuable in its own right.

Conclusion

The greatest contribution of Colours of My Mind is perhaps its demonstration that citizenship is more than voting, paying taxes or complaining about government. Citizenship also involves thinking, arguing, remembering and holding oneself and one’s community accountable.

That is what Emaduku attempts throughout these pages.

Crispin Oduobuk is a former acting editor of Weekly Trust.

World.title: How NDC is funded – Spokesperson
World.content:
The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has said its activities ahead of the 2027 general elections are being funded through donations, levies and contributions from members, stakeholders and well-wishers.

The party stated this in a statement issued by its National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director, on Tuesday, while providing clarification on its funding and candidate selection processes.

Mr Director said that the party, being a new political organisation without elected public office holders, had to develop mechanisms to raise resources for its operations and election-related activities.

He said that the party’s constitution provided for contributions from aspirants, members, stakeholders and members of the public to support its activities.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to him, all contributions and levies are paid directly into the designated party account and managed by the appropriate organs of the party.

He maintained that the NDC National Leader, Seriake Dickson, did not demand or receive money from any aspirant for personal use.

“All funds were duly received, receipted and accounted for in line with global best practices,” he said.

The publicity secretary said the party would render a full account of its finances in accordance with the Electoral Act and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) guidelines.

He explained that funding was an important aspect of election planning, particularly for an opposition party seeking to field candidates across the country within months of general elections.

Mr Director said the party’s decision to seek donations and levies from members was intended to support its operations and national mobilisation.

He added that the party was not funded with money from government treasuries, but through contributions from members, stakeholders and supporters.

The NDC spokesperson also said the party’s presidential and vice-presidential tickets were offered without charge, adding that the same principle applied to several other political positions and candidates.

He expressed the party leadership’s commitment to transparency, due process and justice in its operations.

Mr Director urged members of the public and the media to rely only on verified information concerning the party’s activities and finances.

He said that NDC would remain focused on its preparations for the 2027 general elections and its objective of building a broad-based political movement.

(NAN)

World.title: Why you shouldn’t miss FirstBank’s Agric and Export Expo 2026
World.content:
As Nigeria continues to diversify its economy beyond oil, agriculture and non-oil exports are emerging as powerful drivers of growth, job creation, food security, and foreign exchange earnings.

To advance this conversation, FirstBank will host the 5th edition of its Agric and Export Expo on 16 and 17 September 2026 under the theme: “From Farm to Global Markets: Building Nigeria’s Export Value Chain.”

The two-day event will bring together policymakers, regulators, agribusiness leaders, exporters, investors, and development partners to discuss practical solutions for strengthening Nigeria’s agricultural value chain and expanding access to global markets.

The Minister of Agriculture and Food Security, Senator Abubakar Kyari, will deliver the keynote address, sharing insights on boosting agricultural productivity and strengthening food systems.

The Governor of Niger State, Mohammed Umar Bago, will deliver a goodwill message.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Participants will also hear from respected industry leaders, including:

• Olasunkanmi Owoyemi, MD/CEO, Sunbeth Global Concepts Limited

• Taiwo Ayoade, Deputy Managing Director, Agro Traders Limited and Plantation Industries Limited

• Sunil Kumar Chauhan, MD/CEO, Dangote Fertiliser Limited

• Ayodele Abioye, MD/CEO, BUA Foods Plc

• Dr. Agboola Zubayr Belgore, MD Amo Byng Nigeria Limited

• Amit Bose, Chief Financial Officer, Valency Agro Nigeria

Interested participants are encouraged to register here

Now in its fifth year, the FirstBank Agric and Export Expo has become a leading platform for promoting collaboration, innovation, and investment across the agriculture and export ecosystem. The conference will explore emerging market opportunities, export financing, value addition, technological innovation, and policy frameworks that can help Nigerian businesses compete globally.

Whether you are a farmer, exporter, agribusiness owner, investor, or entrepreneur, the Expo offers a unique opportunity to gain valuable insights, build partnerships, and discover new growth opportunities.

World.title: From “Coat of Many Colors” to “Colours of My Mind,” By Foster Akpore
World.content:
Dolly Parton once turned a poor child’s “Coat of Many Colors” into a story of dignity… In Egini, Austin Emaduku has given “Colours of My Mind” another meaning by placing books within reach of the community and creating opportunities for young people to engage with literature themselves… One began with a coat made from scraps… The other begins with shelves filled with knowledge…. Both carry a message that deserves to travel far beyond Tennessee and Egini: circumstances may shape where a child starts, but access to education can help determine where that child goes.

There was a remarkable coincidence in Delta State on Tuesday, 25 August.

On the day the world mourned Dolly Parton, the American country music legend whose childhood poverty inspired “Coat of Many Colors” and whose later life became closely associated with childhood literacy, Egini in Udu Local Government Area of Delta State was opening a new chapter of its own.

At the Egini Community Town Hall, Dr Austin Emaduku presented his 275-page book, Colours of My Mind, and formally opened the Egini Community Public Library, a facility he donated to the public to mark his birthday.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

There is no evidence that the two events were connected. Yet the coincidence provides a remarkable opportunity to reflect on the relationship between poverty, books, education and the responsibilities of those who have the means to give back.

Dolly Parton’s “Coat of Many Colors” was born from a childhood experience of poverty. Her mother made her a coat from pieces of discarded cloth. To the outside world, such a coat could have represented deprivation. To the young Dolly, it represented her mother’s love, sacrifice and dignity.

Decades later, that same child who grew up with very little would establish the Imagination Library, a programme that provides free books to young children. Her father’s difficulty with reading and writing helped shape her appreciation of literacy and the opportunities that books can provide.

That journey from “Coat of Many Colors” to the Imagination Library offers a powerful lesson. Poverty can restrict what a child possesses, but it should never be allowed to determine what that child can learn, imagine or become.

It is a lesson that resonates strongly with what Emaduku has done in Egini.

Colours of My Mind is, in many respects, an intellectual record of the author’s engagement with his society. Published by Premium Times Books, the volume contains 69 articles examining contemporary issues affecting Udu, the Urhobo nation, the Niger Delta and Nigeria. Its subjects include politics, governance, culture, religion, human rights and the challenges confronting communities.

Professor GG Darah, one of Nigeria’s respected scholars and literary critics, described Colours of My Mind as a literary masterpiece and encouraged Emaduku to continue producing works that interrogate contemporary issues and stimulate intellectual engagement.

Mr Emmanuel Ogheneochuko Arodovwe of the Department of Philosophy, Delta State University, Abraka, who reviewed the book, described its language as lucid and simple, while noting the depth of the ideas contained in the work. He presented Emaduku as a social commentator whose writings reflect sustained engagement with the realities around him.

But perhaps the most important decision surrounding Colours of My Mind was not what Emaduku wrote in the book. It was what he chose to build around it.

He donated a library to the public.

In his welcome remarks, Emaduku explained that the library was, in his view, the most important part of the ceremony.

He said the journey towards establishing the library began in 2023 during his tenure as President-General of Udu Kingdom, when he provided and fitted the space within one of the rooms of the Egini Community Town Hall with bookshelves and reading pews and stocked it with books. He acknowledged the community leadership and his childhood friends for making the space available, as well as the memory of his late brother.

For Emaduku, the purpose is clear. He wants to revive reading among youths and adults in Egini and other Udu communities, while helping people who, for economic reasons, cannot easily obtain reading materials.

The library has been stocked with 600 books and equipped with a 4.2 KVA solar inverter, providing 24-hour power supply, as well as air conditioning. Emaduku described the facility as an environment designed to provide an escape from distraction and create suitable conditions for reading and research.

He described the library as a “mustard seed,” expressing the hope that it would eventually put Egini and Udu on the world map.

That vision deserves serious attention.

A library cannot, by itself, eliminate poverty. But it can remove one of poverty’s barriers by giving children and young people access to books, knowledge and opportunities to learn.

The Egini project therefore represents more than a philanthropic donation. It is an attempt to create an institution that can continue serving the community long after the opening ceremony has ended.

From Coat of Many Colors to Colours of My Mind

This is where the connection between Dolly Parton’s “Coat of Many Colors” and Emaduku’s Colours of My Mind becomes particularly meaningful.

Dolly’s coat was made from scraps because that was what her family could afford. Yet it became a symbol of love and dignity.

Colours of My Mind is a collection of ideas shaped by years of observation, activism and engagement with society. The Egini library now provides a place where those ideas, along with the works of other writers, can encounter new minds.

One is a story about the colours of a child’s coat.

The other is about the colours of an adult’s mind.

Both remind us that what appears ordinary can carry extraordinary meaning.

Emaduku also explained that the book represents a reflection of his life and interventions on national issues between 2015 and 2023. He described the work as a weaving together of his views, social commentary and fictional writings around the experience of living in community.

He acknowledged several people who encouraged the book’s journey, including Dr Chido Onumah, whom he credited with conceiving the idea of gathering his writings, arranging the articles, reading the manuscript, and introducing him to the publisher.

He also acknowledged Professor Godwin Darah for his encouragement and for accepting to chair the event, saying that having Darah’s name on the cover was an endorsement of considerable value.

The library and the book therefore emerged from the same intellectual conviction: that ideas should be preserved, shared and made available to future generations.

The Book Leaves Egini

The initiative becomes even more encouraging because Colours of My Mind is already travelling beyond Egini.

Nigerian-American writer EC Osondu, an internationally recognised author and professor of English at Providence College, Rhode Island, United States, purchased and donated 10 copies of Colours of My Mind to secondary schools in Urhobo land. The books are expected to be delivered to the benefiting schools through the Chairman of the Association of Local Governments of Nigeria.

That gesture reinforces the principle behind the library. Books should circulate.

They should enter classrooms, libraries and homes. They should be read by students who may agree with the author, question his arguments or find ideas that inspire their own writing.

A book should not end with its launch.

Its journey begins when a reader opens it.

The Same Annual Literary Awards

Emaduku has also taken the literacy project beyond the provision of books by establishing the Salor and Mabel Emaduku Annual Literary Awards, known as the SAME Annual Literary Awards.

The first initiative under the programme will be an essay-writing competition involving secondary schools in Udu and Ughievwen Kingdoms, which Emaduku described as his paternal and maternal kingdoms respectively.

The first prize will be ₦100,000, the second prize ₦60,000, and the third prize ₦40,000.

The grand finale will be held during the anniversary of the Egini Community Library.

This explains the invitation extended to the Chief Inspectors of Education of Udu and Ughelli South Local Government Councils at the event. The competition is intended to become an annual platform connecting schools across the two kingdoms through writing and intellectual engagement.

Emaduku also announced plans for regular literary competitions and debating society competitions among schools in Udu and Ughievwen, under the auspices of the SAME Annual Literary Awards and the library.

This is an important development because a library should not be reduced to a collection of books.

It should become a place where young people read, write, debate, question, research and develop confidence in expressing ideas.

A Book Reading Breakfast could bring children, teachers, parents, writers and community leaders together around selected books. Spelling bee contests could strengthen vocabulary among younger pupils. Quiz competitions could encourage wider reading across history, science, culture and current affairs. Storytelling sessions, poetry readings, young writers’ clubs, debates, holiday reading programmes, career talks, digital literacy classes and meetings with Nigerian authors could further expand the library’s role.

The SAME Annual Literary Awards could eventually provide the framework for many of these activities.

Emaduku said the longer-term ambition is even greater. He hopes that the awards can eventually reach a level where prizes of ₦1 million, $2,000, and more can be offered.

His stated ambition is that when that happens, people from around the world will have reason to come to Egini.

That may sound ambitious, but ambitious institutions often begin with modest foundations.

The 600 books on the shelves today can become thousands.

The ₦200,000 essay prize can grow.

A school competition can become a regional literary event.

A community library can become a centre for research and intellectual activity.

That is how institutions grow.

A Lesson for Other Philanthropists

This is the lesson other philanthropists should learn from Emaduku.

Nigeria does not need every wealthy individual to build a monument bearing his or her name. Communities need institutions that continue to serve people after the donor has moved on.

If individuals who have benefited from education established or supported libraries in their communities, the cumulative effect would be significant.

One community could have a library.

Another could have a reading centre.

Another could renovate an abandoned library.

Another could provide books.

Another could support internet access and computers.

Another could sponsor reading competitions and scholarships.

The result would be a network of community-based educational resources built alongside government schools and public institutions.

The donation of a library is therefore only the beginning.

The greater contribution lies in creating a culture around it.

Let children be encouraged to read.

Let schools compete.

Let young writers be discovered.

Let debates return to schools.

Let communities celebrate intellectual achievement as enthusiastically as they celebrate sporting and social accomplishments.

Let philanthropists understand that a functioning library can become one of the most enduring gifts they leave behind.

The Significance of 25 August

On 25 August, while Dolly Parton’s death was being reported around the world, Egini was opening a library.

There is no documented connection between the two events. But the coincidence allows us to place two stories side-by-side.

One began with a poor child wearing a “Coat of Many Colors” made from scraps.

The other is represented by Colours of My Mind, a book born from years of intellectual engagement and accompanied by a library intended to make knowledge accessible to a community.

Dolly Parton’s story reminds us what can happen when childhood experiences of poverty become a lifelong commitment to literacy.

Emaduku’s story reminds us that philanthropy can move beyond financial assistance and create institutions that expand opportunity.

The two stories meet in one simple idea.

Give people access to books and you give them access to worlds beyond their immediate circumstances.

That is why Emaduku’s initiative deserves more than congratulations.

It deserves replication.

Let philanthropists build libraries in their communities.

Let writers donate books to schools.

Let businesses support reading programmes.

Let traditional institutions encourage young people to read.

Let local governments support community libraries.

Let schools make use of them.

And let initiatives such as the SAME Annual Literary Awards give young readers and writers opportunities to compete, create and be recognised.

Dolly Parton once turned a poor child’s “Coat of Many Colors” into a story of dignity.

In Egini, Austin Emaduku has given Colours of My Mind another meaning by placing books within reach of the community and creating opportunities for young people to engage with literature themselves.

One began with a coat made from scraps.

The other begins with shelves filled with knowledge.

Both carry a message that deserves to travel far beyond Tennessee and Egini: circumstances may shape where a child starts, but access to education can help determine where that child goes.

And if the Egini Community Public Library, the SAME Annual Literary Awards and the first school essay competition inspire other Nigerians to make similar investments, then the most important chapter of Colours of My Mind may not be the one already written.

It may be the chapters that young readers and young writers are yet to write.

Foster Akpore is a media practitioner, media and public relations officer of Orogun Kingdom, and publisher of Oghwoghwa Reporters.

World.title: INEC fixes date for by-elections in four states
World.content:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has fixed 19 September for the conduct of five by-elections in four states: Gombe, Kano, Bauchi and Delta.

The Chief Press Secretary to the INEC Chairman, Tunde Oketola, disclosed this in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Tuesday in Abuja.

Mr Oketola said that the by-elections comprised one federal and four state constituencies.

According to him, the by-elections will take place at the Gombe/Kwami/Funakaye Federal Constituency in Gombe, while the state constituencies shall take place at the Disina and Sakwa State Constituencies in Bauchi State; and at Udu and Dawakin Kudu in the Delta and Kano State Constituencies, respectively.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The seats became vacant for different reasons.

INEC has scheduled the general election for early next year.

While the presidential and National Assembly elections hold on 16 January 2027, the governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections take place on 6 February 2027.

Winners of the 2027 elections will be inaugurated on 29 May.
