“I looked at Linky, she looked at me, and we were like, if it’s good enough for Billie Jean, it’s got to be good enough for us. We’re in!”

Kloss’s role on the WTA board mattered.

“We wanted people to think it wasn’t only for Americans, that it was global. Because I was from Africa, I got put on the board, and it was an unbelievable education. That’s why I tell any young person: understand the business you’re in. If you understand the media, sponsor and tournament director’s role, then you understand why you get paid and what obligation you have to grow the sport.”

Renamed

The venue adds crucial colour to this story.

The USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, a 46.5‑acre complex in Flushing Meadows, was renamed in King’s honour on 28 August 2006, the first major sports venue named after a woman, approved unanimously by the USTA board.

King, who grew up on public courts in Long Beach, called the honour humbling, noting that the venue is a public space open to everyone.

Her legacy sits alongside that of her friend Arthur Ashe, whose name crowns the main stadium.

Its naming wasn’t straightforward.

The USTA first proposed naming one of the three main stadiums after King.

Louis Armstrong Stadium stayed as is, agreed with Armstrong’s wife as a nod to its past life as a music venue.

The main stadium was named for Arthur Ashe in 1997.

So, the USTA offered the third option, the Grandstand court: “They talked about naming the Grandstand court for her, because Louis Armstrong Stadium had to remain Louis Armstrong.”

Turned down the offer

But King turned them down.

Kloss explains: “She said, I do not want a woman at the third court” (the other two bigger stadiums were named after men)”.

King rejected the USTA’s offer, saying that she would rather have nothing. Her point reverberated. As a result, “they ended up naming the entire centre around her. So, you know what? Sometimes you have to be willing to give up something, to potentially get something”.

The interview wraps up with a full‑circle moment.

Kloss is wearing something deeply symbolic. Her striking blue suede shoes are a new limited‑edition Adidas re‑release of the iconic pair King wore during 1973’s ‘Battle of the Sexes’.

Kloss highlights the details: “1973” on the left heel, the match’s set scores on the right heel, Billie Jean King’s signature in gold, and the number “39” stamped on the tongue, marking her total grand slam titles. The shoe was a long time coming: “Stan Smith has one, so how about a woman’s shoe?”

‘Incredibly innovative’

Looking ahead, Kloss is optimistic about the US Open’s new CEO, fellow South African Craig Tiley, as the figure to unlock more from the venue, it’s US Open fortnight.

“He’s incredibly innovative, and will push people to do better,” she said.

“I hope he can unlock some opportunity and access.”

For Kloss, the philosophy that built the WTA and that earned King her name on the gates is the same one she carries home: “You can’t just say it, you have to be it.”

Amisha Savani is reporting exclusively for The South African from the 2026 US Open in Flushing Meadows, New York

World.title: South Africans feel safe by day, but fear crime after dark
World.content:
South Africans generally feel safe walking alone in their neighbourhoods during the day, but that confidence drops sharply after sunset. Image: Wikimedia Commons

South Africans generally feel safe walking alone in their neighbourhoods during the day, but that confidence drops sharply after sunset, according to the latest Statistics South Africa (Stats SA) Governance, Public Safety and Justice Survey (GPSJS).

The 2025/26 survey found that 80.7% of individuals felt safe walking alone in their neighbourhood during the day, down marginally from 81% in 2024/25.

After dark, however, fewer than four in 10 people felt safe walking alone.



Just 37.9% said they felt safe walking alone in their neighbourhood at night, although this represented an improvement from 36.1% the previous year.

The findings highlight how crime continues to influence the way South Africans move around their communities and protect themselves.

Limpopo feels safest

The province with the strongest sense of safety was Limpopo.



According to Stats SA, 98% of individuals in Limpopo said they felt safe walking alone in their neighbourhood during the day, while 69.1% said they felt safe doing so after dark.

The national figures show a much more cautious picture.

The proportion of people who had taken steps to protect themselves against crime increased from 43.3% in 2024/25 to 46.6% in 2025/26.



The most common response was limiting walking to safer hours, reported by 31.5% of individuals.

A further 29.9% said they had installed physical security measures, including burglar doors, to protect themselves against crime.

Housebreaking remains a major threat

At household level, housebreaking or burglary remained the most common crime experienced in 2025/26.



Stats SA estimates that around 1.5 million housebreaking incidents occurred during the year, affecting 5.3% of households nationally.

Male-headed households, households where the head had a post-school qualification, and households in KwaZulu-Natal and the Northern Cape were among those most affected.

Despite the scale of the problem, many cases never reached the police.



Only about 48% of households affected by housebreaking reported the crime, although this was an improvement of 4.8 percentage points from the previous year.

That means more than half of affected households still did not report their experiences to police.

Theft affects millions

For individuals, theft of personal property was the most common personal crime.



Approximately 1.2 million people, or 2.6% of individuals aged 16 and older, experienced personal theft during the year.

There were an estimated 1.4 million incidents.

Western Cape and KwaZulu-Natal recorded higher levels of personal theft, while men were more likely than women to experience it.



Once again, reporting rates remained low.

Almost two-thirds (62.7%) of victims did not report their experience to police, while 37.3% reported some or all of the incidents.

Street robbery was the second most common personal crime, although incidents declined from an estimated 529,000 in 2024/25 to 515,000 in 2025/26.



The proportion of street robbery incidents reported to police increased from 36.4% to 41.7%.

Assault cases increase

Not every crime showed a decline.

The number of individuals who experienced assault rose from 363 000 in 2024/25 to 408 000 in 2025/26.



Men were more likely to experience assault than women, but Stats SA found a significant difference in the relationship between female and male victims and their attackers.

Almost one-third (31.4%) of female assault victims said their perpetrator was a spouse or intimate partner, compared with just 2.2% of male victims.

Knives were the most commonly used weapons in assaults, followed by sticks or clubs.



The Stats SA findings provide a picture of crime that goes beyond police statistics, revealing how crime affects people’s perceptions of safety, daily routines and decisions about whether to report incidents.

For many South Africans, the impact is therefore not limited to becoming a victim of crime. It also determines when they walk, where they go and how heavily they secure their homes.

Out of 10, how safe do you feel walking around your neigbourhood during the day and night?

Let us know by clicking on the comment banner below …

World.title: WEATHER: Where South Africa felt the coldest this past week
World.content:
Cold weather blankets parts of South Africa as a sharp cold snap brings winter-like conditions to several areas. Image: Unsplash

South Africa experienced a sharp return of winter-like conditions last week as a cut-off low brought cold air, rain, snow and severe storms to several parts of the country.

The coldest conditions affected mainly the high-lying interior, where temperatures dropped sharply as the system moved across the country.

The South African Weather Service (SAWS) warned of very cold conditions in places over the eastern interior, particularly the high ground, during the weekend.



High-lying areas bore the brunt of the cold

The Free State, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga and parts of KwaZulu-Natal experienced some of the most noticeable temperature drops during the week.

The cold was particularly pronounced in elevated areas, where temperatures can drop quickly overnight and in the early morning.

By Saturday, SAWS forecast cloudy, windy and cool conditions across the Free State and North West. Mpumalanga would remain cool to cold, with morning fog along the escarpment.



KwaZulu-Natal also saw a marked change, with cold conditions, rain and thunderstorms moving across the province as the weather system shifted eastwards.

A dramatic change from the start of spring

The cold spell arrived just days after the start of meteorological spring on 1 September.

Instead of a widespread warm-up, a cut-off low pushed colder air into the interior and created a mix of rain, thunderstorms and winter-like temperatures.



The system also produced severe weather. By 5 and 6 September, SAWS warnings covered large parts of the Northern Cape, North West, Free State, Gauteng and Mpumalanga, with risks including severe thunderstorms, hail, damaging winds and flooding.

The cold did not affect every province equally

Coastal areas generally experienced milder conditions than the high interior.

The difference is largely linked to elevation. South Africa’s inland plateau sits considerably higher above sea level than the coast, allowing temperatures to fall much lower during cold spells.



That is why places in the interior can experience freezing mornings while coastal areas remain comparatively mild.

Was this South Africa’s coldest province?

There is not enough publicly accessible station data from SAWS for 1–7 September to reliably rank all nine provinces by their lowest recorded temperature.

Rather than naming a province without complete observations, the available evidence points to the high-lying central and eastern interior as the main focus of the week’s cold spell.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE | From GoFundMe to US Open: Yuliia Starodubtseva’s unconventional rise
World.content:
For most aspiring professional tennis players, the road to the top begins early, with junior international tournaments, private coaches and substantial financial backing. Image: Dave Marshall

The path to elite professional tennis is typically rigid and paved from early childhood: specialised academies, junior ITF circuits, private touring coaches, and heavy financial backing.

Ukrainian star Yuliia Starodubtseva, however, shredded that playbook entirely.

Her journey to breaking into the world’s Top 60 and electrifying the grandstands at Flushing Meadows is a story of sheer resilience, crowdsourced faith, and an improbable coaching partnership with deep South African ties.



A Unique Collegiate Foundation

Unlike many of her peers on the WTA Tour, Yuliia Starodubtseva didn’t jump straight into professional competition as a teenager.

Instead, she spent five years at Old Dominion University in the United States, competing in the high-pressure collegiate system while earning a master’s degree in Sports Management.

It was an extended stint made possible partly by an extra eligibility year granted during the Covid-19 pandemic.

“I don’t think that I would ever change my path, the way I went through college,” Starodubtseva reflects.

“The most important part wasn’t even tennis or mental strength but maturing. Taking those five years, being on my own, solving my own problems, and not being around my parents … I felt like I was someone before I entered the tour, you know? I wasn’t just thrown as a kid into the tour, constantly living in hotels, going tournament to tournament, seeing no other life.”

That independence became her bedrock when she transitioned out of college in the summer of 2022.



Balancing an internship with coaching in New York, Yuliia Starodubtseva held vague ambitions of testing the professional waters if she could scrape together sufficient funds.

To stay sharp, she approached a local academy director in New York, asking if she could train alongside the academy’s top junior boys free of charge.

“I asked if I could practice with the boys from the academy. I said, ‘I don’t have much money to pay, but it’ll be good for your boys, and good for me.’ I trained myself with them while still coaching on the side,” she recalls.

The $17 000 Grassroots Miracle

Recognising her immense natural talent and ferocious work ethic, supporters at the academy stepped in with an unexpected lifeline: they launched a GoFundMe campaign, raising approximately $17 000 (around R300 000) from friends and well-wishers to launch her professional career.

That modest grassroots war chest proved transformative.

Deprived of an initial ITF ranking, Yuliia Starodubtseva used the funds to travel to Universal Tennis Rating (UTR) events at the start of 2023, earning wildcards into lower-tier ITF tournaments.

Within just six months, she achieved what many spend years striving for: qualifying for the main draw of the 2023 US Open without having ever played a single WTA main-draw match prior.

Her sudden exposure to the upper echelons of the sport was a baptism by fire.

By early 2024, she had qualified for the Australian Open, drawing former world No 2 Ons Jabeur under the bright lights of Margaret Court Arena.

“I could not see the ball properly,” Starodubtseva laughs, recalling the overwhelming spectacle.

“She came out in her cloak … It was like an entrance! I didn’t even know where to put my bag on court. But you adapt quickly.”

South African Passion & Grand Slam Heartbreak

Behind Yuliia Starodubtseva’s meteoric rise is a distinctive dual-coaching set-up combining South African expertise and Australian flair.

Her coaching team features South African veteran coach Marcel du Coudray alongside her Australian partner and co-coach, Pearse Dolan.

The coaching dynamic brought raw emotional drama to the 2026 US Open during Starodubtseva’s epic second-round victory over former top-10-star Maria Sakkari.

After dropping the opening set 6-1 and facing multiple match points in the second, Starodubtseva staged a heroic fightback.

Battling severe full-body cramping in the decider, to the extent that she was forced to execute a desperation underarm serve at 5-2, she gutted out a memorable 1-6, 7-6 (7/4), 6-2 victory.

The sheer tension of the comeback pushed her South African coach to his emotional limits.

Following the match, Du Coudray was moved to tears in the player box before sprinting off into the facility corridors just to burn off the surging adrenaline.

“He went to do sprints after because he had too much adrenaline in him!” Starodubtseva laughs.

“I didn’t see him crying on court, but somebody told me afterwards. It means so much to have that level of belief around you.”

In her third-round clash against world No 2 Elena Rybakina, Starodubtseva pushed the Wimbledon champion to the absolute brink, serving for the opening set and holding a set point before falling 7-6 (8/6), 6-3.

Despite the defeat, the Ukrainian proved unequivocally that she belongs on tennis’s grandest stages.

Bridging Cultures: Cricket, Rugby, and South African Tennis

Through her work with Du Coudray, Yuliia Starodubtseva has received a crash course in South African sporting culture, a world vastly different from her upbringing in Ukraine.

“Before I met Marcel, I didn’t know much about South Africa,” she admits.

“He told me there aren’t many tennis players from there right now. In Ukraine, tennis was very popular growing up, alongside football. But Marcel is a huge cricket fan! We don’t have that in Ukraine at all.”

While cricket remains a novel puzzle, Starodubtseva has enthusiastically embraced another staple of southern hemisphere sports culture: rugby.

Having attended her first live match in Sydney last year, she was instantly hooked by the physicality. “I really loved it!” she grins. “They smash each other – no pads, no helmets. I love it!”

With racquet sports currently experiencing an unprecedented boom across South Africa, fuelled by the rapid rise of padel and renewed community tennis interest, Starodubtseva hopes her story serves as an encouraging blueprint for young South African talent contemplating the US collegiate route as a stepping stone to professional success.

Perspective Amid Conflict Back Home

Yuliia Starodubtseva’s fighting spirit on court is deeply connected to the harsh reality she faces off it.

Hailing from Nova Kakhovka, a Ukrainian city currently under Russian military occupation, she carries the heavy emotional weight of a homeland torn apart by war.

Her hometown has suffered severe infrastructure destruction and flooding.

While some of her family members remain in the high-risk region, Starodubtseva faces the heartbreaking reality that she may never be able to return to the place where she grew up.

“It’s very dangerous there… I don’t think I’ll ever be able to come back to where I’m from because our houses are not in good condition anymore. It feels like a big part of me is gone, but as long as my family is safe and fine, I take that.”

To preserve her mental focus during major tournaments, she deliberately deletes social media apps to avoid traumatic news cycles before stepping onto court.

Yet, she draws immense inspiration from the stoic resilience of her people, including her grandfather, who unfazedly went fishing right after catastrophic local flooding.

On tour, Starodubtseva has found strong solidarity, building a close friendship with fellow player Daria Kasatkina, who famously renounced her Russian athletic allegiance to represent Australia while speaking out boldly against the conflict.

“I don’t discriminate against people by where they were born,” Starodubtseva emphasises.

“Dasha showed her opinion, she spoke out, and I appreciate that so much. Only a strong, brave person can do that.”

For Yuliia Starodubtseva, tennis is no longer just about rankings or prize money. It is a platform to display hope, determination, and gratitude.

From crowdsourced dollars in New York to emotional South African coaching celebrations and heroic Grand Slam battles, her journey proves that no matter where you start, or what adversity confronts you, grit and heart will always find a way.

Dave Marshall is reporting exclusively from the 2026 US Open in New York for The South African.

World.title: GBVF national disaster: What’s changed so far?
World.content:
Women For Change says South Africa still lacks a clear implementation plan nearly ten months after GBVF was declared a national disaster: Image Instagram @womenforchangesa

Ten months ago, South Africa reached a milestone that took over a million signatures to achieve.

Today, the organisation behind that petition says it’s time to ask an uncomfortable question about what’s actually followed.

Women For Change fought for this classification, and the government announced it on 20 November 2025, after their petition gathered more than 1.1 million signatures.



how the classification came about

President Cyril Ramaphosa announced the decision at the G20 Social Summit, following the “G20 Women’s Shutdown”campaign.

That announcement followed a wave of nationwide protests.

There, demonstrators lay down in silence for 15 minutes to honour the estimated 15 women murdered daily in South Africa.

Bongani Sithole, head of the National Disaster Management Centre, made the formal classification after reviewing reports from government and civil society.

Those reports showed the ongoing violence met the legal definition of a national disaster.

The classification aimed to unlock emergency funding and drive a more coordinated national response.



It also aimed to redirect government budgets toward implementing the long-standing Emergency Response Action Plan on GBV and Femicide, first introduced back in 2019.

what Women For Change says is still missing

In a recent statement, Women For Change said South Africans still don’t have a clear, publicly accessible, costed implementation plan.

They want to know what will actually be done, by when, by whom, with what budget, and against which measurable targets.

The organisation asked pointedly where the dedicated funding for the disaster response actually is.

They also asked where the transparent allocations for the National Strategic Plan on GBVF have gone.

The group didn’t stop there.

They also pointed to the timing of two new commemorative R2 coins that entered circulation during Women’s Month.

One honours Charlotte Maxeke, the first Black South African woman to earn a university degree.

The other marks the more than 20,000 women who marched to the Union Buildings in 1956.

Women For Change said that recognition matters.

But they called it a painful irony to honour revolutionary women on currency while women today are still fighting for meaningful action against the violence killing them.

Their message was blunt: classification was never meant to be the finish line.

It was only the starting point, and a national disaster cannot exist only on paper.

But in my opinion, “irony” is the perfect word for it.

A R2 coin doesn’t fix the issue at hand, it feels more like a distraction for a minute, while the bare minimum has actually been done since the announcement. And South African women simply aren’t standing for the bare minimum anymore. We demand actual change.

Do you think enough has changed since the classification was announced?

Let us know in the comments below…

World.title: Friday’s New Moon: What it means for coastal tides
World.content:
South Africans heading to the coast on Friday should take note of the stronger spring tides linked to the New Moon. Image: Unsplash

The New Moon arriving on Friday will not only bring darker skies for stargazers. It will also affect the tides along South Africa’s coastline.

As the Sun and Moon broadly align with Earth during the New Moon, their gravitational effects work together to produce a greater difference between high and low tides. Popularily known as the Spring tide

The Moon has a bigger effect on tides because it is much closer to Earth. Although the Sun has stronger gravity, its greater distance means it has a weaker effect on the tides.



Why the New Moon affects tides

Tides are not simply caused by the Moon and Sun pulling the oceans upwards. They result from differences in the strength of their gravitational pull across Earth.

The Moon’s close distance to Earth means its gravitational pull changes more noticeably across the planet. These differences create the tidal forces that cause ocean levels to rise and fall.

During a New Moon, the Sun and Moon are broadly aligned with Earth. Their tidal forces then combine, increasing the difference between high and low tide.



The same effect occurs around a Full Moon.

What is a spring tide?

A spring tide means there is a larger tidal range. Higher high tides and lower low tides than usual.

Spring tides have nothing to do with the spring season. The name describes the stronger tidal range that occurs around the New and Full Moon phases.



People living along or visiting South Africa’s coastline can check local tide times before heading to the beach, fishing, boating or taking part in other activities near the water.

World.title: The hidden tech problem South African businesses should not ignore
World.content:
The Bio-Oil distributor app shows why maintaining and modernising business-critical technology is becoming as important as launching it. Image: Bio Oil website

As South African companies look to get more value from existing digital investments, the Bio-Oil distributor app shows why maintaining and modernising business-critical technology is becoming as important as launching it.

A business app can look perfectly fine on the outside while becoming increasingly difficult, risky and expensive to maintain behind the scenes.

Need to pay attention to

It is the less glamorous side of digital transformation, and one more South African businesses may need to pay attention to.



The issue is not always about launching a shiny new app or introducing the latest platform.

Sometimes, the bigger challenge is keeping an existing digital product alive, secure and useful long after launch day has passed.

Bio-Oil, the skincare brand owned by Union Swiss, offers a useful example.

The brand, which recently celebrated its 39th anniversary, is sold across markets around the world and supported by a large distributor network.

To help keep those distributors connected to company updates, marketing activity, product information and performance data, Union Swiss uses a mobile application developed in partnership with Bluegrass Digital.

But the interesting part is not simply that the company has an app. Plenty of businesses do. The more important question is what happens when that app becomes embedded in the way a business actually runs.



When an app becomes business infrastructure

The Bio-Oil distributor app started with a simple idea: create a more modern way to communicate with distributors across 163 countries.

The concept was initially inspired by the familiarity of Instagram, giving distributors a way to access brand content, view updates, and share images and videos of local marketing activity.

In plain English, it gave different markets a way to see what was happening elsewhere and learn from each other.

Over time, the app’s role changed. It moved from being a more open, social-style engagement platform to a structured communication channel, with selected Union Swiss team members publishing updates directly to the wider distributor network.

That shift matters because it shows how digital tools often evolve in real business environments: what starts as a communication tool can become part of daily operations.

And once that happens, the stakes change. If an app is used to share company updates, campaign information, business performance and market activity, it is no longer a “nice-to-have” digital extra. It becomes part of the operating rhythm of the business.

The critical work that keeps digital products alive

Here is where many businesses get caught out: digital products age. Mobile operating systems change, frameworks are updated, security requirements shift, and new devices and media formats create new demands. What worked well five years ago may still function, but it may no longer be easy or safe to improve.

That was one of the risks identified by Dawie Pritchard, Development Team Lead at Bluegrass Digital, when he joined the Bio-Oil project.

According to Pritchard, the issue was not simply a single broken feature. The greater risk was that the platform had become harder and more expensive to evolve.

“The real risk was not one broken feature, but a system that had become expensive to evolve,” he said.

That is a line many South African businesses should sit with, because ageing technology rarely announces itself dramatically.

It often shows up as slower releases, higher maintenance costs, more fragile updates and nervousness every time a change needs to be made.

What had to change behind the scenes

The modernisation work on the Bio-Oil app included a move to Expo’s Continuous Native Generation approach.

For non-developers, that means changing how the app’s underlying mobile code is managed, reducing complexity and making future updates easier to handle. This was not a small tweak.

The work touched more than a hundred native files and required the team to replace or rework major integrations connected to camera functionality, file systems, permissions, splash screens, background tasks, configuration and image tooling.

In other words, the parts of the app most users never see had to be reorganised so the product could keep serving the business.

Bluegrass also continued upgrading React Native, improving automated testing and strengthening release processes.

It may not sound exciting. It is not supposed to.

But this is the kind of work that helps prevent useful digital products from becoming expensive liabilities.

Why performance still matters

The team also focused on the parts of the app that distributors use most often.

The platform’s feed and media functionality sit at the centre of the user experience, with distributors consuming posts, images, videos, company news and marketing information through these areas.

Improving feed rendering, list performance and media playback may not make for a flashy product announcement, but it can have a meaningful impact on the people using the app.

Anyone who has dealt with a slow internal system, clunky app or unreliable portal knows the problem.

If the tool is frustrating, people use it less. If they use it less, the business loses the value it expected to get from the technology in the first place.

The work also included improvements to monitoring and logging, giving the team better visibility into how the app performs and where issues may appear.

Database architecture, cloud infrastructure and security were reviewed and optimised as part of the broader effort to improve maintainability and manage operational costs.

Again, none of this is the kind of work that usually grabs headlines. But it is exactly the kind of work that determines whether a digital product remains useful.

What South African businesses can take from this

For South African companies, the lesson is not that every business needs a global distributor app. The more useful takeaway is simpler: digital products need maintenance strategies, not just launch plans.

Many businesses have invested heavily in websites, apps, portals, ecommerce platforms, customer systems and internal tools.

Some of those platforms now sit at the centre of how teams sell, communicate, report, support customers or manage operations.

But if those platforms are not modernised over time, the cost of change can creep up quietly.

That can leave businesses stuck with systems that still work, but are slow to update, expensive to maintain and difficult to adapt when the market changes.

In a South African context, where many companies are under pressure to do more with tighter budgets, that matters.

The less visible work of modernising, testing, simplifying and securing digital platforms may be one of the more practical ways to protect earlier technology investments.

The real story is not the app

Bio-Oil’s distributor platform is still doing what it was meant to do: helping Union Swiss communicate with distributors across markets and share company, marketing and performance information.

But the broader story is not just about one app or one brand. It is about what happens once digital tools become woven into the way a business operates.

Launch day may get the attention. The real test comes years later, when the platform still needs to work, still needs to adapt, and still needs to support the people relying on it.

For businesses sitting on ageing apps, portals or digital platforms, that may be the uncomfortable question worth asking now: is your technology still helping the business move, or has it quietly become the thing slowing it down?

World.title: All Blacks to make a big change at flyhalf?
World.content:
Despite the fact that the All Blacks trail 2-1 in the series against the Springboks, coach Dave Rennie is expected to stick to the plan of making several changes to the team for this Saturday’s fourth and final Test.

At flyhalf, Ruben Love – who has played six matches (including all five Tests) this year – is expected to make way after an indifferent showing last weekend at the FNB Stadium.

It could quite possibly open the door for a sensational comeback for Richie Mo’unga, who has not played a Test match for the All Blacks since the 2023 World Cup final against the Springboks, having decided to ply his trade in Japan after that tournament.



New Zealand Rugby have a strict policy whereby overseas-based players will not be eligible for the All Blacks, but Mo’unga recently became available for selection again after playing for Canterbury against Auckland in the NPC on 1 August.

The 32-year-old was only recently called up to the All Blacks’ touring squad as an injury replacement, and he featured in the midweek game against the Lions.

“We sort of always thought we would make changes in the fourth Test regardless of whether we won that third one or not,” Rennie commented after the last Test.



“We want to make sure we are bringing in guys with plenty of energy and sharing the workload. Obviously with three key players missing, it alters that thinking as well. But what we know is we will have a highly motivated 23 guys stripping at the weekend.”

All Blacks have endured injury woes

In reference to the unavailable players, three players have been ruled out after picking up injuries in the third Test against the Springboks. Ardie Savea has a dislocated shoulder; Quinn Tupaea suffered a MCL (knee) injury and Luke Jacobson has injured a tendon in his elbow.

Together with these three players, an additional six players have also returned to New Zealand: Josh Jacomb, Siale Lauaki, Saula Ma’u, Cortez Ratima, Bradley Slater and Ofa Tu’ungafasi.



New Zealand squad for the final Test

Forwards: Asafo Aumua, Codie Taylor, Samisoni Taukei’aho, Ethan De Groot, Tyrel Lomax, Fletcher Newell, Pasilio Tosi, George Bower, Xavier Numia, Jamie Hannah, Sam Darry, Josh Lord, Patrick Tuipulotu, Fabian Holland, Tupou Vaa’i, Simon Parker, Wallace Sititi, Peter Lakai, Ethan Blackadder, Semisi Ta’eiloa.

Backs: Cam Roigard, Kyle Preston, Noah Hotham, Beauden Barrett, Ruben Love, Richie Mo’unga, Jordie Barrett, Anton Lienert-Brown, Timoci Tavatavanawai, Fehi Fineanganofo, Leroy Carter, Emoni Narawa, Rieko Ioane, Josh Moorby, Will Jordan, Damian McKenzie.

World.title: LIVESTREAM | IMC gives update on repatriations
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration is providing an update on the country’s repatriation and deportation efforts.

The committee was established by President Cyril Ramaphosa to strengthen coordination on migration-related matters and oversee interventions announced in his State of the Nation Address.

READ | Four injured during March and March protest

More than 77,000 undocumented foreign nationals have been repatriated since the beginning of the year, according to government figures.

The latest update is expected to provide further details on the progress of repatriations and deportations, as government steps up efforts to manage undocumented migration.

World.title: Kruger on alert for extreme weather as drought looms
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Kruger National Park is preparing for another extreme weather threat, just months after devastating floods forced the evacuation of parts of the park.

Authorities are now bracing for a potentially severe drought, with a strong El Niño weather pattern expected to bring challenging conditions this summer.

The park is still rebuilding key infrastructure damaged by the January floods, including the Letaba bridge.

SANParks says it is now having to prepare for increasingly unpredictable weather while balancing the needs of tourists, staff and wildlife.

World.title: SA cherries get green light for export to China
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - It's a cherry-on-top moment for South African farmers.

Local producers have won access to China's lucrative market.

South African cherries are set to enter the country for the first time after Agriculture Minister Wille Aucamp signed an agreement in Beijing.

China is the world's largest cherry importer, bringing in more than $3.3-billion worth last year.

Government says the agreement will create new export opportunities, boost investment in the sector and support around 600 jobs.

The deal is part of broader efforts to deepen agricultural trade with China, with market access talks for South African blueberries also at an advanced stage.

World.title: POPCRU blames Rooigrond prison infrastructure for inmate escape
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Rooigrond Maximum Security Correctional Centre’s infrastructure, rather than staff inefficiencies, may have contributed to an inmate’s escape.

This is according to the Police and Prisons Civil Rights Union (POPCRU).

The union’s comments come after the Department of Correctional Services (DCS) served eight officials at the facility near Mahikeng with notices of contemplation of suspension following the escape of an inmate.

Edward Khomotso Madiba escaped from the facility on 6 September.

He is serving a 20-year sentence for robbery, possession of a firearm and ammunition, kidnapping and parole violations.

According to DCS, Madiba was being held in the single cells on a further charge relating to a previous escape when he managed to break out of the correctional centre.

DCS spokesperson Singabakho Nxumalo says preliminary information indicates that Madiba cut through the burglar-bar door of the single cells.

Nxumalo says security measures have been activated and officials are working with other law enforcement agencies to locate and apprehend Madiba.

“All necessary measures are being implemented to ensure that Madiba is traced and brought back to custody,” says Nxumalo.

But POPCRU North West secretary Johannesburg Dire says the facility has been in a poor state for a long time, making it easier for inmates to escape.

He says previous escapes have also been investigated, with findings indicating that some were linked to infrastructure problems rather than human error.

“There is a possibility that he could have escaped from the dilapidated parts of the facility,” says Dire.

Dire says that while an inmate may be able to escape from a cell, they would still have to pass through an entrance where an official should prevent them from going further.

If an inmate manages to leave the building, they should then be visible to officers stationed in watchtowers around the facility.

However, Dire claims some of the watchtowers are currently unmanned because of infrastructure problems.

He says an inmate would then have to breach the facility’s perimeter fencing, which is supposed to prevent them from leaving the premises.

Dire says all investigations should be completed before DCS reaches conclusions about the circumstances surrounding the escape.

World.title: 'The ber months': Christmas arrives early in the Philippines
World.content:
MANILA - At a city block-sized market in the Philippine capital, a platoon of plastic Santa Claus figures parachute from the ceiling of a shop already stacked high with Christmas decor despite the holiday being fully four months away.

The site is a familiar one in the Philippines, where September 1 means radio stations playing Christmas carols, homeowners putting up lights, and the country's giant shopping malls unleashing their most impressive displays.

Welcome to the "ber months" -- September, October, November, December -- a months-long countdown to the most anticipated holiday on the calendar in the deeply Catholic country.

"We can smell it coming," sales clerk Cora Lansangan, 73, said during an AFP visit to a Christmas shop that began stacking its shelves on July 31.

The store was already packed with shoppers buzzing around displays of Christmas trees, ornaments, plastic reindeer, mangers and festive lanterns during a recent AFP visit.

World.title: Mongolians wait hours for fuel as reliance on Russia bites
World.content:
ULAANBAATAR - After a five-hour wait for petrol, Mongolian pensioner Nasanjargal is still 10 places from the pump, with dozens of cars behind him in a queue snaking into the arid steppe.

"Fuel is unavailable, there are huge queues everywhere," he told AFP from his motionless Toyota sedan after a one-and-a-half-hour drive from the capital Ulaanbaatar.

Sandwiched between Russia and China, landlocked Mongolia has historically imported more than 95 percent of its petrol from its vast northern neighbour.

But Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities have disrupted supplies in recent months, triggering a relentless fuel shortage that has depleted Mongolia's limited stockpiles and raised questions about its energy security.

The shortages have roiled logistics, lifted costs and ruined the plans of many Mongolians accustomed to taking advantage of the short summer season with a road trip in the picturesque countryside.

Nasanjargal, a former police officer who goes by one name, said he was "out of options".

"I headed out this way hoping things might be better out in the rural areas," he said, his young granddaughter shifting impatiently in the back seat.

"It's the same story everywhere."

World.title: Panama Canal considering more cuts in transits due to El Nino
World.content:
PANAMA CITY - The number of ships sailing through the Panama Canal could be cut further due to drought caused by the El Nino weather pattern, the new administrator of the waterway told AFP on Monday.

Panama has declared a nationwide emergency over El Nino, a phenomenon developing over the Pacific Ocean that is affecting worldwide weather patterns and pushing up global temperatures.

This year's El Nino is expected to be the strongest since record-keeping began four decades ago.

Panama's restrictions come even as use of the canal has risen: shippers are seeking an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has blocked in retaliation for the war launched by the United States and Israel.

The interoceanic Panama Canal -- which handles five percent of global maritime trade -- has already reduced the maximum number of ships allowed through daily, from 36 last month to 32 by mid-September.

It operates using rainwater that collects in two reservoirs, whose levels have dropped due to the onset of El Nino.

Without water, the locks that lift and lower ships at the start and end of their crossing cannot function.

Ilya Espino de Marotta, who took over as head of the Panama Canal Authority on Monday, told AFP that further measures may be implemented if the drought does not subside.

"We do not rule out the possibility that in February or March we may have to lower the limit -- probably not to 24 slots per day, but it could be reduced to 29 or something similar," she said.

- 200mn litres per ship -

Each ship requires about 200 million litres of water, which is then discharged into the sea.

In 2023, El Nino forced a reduction in daily transits from 38 to 22 due to the dramatic reduction in reservoir levels.

Espino de Marotta, the first woman ever to head the US-built canal authority, stated, however, that she does not expect restrictions to reach the levels seen that year.

Apart from reducing the number of vessels, canal authorities have also reduced their maximum draft, from 15.2 meters to 14.6 meters (50 feet to 48 feet).

The draft is the vertical distance between the waterline and the lowest point of a ship's hull. It is a measure of how much water is needed for a ship to float safely without running aground.

Experts have warned that long-term restrictions on canal crossings could lead to higher shipping costs and longer waiting times for deliveries.

The United States and China are the main users of the canal, which is the fastest maritime route between the east coast of the United States and China.

The canal connecting the Atlantic and Pacific handles around 40 percent of US container traffic.

The Iran war has pushed up traffic through the channel.

With shipping at a standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for a fifth of the world's oil and gas, the Panama Canal has become a fallback route for energy shipments.

World.title: Third absence for injured Hadjar as Lawson fills in again in Spain
World.content:
MADRID - Isack Hadjar, who has missed the last two Grand Prix with a wrist injury, will again be absent from this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, his Red Bull team announced.

The young Frenchman will again be replaced by New Zealander Liam Lawson, who will line up alongside Max Verstappen.

Lawson's seat in the Racing Bulls will be filled for the third race in a row by Japanese driver Yuki Tsunoda.

"After racing for the team in Zandvoort and Monza, Liam will continue to drive alongside Max at this week's Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid," Red Bull said in a statement.

"The decision has been taken as Isack's recovery continues to progress positively. While he is not yet ready to return to the cockpit, he will be in Madrid supporting the team."

Hadjar, who turns 22 at the end of the month, injured his left wrist during a training session over the summer break.

He currently sits eighth in the world championship with 71 points, making the podium at the Monaco GP.

Lawson finished seventh at Zandvoort but could manage only 14th on Sunday at Monza.

World.title: You have 90 days: State walks back snap order on foreign traders
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Burundian nationals in Kenya at their embassy of the republic of Burundi chancery at Dennis Pritt road on September 8, 2026 [David Gichuru, Standard]

Kenya has extended a five-day shutdown order against foreign small-scale traders to a 90-day window to regularise their immigration status, work permits, business registration and licensing.

State House Spokesperson Hussein Mohamed announced the extension in a statement on Tuesday, a day after the Government's original deadline lapsed and amid panic among foreign traders, particularly Burundians who queued at their embassy in Nairobi for travel documents.

President William Ruto had, on September 2, ordered foreign nationals in hawking and small-scale retail to shut their businesses from September 7, arguing they should not compete with Kenyan traders.

The order triggered business closures and reports of harassment in parts of the country.

Under the revised approach, government agencies will guide affected foreign nationals and administer the requirements fairly and consistently over the 90 days, according to Tuesday's statement.

"At the conclusion of the 90-day regularisation period, immigration, work permit, registration and licensing requirements will be enforced firmly and strictly in accordance with the law and due process," noted Mohamed.

The Government said it would continue protecting foreigners who are lawfully resident, employed, investing or conducting business in Kenya.

"Kenya will protect economic opportunities for its citizens, especially within the micro and small-enterprise sector, while remaining open to lawful foreign investment, enterprise and employment," the statement said.

Officials have directed that the Local Content Bill, 2025, currently before Parliament, be expanded to establish a framework governing participation in small-scale trade.

The Bill, which Ruto linked to the original crackdown, proposes that foreign firms source most of their goods, services and staff locally.

"No individual or group has the authority to harass, intimidate, threaten or interfere with foreign nationals or their businesses. Any person engaged in such conduct will face firm action in accordance with the law," explained Mohamed.

Opposition leader Kalonzo Musyoka had criticised the original order as chaotic, pointing to scenes outside the Burundian Embassy as evidence of poor planning.

The Government reaffirmed Kenya's commitment to the East African Community and regional integration.

"We will continue to facilitate the movement of people, labour, services and capital in accordance with applicable legal and regulatory frameworks," the statement said.

"Legitimate concerns about economic opportunities can never justify discrimination, excuse lawlessness or sanction violence. Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country," Mohamed added.

World.title: Centum taps insider as Mworia exits after nearly two decades
World.content:
Centum Investment Company PLC acting Group Chief Executive Thomas Omondi-Achola. [Courtesy]

Centum Investment Company PLC has appointed Thomas Omondi-Achola as acting group chief executive, tapping an internal candidate to succeed long-serving CEO James Mworia, who is leaving to head Kenya’s newly established National Infrastructure Fund (NIF).

The transition, effective immediately, marks the end of an 18-year tenure during which Mworia transformed Centum from a small investment firm into East Africa’s largest diversified investment platform, the company said in a statement.

World.title: Ruto: Kenya to end raw mineral exports
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during a thanksgiving service in South Horr, Samburu County on September 6, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto says Kenya will no longer allow its mineral wealth to leave the country in raw form, coming days after the controversial saga surrounding Tata Chemicals’ operations at Lake Magadi.

Ruto defended the government’s decision to suspend Tata Chemicals’ operations at Lake Magadi, Kajiado County, arguing that Kenya has not been receiving sufficient value from the natural resource and that more investors should be given an opportunity to develop the area.

“We want to give five, six or even 10 companies an opportunity to use the resources there to create jobs, value, create wealth and reduce poverty,” Ruto said.

The President made the remarks during a thanksgiving service in South Horr, Samburu County, on Sunday, where he announced a broader government policy aimed at shifting Kenya from exporting raw materials to processing them locally.

“Going into the future, our position as the government. Whether we are talking about Magadi Soda or oil or all our minerals, we have taken the decision that we will no longer export raw materials,” Ruto said.

“We are going to process all minerals available in Kenya.”

The declaration puts the long-running Lake Magadi dispute at the centre of a much wider economic strategy.

Tata Chemicals has been associated with soda ash production at the lake for more than a century. Its Kenyan operations trace their history to 1911, when the Magadi Soda Company began extracting trona from Lake Magadi.

Operations were suspended on July 28, 2026, following a directive from the Ministry of Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs over compliance and licensing issues.

Ruto has argued that the resource should generate greater benefits for Kenyans through expanded investment, job creation and local value addition.

He accused the existing model of allowing valuable resources to leave the country while Kenya receives less economic benefit than it could.

The President’s comments reflect a longstanding challenge facing Kenya’s extractive sector: how to turn mineral deposits into manufacturing opportunities rather than simply exporting commodities.

Under the proposed approach, minerals such as gold, limestone, iron ore, graphite, titanium and soda ash would be processed or refined in Kenya before being exported.

The government says this would create industrial jobs, strengthen local supply chains and increase the value of exports.

Ruto cited planned cooperation with Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote as an example of the investment model the government wants to pursue.

He said talks were underway to establish an oil refinery and petrochemical complex in Lamu, alongside efforts to attract investors into mineral refining.

“It is imprudent for any government to export raw materials, create jobs and value in other countries while we have a big population of young people who need jobs,” Ruto said.

World.title: Sifuna condemns abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Busia County Senator Okiya Omtata, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, Bumula MP Jack Wamboka during the burial service of Mary Gorreti Okiya at Kabula, in Bumula on September 5,2026. [Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has declared that the fight to restore democracy, media freedom and the rule of law following the abduction of Standard Group Senior Editor will form the centrepiece of the Linda Mwananchi government vowing to defeat President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election.

Sifuna accused President Ruto’s administration of undermining constitutional freedoms and creating an atmosphere of fear, saying the country must be returned to what he described as “the rail of the six important values” enshrined in the Constitution.

Speaking in Bumula Constituency, Kakamega County during the burial of Mary Goreti, the sister of Busia Senator Okiya Omtatah, Sifuna strongly condemned the abduction and arrest of a Standard Group Associate Editor, Alex Kiprotich, arguing that journalists must be protected if Kenya is to remain a democratic country.

“It is impossible that you are driving on the road and you are taken away the way the way the Standard Group Journaliat and Editor Alex Kiprotich was taken. Kenyans want to live in a free country. We do not want to live in fear,” said Sifuna.

He questioned the circumstances surrounding the incident and accused the Government of failing to protect media freedom, adding that the Linda Mwananchi movement would seek to restore institutions and constitutional safeguards if elected to power, arguing that democracy could not survive where citizens, journalists and political opponents lived in fear.

"You cannot just arrest a senior journalist in the middle of the road with police carrying firearms, then you dump him some 500kilometres near the dam, a country cannot have democracy if media is not being respected and allowed to do it's work as per the constitution," said Sifuna.

He said the movement’s agenda was not merely about removing the current administration from power but it's main plan is rebuilding systems of governance around constitutionalism, democracy, individual freedoms and the rule of law.

“With less than 11 months remaining, we want to tell Kenyans that our entire plan is to return this country to the rails of the six important values contained in our Constitution, including democracy, freedom of citizens and the rule of law,” said Sifuna.

Sifuna also accused the Government of using threats against political opponents, saying leaders should not threaten citizens with arrest, expulsion or other forms of intimidation.

He challenged religious leaders to remind politicians that the power to determine the length of a person's life belongs to God.

Sifuna further linked the rule of law to economic growth, warning that investors would be reluctant to establish businesses in Kenya if government could arbitrarily order them to leave.

He said Kenya could not rely on government alone to create employment for millions of young people, arguing that the country needed both local and foreign investors.

“No investor can bring his project to a country where he can wake up one day and the President tells him, ‘Pack and go.’ It is impossible,” Sifuna said.

He argued that investor confidence was also affected by the possibility of commercial disputes being referred to foreign jurisdictions because investors lacked confidence in Kenya’s legal system.

Sifuna also criticised the government over the ongoing nurses and midwives strike, saying the rule of law required the State to honour agreements signed with workers.

World.title: Murkomen reaffirms IG Kanja's command of National Police Service
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has reaffirmed that the Inspector General of Police retains constitutional command of the National Police Service, saying the government will continue to respect the independence of the office.

Speaking during the passing-out parade of new Administration Police recruits in Nairobi, Murkomen said the Inspector General has authority over key operational matters within the service, including investigations, promotions and deployment of officers.

“Your Excellency, the Inspector General of Police retains the command of the National Police Service, especially on matters of investigation, promotion and deployment of officers without interference from anyone, including the Cabinet Secretary. We will continue respecting Article 245 of the Constitution,” Murkomen said.

His remarks come amid public debate over the relationship between the Interior Ministry and the National Police Service, particularly allegations that political leaders sometimes issue direct instructions to police officers.

Murkomen dismissed criticism directed at the office of the Inspector General, describing some of its proponents as tribalists and propagandists. He maintained that the Inspector General is carrying out his responsibilities and said he had confidence in the leadership of the police service.

“I have full faith in the IG and believe that every act that is done by the National Police Service is guided by the Constitution,” he said.

The Cabinet Secretary also addressed concerns over his role in directing the police, saying that his responsibility is primarily to provide policy direction rather than interfere with the operational command of the service.

“When required to give policy direction, I always give it in writing and we will continue to support the independence of the National Police Service from external interference,” Murkomen said.

During the ceremony, Murkomen also cautioned the newly graduated officers against corruption, excessive alcohol consumption and conduct that could undermine the reputation of the police service.

He urged the recruits to uphold discipline and protect the dignity of the police uniform, noting that the respect they receive from members of the public would depend largely on their conduct.

The Cabinet Secretary encouraged the officers to understand the responsibility that comes with joining the National Police Service and to discharge their duties within the confines of the Constitution and the law.

The passing-out ceremony marked the entry of the new recruits into the police service that made the CS use the occasion to emphasize professional conduct and respect for the constitutional framework governing policing in Kenya.

World.title: Ruto assures Kajiado residents of full control of Amboseli National Park
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto inspects the Rombo Clusters Irrigation Development Project in Kajiado County on September 3, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

President William Ruto has assured Kajiado residents that they will soon have full control of the management of Amboseli National Park, following his decision to return the park to the county in November 2025.

However, he said the transfer has been temporarily halted by the court.

The President hit out at those he accused of frustrating the move, saying they will be in for a rude shock.

“They took us to court over the Social Health Authority and the Affordable Housing Programme, but these programmes are progressing well. Similarly, I want to assure the people of Kajiado that, before the end of this year, Amboseli will be fully in the hands of Kajiado County,” he said.

Speaking in Kajiado County on Thursday during his development tour, President Ruto reiterated that he will not relent in his pursuit of equity and inclusive development across Kenya, saying that longstanding inequalities have unduly benefited certain regions at the expense of others.

He revealed that the securitisation of the Road Maintenance Levy Fund and the Sports Fund has enabled the Government to clear pending bills in the roads sector and construct 6,000km of new roads, and accelerate the construction of 32 new stadia across the country.

"The Road Maintenance Levy Fund was misused to only build roads in some parts of the country. Those opposing securitisation are unhappy that we are advancing equity," he said.

The President began his tour at Oloirien in Kajiado South Constituency by inspecting progress of the 67km Illasit-Rombo-Chala-Njukini-Taveta road, which is 48 per cent completed.

The Sh9.4 billion project will cut travel time between Kajiado and Taita-Taveta counties from two hours to just 40 minutes, thus easing the movement of goods and people.

The Head of State announced that eight new roads of 220km are being built across Kajiado County at a cost of Sh13 billion to open up the region and improve transport.

The President commissioned Sh221 million Rombo Clusters Irrigation Development Project, which is expected to enhance livelihoods and boost irrigation in the area.

He also inspected progress of the Sh2.2 billion Loitoktok Affordable Housing Project, and laid the foundation stone for the Sh220 million Loitoktok Kenya Medical Training College student hostels with a 580-bed capacity.

At Kimana, in Kajiado South Constituency, President Ruto commissioned the Sh2.7 billion Sultan Hamud-Loitoktok 132kV Transmission Line and Loitoktok Sub-Station, which will serve the residents of Kajiado South and parts of Makueni County.

He inspected construction of the Kimana modern market, which is aimed at giving traders dignified working environment.

At Namanga, Kajiado Central Constituency, the President commissioned the Namanga Sub-Station, a project of the Kenya Electricity Transmission Company (KETRACO), which is part of the 132KV Machakos- Konza-Isinya-Namanga Transmission Project.

Namanga Modern Market, which is under construction at a cost of Sh50 million, will benefit 120 traders at the border town.

In Kajiado town, the President toured the construction of the Kajiado Affordable Housing Project, a Sh473 million investment that will deliver 196 housing units, as well as the 100-unit police housing project at a cost of Sh137 million.

He also inspected the progress of the 580-bed student hostels at Maasai National Polytechnic, which is being built at a cost of KSh216 million.

Ruto ordered the closer of Tata Chemicals, saying the government will identify a new and responsible investor to take over soda ash mining operations at Lake Magadi.

The President said Tata Chemicals had failed to adequately modernise the plant, create sufficient employment opportunities for residents, and deliver meaningful economic benefits to the people of Kenya.

“It is unfair for one company to dominate the ownership and operations of Magadi Soda for years, yet it has done little to improve the factory or create employment opportunities for our youth,” he said at Rombo in Kajiado South Constituency.

He added: “Because they have been unable to do anything meaningful with the plant for more than 100 years, I have directed them to pack up and go.”

The Ministry of Mining suspended the company’s mining operations in July 2026 over concerns relating to regulatory compliance, value addition and licensing.

The ministry also ordered the closure of the company’s depot in Kajiado Town for contravening environmental regulations.

In addition, the company has been unable to reach an agreement with the Kajiado County Government over a land rates dispute following the expiry of its operating licence in 2023.

The plant produces soda ash, or sodium carbonate, a key industrial mineral used in the manufacture of glass, soap and laundry detergents, among other products.

Despite being Africa’s largest soda ash producer, President Ruto noted that the operation had not delivered commensurate benefits to Kenyans over its more than 100-year history, particularly because much of the soda ash produced is exported for processing and consumption in overseas markets.

The Government, the President said, would therefore prioritise an investor capable of modernising the facility, expanding local value addition, creating jobs for young people, and ensuring that Kenya derives greater economic value from its natural resources.

World.title: IG Kanja orders probe into abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Standard Group PLC Associate Editor Alex Kiprotich. [Stafford Ondego, Standard]

The Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja has ordered immediate and transparent investigations into the alleged abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor Alex Kiprotich in Gilgil.

The National Police Service (NPS) said it had taken note of reports that Kiprotich was allegedly kidnapped on Tuesday and had moved swiftly to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

NPS spokesperson Muchiri Nyaga said the police service treats kidnapping and abduction with the utmost seriousness, describing the offences as a threat to the lives, liberty and security of Kenyans.

“The Inspector General of Police has accordingly ordered immediate investigations to determine what transpired, including the identity of the heavily armed individuals reportedly seen ordering occupants out of their vehicle,” Nyaga said in a statement.

The NPS said its Anti-Abduction Unit, established to investigate abductions and disappearances, had taken up the matter and would work to ensure that those responsible are brought to justice.

“We unequivocally condemn any act of kidnapping, abduction, or intimidation intended to interfere with press freedom or any other constitutional right,” Nyaga said.

The police service assured the public that the investigation into the Gilgil incident would be conducted transparently, stressing that no one was above the law.

The development comes amid growing condemnation of Kiprotich’s alleged abduction, with the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also calling for an immediate investigation.

CPJ Africa Director Angela Quintal described the incident as a “shameful indictment” of the Kenya Kwanza administration, raising concerns over the safety of journalists and press freedom in the country.

“The attempt to forcibly disappear Alex Kiprotich, three days after President William Ruto railed against The Standard Group, reflects the growing dangers that journalists face in Kenya, despite the president’s earlier promise to allow the press to work freely,” Quintal said.

The New York-based press freedom organisation further expressed concern over what it described as an escalation in cases of abductions and enforced disappearances in Kenya.

World.title: Trumpets of reforms blow louder as Kenya marks 16 years under 2010 Constitution
World.content:
The Constitution, Kenyan flag and the National anthem. [PCS]

On Thursday, August 27, a group of people largely composed of the youth gathered under some trees at Jeevanjee Gardens in Nairobi, carrying Kenyans flag, and banners and placards inscribed with "implement the constitution. Kenyans first" words.

These were in protests against what they believed is deliberate failure of those in authority to fully implement the 2010 Constitution.

World.title: Democrats might win in the midterms — but a whole new set of problems await
World.content:
The left wing of the Democratic Party flourished this summer as fed-up liberals in key races across the country have eschewed traditional, more moderate candidates in favor of hard-charging progressives.

But behind the scenes, ultra-progressive House members and candidates are pushing their own party leaders to reflect more of that mood — arguing that Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and his allies are, so far, failing to grasp the demands of far-left voters who showed up in droves this summer.

Those liberals watched in alarm in recent weeks as Jeffries publicly disavowed their marquee “Medicare for All” bill while a pro-Israel Democrat was elevated to a key foreign policy role within the caucus. They also argue his allies were working to undermine a pair of progressive candidates in Michigan and California.

“I was very confused and surprised by that,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a senior progressive and author of the House’s “Medicare for All” bill, told CNN about the leader’s comments about her signature bill. She added that she has been having “direct” conversations with Jeffries about it.

The emerging frustrations on the left offer a preview of some of the pressures that await Jeffries if the party can flip the chamber next year, particularly as a new crop of far-left progressive candidates threaten not to support him for leader post-election.

“I think what we’ve seen around the country is that people all over are dissatisfied. They’re not happy with the administration. They’re not happy with the current leadership in the Democratic Party — and are looking for a change,” Dr. Adam Hamawy, a progressive candidate who is likely to win a deep blue seat in New Jersey this November, told CNN. Hamawy is among several candidates fresh off primary victories who have not decided whether to back Jeffries.

“Most Democrats, I think, agree that the current leadership is failing to face the moment,” Hamawy told CNN when asked if he’ll support Jeffries. “I have to see what the choices are and what the situation is.”

Adam Hamawy speaks during an AFP interview in Washington DC, in June 2024. Drew Angerer/AFP/Getty Images

Tensions have long simmered within the Democratic Party, including in its fractious House caucus, where many centrists are privately pleased with what they see as Jeffries’ effort to distance the party from a far-left agenda ahead of a critical election. But the rise of the democratic-socialist wing of the party has drawn new urgency to a major question now facing Jeffries: How much should the party embrace its insurgent left when it’s also trying to win dozens of seats in GOP turf in November?

Nearly all progressives who spoke to CNN said Jeffries is still on track to become speaker next January if Democrats flip the chamber, according to conversations with more than a dozen Democrats. Privately, Jeffries has already met or made plans to meet with five of those insurgent Democrats: Hamawy in New Jersey, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, and Melat Kiros in Colorado, according to people familiar with the discussions.

Still, the recent frustrations on the left illustrate the challenge for Jeffries and his leadership team as they navigate the anti-establishment midterm mood within their party. The dissatisfaction goes beyond the upper echelons of leadership: there are preliminary internal discussions among current progressive members about challenging committee leaders and, possibly, instituting term limits for key roles, multiple people told CNN.

“Defeating 10, 30-year incumbents should be a wake-up call to the Democratic establishment that the base is moving underneath them,” Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for a group helping to power the far-left wins, Justice Democrats, told CNN. (This cycle, nine of the group’s endorsed candidates won primaries, its biggest year to date.)

Andrabi specifically pointed to Jeffries’ comments on “Medicare for All” – in which Jeffries recently said he did not support the legislation: “Unfortunately, it often feels that the Democratic leadership and establishment don’t even want to acknowledge the ground is moving.”

Progressives, including Hamawy and Avila Chevalier, made clear in interviews with CNN they are coming to Washington to make real progress on an ambitious agenda on affordability and anti-corruption — not to simply antagonize leadership.

“We’re not really going in to fight, we’re going in to deliver on what people want,” Hamawy said.

Yet even Jeffries’ allies acknowledge the challenge awaiting him in January: navigating an intraparty battle over the party’s ideological future. While an emboldened left wing is pushing for a major shake-up in Congress, Jeffries could also face an expanded centrist bloc that humiliated leadership last week when some of its members showed they were willing to defy the party line on key priorities — even if it meant helping Republicans.

That centrist rebellion has since triggered a messy internal feud among House Democrats. Privately, Jeffries and his team are discussing ways to crack down on any of their members voting for procedural motions that hurt the party – a proposal that has infuriated the left and centrists alike, according to Democrats from both factions.

A tense debate has since unfolded over whether party leaders should create new rules for next year to punish members who defy leadership. In a closed-door meeting on Wednesday about leadership’s push, Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar of Texas pushed back firmly, arguing that members need to be able to voice dissent, according to multiple people familiar with the discussions. But he was immediately confronted by others, including Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Florida, who argued Democrats shouldn’t be willing to go rogue on the floor.

Those dynamics will be on full display starting with the speaker’s vote in January, if Democrats win the majority.

Avila Chevalier, a community organizer who shook New York City politics by unseating a long-time incumbent this summer, told CNN that she recently had a “positive” conversation with Jeffries.

But she said she hasn’t “come to any final decisions on that yet,” when asked whether she would support Jeffries as party leader, adding: “It’ll be the first vote I make. It’ll set the tone for the kind of representative that my district will have, and I want that vote to mean something to my community.”

Darializa Avila Chevalier stands for a portrait at Marcus Garvey Park in the Harlem neighborhood of New York on August 12. Marco Postigo Storel/CNN

Even if many of the far-left incoming Democrats ultimately do support Jeffries, it’s to their advantage not to show their cards just yet – creating what could be powerful leverage to negotiate for their priorities when they first arrive in Congress.

Asked more broadly about her agenda for next year, Avila Chevalier offered a range of “day one” priorities such as ending the sale of weapons to Israel, the Green New Deal for Public Housing and abolishing super PACs – as well as other ideas that are widely backed by the party like universal childcare and raising the minimum wage.

“It’s time that folks who are in DC or elsewhere who might be comfortable with the status quo to recognize that the vast majority of the people of this country are hungry for something different,” she said.

Angst over the emerging Democratic agenda

Many liberal Democrats are careful not to openly criticize their own leadership just ahead of a must-win midterm election.

But privately, progressive members and candidates remain concerned by Jeffries’ comments publicly disavowing “Medicare for All” and saying he does not support the Democratic Socialists of America agenda in an interview last month with NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

Asked if he supports the bill, Jeffries said: “No, as you indicated, I haven’t cosponsored the ‘Medicare for All’ legislation that has been introduced over the last several years,” adding: “I do think we need to figure out how to fix our broken health care system and then build something better.”

Jeffries’ allies said his comments also reflect one of his long-time beliefs — that House leaders should not support major bills until there’s broad support in the caucus.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks during a press conference in the US Capitol on September 3. Finn Gomez/Getty Images

Other progressives are concerned that party leaders are not adequately responding to the movement’s vocal pro-Palestine push. They are, in particular, concerned about the recent elevation of prominent Israel supporter, Rep. Jared Moskowitz of Florida, to a Foreign Affairs subcommittee post that could give him influence over foreign policy next year.

Multiple Democrats told CNN that Jeffries was not involved in the move – saying instead that it was arranged by Rep. Brad Sherman, another Israel ally, who inherited the role after a colleague’s resignation. Moskowitz, who’s facing a tough reelection, asked Sherman if he could have the spot on the panel to help him with pro-Israel voters back home, those people said.

Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, dismissed the left’s criticism, calling the hand-off “standard committee procedure.” He added that Moskowitz had already held an important role on the committee – the top Democrat on the oversight subcommittee, which has since been passed off to Rep. Jonathan Jackson of Illinois.

“I don’t know what the left’s problem is,” Meeks said, adding that he believes his committee is “very balanced” on the issue of Israel.

Still, the rise of Moskowitz has emerged as a major flashpoint among progressive lawmakers and candidates, especially after Jeffries had appealed to the left earlier this year by declaring that “American policy in the Middle East must change” after he opposed cutting taxpayer aid to Israel during a landmark vote earlier this year.

A ‘shocking’ intervention in California

Then there are party leaders’ recent moves on the campaign trail.

In California, progressives are furious that their state’s delegation leader, Rep. Zoe Lofgren, tried to tank a left-wing candidate in a bitter fight to fill the seat of former Rep. Eric Swalwell.

Rep. Zoe Lofgren arrives for a Democratic caucus meeting on September 1. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Progressive candidate, state Sen. Aisha Wahab, won the state party’s endorsement and secured the most votes in two separate primaries for the seat (including a special election) – though she failed to top the 50 percent needed to avoid a runoff.

Ahead of that August 18 runoff, Lofgren, a leadership ally, released a video statement questioning Wahab’s fitness to serve in Congress and instead endorsed a more moderate candidate for the upcoming runoff.

The drama began after Lofgren and others, including No. 3 House Democrat Rep. Pete Aguilar, argued that California Democrats needed to fill the seat as quickly as possible and should install a “placeholder” Democrat to the seat temporarily.

But progressives argued Lofgren was simply trying to keep Wahab out of the role, giving the more moderate — and AIPAC-backed — candidate a better chance of winning a full term for the seat in November. (A person familiar with the subject said the congresswoman wasn’t opposing her due to her progressive policy stands, but rather because of Wahab’s refusal to back the push to install a “placeholder” Democrat to the seat through January.)

Wahab still won and was sworn into the House last week. But the cost, progressives say, was millions of dollars in spending in the election that could have gone toward defeating Republicans.

Rep. Aisha Wahab speaks with Speaker of the House Mike Johnson just after she was sworn in, at the US Capitol on September 2. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Wahab has since spoken with both Lofgren and Aguilar and they congratulated her on her win, she told KCRA 3 News. But one of Wahab’s most vocal supporters, Amar Shergill, a prominent progressive activist in California, told CNN that he still blames party leaders for allowing such a “shocking” intervention against the candidate endorsed by the state party.

“I’ve never seen anything like it, it was unprecedented,” Shergill said. “Lofgren leads the largest congressional delegation in the country. When she makes moves behind the scenes, everybody hears about it. It’s impossible for DC leadership not to know what she’s doing.”

“It was a tough primary but we’re looking forward to everyone coalescing around her and putting the primary behind us,” said Evan Brown, executive director of the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC.

Frustrations after bitter primary in Michigan
