Meanwhile, in Michigan, progressives are fuming that the House Democrats’ campaign arm has refused to publicly promote left-wing Democrat, Will Lawrence, roughly a month after he won a nasty three-way primary there.

At issue: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has so far declined to add Lawrence to a coveted list of their priority House candidates, in part out of deference to leaders of the Congressional Black Caucus, multiple people involved in discussions about the issue told CNN.

The CBC has yet to endorse Lawrence after their public battle with him during the primary over his 2024 comments criticizing Black political leaders. Lawrence, a White climate activist who recently let his DSA membership lapse, came under fire from senior Black Democrats, including Jeffries and Meeks for saying Black political leaders “defang the White left.”

Lawrence, in previous interviews with CNN, has apologized for his “choice of words” in that statement. And some House progressives are “absolutely apoplectic” that party leaders have not yet backed him, according to one of those people.

US House candidate William Lawrence speaks at a rally with US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in Lansing, Michigan, on July 19. Andrew Roth/Sipa USA/AP

“We’re working on a path forward when it comes to being able to support him,” a Black Caucus strategist with knowledge of the situation told CNN.

The list, run by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, is effectively seen as a “stamp of approval” from party leaders — a flashing sign for party groups and donors to put their support behind the strongest candidates. Lawrence’s absence, progressives say, is depriving him of a big fundraising boost to help defeat GOP Rep. Tom Barrett.

The flare-up in Michigan comes after party leaders did get behind a slew of other progressive candidates in key races – including some who defeated party-preferred candidates – such as Randy Villegas in a pivotal California swing seat.

The DCCC and Lawrence’s campaign declined to comment. But one person familiar with the inner-workings of the DCCC told CNN that the group has been “working every day” with Lawrence’s team to defeat Barrett in November.

Meeks, who runs the Black Caucus’s PAC, said he’s had “good conversations” with Lawrence over the phone and is looking forward to sitting down with him in Washington soon.

“We’ll talk. I think we’re going to get that resolved,” he said. “If you look at him, compared to who he’s running against, we want him to win.”

World.title: Trump’s blockade pushes Iran toward military escalation
World.content:
As Washington abandons talks with Iran for an aggressive economic pressure campaign, a cornered Tehran is now threatening military escalation and a wider war to force negotiators back to the table.

US President Donald Trump has dismissed diplomacy with the Islamic Republic, calling a June ceasefire agreement one that “isn’t worth the paper it’s written on.” His administration has instead piled pressure on Iran through a global sanctions campaign, military strikes and a maritime blockade that stops goods from leaving or entering the country.

The multifront campaign has put Iran under unprecedented pressure, forcing its fatigued population to endure still more strain. Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile, remains conspicuously absent. Tuesday will mark his sixth month in hiding in an attempt to avoid the fate of his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in an airstrike at the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran in late February.

Iran’s military officials are increasingly touting new tactics in response to the pressure, threatening to target nations taking part in the blockade and warning that they could broaden the conflict.

On Monday, a wave of attacks from the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen hit several Saudi towns and cities, wounding at least 73 civilians and causing fires at energy facilities. Global oil prices climbed one percent.

Iran’s Supreme National Security Council leader, Mohsen Rezaei, said in an interview with Iranian media on Sunday that “new strategies must be adopted in the war, in negotiations, and in confronting the blockade.” He also suggested that Iran could expand its own blockade beyond the strait by introducing a new “exclusion zone” in the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman.

“In recent days, Washington has received a clear warning from Iran’s new missiles. Economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to the blockade perimeter. The operational posture toward US warships and bases has been fundamentally recalibrated,” he wrote on X on Tuesday.

Over the past few weeks, Iran and Oman have been slowly negotiating management of the Strait of Hormuz. On Monday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said a “temporary safe route” through the strait would likely be registered with the International Maritime Organization in the “coming days.” It’s unclear if the US would recognize the agreement being negotiated between Iran and Oman.

For now, mediators have identified two main obstacles to resolving the conflict, Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari told CNN’s Becky Anderson: political will and technical solutions.

“Political will is based on narrative, meaning that we find the right narrative for the parties of the conflict to get out of this crisis. And it’s juggling four or five balls at the same time in trying to find all the solutions needed,” he said.

A boatman sails in the waters of the Five-Step local fishing harbour in the port city of Bandar Abbas in southern Iran on September 5, 2026. Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images

Despite the diplomatic stall, Iran’s top officials, including President Masoud Pezeshkian, have repeatedly signaled their desire to return to the June agreement — one widely viewed by observers as favorable to Tehran. Domestically, however, hard-line conservatives remain critical of any agreement with the US, accusing the Iranian president and his negotiators of compromising Iran’s wartime gains.

“Tehran is trying to reconcile two pressures: a war-weary population that needs economic relief and an ideological base that does not want capitulation,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN. “That is why the preferred outcome is diplomacy, but diplomacy that can be presented domestically as the result of Iranian strength rather than retreat.”

Cornered, Iran now faces a quagmire. Without compromise on its demands over control of the Strait of Hormuz, its nuclear program or sanctions relief, pressure from Washington is unlikely to ease, while any compromise with Washington would leave Iran’s top officials answering to ideologically driven hard-line factions within the regime.

“The Iranian nation accepts neither threats nor coercion, nor negotiations whose outcome would be the weakening of the country’s rights,” Hossein Taeb, head of the hard-line Basij paramilitary volunteer group, said Monday. “Negotiations are for securing the nation’s rights, not surrendering them.”

“Playing out the inevitable”

Despite Iranian and Qatari officials talking up efforts to reestablish diplomacy, Trump maintains that his tactics do not seek to “force” Iran back to the negotiating table, instead, signaling Washington’s comfort with the status quo.

“I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week. “They are just playing out the inevitable,” he added, before calling on Iranian people to “rise up and fight” the regime.

The memorandum of understanding set a roadmap for further negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program and sanctions relief, while preparing for a future in which Tehran would have a role in managing the Strait of Hormuz, which is crucial for the transport of a fifth of the world’s oil supply.

In the weeks that followed the signing of the agreement, Iran attempted to control traffic across the Strait of Hormuz, while the US launched a heavy barrage of strikes on Iranian targets along the coastline.

The US Navy also began escorting vessels carrying crude out of the Strait of Hormuz, slowly ramping up the transit of oil to relieve pressure on markets, while regional countries such as the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia have shifted away from Hormuz to export oil to their clients.

“Our energy exports will not be held hostage, nor will our trade and economic activity,” UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said at the Hili Forum in Abu Dhabi on Monday.

“We are actively expanding port capacity along our eastern coast. Together with the pipelines, railways and trade links needed to connect alternative corridors for cargo are being developed and strengthened,” he added.

Red lines

Washington has also not let up military pressure, ordering strikes on Iranian targets, including last week, when an attack killed 18 people. Among them were four people at a wedding celebration, including a child, after shrapnel from a US strike hit a house in a village along the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian officials.

People gather near damaged buildings on September 6, 2026 following a US strike in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province. Iranian authorities say a US strike hit a wedding celebration on the night of September 2, 2026 killing at least four people and wounding 68 others. Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images

In response, Iran has targeted regional countries and vessels transiting the strait, while its proxies in Yemen have attacked Saudi oil facilities. But the ferocity of the strikes do not compare to the early days of the war when Iran launched hundreds of rockets and drones on regional targets, including Israel, heavily disrupting livelihoods and inflicting damage on stable countries.

“The logic is that Tehran cannot simply wait while the US gradually erodes its military and economic leverage,” Azizi, of the ICG, said. “This does not necessarily mean Iran wants another large-scale war. More likely (it) would be calibrated escalation in the sense of greater pressure on shipping, expanding the attacks on US bases or targeting its naval assets, or potentially some targets related to regional energy infrastructure.”

Amid the growing pressure, Iran’s lawmakers are sending deterring messages, warning the region of new weaponry and tactics, including attacks on warships and bases, while its military commanders claim that the Iranian army has now updated equipment and systems “in line with new threats.”

The objective would be to make the “current situation sufficiently costly” for the US that diplomacy again “becomes preferable,” Azizi said.

Such a strategy carries risks, however.

“Once both sides begin testing each other’s red lines, the risk of miscalculation increases significantly. An Iranian attack causing substantial US casualties, or a US response crossing one of Tehran’s red lines, could quickly take the confrontation beyond calibrated escalation and back toward full-scale war,” Azizi said.

World.title: UK set to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank in major reset of relations
World.content:
The United Kingdom is expected to unveil sanctions targeting Israel on Tuesday over the massive expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank under the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, marking a significant “reset” of the UK’s relations with the country.

Previewing the expected measures, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the sanctions were an effort to prevent the destruction of the two-state solution.

The decision marks a significant clash between Israel and what had been one of its top Western allies and comes amid mounting international criticism over Israel’s policies in the West Bank, where settler violence against Palestinians has surged in areas the international community views as part of a future Palestinian state.

Sanctions on settlement products will likely have little impact on the approximately $8 billion in annual trade between the two countries, only a tiny fraction of which comes from the West Bank. The top UK export to Israel is medicinal and pharmaceutical products, according to its Department for Business and Trade, while the top imports are fruits and vegetables.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog said sanctions would be a “serious error in judgment and choosing the wrong side of history.” At an event marking three decades of relations with the European Union on research and innovation, Herzog said, “Sanctions are not a solution. Dialogue is.”

The UK sanctions could also trigger a response from the Trump administration. US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, who has defended Israeli settlements in the West Bank, told BBC News on Tuesday, “I think without a doubt there will be (a reaction),” warning it could have a “huge impact on British businesses.”

The sanctions come amid Israel’s push to advance the internationally-condemned E1 settlement project, which critics say divides the West Bank into north and south, making a contiguous Palestinian state virtually impossible.

It also splits East Jerusalem – the envisioned capital of a Palestinian state – from the rest of the territory. In late-August, Israel’s Housing Ministry invited bids for the construction of more than 1,200 housing units in E1. The plan aims to create a continuous bloc of Jewish settlements from East Jerusalem to the West Bank.

Israel’s far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has explicitly championed the expansion of settlement as a way to “bury” the idea of a Palestinian state. “The Palestinian state is being erased from the table not with slogans but with actions,” Smotrich said when E1 received its final approval.

Last year, the UK and others sanctioned Smotrich and far-right Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir for “repeatedly inciting violence against Palestinians.”

Israel captured East Jerusalem and the West Bank in the 1967 war. Both are considered occupied territories under international law, and Israeli settlements there are widely regarded as illegal.

Miliband condemned the plan earlier this month, calling it an “unacceptable and destructive act” and one that crosses a “red line.” He demanded its “immediate reversal” summoning the Israeli Chargé d’Affaires in London in August.

“The impact of settler violence and terrorism has been catastrophic for Palestinian communities,” Miliband said. The expansion of settlements, he warned, “threaten(s) peace, security and the prospects for a viable Palestinian state.”

In May, the UK was one of several European countries who warned international companies against participating in the construction of E1 because of legal and reputational risks and consequences. The statement, which also had the backing of Canada, Australia and New Zealand, said the situation in the West Bank has “deteriorated significantly” as settler violence has reached “unprecedented levels.”

“Britain will not stand back and accept the destruction of the Two-State Solution,” he said, referring to a peace plan that calls for an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel.

Miliband told British lawmakers on Monday that he would be setting out a “comprehensive set of measure in the coming weeks.”

An excavator demolishes a Palestinian-owned building as Israeli forces carry out a raid in the Taawun Alawi area of Nablus, West Bank, Palestine, on August 31, 2026. Nedal Eshtayah/Anadolu/Getty Images

Last week, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar told local media that his government would retaliate against the UK if sanctions were imposed.

“If Britain acts against the State of Israel, the State of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools,” he told Ynet News. “The period is over when people act against the State of Israel and the State of Israel doesn’t respond.”

Israel gave final approval for the E1 plan last year, greenlighting more than 3,400 housing units.

“Every settlement, every neighborhood, every housing unit is another nail in the coffin of this dangerous idea,” he added.

The E1 plan has been accelerated under Netanyahu’s hardline government, which has made settlement expansion a priority. While most Israeli settlements are state-run projects, many settler groups have also established dozens of unauthorized outposts in recent years – often through violence and physical force – that eventual secure Israeli government approvals.

Human rights and monitoring groups, including Amnesty International, have said that Netanyahu’s government turns a blind eye to violence, calling it part of a broader ecosystem of “state-supported settler violence.”

World.title: Nation’s largest school district bans AI in the classroom through 8th grade
World.content:
New York —

New York City is banning the use of generative artificial intelligence for public school students from 2K through 8th grade, part of a larger move to restrict classroom technology in the nation’s largest school district.

The one-year moratorium will affect nearly 600,000 public school students, nearly two-thirds of the district’s total enrollment. As part of the policy rollout, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the district will “discontinue or disable the AI components of more than 38 previously allowed programs that do not meet our new safety and oversight standards.”

Mamdani announced the policy on Wednesday with New York City Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels, saying it’s designed to protect students’ critical thinking abilities as well as the relationships between students and teachers.

Many communities across the country have pushed for stricter limits on screentime and AI use, amid growing fears that the technology could stunt students’ learning and development or pose safety risks. Meanwhile, AI companies have rolled out tools for learning and education, and provided funding to teachers’ unions to help develop AI training curricula.

The Los Angeles Unified School District this year announced major restrictions on classroom screen use and recently moved to “restrict student access to generative AI platforms” while the district reviews safeguards, a LAUSD spokesperson confirmed Wednesday.

New York state last year banned students from using personal phones during the school day. But Mamdani’s office called Wednesday’s announcement the country’s “most expansive” limits around AI use in schools.

In New York City, the education department banned the use of ChatGPT from school devices and networks in 2023, before reversing course months later. Under the policy announced Wednesday, a new Technology in Schools Coalition of educators, parents, students and others will evaluate the impacts of the moratorium and make recommendations for future school years.

New York City high school students will have access to a limited slate of AI tools and receive “AI critical thinking” courses. Companion chatbots, as well as mainstream services such as ChatGPT and Claude, will be blocked for all grades.

The district will also limit individual screen time for students based on grade level. The policy includes exceptions for students with disabilities and English learners.

Teachers will be allowed to use AI for lesson planning and other “operational tasks,” but not for grading or student assessments.

Michael Mulgrew, president of the New York-based United Federation of Teachers, lauded the screentime limits and carve-outs for students with special needs in a statement Wednesday. But he questioned how the education department will evaluate learning tools’ AI safeguards going forward, saying schools or educators could be left uncertain about which products are approved for use.

Samuels on Wednesday acknowledged the challenge of preventing students from using AI at home, for example, to help complete homework. He said the policy “seeks to expand our teachers’ and our understanding of how to combat the external use of AI,” but also called on parents to help monitor their kids’ tech use at home.

Still, Mamdani said he believes the policy will benefit students and educators.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI in early education is not only inevitable, but that it is necessary,” Mamdani said during Wednesday’s press conference. “We do not see it that way.”

World.title: Tycoon Salah Diab proposes solution to Egypt’s water crisis: “We will cultivate 100 million feddans”
World.content:
Prominent Egyptian business tycoon and founder of Al-Masry Al-Youm, Salah Diab, has urged a sweeping transition from traditional flood irrigation to modern drip systems to combat Egypt’s escalating water crisis, citing tenfold consumption cuts in agricultural trials.

Speaking during an interview on Al Arabiya’s “First Class” show hosted by Fatima Al-Daawi, Diab argued that traditional flood irrigation consumes up to 10 times more water than modern techniques while yielding far lower efficiency.

“In one of our farms located at the tail end of an irrigation canal, we faced severe water shortages when attempting to cultivate 16 feddans of bananas,” Diab explained.

“After adopting drip irrigation, we expanded cultivation on that same farm to 260 feddans while simultaneously reducing fertilizer usage and pump fuel consumption by 90 percent.”

Diab proposed phasing in modern irrigation systems across two governorates each year.

He estimated that a nationwide rollout could free up enough water to expand Egypt’s cultivated land area from 10 million feddans to 100 million feddans.

The agricultural sector and national water strategy

In an effort to mitigate Egypt’s chronic water deficit and maximize agricultural output, prominent figures and state ministries are prioritizing a shift away from traditional flood irrigation:

Modernization drive: Transitioning to high-efficiency drip systems cuts farm water consumption by up to 90% while significantly boosting crop yields and lowering fertilizer/fuel costs.

Transitioning to high-efficiency drip systems cuts farm water consumption by up to 90% while significantly boosting crop yields and lowering fertilizer/fuel costs. Structural interventions: The initiative relies on national canal-lining projects (Hayah Karima) to prevent seepage at canal tail-ends, alongside strict enforcement on water-intensive crops (rice, sugarcane, and bananas) to safeguard Egypt’s fixed 55.5 billion cubic meter Nile quota.

Urban forestry controversy and local backlash

In parallel, urban infrastructure expansion has sparked heavy public and media criticism.

Widespread street-widening projects—notably along Gamaat al-Dowal al-Arabiya Street and corridors in Zamalek, Dokki and Heliopolis—led to the removal of decades-old trees.

Critics noted that this intensified urban heat-island effects and degraded per-capita green space.
