World.title: Iran-backed Houthis attack Saudi oil facilities, injuring dozens
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis attacked four cities in the south of U.S. ally Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a major expansion of the six-month-old Middle ‌East war.

The Houthis, who control most of Yemen's populated areas, including the capital, said they had launched a broad operation deep into Saudi territory. They used drones and missiles to strike a Saudi airbase in the southern city of Khamis Mushait, and targets belonging to Saudi Arabia's state oil company in nearby Abha, Najran and Jazan, a major Red Sea port.

Saudi authorities described blazes at the sites and said women and children were among the 73 ​people hurt. The reports of such large numbers of wounded suggested the attacks were among the biggest ​carried out against Saudi Arabia since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.

Confirmed images of the aftermath of the attacks were not immediately available. The Houthis released pictures of an explosion of what they said were trucks from Saudi Arabia ​they had struck at the border in another area.

Houthi attacks on southwestern Saudi Arabia have the potential to worsen the war's global economic impact by disrupting Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

After a month of calm in August, fighting in the Gulf has resumed, with ⁠Iran and the U.S. exchanging fire, sending ⁠global oil prices back up to levels unseen since July. Brent crude prices were up more than ‌two per cent on Tuesday, above $99 US a barrel.

The ⁠fighting has caused global shortages of crude oil and, more acutely, the fuels that are produced by refining it. Diesel fuel in the United States is now at a record average retail price of more than $5.90 a gallon less than two months before midterm elections that could threaten the hold of Donald Trump's Republicans on one or both chambers of U.S. Congress.

Test of wills

Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling against the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade. That war had calmed in recent years, but a ceasefire there has broken down, with the Houthis threatening shipping at the mouth of the Red Sea.

"The coalition ⁠will take all necessary operational measures to deter this terrorist militia and resolutely confronts its hostile approach," Col. Turki al-Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said in a statement on X.

Smoke rises from a burning truck during what the Houthis say was an attack targeting trucks coming from Saudi territory, at Al-Wadiah border crossing on the Saudi-Yemen border, in this image obtained from a handout video. (Houthi Media Centre/Reuters)

Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree accused Riyadh of having escalated the war by launching airstrikes on Yemen, and said the Houthis would respond.

The war in the Gulf has turned into a test of wills ‌between the U.S. and Iran, with each side hoping that economic pressure from competing blockades will force the other to yield.

Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf, while cutting off Iran's exports with a blockade just beyond it.

Tehran has announced new measures to seal off the strait, saying it will soon unveil details of a "maritime exclusion zone" that will extend from the ​perimeter of the U.S. blockade, through the strait and into the Gulf itself.

The U.S. fired at Iranian tankers over the weekend in retaliation for Iranian fire at American warships. Iran said it had used new, more capable ballistic missiles to attack.

"In ⁠recent days, Washington has received a clear warning from Iran’s new missiles," Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said on X. "Economic warfare will be met by a ⁠maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to the blockade perimeter. The operational posture toward U.S. warships and bases has been fundamentally recalibrated."

Thousands on the move in Yemen

Despite U.S. barrages that have degraded Iran's ⁠conventional forces and ⁠punished its already ailing economy, Iran still possesses missiles and drones ​that can threaten oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and have been used to attack U.S. military bases scattered throughout the region.

About one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural ​gas shipments passed through the strait before the war.

The flare-up between the Saudis and Houthis has displaced about 18,500 people in Taiz and Hodeida in southwestern Yemen, further pressuring communities in southern Taiz and the West Coast, according to the International Organization for Migration.

"Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," said Abdusattor Esoev, IOM chief of mission for Yemen. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before."

Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and much of northern Yemen and forced the government into exile. A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year to try to restore the government to power.

The civil war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to UN estimates, and at times pushed the country to the brink of famine.

World.title: Back to school: Everything you need to know about Ontario's education policy changes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tuesday marks the official return to school for hundreds of thousands of Ontario students, but the academic landscape inside those halls will look a little different this fall.

If you’ve just come off a busy summer full of beach days and cottage trips, here are some of the major updates you may have missed.

Mandatory final written exams for high school courses

In June, Education Minister Paul Calandra announced a string of changes, including making final written exams mandatory for most high school courses.

The move is “intended to provide a more consistent approach to assessment and evaluation for students in Grades 9 to 12,” according to the province’s website.

WATCH | Education minister announces policy changes for 2026-27 school year: Why Ontario is changing high school attendance, exams rules | Duration 1:01 Ontario Education Minister Paul Calandra announced changes to the province’s English school systems, including mandatory written exams and incorporating attendance and participation into high school students’ final marks.

For Grades 9 and 10, mandatory final written exams are now worth 20 per cent in core subjects like english, math and science. The EQAO Grade 9 mathematics assessment counts as a written final exam.

In Grades 11 and 12, exams account for 25 per cent of the grades in core subjects, while non-core subjects split final evaluations between a written exam and a culminating project.

Workplace preparation, co-op and special education courses remain exempt from written exams, though final non-written evaluations are still required.

Attendance will now factor into final grades

Starting this school year, attendance and participation will account for 15 per cent of a final mark in Grades 9 and 10. In the upper years, it will count for 10 per cent.

A student who has more than two unexcused absences won't be able to get that full 10 or 15 per cent.

After the change was announced in June, Calandra told The Canadian Press attendance rates in Ontario high schools have been among the worst in the country.

"My advice to parents is, keep them in school," he said at the time. "Education should be their priority.”

Illnesses and religious holidays are categorized as excused absences and will not affect grades.

New financial literacy graduation requirement

Ontario high school students also now need to pass a financial literacy test in order to graduate.

Grade 10 students will take the new standardized financial literacy evaluation in Career Studies (GLC2O) and must score at least 70 per cent to pass.

According to the province's website, students will have two opportunities during the course to achieve that benchmark. If they don’t succeed, they will be provided more opportunities outside the course.

WATCH | How parents feel about Ontario's education changes: Parent reacts to Ontario's planned mandatory exams changes | Duration 0:45 Ontario is planning to introduce mandatory written exams on 'official exam days' for grades 9-12. We spoke to one parent who is concerned about the changes, particularly for students who don’t perform well on exams.

The education minister announced the requirement last spring, saying students need practical, real-world skills, including on how to manage money and budgets.

The evaluation will focus on essential financial life skills, including household budgeting, interest rates, credit cards, saving strategies and consumer awareness, the province says.

Student and family support offices at all school boards

Last week, the province announced student and family support offices will open at all 72 school boards.

The province first announced the program last fall, when it placed five school boards under provincial control for alleged mismanagement, ordering those boards to open support offices by January 2026.

When announcing the program expansion in Hamilton last week, Calandra said the offices are meant to give parents and caregivers a clear next step when concerns cannot be resolved at the school level.

“We know there are going to be times when parents have questions and concerns,” he said. “Most of these can and should be resolved with the teacher or principal.”

But parents should not have to spend weeks trying to determine who is responsible for handling more complex issues, Calandra said.

New 'back to basics' kindergarten curriculum

A new kindergarten curriculum will take effect this school year.

The new "back-to-basics" curriculum shifts away from play-based learning towards academic rigour, according to the province.

It includes new learning requirements in math, science and language skills, where the previous curriculum emphasized learning through exploration and play.

Some teachers have expressed concern over whether the new expectations are age-appropriate for four- and five-year-old children.

The province says the curriculum maintains learning through play while introducing more structured lessons in reading, writing and math.

World.title: Thieves steal paintings from Renoir Museum on French Riviera
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Thieves stole four paintings from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera, the local mayor said, but dropped two of them in the gardens ​as police, alerted by alarms, gave chase ​early Tuesday.

The most valuable works of the impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir have fetched dozens of millions of dollars at auctions.

Mayor ​Bryan Masson said the thieves broke ⁠into the museum a little ‌before 6 a.m. through a hole made in a garden fence to snatch four paintings — the latest of a series of brazen art thefts in the country.

"Attacking the Renoir Museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer. These actions are particularly serious," Masson said.

The ‌two stolen paintings were Madame Colonna Romano and Young Woman at the Well, the municipality said. Both belong to Paris's famous Orsay Museum and were on loan to Cagnes-sur-Mer's Renoir Museum.

"It's Renoir's, it is priceless, you ⁠cannot sell it like that," the mayor told reporters, speaking in front of the museum.

The museum was created in 1960 in the mansion of the artist on a hill in Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, where Renoir died in 1919. The collection on display in the museum includes 13 paintings from the master and some 40 sculptures, furniture and photographs.

Theft follows 2025 Louvre heist

Art thieves in Europe are committing more violent robberies, and specialist gangs have been replaced by ad hoc ​opportunists recruited through social media, pan-European police body Europol said last month.

The heist at ‌the Louvre Museum in Paris in October of last year was a prime example of this, Europol said, as the thieves threatened guards and visitors and stole €88 million ($141.5 million Cdn) worth of jewels, such ​as Empress Eugenie's tiara.

World.title: Why thousands are paying to watch people play Dungeons & Dragons live
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There is no script, no fixed ending and no guarantee the heroes will make it out alive.

Onstage, performers build a fantasy world together while dice rolls and split-second choices can send the story to places nobody planned.

On Sept. 10, nearly 2,800 people will fill Vancouver's Queen Elizabeth Theatre for a sold-out performance of Endless Dungeon, led by comedian and game master Brennan Lee Mulligan. The Vancouver date follows a sold-out May performance at Toronto's Coca-Cola Coliseum.

Endless Dungeon is part of the growing world of "actual play" — tabletop role-playing games performed for an audience — a genre combining improvisational theatre, collaborative storytelling and game mechanics, with dice helping determine whether characters succeed or fail.

For performers and scholars, the appeal lies in uncertainty, intimacy and collaboration — and in knowing that no two performances will be exactly alike.

Mulligan told CBC News that part of the attraction is simply "the joy of live theatre."

"It's happening in front of your face," he said, adding that the audience reactions become part of the draw. "You are there, your gasps, your laughs, your groans at a bad D&D pun."

WATCH | CBC Exclusive: Brennan Lee Mulligan on the popularity of live D&D: Why live D&D is drawing thousands — and changing who gets seen | Duration 8:08 Brennan Lee Mulligan on why audiences are filling theatres for live D&D, how performers preserve the intimacy of friends creating stories together, and how the form has made queer, trans and other marginalized players more visible.

A roller coaster with no track

The term "actual play" is recent, but the practice is a longstanding one according to Emily Friedman, a professor of English at Alabama's Auburn University who studies the format.

Online shows such as Critical Role, Mulligan's Dimension 20 and The Adventure Zone helped bring actual play into the mainstream. Live performances are often self-contained, with clearer character goals and story beats designed to reach an ending in a few hours. That makes the action "heightened and brightened and made sharper and quicker and faster," Friedman said.

She compared its appeal to being on a roller coaster where "the track is being laid in front of you at high speed."

Vancouver comedian Jess Lupini, who is joining Endless Dungeon for this stop, compared it to another form of unscripted entertainment.

"Watching actual plays is exciting in many of the same ways that watching hockey is exciting," she said. "You don't know what's going to happen."

Emily Friedman, left, and Brennan Lee Mulligan on an episode of Adventuring Academy, a series on the streaming service Dropout. Friedman says live actual play is like a roller coaster whose track is being laid as the performers race forward. (Submitted by Emily Friedman)

'The feeling of being in the room'

But that unpredictable nature only partly explains why people pay to see a format they can watch online.

Abdul Aziz, a Vancouver comedian joining Mulligan for this Endless Dungeon performance, says the attraction is "probably the feeling of being in the room."

Aziz also performs on the actual-play podcast Spout Lore, which has tried to preserve the atmosphere of friends playing together even as those conversations became entertainment for strangers.

"We sort of are more focused on each other while playing than we are focused on the audience," Aziz said.

Friedman says audiences are watching two things at once: fictional characters and the real people creating them reacting genuinely when another player's choice surprises them.

Mulligan says performers have to make the audience feel included without sacrificing their connection to one another.

"The best part of live theatre is the preservation of authentic connection between performers and feeling totally invisible as an audience member, even as everything has been arranged to include you," he said.

"Whatever you do to delight your players will delight the audience."

Abdul Aziz, a Vancouver comedian and actual-play performer, says tabletop role-playing games let people put parts of themselves into their characters, creating an authentic connection with audiences. (Submitted by Abdul Aziz)

A place to imagine differently

For Aziz, fantasy also offers room to question rules that can seem fixed in the real world.

Aziz, whose parents are from Egypt and who immigrated to Canada as a child, says growing up in a mainly white community gave him an outsider's perspective on cultural conventions.

That carried into Spout Lore. While building his barbarian character's homeland, Aziz drew heavily on Middle Eastern cultures.

"In a very literal sense, the outsider's perspective was immediately useful in our show," he said.

Jess Lupini, centre, a Vancouver comedian and actual-play performer, appears with fellow BlackwaterDnD cast member Sean Depner, left, and game master Tim Carlson. Lupini says role-playing gave her a safe way to explore her gender identity before transitioning. (Submitted by Jess Lupini)

For Lupini, who is also a recurring cast member on BlackwaterDnD, an actual-play show streamed on YouTube and Twitch, taking on different characters became a way to explore herself.

Lupini, who is transgender, says tabletop role-playing games give people a chance to try on different identities, pronouns and personalities.

Before transitioning, she played characters who used she/her pronouns.

"That was really liberating and felt like a safe way of exploring a piece of myself that I had been conditioned to be really afraid of exploring," she said.

Friedman says women, gender-nonconforming people, 2SLGBTQ+ people and disabled people have always been part of tabletop gaming as players and creators, but were not always visible in traditional gaming spaces.

"It's just the shift of the spotlight in a lot of ways," she said.

Mulligan agrees, saying actual play didn't create those experiences, but made them easier to see.

"Actual play provided visibility for a reality that was always there," he said.

Em Carlson, CEO and creative director of the Vancouver-based actual-play show BlackwaterDnD, says audiences want stories that make them feel included in the narrative. (Submitted by Em Carlson)

A safe place to play

That kind of exploration depends on trust, says Em Carlson, CEO and creative director of BlackwaterDnD and another performer joining Vancouver's Endless Dungeon.

Carlson, whose professional background is in mental-health therapy, says the group does extensive preparation around safety and collaboration and notes that "play can't happen if you're not safe."

Tabletop role-playing culture still hasn't fully achieved its ideals of inclusion, Carlson says, but the stories reaching audiences have broadened as people want stories that help them feel included in the narrative.

"They can be a part of that joy that the players experience at the table."

For Carlson, Endless Dungeon offers something increasingly uncommon in an era of endlessly replayable media: a story created once, for the people present.

"It's a one-night experience where a fantastic, amazing audience gets to come in and laugh with us and cry with us and feel big feelings and cheer."

World.title: Parents are pushing back on classroom screen time in a 'techlash' over too much technology in schools
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As an occasional substitute teacher for middle- and high-schoolers in Nova Scotia, Kim Herrick often gets a front-row seat seeing how teens use tech at school.

Whether students are tasked with assignments, work for another class or granted free time, Herrick regularly sees them checking Snapchat, TikTok or Instagram accounts, shopping online, gaming or even trading Bitcoin — easily bypassing school board security methods aimed at blocking such use.

The ubiquity of students engaging in non-educational online activities — and the futile attempts to clamp down on it — have contributed to her view that we need to reconsider the tech used by default in classes today.

But the alarm bells really started going off for Herrick when she discovered her elder daughter — who's starting Grade 2 this fall — has had a school Google account for three years, without Herrick knowing. Herrick said she couldn't log into the account and school officials said she couldn't opt-out or have it deleted, saying it was necessary for access to educational apps and "a requirement" for learning.

We have hundreds of years of going to school as humans, Herrick said. "We do not need a Google account to learn."

Many parents, educators, advocacy groups and experts are pushing back against the amount of screen time in schools and the prevalence of tech tools woven into the current education system, with some making links to a range of woes, from behavioural issues to distracted students to data breaches that put youngsters' privacy at risk.

Yet a rollback to classroom practices of the past isn't the answer to the current "techlash," say some education experts, who favour intentional and thoughtful use of technology as the way forward.

WATCH | Where did 'techlash' come from?: What's a techlash? | Duration 0:23 Tom D'Amico, recently retired director of education for the Ottawa Catholic School Board, explains a movement pushing back and questioning device and technology use in schools.

Changing approach to tech in education

For years, a one-to-one student-to-device ratio, web access and learning through game-like applications have been seen as symbols of educational progress. But amid a worldwide push to reduce teen smartphone and social media use, a vocal wave of parent groups — including Skills Before Screens in Canada, the U.K.-based Close Screen Open Minds, as well as Schools Beyond Screens and ScreenSense in the U.S. — is broadening this scrutiny to encompass educational tech usage more generally.

After having prioritized digital schooling for the past decade, for instance, Sweden has recently shifted back toward physical textbooks, pen-and-paper homework, reinvesting in libraries and screen-free classrooms (particularly for younger students), citing falling scores on international assessments.

Poor reading scores have tech-friendly Norway making a similar return to physical books in its schools, as well as introducing a near-ban on Generative AI usage in elementary, with restrictions for high-schoolers.

In the U.S., parental demands have led to stricter tech policies at the country's two largest school boards. The Los Angeles Unified School District has already started the school year with limits on screen time in every grade, including a total device ban before Grade 2. On the opposite coast, New York is restricting one-to-one device time for Grade 2 and below and suggesting caps for older elementary students. It's also halting student-facing Generative AI use through Grade 8 and limiting use for high schoolers, for now.

Kim Herrick, seen playing a game at home with her husband and daughters, has had a front-row seat into classroom tech use across different grades and ages, both as a parent to two young kids and an occasional substitute teacher for middle and highschoolers in Nova Scotia. (CBC)

Herrick says many parents, such as herself, are in the dark about the screens and apps their youngsters access in class, let alone what the responsible use or data privacy agreements are regarding those apps and school accounts.

Beyond privacy, the mother of two and former wilderness leadership educator in the U.S. is also concerned about what unfettered school tech use means for the long term.

She worries about susceptibility to distraction — she's had secondary students claim they're multitasking as they juggle a bevy of browser tabs, apps or screens — not to mention negative impacts on their mental and physical health down the road.

In the meantime, overreliance on tech also bogs down educators' precious time with policing student usage and dealing with tech support, rather than teaching, Herrick said.

Herrick says she worries about wide-ranging impacts of overrelying on technology in schools, from the effects on student cognition, mental and physical health to data breaches that leak their info online. (Paul Poirier/CBC)

Intention versus novelty

Classroom tech use varies across Canadian regions, schools and educators, but it's indeed integrated into teaching today, according to Johanathan Woodworth, an assistant professor at Mount Saint Vincent University in Halifax.

Whether teachers are getting students to research a project online, study the solar system via a virtual reality simulator or test out an AI chatbot, Woodworth emphasizes that tech use must be intentional, thoughtful and directly connected to the skills students are expected to learn.

"A lot of times teachers use technology in the classroom because of the novelty effect and engagement — but the novelty effect wears off," Woodworth said from Halifax, where he teaches educational technology to existing and prospective teachers.

When he's teaching educators about how to incorporate tech in their classrooms, Mount Saint Vincent University assistant professor Johanathan Woodworth emphasizes intention, judiciousness and connection to students learning goals. (Eric Wiseman/CBC)

"The first step is to think about 'Do I even need to use it? What is the purpose of me using it? Does it actually help me in my classroom?'"

It's important teachers are supported with guidelines and enough training on how to carefully and effectively use technology, he says, in order to understand it and, in turn, teach and model that knowledge to their students.

Striving for balance

Rolling back to no-tech classrooms isn't necessarily the answer either, Woodworth said, since a main reason schools employ tech today — text-to-speech and speech-to-text applications, for instance — is to accommodate students with disabilities.

Schools must balance "purposeful" tech use with the need to prep students for a tech-filled world, while also ensuring it's "not used as a distraction," according to education consultant Tom D'Amico, former director of education of the Ottawa Catholic School Board.

Tom D'Amico, the former director of education for the Ottawa Catholic School Board, says he's seeing a shift across Canada toward schools taking a more developmentally and age-dependent approach to incorporating tech in classrooms. (Mathieu Theriault/CBC)

He says the concerns raised by parents — both the ones driving the current "techlash" and those pushing for their kids to build tech skills — are contributing to a "balanced and focused" approach by school boards.

In his current work advising school districts across Canada about artificial intelligence, D'Amico says he's noticing a shift: schools taking a more developmentally and age-informed approach to technology.

For instance, "that means regardless of the province, you're looking at the earliest grades not having a lot of device time, but still getting AI literacy. They still need to learn about digital citizenship, what it means to use a computer," he said, noting gradual introduction of more technology in middle and high school.

"Critical thinking can be [taught] without the technology as well in the early ages," D'Amico added, emphasizing that this learning must be "embedded in the curriculum, so it happens every single year, in an age-appropriate manner."

Ultimately, he says, the top focus of schools should be student learning and strengthening students' connections with teachers and their classmates.

"What's the number one technology in a classroom? It's the student and their brain," he said.

World.title: Russian drone and missile strikes on Kyiv kill 2, ending pause in attacks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Russia pummelled Kyiv with drones and missiles early on Tuesday, resuming its air attacks after a brief halt for the visit of U.S. peace negotiators, killing two people and triggering fires across the Ukrainian capital.

Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 10 more had been injured in the city, while falling debris in one district caused fires at a five-storey apartment building and a three-storey residential block.

The attack damaged at least 14 highrise buildings, a dorm, a school, a clinic, warehouses and other sites, officials said.

Russia resumed its attacks after U.S. peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff left Kyiv following a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday, as the Trump administration renewed its push to end Russia's 4-1/2-year war in Ukraine.

They arrived from talks in Moscow, after which the Kremlin said it did not rule out the resumption of the three-way negotiations.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 10 people had been injured in the city, while falling debris in one district caused fires at two residential buildings. (Efrem Lukatsky/The Associated Press)

"The moment the U.S. president's peace envoys left, (Russian President Vladimir) Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.

"His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy," Sybiha said, urging allies to ramp up pressure on Moscow, as well as to provide interceptors to down ballistic missiles, since Kyiv's stocks of these run critically low.

Kyiv resident Iryna Barisenkova, 61, said she heard explosions while travelling on public transport and was told there was a large fire near the Darnytskyi Vehicle Repair Plant, or DVRZ, area on the capital's left bank.

"Everything was thundering on the left bank," Barisenkova said. "It was just brutal."

Prior to the talks, Russia stepped up air attacks on Kyiv and nearby areas to nearly round-the-clock for several days, rather than mainly at night, using faster jet-propelled drones that killed residents and disrupted activities.

The Russian defence ministry said Moscow hit military and logistic targets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, as well as in the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, Russian newswires said.

WATCH | U.S. officials visit Kyiv following Moscow trip: U.S. officials optimistic after Kyiv trip | Duration 1:53 American special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were optimistic about Russia-Ukraine peace talks during a visit to Kyiv at a time when both sides have escalated airstrikes.

Poland activates aircraft

Amid explosions heard in Kyiv, neighbouring Poland, a NATO and European Union member, launched preventive operations against Russian missile attacks on Ukraine, the Polish army said.

Poland's Lublin airport has temporarily suspended flights because of the military operations.

In Russia, Ukrainian drones damaged civilian infrastructure and injured people in the Volga river city of Saratov, some 730 kilometres southeast of Moscow, the regional governor said.

The area is home to a large oil refinery run by state oil company Rosneft, as well as other industrial and military facilities.

Meanwhile, two people ‌were killed and ​one ​wounded ⁠in ⁠a ‌Ukrainian attack on ⁠the Crimean peninsula, which ‌was annexed by Russia ​in ⁠2014, ⁠Sergei ⁠Aksyonov, the ⁠Moscow-appointed ​regional governor, ​said.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with human rights office over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.

World.title: Judge orders Colombia’s military to suspend air strikes on illegal armed groups
World.content:
A court ordered the government and the military to suspend air strikes on suspected members of illegal armed groups while studying the risk of harm to child forced recruitment victims.

In a preliminary sentence, the Bogota family court in response to a lawsuit that was filed by a civilian who claimed the State ignored its obligation to protect children when carrying out air strikes on illegal armed groups.

TO ORDER the PRESIDENCY OF THE REPUBLIC, the MINISTRY OF NATIONAL DEFENSE, the GENERAL COMMAND OF THE MILITARY FORCES, the NATIONAL ARMY, the COLOMBIAN AEROSPACE FORCE, and the NATIONAL NAVY, through the appropriate channels and within the scope of their respective authorities, that, pending a decision on the merits in this constitutional protection action, they refrain from conducting offensive air operations against targets regarding which there is certain, objective, or reasonably verifiable information regarding the presence of children or adolescents recruited or used by armed groups, until the necessary precautionary and protective measures have been adopted and verified, and it has been determined, based on the available information and applicable operational protocols, that there is no less harmful operational alternative that would allow the legitimate military objective being pursued to be achieved Bogota family court

According to Radio Caracol, at least 107 minors were killed in air strikes on illegal armed groups since they were resumed by former President Ivan Duque in 2018.

The sentence comes a day after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the military killed 23 “narcoterrorists” in the deadliest air strike during the peace process that started in 2016.

The president vowed to resume bombing campaigns that were all but suspended by former President Gustavo Petro as he sought peace and demobilization talks with multiple illegal armed groups, a strategy rejected by the new far-right government.

Following the killing of at least three children in an air strike carried out in August, Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora blamed guerrilla organizations for the deaths, claiming they were recruiting children for human shields and combatants.

World.title: Colombia’s education minister resigns after less than a month
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella replaced his education minister after she resigned, claiming “an unexpected family situation.”

De la Espriella announced on social media platform X that he had accepted the resignation of the evangelical Education Minister Viviane Morales, who took office on August 7, the first day of the administration.

I bid a nostalgic farewell to my dear friend Viviane Morales. God’s designs are inscrutable, and she must leave us early to take charge of a personal situation that I sincerely hope she can resolve very soon. President Viviana Morales

In the same post, De la Espriella said he had appointed Ilva Myriam Hoyos, stressing that “I am confident that she will be an outstanding minister and that she will serve Colombia with dedication, character, and conviction.”

While in office, Morales lead the government’s Culture War in education and vowed to remove “gender ideology” from Colombia’s classrooms, and proposed a law that would allow churches to provide public education services.

Hoyos, a catholic, warned in 2016 that a peace deal between the government of President Juan Manuel Santos and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC promoted gender ideology.

The new education minister used to work with Alejandro Ordoñez, Colombia’s notoriously far-right former Inspector General and the country’s current ambassador to the Organization of American States.

World.title: De la Espriella claims Colombia’s military killed 23, arrested 6 EMC guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella claimed Wednesday that Colombia’s armed forces killed at least 23 members of FARC dissident group EMC and captured another six.

In a video, De la Espriella said that “Operation Azarias,” targeted the EMC’s Carolina Ramirez Front and killed one of its commanders, a man called “Tigre” or “Pintado,” in the south of the Guaviare province.

A second guerrilla commander, “Victor,” was among the six alleged EMC members who were arrested during the operation, which included air strikes.

The president claimed that Victor carried out attacks against the military “during the elections, as part of the ‘gunpoint vote’ strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict.”

That narcoterrorist, whom we have now taken out of circulation, carried out attacks against members of the National Army and the Navy. During the elections, as part of the “gunpoint vote” strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict, this criminal ambushed a unit that was on the move precisely to protect citizens’ right to vote freely. President Abelardo de la Espriella

There is no evidence to suggest that De la Espriella’s predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro, employed illegal armed groups to coerce voters into voting against his would-be successor.

One minor allegedly survived the attack and was surrendered to family welfare agency ICBF. The Medical Examiner’s Office is expected to investigate how many minors were among the alleged “narcoterrorists.”

At least three minors were killed in a previous operation in Guaviare that killed at least nine alleged members of the EMC’s main rival, FARC dissident group EMBF, the Medical Examiner’s Office said earlier this week.

Air strikes against illegal armed groups are controversial as they could imply the blanket killing of victims of child recruitment, a war crime according to international humanitarian law.

The government has long insisted that those recruiting children and minors are responsible for the deaths of their victims.

World.title: 1 killed, 15 injured in northeast Colombia car bomb attack on police station
World.content:
At least one person was killed and another 15 injured in a car bomb attack on a police station on the outskirts of Cucuta, the capital of Norte de Santander.

According to the National Police, the bomb exploded on Monday evening outside of the police station in Los Patios, a municipality that is part of Cucuta’s metropolitan area.

Apart from the casualties, the blast also damaged buildings and vehicles that were parked near the police station, police told local media.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had convened a security council meeting “with the entire top brass of the security forces.”

“Wherever the terrorists try to sow fear, that is where the State will be with all is might,” said De la Espriella.

We will pursue with an iron fist those who threaten Colombians, until we capture them, dismantle their networks, and restore peace to our communities. Abelardo de la Espriella

In the region around Cucuta, guerrilla organizations ELN and EMBF have been fighting each other. Organized crime groups operate mainly inside the urban area of the capital of the Norte de Santander province.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

World.title: Vote to move Uribe’s massacre probe to Congress triggers infighting among Colombia’s left
World.content:
Internal fractures within Colombia’s leftist opposition burst into the open following a vote by five representatives of the Historic Pact (PH) party to transfer a criminal investigation against former President Alvaro Uribe to Congress’ Accusations Commission.

The controversy erupted after the five PH members of the committee backed a motion of Uribe’s Democratic Center (CD) party to assert legislative jurisdiction over long-standing criminal cases against Uribe, including investigations into the massacres of El Aro (1997) and La Granja (1996), and the 1998 assassination of human rights defender Jesus Maria Valle.

PH members

David Alejandro Toro

María del Mar Pizarro

Heráclito Landínez

Jorge Bastidas

Gabriel Becerra

As the former governor of Antioquia, Uribe would have been in on the massacres carried out by the Bloque Metro and AUC paramilitary groups, according to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which refused to turn over the investigations.

The commission claimed jurisdiction over the Uribe file because the paramilitaries didn’t demobilize until after 2002, when he became president.

Critics of the decision, including the prosecution and PH Senate chief Ivan Cepeda, argued that Uribe’s alleged involvement in the crimes happened years before he was granted presidential immunity.

Cepeda spent much of his career fighting Uribe in court over his alleged ties to the AUC.

Because of the committee vote, the Constitutional Court will have to rule on who gets to investigate Uribe’s alleged crimes against humanity, which could delay the investigation.

Journalists who reported on the PH support for the fabricated conflict suggested that this may be part of a political deal between congressmen political deal between Uribistas and Petristas, supporters of former President Gustavo Petro.

Becerra, who is close to Cepeda, said in a statement that there “existed nor will there exist any political deal that would compromise justice, truth or the rights of victims.

According to the house representative, the PH lawmakers “initially considered it reasonable and legally appropriate to clarify the jurisdiction of the authority responsible for conducting the investigation,” but changed their mind in response to the controversy and calls for their resignation.

Lawyer Miguel Angel del Rio, the victims representative in the Uribe case, told Tercer Canal that “the ethic committee of the Historic Pact should investigate these five congressman,” adding that “what we have here is solidarity with impunity and this cannot be allowed.”

The Historic Pact became Colombia’s largest political party after congressional elections in March, but has seen an increase in internal tensions after Cepeda’s failure to win the presidential election in June.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.

“I can’t afford to pay you both, so one of you has to go,” Steve told us one morning. “I’ll leave it up to you two to decide which one.” And so we did—over a liter of beer, even though it was like nine-something in the morning. The co-editor (still a dear friend of mine) offered to go. But I’d leave too, I decided. A month or so later. The job had run its course, I thought.

We were frustrated and certainly taken aback—especially by the “decide amongst yourselves who stays and goes” part of the equation. And yet, neither of us was really surprised, because even then, we’d seen enough of Steve and his herky-jerky management style to know that this was precisely the kind of situation that could and would, as it turned out, unfold.

We couldn’t really be angry either. Or at least not stay angry. Because again, with Steve, what you saw is what you got. He was passionate about his project, but not always clear about how to make it grow. Often he’d have a new idea, and then charge ahead. And in those cases, there’d be a flurry of positive changes—new computers maybe, a new paid staff person, a larger office space. But then a particularly capable group of interns would move on, money would run scarce, the whole operation would contract, and we’d be back to square one, or so it felt.

I know this because later I joined Steve for a second, longer stint. What never varied, though, was his fighting spirit. A feisty advocate for the underdog, he was always chomping to champion a good cause—demanding accountability for human rights violations, defending the environment, shining a light on corruption and hypocrisy.

The Santiago Times was his platform, and he committed himself tooth-and-nail to making it survive, if not prosper. And in the meantime, the interns, editors, photographers and other collaborators kept coming through. They kept using Steve’s office and humble little publication as a landing point for early-career, working-abroad experiences, and as a launching pad for further adventures and professional endeavors.

If there was a method to Steve’s madcap approach, it was that with each new idea he had for the Santiago Times, with each new push to improve or revive it, he bought the business a little more time. Months turned into years and then decades. And all the while, people like myself were given an opportunity to work and learn—in large part through trial and error, because although Steve had things to teach, he also gave us space to teach ourselves.

It was his special tenacity, though, that kept the whole thing going, that gave so many people the chance, year after year, to develop their skills. We had fun too. So much fun. The office on Av. Santa María produced lasting, globe-spanning friendships, even love stories. And that was also part of Steve’s gift to us all.

He was an unabashed eccentric. Smart. Complicated. He had an entrepreneurial spirit but no real nose for business. Steve was a lawyer who wrote about politics and fruit exports. An editor with a penchant for typos. Part idealist, part cynic. A campaigner with no patience for diplomacy. He was perpetually cash-strapped, but generous. He was impulsive and impatient at times, but also deeply committed—to his various projects and causes, and to his family and colleagues. He was a teacher and a mentor. A doting father. A friend.

Goodbye Steve. Paz. And thank you.

World.title: Anti-vaccine mandate protests spread across the country, crippling Canada-U.S. trade
World.content:
Speaking to reporters at a press conference in Ottawa, Emergency Preparedness Minister Bill Blair said the blockade at Windsor’s Ambassador Bridge is particularly alarming because a quarter of all Canada-U.S. trade moves through that one crossing, which connects Canada with Detroit and points beyond.

Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of products have been held back for three days as 50 to 75 vehicles and about 100 anti-mandate protesters camp out on the main road that leads on and off the bridge.

The Canada Border Service Agency (CBSA) has closed the bridge to commercial traffic temporarily, diverting trucks to the Blue Water Bridge in Sarnia, Ont. instead. CBSA is reporting wait times in excess of four hours to make the short trip across to Port Huron, Mich.

We’ve seen the criminal acts, acts of thuggery and the obnoxiousness that they’ve inflicted on the people of Ottawa. Now they’re blocking the highways leading into our ports of entry. They’re putting their foot on the throats of all Canadians.

Labour unions representing auto workers have reported some idled Windsor plants have sent workers home while the trucker convoy holds up much-needed parts coming from the U.S.

Transport Minister Omar Alghabra said central Canada could soon see empty store shelves because so much of the region’s fresh food and produce comes into the country across that bridge.

To be honest, I find it ironic that the same people who were trying to sell Canadians fake stories about empty shelves are now causing those shelves to go empty, Alghabra said.

Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens said the protesters appear to be determined to stay. They feel such a passion for this particular cause that they’re willing to die for it, he said.

Speaking briefly to reporters before question period, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said his government is working with Ontario and the City of Windsor to put an end to the blockade.

World.title: Excellent prospects for Mercosur beef exports, except Argentina
World.content:
The Argentine beef industry is optimistic about world meat production and global demand this year, with China again playing a leading market role. A report issued by Argentina’s Rosario Stock Exchange (BCR) and the Mercado Ganadero Department (Rosgan), world beef production will reach 58 million tons, representing a 1% increase over 2021.

This prospect would reverse the downward trend seen in 2021, mainly because of the recovery of the meat-packing industries in Brazil and Australia, the world’s first and third-largest meat exporters, respectively.

As for the global flow of imports, the expected average, according to analysts at BCR/Rosgan, is 10 million tons, which would imply an increase of 2.7% compared to last year.

China, which reduced the pace of international beef purchases in 2021 to 950,000 tons compared to more than 1.1 million tons in 2020 will once again represent 32% of global consumption. According to BCR/Rosgan, China accounted for 13% of global meat demand in 2017.

At that time, Argentina was in the top five beef exporters, having previously been in the top three. But Argentina has dropped out of the top ten beef exporters in recent years, owing to government restrictions on beef exports with the purpose of supporting the domestic market and helping with lower prices.

Nevertheless the Brazilian and Argentine beef markets had an unusual year in 2021. Traditional animal protein producers, the two countries witnessed declines in their exports, particularly in the last months of the year. Overall compared to 2020, Brazil beef sales dropped 9,92% while Argentine exports decreased 13,84%.

The reduction experienced by Brazil can be explained by the beef embargo imposed by China. In effect on September 2021, Brazil voluntarily suspended exports to China after the identification of two cases of mad cow disease in the country.

The World Organization for Animal Health (OIE) recognized that these were atypical episodes and that the risk to the national herd was negligible. Despite this, China insisted in freezing Brazilian beef exports for over three months until December 15.

The drop in Argentine beef shipments were motivated by the high price of the product in the domestic market, and thus the government suspended all exports in May 2021. ” As a consequence of sustained increases in the price of beef cuts in the domestic market, the national government decided to implement a set of emergency measures to better organize the sector, restricting speculative practices, improving the traceability of exports and avoiding tax evasion,” said the decree issued at the time.

Further measures were implemented, and given the deteriorating economic situation of Argentina and its impact on inflation, the country’s export ban on certain beef cuts was extended until the end of 2023.

As a result of this situation, Mercosur junior member Uruguay strongly benefitted and saw beef shipments increase 35%. The same can be said of the other Mercosur member, Paraguay, that also experienced a record year of beef exports in 2021.

World.title: Unemployment in Chile almost back at 2019 levels
World.content:
Chilean authorities have reported Monday that unemployment nationwide had fallen in 2021 to 7.2% while in the same period of 2020 it had hit 10.3%. In the middle of the social uprisings of 2019 it had been recorded at 7.1%.

“It is the eighth consecutive annual decrease in the unemployment rate,” said Leonardo González of the National Institute of Statistics (INE), which also reported the unemployment rate for women stood at 7.4%, and for men at 7.1%.

In the quarter of the year, 119,930 jobs were created compared to the previous quarter. With seasonal adjustment, González specified, the number of jobs recovered quarterly reached 49,625.

Around 1,436,000 jobs have been recovered, which represented 77.5% of all jobs lost during the worst part of the COVID-19 pandemic, with 81.8% accounting for jobs held by men and 73.1% for those carried out by women.

The INE also said 80.1% of formal jobs and 94.5% of informal jobs had been recovered.

“If we continue at this rate, we estimate that we will soon be able to recover all the jobs that were lost in the worst moment of the pandemic,” González stressed. He warned, however, that “we have been consistently seeing these rates rise, but we are not yet seeing pre-pandemic levels.”

Employment ended 2021 at 54.3%, while the labor force participation rate ended at 58.5%, an 8.1% yoy increase, driven by women (11.7%) and men (5.7%).

Jobs were boosted by construction (22.2%), commerce (8.5%) and the hotels and restaurants (30.9%).

Economy Minister Lucas Palacios said that during “2021 we met the goal of strongly recovering economic activity and also employment.”

“We have recovered 80% of the jobs that the pandemic and recession destroyed. It was necessary to create health, operational security and certainty conditions to reactivate the economy and especially investment, which is the main source of opportunities,” Palacios said.

Palacios also highlighted joint efforts by the public and private sectors. “Incentives from the State can be very relevant to promote investment and employment,” the minister explained.

Labor Minister Patricio Melero agreed the unemployment figures meant “great news” and praised “the measures adopted by the government, both in economic and health matters,” which were yielding “results which are very positive for the country.”

(Source: ANSA)

World.title: Six in ten Argentines attribute Milei's shift on the Falklands to political convenience
World.content:
Six in ten Argentines attribute Milei's shift on the Falklands to political convenience

8th Tuesday, September 2026 - 10:02 UTC Full article

The sovereignty claim enjoys majority backing in Argentine society, but Milei's call for unity inspired confidence in 41% of those consulted and distrust in 56%

Some 61.1% of Argentines believe President Javier Milei adopted his current position on the Falklands out of political convenience, against 24.7% who attribute it to conviction, according to a survey by the consultancy Management & Fit of a thousand respondents with a margin of error of 3%.

The poll was released after the address the president gave to the nation on Thursday, in which he said the islands “are Argentine by history and by right, there is no discussion about it” and announced he would speed up sanctions against oil companies operating in the area without Argentine authorisation. Nine in ten respondents were aware of that address.

The figures distinguish between support for the position and the credibility of the shift. The sovereignty claim enjoys majority backing in Argentine society, but Milei's call for unity inspired confidence in 41% of those consulted and distrust in 56%. On the content of the speech, 44.6% considered he had announced concrete measures and 44.2% that he had confined himself to general statements, a tie within the margin of error.

The position marks a change from his earlier statements. Milei has repeatedly declared his admiration for Margaret Thatcher, British prime minister during the 1982 conflict, and had acknowledged the islanders' right to self-determination, arguing that Argentina should persuade them to prefer being Argentine. That possibility was ruled out in Thursday's message.

After the speech, the Office of the President circulated the results of an open poll run by the newspaper Clarín on its social media accounts, according to which 81.3% of those who responded supported the announced measures. Such polls are not representative samples and are not comparable with probability-based surveys.

The government is drafting a national sovereignty defence bill to send to Congress, along with the terms of the National Security Council the president announced. Officials calculate the opposition will find it difficult to reject legislation strengthening the defence of national interests.

The issue emerged at an adverse moment for the government's economic agenda, little more than a year before the 2027 presidential elections. Unemployment tops Argentines' concerns at 36%, ahead of corruption and inflation; arrears on credit to individuals reached 17.5% in June, and 60% of respondents in another survey expect their personal situation to worsen in coming months. Peronist lawmakers are preparing a session in the Chamber of Deputies on Wednesday on maintaining treatment for people with disabilities and relief measures for indebted households.

The United Kingdom has administered the archipelago since 1833 and Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed retaining British overseas territory status, with three votes against. Milei's speech followed remarks by Donald Trump, who said he reviews “every position” when asked about sovereignty over the islands, without committing to any decision.

World.title: Falklands: Lords confirm UK’s unwavering support for Islanders right to self-determination
World.content:
Falklands: Lords confirm UK’s unwavering support for Islanders right to self-determination

8th Tuesday, September 2026 - 10:00 UTC Full article

Baroness Winterton, “we have made clear to Argentina that the measures announced by president Milei will not change the UK’s unwavering commitment to the Islands”.

The issue of President Javier Milei’s speech last week with its threats to the Falkland Islands, Islanders right to self-determination and the Islands’ right to develop its resource, was addressed by the House of Lords on Monday.

Lord Callanan made a question on the matter to Baroness Winterton, who repeatedly replied on UK’s unwavering support for the Islanders and the Islands.

Lord Callanan, C, said, “my Lords I beg leave to ask a question of which I have given prior notice, the question is as follows, ‘To ask her Majesty’s government what recent discussions they have had, if any, with one, the government of Argentina and two, the government of the United States pertaining to the future of the Falkland Islands and what steps they are taking to ensure the security of those Islands.

Baroness Winterton of Doncaster, and Under Secretary of State for the Indo-Pacific, FCDO replied, My Lords, the UK remains steadfast in its support for the Islanders right to self-determination. This is not the first time Argentina has made economic threats against the Falklands.

These threats have not prevented the community’s remarkable economic development and we have made clear to Argentina that the measures announced by president Milei will not change the UK’s unwavering commitment to the Islands.

The United States is our closest ally, they can have no doubt about our unwavering support for the Islanders.

World.title: Germany: why AfD won in Saxony Anhalt, and what happens next
World.content:
Germany: why AfD won in Saxony Anhalt, and what happens next

8th Tuesday, September 2026 - 09:21 UTC Full article

The polarized nature of the election, with 41% of voters surveyed beforehand wanting an AfD-led government but 46% favouring one led by the CDU, had some surprising effects

By Ed Turner (*)



The results of Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state election on September 6 were far worse than feared for the country’s mainstream political parties. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came close to winning a majority of votes, with 43.8%. This was about 4% higher than polls had suggested.

Support for the centre-right Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU), on the other hand, imploded. It won 17.2% of the vote, down from 37.1% in 2021, performing substantially worse than predicted.

At nearly 78%, turnout was up substantially compared with 2021 – in a way that helped the AfD. Analysis suggests the growth in its support came mostly from former non-voters, joined by a substantial number of erstwhile CDU supporters.

The polarized nature of the election, with 41% of voters surveyed beforehand wanting an AfD-led government but 46% favouring one led by the CDU, had some surprising effects. One was that it flattered the social democratic SPD and the Greens.

Both the SPD and Greens received tactical support from CDU and Left Party voters to make sure they reached the 5% of votes required to win seats in the state parliament.

The AfD, which has sais it would only seek to govern if it had a majority, now has several paths to seeing its candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, elected as Saxony-Anhalt’s minister president. Most likely is a deal with the Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW), a party that combines left-wing economic policies with conservative ones on topics such as migration.

On election night, the BSW made clear it had “overlaps” with AfD positions in some areas and that it would be “completely undemocratic” for the AfD to be excluded entirely from government.

If this failed, some support from the CDU would be a further route. The election of minister president is a secret ballot, and several CDU MPs reelected on Sunday have a long history of suggesting there should be more openness to working with the AfD.

Support across society



The AfD did best in Saxony-Anhalt among working-class voters (59%), as well as those with a lower level of education (57%) and those who perceived their economic situation as bad (65%). But even among graduates (30%) and voters who saw themselves in a good economic situation (37%), the AfD performed respectably.

It also secured over 40% of support among all age groups apart from the over 70s (31%). So the AfD can really claim to be a Volkspartei or “people’s party”, with support from across society, across the state.

By no means was this a single-issue election. Exit polls revealed immigration was one motivating factor for AfD voters, with 91% of them agreeing with the statement that they “were very worried too many foreign people live in Germany”. But so too was concern with security and the economy.

There was also real dissatisfaction (66% of all voters) at the state government, which had been led by the CDU since 2002. But the standing of Friedrich Merz’ government in Berlin was worse, with 83% taking the view it was insufficiently concerned with the problems of ordinary people. Just 20% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt trust it to improve the country substantially in the coming years.

Accompanying these sentiments, which can be found across Germany albeit more strongly in Saxony-Anhalt and other eastern states, there is a strand of dissatisfaction particular to the east. Seventy-three percent of all voters in Saxony-Anhalt believed easterners were still second-class citizens in many situations.

This view is taken by 83% of AfD voters. The AfD has been rather successful in mobilising grievances about reunification and some nostalgia about the days of the communist East Germany.

Assuming the AfD does form a government, there will be close scrutiny of the extent to which it can implement its hard-right manifesto – and, indeed, whether it confirms the view of German intelligence that the party is demonstrably “right wing extremist” in the state.

In fields such as education, culture, law and order and public broadcasting it will go on the front foot, though there may well be persistent legal challenges to more radical measures. These include attempts to force teachers to represent particular ideological positions in schools.

The AfD will also use its position for further publicity, and of course each time it is blocked from realising its aims by courts or other parties, it can claim to be a victim of establishment stitch-ups. This is a common populist tactic.

Wider political consequences



The results make Merz’s position even harder. Already as unpopular as any German chancellor has ever been, he stands no prospect of any boost from the state election in Mecklenburg West Pomerania on September 21. That election is set to be a clear battle between the AfD and SPD.
