On the same day, the state of Berlin, with its highly fragmented politics, might offer the chance of a first-place finish for Merz’s CDU on a low vote-share. But that would not be a game-changer.

Crucially, many of his MPs will demand changes. Most will push for a rightward shift to close down an open flank the AfD can exploit. But that can hardly be achieved in coalition with its current coalition partner, the SPD.

Others will push for reopen major reform packages, such as pensions, slated for decision in the Autumn, noting the loss of ground among working-class voters. However, that would rub up against Merz’s analysis of what Germany needs to do to get its faltering economy back on track.

Saxony-Anhalt may be asking a very hard question not just of Merz, but of German society: is the country now so fragmented politically that it is becoming almost ungovernable?

Coalitions of easy bedfellows (Christian Democrats with Liberals or Social Democrats with Greens) would barely get 25% of the vote at a federal election. So mainstream parties are forced to form governments with parties with whom they fundamentally disagree simply in order to keep the AfD out.

These governments quarrel, they put off decisions as they cannot agree, and they collapse. And from this negative dynamic, the AfD is able to profit.

World.title: Jaguar-Land Rover will cut 4.000 jobs to compete with Chinese electric carmakers
World.content:
Jaguar-Land Rover will cut 4.000 jobs to compete with Chinese electric carmakers

8th Tuesday, September 2026 - 04:29 UTC Full article

Falkland Islands are considered the land of the ‘Landy’ Rover

Jaguar Land Rover announced on Monday it will cut 4,000 jobs across its global workforce as it tries to cut costs and compete with Chinese electric carmakers. Britain’s biggest automaker said the job cuts will take place over the next two years as it targets 1.7 billion pounds (US$2.3 billion) in savings to make it more competitive as the industry transitions to electrification.

“The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty,” chief executive PB Balaji said in a statement.

The job cuts and savings will help the company invest 15 to 18 billion pounds (US$ 20-24 billion) over the next five years in electrification, digital technologies and other areas, he added.

Jaguar Land Rover, which makes the Range Rover, Discovery and other luxury SUVs, has faced pressure amid intense competition from cheaper Chinese EVs, soaring costs and the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Its sales were also hit last year when a cyberattack forced it to halt production for a month.

The company, owned by India’s Tata Motors, makes most of its cars in factories across the U.K. It employs around 34,000 people in the country and the majority of the job cuts are expected to affect its U.K. operations.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said Monday that while market conditions are challenging for the automotive sector globally, Britain’s government will not consider a bailout for Jaguar Land Rover.

World.title: The Falklands pay tribute in London to the merchant seafarers who served in 1982
World.content:
The Falklands pay tribute in London to the merchant seafarers who served in 1982

7th Monday, September 2026 - 19:26 UTC Full article

Hyslop with Lord West of Spithead (central) and Chris Locke (right), former Royal Fleet Auxiliary (RFA) Chief Officer, Marine Officer, alongside other attendees at the Navy Day Memorial

The Falkland Islands Government Representative to the United Kingdom and Europe, Richard Hyslop, laid a wreath on Sunday on behalf of the people and Government of the islands during the annual Merchant Navy Day service held at Trinity Square Gardens in London.

The ceremony took place at the Falkland Islands Memorial, within the grounds of the Merchant Navy Memorial. Hyslop was joined by veterans of the South Atlantic Medal Association, which brings together those who served in the 1982 conflict, and by Lord West of Spithead, patron of the Merchant Navy Association, a former First Sea Lord and himself a veteran of that campaign. Also present was Chris Locke, a former Royal Fleet Auxiliary chief officer who served as Falkland Islands Marine Officer and Harbour Master.

“Each year, we pause to remember the service and sacrifice of merchant seafarers who served during the Falklands War to defend the freedom and right to self-determination of Islanders,” Hyslop said. “We remain hugely grateful to the Merchant Navy, both past and present, for their invaluable role in supporting the Falklands and allowing our modern Islands to prosper.”

The commemoration falls each year on September 3, the date on which the SS Athenia was sunk in 1939, the first British merchant vessel lost in the Second World War. The Red Ensign, the merchant navy's flag, is flown in recognition of a sector that carries more than 90% of the United Kingdom's trade.

During the 1982 conflict, the British Ministry of Defence requisitioned or chartered dozens of civilian vessels under the arrangement known as Ships Taken Up From Trade, among them the liners Canberra and Queen Elizabeth 2, used as troop transports. The costliest episode was the loss of the Atlantic Conveyor, a converted container ship struck by a missile on May 25, 1982, which sank with the loss of twelve lives, including that of its master, Ian North. Heavy-lift helicopters intended for the land campaign went down with her.

Maritime transport remains central to the archipelago, which depends on shipping for its supplies and for the export of its fisheries production, the main source of income for its economy.

World.title: A port dispute in Montevideo blocks a second ferry operator on the Buenos Aires route
World.content:
A port dispute in Montevideo blocks a second ferry operator on the Buenos Aires route

7th Monday, September 2026 - 19:20 UTC Full article

Port of Montevideo

Uruguayan ferry company Colonia Express obtained authorisation from the Ministry of Transport and Public Works at the end of July to operate the passenger and vehicle route between Montevideo and Buenos Aires, but cannot begin the service because the only ramp at the Montevideo port suitable for unloading cars belongs to Buquebus, the company that currently runs the crossing alone.

A pontoon of this kind is the floating platform that allows vehicles carried in ships' holds to be loaded and unloaded. The one at the Maciel pier was built by Buquebus after it obtained the passenger terminal concession in 1996, and ceased to form part of public infrastructure in 2016, when the National Ports Administration terminated that concession. Colonia Express is asking the authorities to establish shared use; Buquebus opposes it.

Sources at the National Ports Administration told the Montevideo newspaper El País the matter is one “between private parties” and that the body has received no formal documentation on the authorisation. They said any ferry operation may use public berths or be agreed privately, but that the pontoon is not part of the authority's pier, so the decision on its use rests with its owner. Ministry officials said the file is within its review period and that administrative appeals are under way.

Colonia Express director Sebastián Planas announced the company will go to court seeking an injunction against both the ministry and the ports authority. “The ministry must respond to us and give us a solution, but on the other hand it is the ports authority that should require Buquebus to share the pontoon or remove it,” he told the outlet El Observador. The company also argues the state of the Maciel pier does not allow a second platform to be installed, and it aims to operate during the coming summer season.

The pier, 380 metres long with a five-metre draught, has dredging problems and maintenance shortfalls that cause periods of inactivity. A tender for its reconstruction is under way, with specifications still being drawn up. In March, the National Ports Administration declared of interest a private initiative submitted by Buquebus to rebuild the pier and modernise the terminal, valued at between 66 and 100 million dollars with a concession estimated at fifty years. That declaration gives the company preference in the tender process.

Between January and July, more than 500,000 passengers and 57,000 vehicles crossed the River Plate on this route. Buquebus, owned by Argentine businessman Juan Carlos López Mena, recorded 70,000 more boarding and disembarking movements than in the same period last year. Colonia Express has operated since 2007. The company has made no public statement on the pontoon.

World.title: The Falklands claim, one of the few issues that cuts across Argentina's political divide
World.content:
The Falklands claim, one of the few issues that cuts across Argentina's political divide

7th Monday, September 2026 - 09:10 UTC Full article

President Javier Milei addressed the nation on Thursday following Donald Trump's remarks about a possible review of US neutrality

The sovereignty claim over the Falklands is one of the few points of consensus that cuts across Argentina's political fracture, known locally as “la grieta”, a polarisation that splits the country into two opposing camps on almost every public question. That cross-cutting quality explains both its constant presence in popular culture and its recurrence in political discourse.

Political scientist Mariana Altieri, author of a comparative study of the archipelago and Gibraltar, links that centrality to Argentina's founding narrative. “When Argentina became independent from Spain, the islands were part of it and then they were taken from us, and that is associated with Argentina's trauma, with what could have been and is not,” she says. Anthropologist Rosana Guber, a researcher at Conicet and a specialist on the 1982 conflict, suggests understanding it as a symbol comparable to the flag or the anthem: “They speak to people who may hold different positions on everything else.”

The attachment is strongest in the far south. In Río Grande, less than 600 kilometres from the islands and almost 12,800 from British shores, the outline of the archipelago appears on school uniforms, sports kit and numerous murals. The anthem of Tierra del Fuego province is the March of the Malvinas, and the vigil held every April 1 draws up to 20,000 people, according to historian Esteban Rodríguez.

Concrete knowledge of the territory, by contrast, is limited. Journalist Nicolás Cassese, who has travelled to the archipelago three times, estimates that fewer than 1% of Argentines have visited it. “Of Messi and Maradona we have an enormous amount of information, and of the islands we know almost nothing,” he says. He recounts that when he published a novel set in Stanley some readers did not recognise the place name, and notes the settlement was founded in 1845, when the British already administered the islands, and that Argentines themselves used that name for decades.

That consensus has made political use easier. President Javier Milei addressed the nation on Thursday following Donald Trump's remarks about a possible review of US neutrality, announcing sanctions on companies operating in the area without Argentine authorisation and the construction of a military base in the south. The opposition noted that a 2011 law already provides for such sanctions and that construction of the base had begun before his own government halted it. The La Plata veterans' centre criticised his use of the claim as a “lifebelt”. In 2025 Milei had argued that islanders should decide: “We hope the islanders choose to vote for us with their feet.” Altieri describes Thursday's speech as “a 180-degree turn”.

The United Kingdom has administered the archipelago since 1833 and maintains that its status depends on the wishes of its inhabitants. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to remain a British overseas territory, with three votes against.

World.title: An Argentine court returns an 18th-century work to the heirs of a Jewish art dealer
World.content:
An Argentine court returns an 18th-century work to the heirs of a Jewish art dealer

7th Monday, September 2026 - 09:01 UTC Full article

An Argentine federal court on Friday ordered the return of the painting Portrait of a Lady to the family of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, almost 90 years after the Nazi regime looted his collection in Amsterdam. The work surfaced last year at a house in Mar del Plata, 400 kilometres from Buenos Aires.

The ruling was issued at a hearing chaired by federal judge Santiago Inchausti, attended by prosecutors, the heir's lawyers and the defendants. Patricia Kadgien and her husband, Juan Carlos Cortegoso, had been accused of possessing and concealing a work of art stolen in the context of a genocide. After initially arguing they were the legitimate owners by inheritance, they accepted an agreement with prosecutors to avoid trial and irrevocably renounced any right over the painting. The deal includes a donation of 4.8 million pesos, around 3,200 dollars, to the support association of a maternal and child hospital. Prosecutor Carlos Martínez said the outcome amounts to “a reparation of a historic character for the victims”.

Patricia Kadgien is the daughter of Friedrich Kadgien, an SS member and financial expert for the National Socialist regime from 1938, with a prominent role in currency purchases and in the plunder of occupied territories. A 1945 US report described him as “a snake of the worst kind”. He fled to Switzerland, then Brazil and finally Argentina, where he established himself as a businessman and died in 1978 without ever facing trial.

The discovery came through a property listing. In August 2025, marking eighty years since the end of the Second World War, the Dutch newspaper Algemeen Dagblad sent correspondent Peter Schouten to Mar del Plata to try to contact Kadgien's daughters. No one answered, but he noticed a for-sale sign on the front of the house. Searching for the listing on the estate agency's website, he found among the interior photographs the painting hanging in the living room. The couple were held for 72 hours until they handed the work over.

The piece is an oil on canvas measuring 119.5 by 89 centimetres. Goudstikker's records attributed it to Giuseppe Ghislandi, but analysis by Argentina's National Academy of Fine Arts confirmed it is by Giacomo Ceruti, the 18th-century Italian painter known as Il Pitocchetto. Its market value is estimated at around 250,000 euros.

The painting will be handed to Marei von Saher, the dealer's daughter-in-law, who has spent decades tracing pieces from the collection of more than 1,100 works. Through her lawyers she said she does not accept “86 years of plunder” but is not seeking revenge or compensation. Her intention is for the painting to be exhibited on loan at a museum in Buenos Aires before its return. It remains in the custody of Argentina's Supreme Court.

World.title: Alfonso Cuarón enters the gothic-horror realm of Dungeons & Dragons
World.content:
Alfonso Cuarón, the Mexico City-born director of “Y tu mamá también” and “Roma,” is heading back to Netflix — this time to executive produce a series set in the gothic-horror world of Dungeons & Dragons.

“Ravenloft” is a live-action series set in the Dungeons & Dragons universe that follows the transformation of Strahd von Zarovich into the evil Darklord, the vampire ruler of Barovia.

According to Deadline and other reports last week, Cuarón, 64, will executive produce through London-based Esperanto Filmoj, the company he co-founded in 2002. (Filmoj is an Esperanto word meaning “films.”)

The series marks Cuarón’s return to Netflix, which showcased his semi-biographical “Roma” in late 2018 following a short release in theaters — a flashpoint in the early debate over streaming films’ theatrical releases.

The black-and-white drama, set in Mexico City of the early 1970s, went on to earn Netflix its first Academy Award best-picture nomination, among 10 total nominations. It lost to “Green Book” for best picture, but did win Oscars for best director, best cinematography and best foreign language film, now called best international feature film.

“Ravenloft” is being written by John August, whose background in gothic fantasy is a good fit for the series’ horror and dark-romance premise. His co-writing credentials include five Tim Burton films, including “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” “Corpse Bride” and “Dark Shadows.”

What is Ravenloft?

Watch this video on YouTube

First introduced in 1983, Ravenloft became one of the tabletop game’s best-known settings. Its realm of Barovia is a mist-shrouded gothic-horror world ruled by Strahd, who is both its tyrant and its prisoner.

The project is separate from “The Forgotten Realms,” a previously announced Netflix Dungeons & Dragons series no longer in development.

For “Ravenloft,” Netflix has not announced a cast, director, production start date or release date. Late 2027 would be the earliest plausible release time, though 2028 is more realistic.

Cuarón won Oscars for directing and editing the 2013 space thriller “Gravity,” becoming the first Mexican-born winner of the Best Director award. He had already directed “Y tu mamá también” (2001), “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban” (2004) and “Children of Men” (2006). He co-wrote “Y tu mamá” with his brother, Carlos.

More recently, he wrote, directed and executive produced the limited series “Disclaimer,” and he is also co-writing and executive-producing the forthcoming drama “Ascension,” both for Apple TV.

With reports from Excélsior, EFE and Deadline

World.title: 2 years into operations, Olmeca Refinery reports its best month yet
World.content:
The Olmeca Refinery in the Gulf coast state of Tabasco had its best-ever month for fuel production in July, according to data from the state oil company Pemex.

The refinery, built on the Tabasco coast during Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency, produced an average of 252,498 barrels of fuel per day in July.

That figure — which includes premium and regular gasoline as well as diesel, among other fuels — represented a 78.8% increase compared to June and an annual gain of 62.4%. Production of regular and premium gasoline rose even more sharply at the Olmeca Refinery in July, increasing 127.9% on a month-over-month basis and 89.5% annually to reach an average of 108,548 barrels per day (bpd).

The sharp increases in production in July came after refinery equipment was restored and upgraded between April and June. A number of fires have occurred at the US $21 billion facility, including in March, April and July of this year.

Output from the Olmeca Refinery in July exceeded 200,000 bpd across an entire month for just the third time. López Obrador inaugurated the refinery, located at the Dos Bocas port, in July 2022, even though it was unfinished and not refining crude at the time.

The facility is one of seven refineries operated by Pemex in Mexico. The Salina Cruz Refinery had the highest output in July, followed by Olmeca, which contributed 21.2% of Pemex’s total production of 1.19 million bpd of fuel in July.

Olmeca had its second-best month for crude processing in July

Pemex data also shows that the Olmeca Refinery processed an average of just under 229,000 barrels of heavy Maya crude per day in July. That figure represented a 62.2% month-over-month increase and a 53.9% year-over-year gain. The only month when the Olmeca Refinery processed a larger quantity of crude was last December. Before July, its processing volumes declined on a sequential basis during six consecutive months.

The Olmeca Refinery only refines heavy “Maya” crude, whereas other Pemex facilities also process light and super light crude. In July, it was Pemex’s second-largest refiner after the Salina Cruz Refinery, which processed an average of 246,838 barrels of crude per day. Pemex’s seven refineries in Mexico collectively processed an average of 1.22 million bpd of crude in July.

At full capacity, the Olmeca Refinery can process 340,000 bpd of crude. The processing volume it achieved in July represented 67.3% of that capacity.

With reports from La Jornada, Imagen Radio, El CEO and El Financiero

World.title: 16 presumed Los Ardillos cartel members arrested in Guerrero
World.content:
Guerrero state authorities took into custody 16 cartel members linked to the “Los Ardillos” crime gang as part of an operation deployed after the dismembered body of a vacationing National Guard member was identified along the Mexico City-Acapulco highway.

The Guerrero Attorney General’s Office (FGE) reported the arrest of the 16 people, the result of a coordinated response carried out on Sept. 5 along with the Army, the National Guard and state police.

On Sunday afternoon, the Defense Ministry (Defensa) confirmed the FGE report about the arrest of the alleged cartel members in the towns of Pablo Galeana, Río Verde and Xaltianguis, all within the municipality of Acapulco.

Among those apprehended was a person identified as Los Ardillos’ “financial operator.”

Among four mangled bodies discovered was that of National Guardsman Eduardo Bustos, who was off-duty. Prior to being murdered, Bustos was apparently forced to film a video in which he stated that state security agents — identifying two by name — receive payments of up to 600,000 pesos per month (US $35,500) from the “Los Tlacos” crime gang to harass their rivals in Guerrero, Los Ardillos.

Defensa issued a statement confirming the death of the guardsman, condemning the violence in Guerrero and “reaffirming its commitment to collaborate closely with civilian authorities in the investigations to clarify the facts, including the circumstances surrounding the statements” made by Bustos in the video.

Also in Guerrero, feds raid and dismantle 3 meth labs

Federal forces deployed in the state of Guerrero located and dismantled three clandestine laboratories used to produce methamphetamine, officials announced over the weekend.

In a statement on social media, federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said the three drug labs were situated in remote areas in the mountainous state. He praised the Army for the successful operations in “inaccessible, high-risk places.”

Two of the labs were in Zirándaro de los Chávez and one in Coahuayutla de José María Izazaga. García Harfuch did not specify when the operations took place.

A trove of drug-producing chemicals and equipment was seized, including more than 260 200-liter drums, 11 500-liter containers, nine reactors, more than 60 gas tanks, 150 sacks of caustic soda, 663 kg of ammonium chloride, approximately 2,400 kg of chemical substances, reactors, condensers, distillers and approximately 1,000 kg of chemical precursors.

Besides ingredients and equipment used for drug production, the operation seized 12 firearms, more than 36,700 cartridges, 17 doses of methamphetamine, 10 slot machines, two motorcycles and a vehicle.

With reports from Milenio, El Financiero, Proceso and Infobae

World.title: After renaming the Gulf and a Great Lake, Trump proposes a ‘more prestigious and beautiful’ name for New Mexico
World.content:
The Gulf of America, Lake America and … New America?

U.S. President Donald Trump has already renamed the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” for U.S. federal purposes. Similarly, Trump renamed Lake Ontario, which straddles the U.S.-Canada border, “Lake America.”

Now, he would apparently like to rename New Mexico “New America,” even though he has no legal authority to change the name of a U.S. state.

Trump shared a map of the U.S. border state to his Truth Social account on Sunday. On the map, the word “Mexico” in “New Mexico” is crossed out and below it appears “America.”

Trump subsequently shared an AI-generated video showing him putting an “America” sticker over “Mexico” on a “Welcome to New Mexico” sign. Above the video, he wrote:

“Many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote-cheating states of all time, to NEW AMERICA. So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State. Wow, I Love It!!! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Trump kept up his social media campaign on Monday, posting another map with New Mexico labeled as “New America.”

On Sunday, New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Gresham rejected the president’s suggestion that the state she governs could be renamed.

“New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate — it’s been ours since before the United States existed. What is up for debate? Who’s showing up for working families,” Lujan Grisham wrote on X.

“… While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo México is busy doing the work,” she wrote.

New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate — it’s been ours since before the United States existed. What is up for debate? Who’s showing up for working families. While the President tries to distract Americans from his disastrous war in Iran, gas prices keep soaring. Americans are… pic.twitter.com/tnX1gPItDH — Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham (@GovMLG) September 6, 2026

The New York Times reported on Monday that “Mr. Trump has no legal authority to rename any state, which in New Mexico’s case is written into its Constitution.”

“Any proposed change would have to originate within the state, a prospect that New Mexico’s Democratic leaders rejected forcefully on Sunday,” the newspaper reported.

The Times also wrote that the origins of New Mexico’s name predate the founding of the United States.

“In the 16th century, Mexicans called the territory north and west of the Rio Grande ‘New Mexico,’ according to the Bureau of Indian Affairs,” the Times reported.

Most of the land that now makes up New Mexico, as well as all of California, Nevada and Utah and parts of several other modern-day U.S. states, was ceded to the United States by Mexico under the terms of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which ended the Mexican-American War of 1846–48. New Mexico’s southwestern corner was acquired by the U.S. later, in the 1853 Gadsden Purchase.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Fireworks blast in México state kills 10, injures dozens more
World.content:
At least 10 people were killed and 82 wounded after an unknown quantity of fireworks detonated during a celebration for a patron saint in the town of Santa María Canchesdá, in the municipality of Temascalcingo, México state.

Local authorities said the explosion occurred at around 9:30 p.m. on Saturday night in the vicinity of the Nuestra Señora de la Luz (Our Lady of Light) church. Temascalcingo, a municipality of 66,000 residents, is located around 160 kilometers northwest of Mexico City.

Videos shared online show festival attendees carrying a straw bull, with fireworks shooting from the effigy. Shortly after, additional fireworks being stored next to the church ignited, which caused a roof and a nearby wall to collapse, burying several people in the rubble.

“It is with profound sorrow that I received the news of what happened in Santa María Canchesdá, Temascalcingo,” México state native and president of the Senate, Higinio Martínez Miranda, announced on social media.

“I contacted the mayor to reiterate my full support and offer my assistance… My solidarity and most sincere condolences go out to the families who are facing the loss of their loved ones. To those who were injured, I wish a speedy recovery.” Governor Delfina Gómez also communicated her condolences.

Hundreds of people from over 40 nearby communities were preparing to watch the fireworks display as part of the annual religious festival when the explosion occurred.

Civil Protection authorities, firefighters, state police and paramedics were quickly mobilized and continued recovering bodies from the debris and working to remove the collapsed structures until the early hours of Sunday morning.

Two priests were injured but are expected to survive, according to the diocese of the nearby municipality of Atlacomulco. Of the 82 total people treated, 62 have already been discharged, eight remain hospitalized and 11 have been referred to other medical facilities.

The state Attorney General’s Office has initiated an investigation into the cause of the accident.

This is not the first time that the storage of fireworks has turned deadly in Mexico. In 2016, an explosion at a fireworks warehouse in Tultepec, México state, killed 42 people.

With reports from Al Jazeera, CNN, NMás, Sol de México and Quadratín México

World.title: Mexico’s foreign affairs head seeks common ground with China in Beijing
World.content:
Mexico’s Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on Monday, marking Velasco’s first official trip to the Asian country and signaling hope for improved political and economic cooperation amid an ongoing trade dispute.

The visit to China takes place under the shadow of trade tensions stemming from the tariffs Mexico applied in January to imports from countries without a free trade agreement, including China.

The package modified duties for 1,463 tariff lines across 17 sectors — with rates of up to 50%. Beijing has questioned the decision, while Mexican authorities maintain that it is not directed at any particular country.

However, a statement issued by the Foreign Affairs Ministry (SRE) downplayed the trade topic, instead describing the meeting as an opportunity to discuss mechanisms for strengthening political, economic, cultural and academic exchanges between Mexico and China.

Velasco highlighted the Mexican government’s readiness to maintain a constructive relationship with China, based on mutual respect, equal sovereignty and non-interference.

The Mexican official proposed strengthening the political consultation mechanism between the two foreign ministries in order to maintain communication and make progress on concrete agreements.

The areas of cooperation highlighted by Mexico include health, education, scholarships, science, technological innovation, the environment, rural development, and cultural exchanges.

The SRE indicated that both parties examined options to expand ties in these areas and leverage existing opportunities for collaboration.

During the meeting, Velasco highlighted coordination between Mexico and China in multilateral forums, including the Group of 20 (G-20) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. He also acknowledged China’s role as host of the upcoming APEC leaders’ summit, scheduled for November in Shenzhen.

Regarding culture, Velasco noted that artistic exchanges offer valuable opportunities to deepen mutual understanding between the two peoples and highlighted the exhibition “On Top of the World Tree: Ancient Civilizations of the Americas” at the Shanghai Museum, which brings together nearly 3,000 archaeological and artistic pieces from Mexico.

Velasco’s trip to China includes the inauguration of the Mexican Consulate in Chongqing, one of the major cities in the western part of the country.

With reports from La Silla Rota

World.title: Trump says Mexico is only good for ‘tamales and tomatoes.’ Trade data says otherwise
World.content:
Listen to this article

U.S. President Donald Trump reasserted on Friday that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs — apart from “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” — and therefore the U.S. could cease trading with its southern neighbor.

However, Trump said he didn’t want to end trade with Mexico — a country that sent more than US $60 billion worth of exports to the U.S. in July alone — “because we get along very well” with President Claudia Sheinbaum.

🇺🇸🇲🇽 Donald Trump aseguró que México no tiene “nada que ofrecer” a Estados Unidos más allá de “tamales y tomates”, al hablar sobre su política comercial desde el Despacho Oval. Pese a la declaración, el presidente estadounidense descartó por ahora interrumpir el comercio con… — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) September 4, 2026

His remarks from the Oval Office came just hours after he threatened in a social media post to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT,” among which is Mexico, if the U.S. Federal Reserve doesn’t lower its benchmark interest rate, which is currently set at 3.50%-3.75%.

“The Fed Board, with its great new leader [Kevin Warsh], must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen!” Trump wrote on Truth Social ahead of the Fed’s next interest rate decision on Sept. 16.

Later on Friday, the U.S. president told reporters that “we could do tremendous good for ourselves by just not trading with countries.”

“We lose with the European Union $200 billion a year. If I didn’t trade with them, we’d lose nothing — just one swipe of the pen,” Trump said.

“We lose with Mexico $195 billion a year,” he said, referring to the United States’ trade deficit with its southern neighbor in 2025.

“… They have nothing that we have to have — I mean hot tamales, tomatoes, a couple of things,” Trump said.

“But basically they have nothing that we need. We have oil, we have everything,” he said, adding that he didn’t want to end trade with Mexico “because we get along very well with the president.”

“We like the president, [we] respect her a lot, but if we didn’t want to trade with Mexico, if we didn’t want to trade with Canada, we’d save from $60 billion to $90 billion a year, just by not trading with Canada,” Trump said.

The U.S. president has previously asserted that the United States doesn’t need anything from Mexico and Canada, its two largest trade partners.

“With Mexico and Canada we have trade deficits. We should have surpluses with them. We don’t need their cars, we don’t need their lumber, we don’t need their energy, we don’t need anything that they have,” Trump said on June 10, the same day that he declared that he wasn’t seeking to renew the USMCA free trade pact.

Three weeks later, the United States announced that it had declined to renew the trilateral agreement in its “current form,” a move that paved the way for annual reviews of the USMCA, which remains in force.

Trump’s assertion that Mexico has “nothing” that the United States needs collides with the reality that the U.S. and Mexican economies are highly integrated and that Mexico ships huge quantities of goods to its northern neighbor on a daily basis. Among Mexico’s exports to the U.S. are vehicles, auto parts, machinery, medical devices, AI servers, alcoholic beverages and fresh food, including tomatoes.

In July alone, Mexico exported goods worth $60.55 billion to the United States, according to the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. in the first seven months of 2026 were worth $358.7 billion, an increase of 16% compared to the same period of last year.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: MND Local: Sheinbaum and Lemus tackle water crisis amid power outages in Guadalajara
World.content:
This week, we have some positive developments to report on the water crisis in Guadalajara, while electrical outages across the Guadalajara Metro Area (GMA) are becoming more serious.

Sheinbaum discussed Guadalajara’s water crisis with Lemus on a recent visit to Jalisco

On Aug. 26, the governor of Jalisco, Pablo Lemus, met with President Claudia Sheinbaum on her visit to Zapopan, where she voiced her support for badly needed hydraulic infrastructure projects to solve the GMA’s water crisis. Sheinbaum was visiting Jalisco to speak at a graduation ceremony and welcome new officers at the Air Force College in Zapopan.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pablo Lemus Navarro (@pablolemusn)

It was reported that more than 22 billion pesos will be allocated through a combination of federal and state investment, along with additional funds from private sources. Following the meeting, Lemus thanked President Sheinbaum for supporting “the major infrastructure projects that Jalisco needs, especially those that will help us resolve water issues in the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area.”

Governor Lemus further clarified that the federal government plans to invest roughly 5 billion pesos to overhaul the El Zapotillo system to optimize water flow and enable it to operate at a maximum capacity of up to 3,000 liters per second. At the state level, the Jalisco government will invest 7.5 billion pesos in the modernization of the Miravalle Water Treatment Plant No. 1 and construct a Chapala-Guadalajara replacement aqueduct for an estimated cost of 10 billion pesos, leveraging a public-private partnership scheme called CMRO.

Billions in pesos pledged for infrastructure to ease long-standing shortages

For impatient residents anxious to know when the water coming from their taps will improve, Lemus said that gradual improvements will start to become noticeable by this October, with additional gains by the first quarter of 2027.

Last June, in response to mounting public pressure, state leaders announced a plan with more than 30 separate measures aimed at addressing the city’s water crisis. At the time, state leaders said a definitive solution to the current water challenges would require an infrastructure investment of more than 20 billion pesos and a multiyear time horizon.

Some of these projects have yet to be approved by Jalisco’s state congress. Despite continuing questions as to where the funds will come from, Lemus continues to insist that the state will not take on debt, the municipal water system will not be privatized, and water rates will not be increased.

Building a better relationship

Before last week’s meeting, Lemus and Sheinbaum (who do not share the same political party) spent months trading verbal jabs over who was responsible for the city’s water mess. At one point, Lemus claimed the state wasn’t a high priority in Sheinbaum’s federal budget, noting at the time it had received “Zero pesos, zero cents from the federal government … for any infrastructure project in Jalisco. Not for highways, not for water infrastructure, not for anything.”

In response, Sheinbaum defended federal efforts to clean up the Lerma and Santiago rivers to reduce health impacts to those in the GMA who live nearby. She also urged Lemus to take ownership of the problem.

Fortunately for the residents of Guadalajara, their recent in-person meeting appears to have put the relationship on better footing, which will be essential to solving the city’s water woes.

Multiple GMA neighborhoods suffer power outages of up to 20 hours a day

While most of Guadalajara’s news headlines continue to focus on the city’s serious water problems, electricity has quietly crept up the list of concerns residents have about municipal infrastructure.

Long a favorite neighborhood of foreign residents, Providencia is now suffering from many of the same infrastructure issues that have historically plagued less desirable areas. Providencia encompasses Providencia Norte, Providencia Sur and Colomos Providencia. Residents in these areas report that dozens of blocks have been without power for multiple hours a day nearly every day, on top of the previously reported water issues.

The residents’ association president, Piero Vega, stated that when the power goes out, homes can be without electricity for up to 20 hours, causing damage to appliances and spoiling food, which is taking a toll on residents’ quality of life. In a recent interview with Mural newspaper, Vega noted the hardship these outages have put on the neighborhood’s elderly residents:

“Many of them have oxygen concentrators; many have diabetes medications. We have a serious problem with the products or things stored in refrigerators, and several people have already been affected by power surges and dips in their electronic devices.”

Grid strain and aging infrastructure fuel safety concerns

Electrical outages have also heightened feelings of insecurity in the neighborhood, as robberies and assaults across the city have been on the rise in 2026, even as the homicide rate declines.

“(The residents) are already afraid of everything when there is power; now it’s even worse without it, because when the houses lose power, the streets also go dark, and thieves … take whatever they can,” Vega observed.

A similar pattern has been unfolding in recent weeks to the north of Providencia, in north Zapopan. In Ecología Seattle and Colonia Los Maestros, multiple power outages lasting 15-plus hours at a time have left residents frazzled.

For its part, the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) has claimed the recent spate of outages is due to seasonal heavy rains and strong winds. While the storms have certainly done damage, many residents in the affected neighborhoods suspect other factors are in play, namely an overloading of the grid by new businesses, restaurants and power towers, along with inadequate maintenance on transformers and old equipment.

As a resident of this area myself, it is common to hear transformers blow out immediately preceding a power outage, whether there is a storm or not.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

01 A jobs report that changed the direction of travel

The August employment report landed on Friday and reset the debate. Payrolls rose 162,000 against a consensus near 56,000, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1%.

Revisions did as much work as the headline. June was lifted from 20,000 to 31,000, and July from a loss of 23,000 to a gain of 21,000.

Average hourly earnings rose 0.3% on the month to US$37.75, and 3.1% over the year. That pace is not consistent with inflation returning quickly to target.

Markets responded by pricing a rise rather than a cut. UBS moved to forecasting two quarter-point increases this year, in September and December. The shift began in late August, after Chair Kevin Warsh spoke at Jackson Hole.

02 Three central banks moving the same way

The European Central Bank meets on Thursday. Its main refinancing rate is 2.40% and the deposit rate 2.25%, after a quarter-point rise in June that was its first in three years.

The bank held in July and said the pause should not be read as the end of tightening. Markets expect a move to 2.50% this week.

The Bank of Japan holds at 1.0% after an eight to one vote on July 31, with Hajime Takata dissenting in favour of 1.25%. The next decision is on September 18, and yen strength on those expectations is what pushed the dollar index down 0.32% on Monday.

China supplied the week’s upside surprise. August exports rose about 25% from a year earlier on cars and high-technology goods, though imports fell short of forecasts.

03 Latin America’s squeeze: strong commodities, dearer capital

Most of the region did not trade on Monday. Brazil was closed for Independence Day and Wall Street was shut, leaving thin books everywhere else.

Colombia was the standout, with the COLCAP rising 0.82% to a record 2,565.37 and the peso firming to about 3,119 per dollar. Mexico slipped 0.21%, dragged by a 12.7% fall in Televisa after its removal from the index was flagged.

Chile closed flat at 11,451.80 even as copper set a record, because second-quarter output fell 0.2% and July mining production was down 9.3%. Argentina lost 0.50% in a session without foreign flow.

The regional problem is the rate outlook rather than the commodity outlook. Record copper and near-record oil help exporters, but a hiking Federal Reserve raises the cost of the capital that funds them.

What to watch today and this week

Tuesday: China’s August trade data, Chile’s rate decision with a hold at 4.50% expected, and Mexico’s 2027 budget package reaching Congress

China’s August trade data, Chile’s rate decision with a hold at 4.50% expected, and Mexico’s 2027 budget package reaching Congress Wednesday: China consumer and producer prices, with consensus at 0.9% and 3.2%, and Mexico’s full August inflation reading

China consumer and producer prices, with consensus at 0.9% and 3.2%, and Mexico’s full August inflation reading Thursday: the European Central Bank decision, United States producer prices, jobless claims, weekly crude inventories, China credit data and Argentina’s August inflation print

the European Central Bank decision, United States producer prices, jobless claims, weekly crude inventories, China credit data and Argentina’s August inflation print Friday: the United States August consumer price report at 8:30 in New York, the last major inflation reading before the Federal Reserve meets on September 16

the United States August consumer price report at 8:30 in New York, the last major inflation reading before the Federal Reserve meets on September 16 Ongoing: the Gulf tanker war, Iran’s talks with Oman over Hormuz shipping, and expected United States tariffs on refined copper imports

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are markets pricing a Federal Reserve rate rise?

August payrolls came in at 162,000 against expectations near 56,000, with earlier months revised up. Wage growth of 3.1% over the year points the same way.

What does a hiking Federal Reserve mean for Latin America?

It raises the cost of dollar funding and makes United States assets more competitive. That pressures regional currencies even when commodity prices are strong.

Why did gold fall while a war widened?

Gold pays no income, so higher real yields make it less attractive. This week rate expectations outweighed safe-haven demand.

Why was Latin America so quiet on Monday?

Wall Street was closed for Labour Day and Brazil for Independence Day. Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Argentina traded, but without their usual foreign flow.

What is the most important release this week?

Friday’s United States consumer price report for August. It is the last major inflation reading before the Federal Reserve meets on September 16.

World.title: Ghana Has Counted 8,578 Fibre Cuts This Year, and Paid US$20m to Mend Them
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

GHANA · BUSINESS

Key Facts —The count: Ghana has recorded 8,578 fibre-optic cable cuts so far in 2026, according to the communications minister, Samuel Nartey George. —The bill: More than US$20m spent by operators on repairs, money the minister said cannot go into new coverage. —Who is digging: Roads built under the government’s Big Push programme account for about 49% of the cuts. —The mining share: Illegal gold mining, known locally as galamsey, accounts for about 25%. —Where it ends: On the current trend Ghana would finish the year close to 9,000 incidents. —What follows: The National Communications Authority has been asked to prepare a framework for compensating customers hit by network failures.

Ghana fibre cuts have reached 8,578 so far in 2026 and cost telecommunications operators more than US$20m in repairs, the communications minister said on 7 September. Road building accounts for about half of them, and illegal gold mining for about a quarter.

What the Ghana fibre cuts figure actually measures

The number counts physical breaks in buried fibre-optic cable, the strands that carry mobile data, bank transactions and government services between Ghanaian cities. Each break is a repair crew, a trench and hours of degraded service for whoever sits behind it.

Samuel Nartey George gave the figure at the Government Accountability Series, the platform on which Ghanaian ministers report to the public, on Monday 7 September. He put the repair cost at more than US$20m for the year to date.

That is money the operators have already spent, not a projection. It is also money that does not become a new mast in a district that has none.

Roads and mining are doing most of the damage

About 49% of the cuts trace back to construction under the Big Push, the government’s flagship road programme, according to the minister. The state, in other words, is the largest single source of damage to its own digital backbone.

Illegal gold mining accounts for roughly a quarter more. Galamsey pits follow the same river valleys and roadsides that the cables do, and excavators working without permits do not consult utility maps.

The remainder is the ordinary mixture of accidental strikes, cable theft and weather. Together they push the country towards about 9,000 incidents by December if nothing changes.

Why an outside investor should care about a trench

Ghana has spent two years rebuilding its credibility with creditors, and the domestic bond market only reopened at the medium end this month. A digital economy is one of the few growth stories the country can tell that does not depend on gold, cocoa or oil.

That story rests on the cable. Mobile money, remittance corridors and the outsourcing jobs Accra is courting all sit on top of a network that is being cut roughly thirty times a week.

Repair spending is also a hidden tax on coverage. Every dollar mended is a dollar not laid, which slows the rollout in exactly the rural districts the government wants connected.

The galamsey problem keeps arriving in new places

Illegal mining has already been counted against Ghana’s forests, rivers and cocoa farms. The fibre figure adds a fourth ledger, and one that is easy to price.

It also complicates enforcement. A pit that damages a cable is a crime against a private operator as well as a breach of mining law, and the two cases rarely travel together.

What the regulator has been asked to do

The minister said the National Communications Authority will prepare a framework for customer remediation, meaning a route to compensation when service fails. That would move some of the cost of a cut from the subscriber back towards whoever caused it.

No timetable was given for the framework. Nor has the government said whether contractors on the Big Push will be made to carry the repair bill for cables they sever.

How the damage is repaired, and who waits

A cut cable is not a software fault that clears itself. A crew has to locate the break, expose the duct, splice the strands and test the span, and in the rainy season that work slows further.

Most subscribers experience it as a slow afternoon rather than an outage, because operators reroute traffic. The cost appears instead as capacity that was paid for twice.

Banks, mobile-money agents and government offices sit at the sharp end. A district office that cannot reach a national database stops issuing documents until the splice is done.

The regional comparison is not flattering

Nigeria has spent two years addressing the same problem, and its regulator designated telecommunications infrastructure as critical national infrastructure in an attempt to raise the penalties for damaging it. Broadband speeds there rose sharply once the fibre network stopped being cut so often.

Ghana has no equivalent designation in force. The remedy currently on the table is a compensation framework for customers, which addresses the symptom rather than the excavator.

That difference matters for anyone comparing the two markets. Network reliability is now a competitive variable between West African economies, not a technical footnote.

What to watch next

The first test is whether the year closes below 9,000 incidents or above them. The second is whether road contractors start paying for what they break.

A third measure matters more to investors: whether operator capital spending on new sites rises once the repair bill stops growing.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many fibre cuts has Ghana recorded in 2026? Ghana recorded 8,578 fibre-optic cable cuts in 2026 up to early September, according to Communications Minister Samuel Nartey George. On the current trend the year would end close to 9,000. How much have the Ghana fibre cuts cost? Telecommunications operators have spent more than US$20m repairing the damage so far this year. The minister said that money cannot then be used to expand coverage. What causes most of the damage? Road construction under the government’s Big Push programme accounts for about 49% of the cuts. Illegal gold mining, known as galamsey, accounts for about 25%. Will customers be compensated? The National Communications Authority has been asked to prepare a framework for customer remediation over network failures. No timetable for it has been announced. Why does this matter beyond Ghana? Fibre is the base layer for mobile money, banking and outsourcing work across West Africa. Repeated cuts raise the cost of every digital service built on top of them.

World.title: Trump Bombardier Threat Reads Well in Brazil, With Caveats
World.content:
BRAZIL · AEROSPACE

Key Facts — What happened Trump posted on Truth Social that Bombardier may no longer sell aircraft in the United States.

— The condition Unless it manufactures there. If they want our market, they must build here, he wrote.

— When Monday 7 September 2026, hours before Canadian retaliatory tariffs took effect on Tuesday.

— The catch No new tariff was attached to the post. A 50 percent aircraft tariff threat dates from January.

— The Brazil angle Bombardier competes with Embraer in business jets, not regional jets, which it exited in 2020.

— What is missing No Embraer statement or named analyst comment on the threat could be sourced.

The Trump Bombardier post landed hours before Canadian tariffs took effect. Brazilian coverage treated it as good news for Embraer, without an Embraer quote to support it.

An Embraer jet. The live overlap with Bombardier is in business aircraft rather than regional ones. (Photo: “Contour Embraer ERJ-135ER N16511 IAD VA1” by Acroterion, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

The Trump Bombardier threat arrived on Truth Social on Monday. Brazilian outlets read it within hours as help for Embraer.

The wording was blunt. No more selling Bombardier in the United States, the post said, adding that their products are not good enough.

It set a condition. If they want our market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a piggybank.

The post claimed more than half of Bombardier’s revenue comes from the United States. It also complained that Canada had blocked Gulfstream from doing business there.

What the Trump Bombardier Post Did Not Contain

No new tariff was attached to it. No outlet reports a percentage or an effective date tied to Monday’s statement.

A 50 percent tariff threat on Canadian aircraft does exist, but it dates from January 2026. It was tied to a certification dispute over Gulfstream jets.

Canada subsequently certified the Gulfstream aircraft, which resolved that dispute. Reporting this week does not revive it.

The timing was the real content. The post came hours before Canadian retaliatory tariffs took effect early on Tuesday.

Those measures cover around 20 billion Canadian dollars of American goods. They double steel and aluminium duties to 50 percent.

Why Brazil Cares

Bombardier is Embraer’s closest competitor in business aviation. Restricting its access to the American market would leave a gap.

One framing in Brazilian coverage needs correcting. Several outlets describe the rivalry as being in regional jets.

Bombardier left regional jets in 2020 when it sold the CRJ programme to Mitsubishi. The live overlap is business aircraft, the Praetor against the Challenger and Global families.

The United States is the largest business jet market in the world. Any restriction on a major supplier there is material to everyone else selling into it.

The Measure That Actually Helped Embraer

There is a separate American decision that genuinely benefited Embraer, and it was an exemption rather than an attack.

In February 2026 the administration imposed a temporary global import duty under section 122 of the Trade Act. It followed a Supreme Court ruling striking down earlier tariffs.

That duty exempted commercial aircraft, engines and aerospace parts. The exemption is what mattered to Embraer.

Reuters framed that as helping Embraer, which had been facing a duty its European and Canadian rivals were not. In July the administration also declined to impose section 232 tariffs on aircraft and parts.

We found no American measure against a jet-parts maker that benefits Embraer. If that claim is circulating, it needs its own source.

What Bombardier Said

The company responded with an American jobs argument. It says it supports tens of thousands of jobs in the United States and employs around 3,500 people there.

It works with nearly 2,800 American suppliers across 47 states and spends over 2.5 billion dollars a year with them. It builds wings in Red Oak, Texas and flight-control components near Los Angeles.

A facility in Fort Wayne, Indiana is due to open later this year. A Republican senator publicly pushed back on the ban call.

What to Watch

The first marker is whether anything follows the post. A statement without an instrument is not a policy.

The second is Embraer itself. The company has not commented, and its order book will say more than any headline.

The third is the wider Canada trade dispute. Aircraft are one file inside a much larger argument that escalated this week.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly did Trump say?

In a Truth Social post on Monday 7 September 2026 he wrote that Bombardier may no longer sell its aircraft in the United States, that over half its revenue comes from American buyers, and that if it wants the market it must build there.

Is a tariff attached to it?

No new tariff was attached to that post. A separate 50 percent tariff threat on Canadian aircraft dates from January 2026 and was tied to a Gulfstream certification dispute that Canada later resolved.

Does this help Embraer?

Brazilian outlets read it that way, since Bombardier is Embraer’s closest competitor in business aircraft. No Embraer statement or named analyst comment on the threat could be sourced, and the two companies no longer compete in regional jets.

Sources: Fox Business, CNBC, Al Jazeera, CBC, Reuters, CNN, Rio Times.

World.title: Brazil Bank Account Closure Rule Settled by the STJ
World.content:
BRAZIL · LAW

Key Facts — What was decided A bank may end a current account contract unilaterally, and one article of the consumer code does not prevent it.

— The case Theme 1.119, decided by the STJ’s Second Section on Thursday 3 September 2026.

— The rapporteur Minister Humberto Martins. The merits were unanimous.

— The catch The ruling fixes no notice period. The thirty days often quoted came from the facts of the case.

— What was left out Whether a bank must state a reason was deliberately excluded from the theme.

— Who brought it Three companies whose accounts Itau Unibanco closed, citing commercial disinterest. They sued in 2019.

The Brazil bank account closure question now has a binding answer. It is narrower than the headlines, and it fixes no notice period.

Inside a Caixa building in Brasilia. The ruling binds every Brazilian court on the question it answers. (Photo: “Brasilia 3702a” by Yves Picq, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Brazil’s highest court for federal law has settled the Brazil bank account closure question. A bank may end a current account contract unilaterally.

The Superior Tribunal de Justica decided it on Thursday 3 September 2026. The case is Theme 1.119, heard by the court’s Second Section.

The thesis is narrow and specific. One article of the consumer code, thirty-nine item nine, does not reach this situation.

It cannot be used against a bank ending a current account contract on its own initiative. That is the entire holding.

Minister Humberto Martins was the rapporteur. On the merits the section was unanimous.

What the Brazil Bank Account Closure Ruling Does Not Say

It does not say the consumer code stops applying to banks. That is a much larger claim than the court made.

Article 39, item nine bans refusing to sell goods or services to someone willing to pay. It carries its own exception for intermediation regulated by special laws.

Martins read that exception as covering institutions supervised by the national monetary council. That is the whole legal move.

Everything else in the consumer code remains available to a customer with a complaint.

The Thirty Days Are Not in the Ruling

The binding thesis requires prior communication to the account holder and fulfilment of remaining contractual obligations. It fixes no number of days.

Thirty days appears widely in coverage. It comes from the facts of the lead case, where the plaintiffs were given that period.

The only disagreement among the ministers was whether to write the notice obligation into the thesis text itself. Martins’s position prevailed.

Anyone reporting that the STJ imposed a thirty-day notice rule is describing the case, not the holding.

The Reason Question Was Left Open

Whether a bank must give a specific reason was deliberately kept outside the theme’s limits. The court drew that boundary itself.

In the lead case the stated reason was commercial disinterest. Three companies sued Itau Unibanco in March 2019 after their accounts were closed on that basis.

They lost at the Sao Paulo state court before the case reached the STJ. The state public defenders’ strategic litigation group argued for requiring a proven legitimate motive, and lost.

Who Was and Was Not Involved

Itau Unibanco is reported as the defendant bank in the lead case. That detail comes from a single smaller outlet, with the larger legal publications naming only the appeal number.

Nubank and Santander were not parties. They appear in some headlines as examples of banks the ruling affects.

The thesis is written generically about current account contracts. It is not limited to companies, even though the lead plaintiffs were companies.

What It Means in Practice

For foreign residents this matters more than it looks. Account closures without explanation are a recurring complaint among newcomers to Brazilian banking.

The ruling makes clear that a closure with notice is lawful. It does not make an arbitrary or abusive one lawful.

What is still open is what happens when a customer disputes the motive. The STJ left that door unlocked.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the STJ actually decide?

That article 39, item nine of Brazil’s consumer code does not prevent a bank from unilaterally ending a current account contract. It was decided under Theme 1.119 by the Second Section on 3 September 2026, with Minister Humberto Martins as rapporteur.

Does a bank have to give thirty days’ notice?

The binding thesis fixes no notice period. It requires prior communication to the account holder and fulfilment of remaining contractual obligations. The thirty days widely quoted came from the facts of the lead case.

Must the bank give a reason?

That question was deliberately excluded from the theme. In the lead case the stated reason was commercial disinterest, and the state public defenders’ group argued unsuccessfully for requiring a proven legitimate motive.

Sources: Migalhas, ConJur, Brasil em Folhas, Superior Tribunal de Justica, Rio Times.

03 What moved it

The weekend brought the sharpest escalation yet in the tanker war. Central Command destroyed the M/T Downy off Kharg Island, the M/T Stark 1 near Jask and a third carrier in the Gulf of Oman.

Two vessels were described as permanently disabled and one as completely destroyed. The strikes came hours after the Revolutionary Guard fired ballistic missiles at a United States carrier and a destroyer the same day.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy then said it hit three oil tankers and three United States-affiliated ships. It did not name the vessels, and no independent source has confirmed the claim.

Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said on Sunday that the era of proportionate responses was over. That language raised the perceived ceiling on further escalation.

Saudi Arabia was hit too. Aramco’s 400,000 barrel-a-day Jizan refinery came under fresh attack on Monday, the third strike on the plant in two months.

No group claimed the Monday attack. The August strike on the same refinery was attributed to the Houthis, not to Iran.

Petrobras headquarters in Rio. Brazil’s B3 was shut on Monday.

04 The Latin American read

Higher crude is a straightforward transfer to the region’s exporters. Colombia, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana all sell more oil than they buy. Mexico does not, because its fuel import bill now exceeds what it earns from crude sales.

Ecopetrol gains most directly on the fiscal side, because oil royalties feed a Colombian budget already stretched by earthquake reconstruction. Petrobras benefits from price but carries its own equity story.

Argentina is the quieter winner. Vaca Muerta output is rising into a market where the marginal barrel is scarce, which supports both YPF and Vista Energy.

The cost side matters too. Record diesel prices raise freight, agriculture and mining costs across the region.

05 The names to watch

Petrobras had no company news on Monday or Tuesday. Its pending item is the redemption of US$1.08 billion of 5.999% global notes due 2028, settling later this month.

Ecopetrol recently closed its US$1.2 billion purchase of 51% of Brazil’s Brava Energia. That deal moves part of its growth story out of Colombia.

YPF posted a US$1.21 billion second-quarter profit and lifted its 2026 core earnings guidance to US$8 billion. Capital spending guidance rose to US$6.2 billion.

Guyana remains the region’s swing story. The Stabroek Block produces about 900,000 barrels a day, and the Errea Wittu vessel arrived on August 21.

The natural resources ministry expects first oil from that vessel in the fourth quarter. That would push the country past one million barrels a day.

06 The outlook

Iranian loadings averaged about 260,000 barrels a day in August. A year earlier the figure was roughly 1.7 million, a fall of more than 80%.

Hormuz transits ran at five, eleven and six vessels on September 1 to 3. Kpler put the ten-day average at ten vessels a day on Monday, the lowest since May, against about 100 before the war.

Gulf crude exports have roughly halved, to about nine million barrels a day. Direct crude shipments through the strait average about 2.2 million barrels a day.

OPEC+ met on Sunday, September 6, and left output policy for October unchanged, according to Reuters. The group finished unwinding its 1.65 million barrel-a-day tranche in August, though other cuts run to the end of 2026.

07 What to watch

The Iran-Oman corridor talks: Tehran said on Monday a deal to manage Hormuz shipping was days away. Crude rose on the headline, so only a working corridor would test the premium.

Tehran said on Monday a deal to manage Hormuz shipping was days away. Crude rose on the headline, so only a working corridor would test the premium. Jizan refinery repairs: A fourth strike on the same Aramco plant would move the market. Watch Saudi loading data rather than statements.

A fourth strike on the same Aramco plant would move the market. Watch Saudi loading data rather than statements. Errea Wittu startup: Guyana’s fifth vessel is due to begin producing in the fourth quarter. It is rated at 250,000 barrels a day, and an earlier start brings that volume forward.

Guyana’s fifth vessel is due to begin producing in the fourth quarter. It is rated at 250,000 barrels a day, and an earlier start brings that volume forward. United States diesel: The retail average is at a record. Sustained strength feeds straight into Latin American freight and farm costs.

The retail average is at a record. Sustained strength feeds straight into Latin American freight and farm costs. American politics: Reuters and Ipsos put support for the campaign at 31% in late August. Quinnipiac last read 34% support against 60% opposition.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is oil rising this week?

United States forces struck three Iranian tankers on September 5, and Iran said it struck six vessels in reply. Iranian exports have fallen more than 80% in a year.

Was there a Monday close for Latin American oil shares?

No. The New York Stock Exchange was shut for Labour Day and Brazil’s B3 was closed for Independence Day, so the prices shown are Friday’s closes.

How bad is the Strait of Hormuz disruption?

The ten-day average fell to ten vessels a day on Monday, the lowest since May, against roughly 100 a day before the conflict. Gulf crude exports have roughly halved.

Which Latin American producers benefit most?

Colombia and Guyana gain most on the fiscal side, while Argentina’s Vaca Muerta producers gain on volume. Record diesel prices offset part of the benefit region-wide.

World.title: Avibras Howitzer Deal Is a Proposal, Not a Signed Contract
World.content:
BRAZIL · DEFENCE

Key Facts — What it is A proposal for Avibras to assemble 36 self-propelled howitzers for the Brazilian Army.

— The value Around R$800 million (US$156 million), on figures reported in the Brazilian defence press.

— The catch It is not formalised. The proposal went to the Army logistics command in late August and awaits legal analysis.

— The weapon The ATMOS 155mm, designed and made by Israel’s Elbit Systems, selected in a 2024 competition.

— Where Assembly would take place at Avibras’s plant at Jacarei in Sao Paulo state, phased two then thirty-four.

— The second condition The Batista brothers’ takeover of Avibras still needs approval from the competition authority CADE.

The Avibras howitzer plan has a value, a unit count and a factory. What it does not have is a signature.

Avibras Howitzer Deal Is a Proposal, Not a Signed Contract

A plan for Avibras to build howitzers for the Brazilian Army has been widely reported as a formalised contract. It is not one yet.

The Avibras howitzer proposal was presented to the Army’s logistics command, COLOG, in late August 2026. It remains in legal analysis.

No signing date has been reported. The Brazilian defence press describes it as pending rather than concluded.

That distinction matters because two separate approvals still stand between the plan and reality.

What the Avibras Howitzer Plan Contains

The value is around R$800 million (US$156 million). The quantity is 36 self-propelled howitzers.

The system is the ATMOS 155mm, designed and manufactured by Elbit Systems of Israel. Brazil selected it in a competition in 2024.

Delivery would be phased. Two demonstration units would come first, followed by thirty-four more.

Assembly would take place domestically, at Avibras’s plant in Jacarei in Sao Paulo state. That local content is the point of routing it through Avibras at all.

The Two Conditions

The first is the contract itself. A proposal in legal review at COLOG is not a procurement, and Brazilian defence purchases have stalled at this stage before.

The second is corporate. Joesley and Wesley Batista agreed in August to acquire control of Avibras Aeroco through Globe Investimentos.

That acquisition is still subject to approval by CADE, the competition authority. Until it clears, the company’s ownership is not settled.

A contract signed with a company whose control is pending would be unusual. The two timelines are linked whether or not anyone intends them to be.

Why the Deal Exists

The ATMOS purchase has been stalled since selection. Brazilian coverage in July described the government trying to unblock it.

Routing assembly through a domestic manufacturer is the standard mechanism for that. It converts an import into an industrial programme with Brazilian jobs attached.

Avibras is the natural candidate. It has built Brazilian rocket artillery for decades and is the country’s best known name in the field.

It has also been in judicial recovery, with debts reported at around R$600 million (US$117 million). An army contract is exactly what a company in that position needs.

What We Are Not Saying

We are not reporting that Avibras has won an R$800 million (US$156 million) contract. The reporting does not support that.

We are reporting that a proposal at that value exists and is in review. The difference is a signature and a regulator.

Both may well arrive. Neither has yet.

What to Watch

The first marker is a signature at COLOG, or a published contract notice. That would settle it.

The second is the CADE decision on the Batista acquisition. Control of the company comes first in practice.

The third is whether the phasing holds. Two demonstration units before thirty-four is a structure that allows a quiet exit if the first two disappoint.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Avibras signed the howitzer contract?

No. The proposal was presented to the Army’s logistics command COLOG in late August 2026 and remains in legal analysis. No signing date has been reported.

What is the deal worth and what does it cover?

Around R$800 million (US$156 million) for 36 ATMOS 155mm self-propelled howitzers, designed by Israel’s Elbit Systems and selected by Brazil in a 2024 competition. Assembly would be at Avibras’s Jacarei plant, phased as two demonstration units then thirty-four.

What else has to happen first?

The Batista brothers’ agreed acquisition of control of Avibras through Globe Investimentos still requires approval from the competition authority CADE. Until that clears, the company’s ownership is unsettled.

Sources: Revista Sociedade Militar, Forcas Terrestres, Rio Times.

World.title: Petrobras Jet Fuel Up 13.9 Percent, and Up 53 Since December
World.content:
BRAZIL · ENERGY

Key Facts — The rise Petrobras raised the average aviation kerosene price by 13.9 percent, effective 1 September 2026.

— In money That is roughly R$0.68 (US$0.13) a litre added to the refinery price.

— The cumulative figure Aviation kerosene has risen 53.3 percent since December 2025.

— The reason given Petrobras cited international oil prices affected by geopolitical tension and market volatility.

— The catch A separate antitrust complaint against Petrobras is about gas, not jet fuel, and dates from May.

— Who filed it The glass industry association Abividro, which accuses Petrobras of abusing a dominant position.

The Petrobras jet fuel rise is the headline. The cumulative figure since December is the number airlines are actually looking at.

Petrobras Jet Fuel Up 13.9 Percent, and Up 53 Since December

Petrobras jet fuel prices rose 13.9 percent from the first of September. The increase applies to the average refinery price of aviation kerosene.

In money that is about R$0.68 (US$0.13) a litre. The rise took effect on 1 September 2026.

Petrobras said the adjustment follows the dynamics of international oil and product prices. It cited geopolitical tension and greater volatility in global energy markets.

The single month is not the whole story. Aviation kerosene has now risen 53.3 percent since December 2025.

Why Petrobras Jet Fuel Matters More Than Petrol

Fuel is the largest or second largest cost line for an airline. It is far more concentrated than it is for road transport.

Brazilian carriers buy most of their domestic uplift from Petrobras. There is limited practical alternative inside the country.

A 53 percent increase over nine months cannot be absorbed within existing fares. It reaches ticket prices with a lag of weeks rather than months.

Brazil’s domestic aviation market has been financially fragile for years. This is the kind of input move that reopens that conversation.

The Antitrust Case Is a Different Story

A complaint against Petrobras is before CADE, Brazil’s competition authority. It is worth separating from the fuel rise.

It was filed by Abividro, the Brazilian glass industry association. The name appears in some coverage as Abvidro, which is a misspelling.

The complaint concerns natural gas, not aviation fuel. It accuses Petrobras of abusing a dominant position in that market.

It alleges restricted third-party access to gas transport and processing infrastructure. It also cites barriers to new entrants and opaque reference pricing.

A further claim is that domestic supply is artificially compressed through reinjection. The effect, Abividro argues, is to keep industrial gas prices high.

The Timing of That Complaint

The filing is not new. It was originally lodged in May 2026 and expanded in July.

The expansion followed the creation of a special commission on the matter by the oil regulator ANP. CNN Brasil reported the filing on 9 July.

Abividro asks CADE to open a formal investigation and to impose preventive and structural remedies. No decision has been announced.

What the Two Stories Share

Both are about a company that is the dominant supplier in markets its customers cannot easily leave. That is the structural point.

Petrobras prices against international parity by policy. That protects the company’s margins and transmits global volatility straight into Brazilian costs.

Industrial gas buyers and airlines are making versions of the same complaint. One went to the regulator, the other will show up in fares.

What to Watch

The first marker is airline pricing. A 53 percent input rise since December has to appear somewhere.

The second is whether CADE opens a formal case on the gas complaint. That decision is the gate.

The third is the next Petrobras adjustment. The company reviews prices without a fixed calendar, which is itself part of the criticism.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did jet fuel go up?

Petrobras raised the average aviation kerosene price by 13.9 percent, effective 1 September 2026, adding roughly R$0.68 (US$0.13) a litre. The cumulative rise since December 2025 is 53.3 percent.

What is the CADE complaint about?

Natural gas, not jet fuel. The glass industry association Abividro accuses Petrobras of abusing a dominant position by restricting third-party access to gas infrastructure and compressing domestic supply. It was filed in May 2026 and expanded in July.

World.title: Bolivia Constituent Assembly Call Comes From Top Judge
World.content:
BOLIVIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — Who said it Romer Saucedo Gomez, president of Bolivia’s Supreme Tribunal of Justice, in an interview with EFE.

— When and where On 7 September 2026, while attending a forum of BRICS supreme court presidents in New Delhi.

— What he said Let us open the Constitution and see what direction we give the country, with the whole country taking part.

— The catch The context is a budget fight. The judiciary wants its share raised from 0.35 to 5 percent.

— The counter-offer Legislators have proposed 3 percent, well below what the courts are demanding.

— The silence No response from President Rodrigo Paz’s government to this specific call could be sourced.

A Bolivia constituent assembly is not a small proposal. It came from the head of the judiciary, in the middle of an argument about money.

Bolivia Constituent Assembly Call Comes From Top Judge
