However, this is a company-reported result and does not establish the technology as a reliable cancer diagnostic test.

Independent cancer specialists say the findings are promising but need to be confirmed in much larger studies.

"The study is promising, as an early signal," said oncologist Santhosh Kumar Devadas.

"But they need to do the study with a much larger group before we make any definitive conclusions."

A non-invasive approach

The potential application is significant in India, where many cancers are diagnosed only after the disease has advanced.

The process is simple. Patients breathe into a cotton mask for around 10 minutes. The sample is then sealed and taken to the laboratory, without the patient meeting the dogs.

Dognosis hopes the approach could eventually be used as an initial screening step, identifying people who may need conventional medical tests.

The company says it plans further trials as it works towards potential commercial approval.

For now, researchers stress that larger and independent studies will be needed to establish whether dogs and AI can reliably detect cancer in real-world settings.

World.title: Exclusive: Italy proposes no fees for digital euro payments under €10
World.content:
Italy has proposed introducing an exemption for digital euro transactions under €10 in a move that would favour small businesses, according to sources consulted and documents seen by Euronews

 

The move is viewed favourably by the central banking community, in particular by the European Central Bank (ECB), a source from the banking sector told Euronews.

The digital euro is a digital form of payment, expected to complement cash, with the ECB aiming to be ready for a potential first issuance in 2029, assuming the necessary regulation is adopted this year.

As Europe mainly relies on US-based payment schemes such as Visa and Mastercard, the EU is pushing for greater strategic autonomy in payments, with the digital euro seen as one potential solution.

It will have legal tender status, meaning merchants will generally be required to accept it, subject to certain exceptions. For this reason, legislators are negotiating how fees should be distributed among market participants, so that small merchants are not disadvantaged by the adoption of the new digital currency.

The distribution of fees among market participants, known as the "compensation model", is among the most delicate parts of the negotiations in Brussels, alongside the "holding limits", meaning the maximum amount of digital euro that can be held in a wallet.

"The proposal is a merchant service charge cap up to €0.02 for low value transactions, applicable especially to small merchants. But we're open to consider a net zero, as de facto this would be the result anyway," an EU diplomat told Euronews on condition of anonymity.

"Such a solution would also make the framework simpler," the diplomat added.

According to internal documents seen by Euronews in relation to the negotiations, the fee scheme will be temporary, allowing the ECB to gather sufficient data before proposing a new model, if appropriate. The need for better data on payment fees has also been highlighted by the European Court of Auditors. In a 2025 report, the ECA found that the European Commission lacked sufficient data on merchant service charges and costs to effectively monitor the impact of existing price interventions in the payments market.

Other negotiation documents indicate that small merchants typically pay higher fees than large companies because they have weaker bargaining power with international payment schemes. These schemes are difficult for merchants to refuse, particularly when they are widely used. According to an ECB analysis, small merchants can pay three to four times more in fees than larger merchants.

The matter will be analysed by member states, the European Parliament and the European Commission during the next round of negotiations in Brussels, according to an internal document seen by Euronews.

Negotiators will meet again in Brussels on Thursday, 10 September, for further discussions.

World.title: EU warns of new terror menace 25 years after 9/11 as online youths seek violent thrills
World.content:
A quarter of a century after the Al-Qaeda terrorist attacks on the United States, jihadist groups still pose a major threat to security in Europe, but a new menace has surfaced that is driven mostly by young people online and authorities are worried.

 

The exact size of the network behind what is being called nihilistic violent extremism is unclear. But police investigators from nine European countries found about 4,340 URL web addresses linked to “The COM,” as the online community has become known, during a campaign to disrupt it in June and July.

“It’s violence for the sake of violence,” European Union Counter-Terrorism Coordinator Bartjan Wegter said ahead of the 25th anniversary of the 11 September 2001 on New York and Washington in 2001.

Overall last year, 45 terrorist attacks were reported across 10 of the 27 EU countries, although none of them were major, mass-casualty incidents.

About half were foiled or failed, but six people were killed. A total of 486 people suspected of terror links were arrested in 21 member countries, according to the EU police agency Europol.

European Union Counter-Terrorism Coordinator Bartjan Wegter speaks during an interview with the Associated Press in Brussels, 3 September, 2026 AP Photo

Jihadist groups, often guided or inspired by networks outside Europe, were behind 24 of the attacks and accounted for more than 70% of the arrests.

Of all those taken into custody, around one third were aged under 18, mostly boys.

Europol does not keep statistics on nihilistic violent extremism because definitions of it differ and acts can fall into the category of ordinary criminality as well as terrorism.

But in Finland in 2025, a 16-year-old boy stabbed three female student colleagues. He allegedly shared a “manifesto” in WhatsApp groups, recorded the attack on Snapchat, and asked on social media for someone to save and give him the video after his release.

In the “manifesto,” he said that he wanted to do something “significant” and “exciting.” No political motive was given for his rampage, according to an EU document on the emerging threat of nihilistic extremist violence.

Violence as a form of entertainment

“It’s very much a fascination with violence. It’s violence as a means of asserting oneself, as a means of gaining status in those online communities,” Wegter told the AP news agency. “There’s not a direct link with ideology.”

In Italy last year, a 15-year-old boy planned a murder to gain notoriety online, authorities there said. He kept images and videos of assaults, murders, school shootings and child pornography on his smartphone.

Wegter said these kinds of incidents, which have been on the rise for two to three years, are not isolated but organised by online networks that are “often driven by young people, for young people often involving young boys.”

A woman walks by a projection at the Residence Palace in Brussels, 5 April, 2024 AP Photo

He said that they “lead to offline violence. We’ve seen stabbings, a young individual stabbing an elderly person for no reason whatsoever.”

Such attacks are tough to prevent or track. They often involve “young individuals who will not have a criminal record, usually, who don’t leave any footprints other than online perhaps, but then it’s often behind encrypted walls and communities,” Wegter said.

Conspiring online to commit real-world crimes

High on the list of groups authorities’ radar is 764, which was founded by an American high school dropout, Bradley Cadenhead. He’s serving an 80-year prison sentence for child pornography and sex offences, but the group still functions.

In Germany last year, a 20-year-old man believed to be a leading 764 member faced 123 charges over acts of “an unimaginable level of brutality and inhumanity,” including murder, rape and the sexual abuse of children, the EU document said.

Unlike 25 years ago, when extremists, mostly from Saudi Arabia, entered the United States and trained to become deadly pilots, the terror threat facing Europe today is mostly organised online.

“The online environment, for all the good things it brings, it is still too permissive,” Wegter said. He described it as “a petri dish for the connection between different threats.”

The Europol headquarters in The Hague, 10 October, 2018 AP Photo

AI on the rise

Privacy advocates insist that people have a fundamental right to communicate without unjustified intrusion. They accuse the authorities and some companies of undermining protections through spyware and other methods.

But Wegter said that “our law enforcement must be equipped with the instruments and tools to deal with the threat as it exists today.” He noted that 85% of investigations take place in the digital environment. “It means that we have to adjust ourselves to that.”

For the Dutch diplomat himself, it means talking more to authorities and organisations in other countries, notably those that such groups use as a rear base.

Police officers patrol in Udine, 14 October, 2025 AP Photo

“Because what happens outside our borders impacts on our security,” including what’s being amplified online, he said.

Europol said criminals are exploiting images and audio to create and edit propaganda, including through deepfakes, memes and GIFs. AI-powered bots were also used to boost recruitment and promote terrorist ideologies, while AI-driven app were used for research to prepare attacks.

“The kind of violent content, violence inciting content, propaganda, manuals, tactics, everything that is available, is very much amplified by AI,” Wegter said.

World.title: Travel industry piles pressure on EU as ‘shambolic’ EES rollout sparks fresh fears of border chaos
World.content:
Following a summer of long queues, missed flights and border chaos, the EU’s emergency flexibility measures for its Entry/Exit System (EES) came to an end on Sunday (6 September).

 

The temporary rules allowed member states to suspend fingerprint and facial scans in exceptional circumstances to ease congestion.

Now, industry bodies are calling for the measures to be extended beyond September, warning that travellers could once again face lengthy delays at Europe’s borders.

The calls come following wait times rising to as long as five hours in July, according to the trade association Airports Council International (ACI).

Lisbon, Milan, Rome and Krakow airports were particularly hard hit through the busy summer season.

Much of the disorder is down to malfunctioning kiosks, low staffing levels and general kinks in the system.

Representatives from Ryanair, Europe’s largest airline, have criticised EES since its launch in October last year and, this week, its chief operating officer, Neal McMahon, said: “the EU’s handling of EES has been a shambles from start to finish”.

“Airlines, airports and border authorities repeatedly warned Brussels that the rollout was not ready, that it would increase processing times and that it would create excessive queues for passengers. Those warnings were ignored, with EU citizens the ones delayed and disrupted,” McMahon added.

He insisted that the EU Commission should extend the EES flexibility until at least April 2027, adding that “passengers should not be made to pay the price for the EU’s failed EES rollout”.

Meanwhile, Matthew Pack, the CEO of Holiday Extras, has strongly criticised EES, saying: “Since the EU won't say this plainly, we will. These border systems have failed... EES hasn't worked”.

"That leaves two EU borders. There's the one in the announcements, where EES runs smoothly, and ETIAS is on track. And there's the one on the ground, the one holidaymakers actually queue at, haphazardly enforced by border guards, where everyone knows the truth: nothing here is working as planned,” he added.

“A system that needs this much quiet improvisation to function isn't ready. The honest response is to say so, roll it back, and rebuild it properly."

The criticism comes following a statement from the EU Commission, which implies that EES hasn’t been as much of a disaster as some insist it has been.

“The system has broadly worked well over the summer and, until 6 September, we have the possibility to temporarily suspend registration of biometrics in case of exceptional circumstances,” a Commission spokesperson said last week.

“We’re in close contact with those few member states where adjustments are needed.”

World.title: Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade
World.content:
Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Advertising

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan.

The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea.

The agreement lasted a year.

While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University.

“The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It's not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.”

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Growing attacks

In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships.

This surge in attacks comes as both nations rush to export their grain harvests.

Grain prices have risen sharply, by as much as 30 percent, international grain broker Can Atbasoglu said, even as both sides scramble to find new routes for their exports.

“Russia will do their best to export as much as they can, both from Russian Baltic ports and EU Baltic ports like Latvia and Lithuania; they're also exporting,” Atbasoglu said.

“Ukraine will also export as much as they can from Romania as well and through the Danube ports. But the export pace will be definitely lower. So it will definitely stay bullish for the markets. Prices are definitely going to stay like this or can have a further increase.”

Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea

Ships staying put

At one of Istanbul's many shipyards, the docks are crowded with ships that once braved the Black Sea. One vessel bears the scars of a drone attack and is under repair. Others undergo routine maintenance as shipowners hesitate to risk new journeys into dangerous waters.

The superintendent of one ship, speaking anonymously, says repairs are nearly finished, but uncertainty clouds the future.

“We wanted to take the ship out to the Black Sea before entering the shipyard, but because of that risk, we didn’t enter the Black Sea and didn’t take on any cargo. We’ve been in the shipyard for 50 days for repairs, but we don’t know what will happen once the repairs are finished,” the superintendent said.

Turkish shipowners warn that many are on the brink of bankruptcy, as idle ships rack up costs of up to 50,000 euros a month in mooring and crew expenses.

Ziya Ustel, CEO of Turkish shipping company VI-ZA STAR, says high freight rates are being offered for Black Sea routes, but the risks are too great.

“They are offering high freight rates, etc,” Ustel said.

Without a diplomatic solution, few shipowners will be prepared to risk their vessels, Ustel warned.

“The main thing is to find out a real solution,” Ustel added. “Otherwise, no one will try anything anymore.”

Turkish diplomacy

Ankara is expected to step up its efforts to find a solution.

Grain brokers say hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough may be one reason prices have so far remained below the record highs seen at the start of the war.

But if Turkish efforts fail and attacks on Black Sea shipping continue, higher grain prices could have a considerable impact, especially on the world’s poorest nations, many of which depend on Russian and Ukrainian grain.

World.title: UK announces trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
World.content:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the measures were in response to what he called "settler terrorism" in the occupied territories. The measures are part of the UK's efforts to support a two-state solution.

The United Kingdom on Tuesday announced trade restrictions on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The center-left Labour Party government has previously sanctioned some Israeli settlers and illegal outposts over violence against Palestinians and illegal development in the West Bank.

What did Miliband say?

"I can announce today that we will introduce an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced in the House of Commons.

"We will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate for settlement expansion," Miliband said.

The foreign secretary said those financing or facilitating illegal settlement would "face the full force of UK sanctions."

Before announcing the sanctions, Miliband said that "settler terrorism was rampant" and referenced various instances of violence in the West Bank.

Why is the UK restricting trade

The measures appear to be setting the tone for relations between Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Israel.

According to a Downing Street readout of a phone call between the British leader and US President Donald Trump on the phone on Monday, Burnham laid out "the UK's commitment to working towards peace and security in the region," and stressed the importance of the two-state solution two-state solution in Israel and the Palestinian territories.

The United Kingdom recognized Palestinian statehood last year in an attempt to revive efforts to achieve a two-state solution.

It also comes Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government forges ahead with settlement construction in the West Bank, raising fears among some Western governments that it threatens any possible two-state solution.

The measures also come amd flaring tensions in the West Bank that have involved violent attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers.

The UK has previously condemned the violence while calling for civilians to be protected and for those responsible to be held accountable.

Israel warns it will 'act against Britain'

Ahead of the announcement, Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar already indicated that Israel would respond.

"If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain," Saar warned.

Israel's hard-line public security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly recognize the Falkland Islands as "Argentine territory under occupation, which the British violently steal from the Argentine people."

World.title: Japan's empty temples seek new ways to survive
World.content:
With a declining population, shrinking congregations and growing economic pressures, temples are struggling to stay relevant. As more temples are sold or closed, is religion in decline in modern Japan?

The 370-year-old structure has all the attributes of a classically designed Japanese temple, from the curved roof to the timber-frame walls, spacious tatami-mat prayer hall and elaborately decorated altar.

Set in manicured gardens on the Chita Peninsula in central Japan, the 350-square-meter (3,767-square-foot) property is on the market for 482 million yen (€2.66 million). The estate agent's pitch says the price includes dismantling by "expert heritage craftsmen" and delivery to anywhere in Japan, where it would be fully restored into a "stunning" two- or three-bedroom home.

The sale and removal of the temple marks the end of its role in the local community in the hills above the Nagasawacho district, but it is a better fate than many places of worship across Japan.

There are around 77,000 temples across the country, but as many as 17,000 no longer have a full-time resident priest as congregations have shrunk — particularly in rural districts experiencing rapid depopulation — and financial pressures have taken their toll.

That means many temples are being sold off or simply shuttered and left to deteriorate quietly.

A temple brought back to life

Tomomi Iwayama took on the abandoned Ganshu-ji temple in Odawara, a coastal town about 80 kilometers (50 miles) southwest of Tokyo, a decade ago. Today, he is the abbot of a growing congregation.

"The temple had no abbot for 70 years before I arrived because it was just so difficult to operate, and it has taken me until now to get it financially back on track," he told DW.

"Even in a relatively large urban area such as Odawara, which has around 200,000 residents, it has been very hard," he said. "In the countryside, it is much more difficult."

Iwayama's biggest problem is the country's shrinking population: fewer worshippers and falling demand for funerals and other traditional rites make it harder to finance the temple's upkeep. He has worked hard to reach out to the local community and has had success in selling plots in the temple graveyard.

Odawara Castle was built in the mid-15th century [FILE: March 2018] Image: Koji Sasahara/AP Photo/picture alliance

One innovation that has attracted attention is the temple's "smart graveyard," where families scan a card, and a robotic system recovers a relative's ashes from the columbarium.

Temples in rural areas of Japan face far greater challenges, he said.

"Young people in villages usually leave to go to university, and then they find a job in one of the big cities, so they rarely go back," he said. "Maybe they will go back once a year to pay their respects to their ancestors at the village temple, but that is not enough for the temple to get by on."

Equally, when the head priest of a rural temple retires, his children are unlikely to want to take the role on because of these challenges. All too often, Iwayama said, the result is the temple closing.

But he denies the suggestion that religion in Japan is following the same path as in the West, where Christian congregation numbers have plummeted over the decades.

Faith in the Digital Age To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Demand for Buddhism remains

"I sense there is still a lot of demand in Japan for Buddhism," he said, contrasting the fast-paced, technology-focused lives that people typically lead with the serenity that they are often seeking.

"Buddhism is a style of living, of an enlightened person," he said. "A lot of people are looking for that. And while the traditional rituals of funerals and anniversaries are declining and that revenue is shrinking, we are finding that more people want to take part in traditional temple cuisine cooking classes, meditation and other things that we can offer."

Temples that are not able to shift to offer experiences more in tune with modern Japan are at risk of closing, said Joey Stockerman, one of the founders of the Mokomoko online real estate service.

"We have had a temple on our site in the past, and we were approached by a foreign potential buyer, so there is certainly interest when these properties become available," he said.

Other foreigners who are long-term residents are doing their best to protect Japan's religious heritage for future generations. American journalist and author Jake Adelstein is currently a Zen priest at Zenshoin Temple in Tokyo's Toshima Ward and is training to become an abbot.

"I do not think that Japanese are becoming less religious; I believe they are becoming fewer because of population decline and they are becoming less wealthy because of the economic situation," he said.

Meet Japan’s AI Buddhist Robot To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Families want to keep the grave plot that they have had for generations, but for many of them it is just too expensive to maintain, and they often live a long way away, so they are unable to regularly visit to pay their respects," he said.

The annual fee for a grave can be up to 100,000 yen, while memorials and other rites can be an additional financial burden, Adesltein explained.

Young people shun religious careers

"Young people are not interested in a career as a priest because temples earn so little money, so there are positions that cannot be filled, and that is especially a problem in the countryside," he said.

Some temples have amalgamated their operations and share a priest, but that will become more difficult in the future, Adelstein said.

As elsewhere, Zenshoin Temple has started vegetarian cooking classes and Zen meditation sessions to appeal to the local community, and Adelstein hopes that will be enough to keep the temple open.

"The training to become an abbot is very tough, and the economics of a temple today often just do not add up, but I see it as a critical part of this society and this nation," he said.

World.title: Afghanistan's women: A national soccer team without a home
World.content:
The Afghan women's national football team has finally been officially recognized by FIFA. Now the players want to make history both on and off the field.

On the football pitches of Bundesliga club Wolfsburg, the Afghanistan women's national team is training and doing exactly what is strictly forbidden in their home country: playing football.

In the first session of the day, the coaches' main focus is helping the players get to know each other better and have fun. That's because, as of April of this year, these young women are now officially allowed to play football as the Afghan national team.

FIFA, the world's football federation, has amended its regulations, allowing Afghan women to once again represent their country in official international matches and FIFA competitions.

"This was a huge victory for us, a wonderful moment, and one of the moments we're most proud of. Because once again, the women of our country have made history and brought about change," Khalida Popal told DW. The former captain and founder of the organization Girl Power has been a pioneer for women's football in her country.

Karimi: 'I'm incredibly proud'

Since the Taliban took power in 2021, the players and Popal have fought for the recognition that has now become a reality.

"I'm incredibly proud that we can now officially play as a national team," said midfielder Maryam Karimi.

For Karimi, who has been living in Portugal since fleeing Afghanistan, FIFA's decision is more than just a formality.

"I hope that one day we'll be able to play in Afghanistan again with this team."

Almut Schult (fourth from the left) coaching the Afghanistan women's team Image: Irving Villegas/dpa/picture alliance

Until then, however, Afghanistan remains a national team without a home.

"We'll probably be one of the first national teams in history that has no home and no country in which to play," said Popal. "We'll compete from exile and represent our country."

Today, the players are scattered across the world. Many have traveled from England, Italy, Portugal or Germany, but some have also found refuge in Australia.

"We come from different countries and can't play together regularly. But when I see the players, they're incredibly united. They keep going and push each other forward,” said Karimi.

Gaining More Visibility Through Football

The 39-year-old Popal wants to use her experience to help the players and advance their athletic development. She wants the national team to be known not only for what was taken from them, but also for what it achieves on the field.

"The first goal, of course, is to build a strong team that performs well on the field," said Popal. "Because the better we play, the better we can represent our country, and the more visible we'll become."

But that is precisely where the biggest challenge currently lies. In Afghanistan itself, a regular system for women's football cannot be established at this time. As long as the Taliban are in power, women are not allowed to play sports.

So there is nowhere for young talent to be nurtured; there is no funding and no support from the country the players represent. This is because the Afghan Football Federation — unlike FIFA — does not recognize the women's team. For the time being, therefore, the team's future must be built outside the country.

"We have no federation and no country where talent can develop," said Popal. That is why the team relies heavily on the Afghan diaspora. There, the team is looking for players who may never have played for a club in Afghanistan, but who could represent their parents' country in the future.

Popal: 'The Taliban are erasing women from society'

To organize football camps like these, the women rely on outside support. The summer 2026 camp was made possible by an invitation from Volkswagen and Wolfsburg, but Popal and her organization still have a lot of work ahead of them.

Giving players who have fled Afghanistan a place back in international football is one part of the challenge, but so is creating structures and a foundation on which Afghan women's football can be built.

"It will be a team that stands up to the Taliban. Because the Taliban are erasing women from society,” said Popal.

"We will play football to stand up for the women of our country. When the players take the field, they're also playing for those women in Afghanistan who aren't allowed to."

Almuth Schult & Khalida Popal talking at Girl Power Summer Camp Image: Irving Villegas/dpa/picture alliance

Just like the former captain, the other young women on the team feel the same way. Midfielder Karimi wants to use football to draw more attention to her friends and all the women in her homeland.

"I can make my voice heard through the way I play football," Karimi said. "I can make my voice heard from the field."

Popal: "These girls are our future”

Despite a long battle for the human rights taken away from women by the Taliban, Popal keeps pushing because she wants to make sure that the women wearing the national team's jersey today are not the last generation to do so.

"I believe that Afghanistan won't stay this way forever. These dark days will pass. These girls will be the next coaches of the Afghan women's national team, the next directors of football academies, the next president, or the next ministers of our country," said Popal.

"And that is exactly why we are investing in these girls: because they are the future.”

This article was originally published in German.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

World.title: German police arrest suspect in power grid sabotage case
World.content:
Investigators say the suspect used homemade rockets and conductive wire to target high-voltage lines in three German states, apparently as part of a campaign against fossil fuels.

German police on Tuesday said they had arrested a 48-year-old man suspected of carrying out a series of sabotage attacks on the country's electricity network.

The suspect was reportedly spotted near the Weisweiler power station, close to Aachen in western Germany, after being sought by authorities for several days.

How were the attacks carried out?

Investigators suspect the man of trying to cause short circuits at several locations in the states of North Rhine-Westphalia, Brandenburg and Saxony over the past week, using homemade rockets to fire thin conductive wire across high-voltage power lines.

The method appears to have worked in at least two cases.

In Bergheim, west of Cologne, several units at a power station were put out of operation for several days.

At a substation near the Jänschwalde power station in Brandenburg, more than 20 homemade rockets were allegedly used to fire conductive material onto power lines, causing two short circuits.

However, neither incident resulted in a power outage.

Sabotage fears hit Germany's power grid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Last week, armed police located and raided a truck thought to have been used in the attacks.

What was the suspected motive?

Investigators have linked a series of letters claiming responsibility for the attacks to the 48-year-old suspect from Gevelsberg, in the southern Ruhr region.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the letters contained information that could only have been known to the perpetrator.

"The knowledge revealed in these letters is clearly knowledge belonging to the perpetrator," Dobrindt said.

He described the attacks as apparent "climate terrorism" carried out by a lone offender.

In the letters, the suspected attacker reportedly justified targeting the electricity network as part of a campaign against fossil fuels.

"Generating electricity from fossil fuels is a crime," one of the letters said.

Lignite is still mined and used for electricity generation in all three states where the suspected attacks took place. The burning of lignite releases massive amounts of carbon dioxide into the air, a major factor in climate breakdown.

World.title: Hungary orders 10 Russian diplomats to leave
World.content:
Budapest says the expulsions are necessary to protect security and sovereignty after years of comparatively close ties between Hungary and Russia.

Hungary has ordered 10 members of Russia's diplomatic mission to leave the country over activities it said were incompatible with their diplomatic status, Foreign Minister Anita Orban said on Tuesday.

The move marks a significant step by Budapest against Moscow, with Orban saying it was intended to protect Hungary's "security and sovereignty."

Why is Hungary expelling the diplomats?

Orban said a Hungarian Foreign Ministry official had informed the Russian ambassador that the 10 individuals had engaged in activities deemed "unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention."

She did not specify what the individuals were accused of doing.

Hungary's authorities had made the assessment before the government called on them to leave, Orban said.

"This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote.

Does this mean a break with Russia?

Orban stressed that Hungary was not severing diplomatic relations with Moscow.

"It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia," she said, adding that Budapest intended to maintain "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules."

Orban has served as Hungary's foreign minister and deputy prime minister since May, following the change of government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar.

The expulsion is nevertheless a notable deterioration in relations with Moscow, particularly given Hungary's previously close relationship with Russia under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

World.title: US-Canada tariff dispute weighs on cross-border ties
World.content:
As Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect, Canadian and US car industries fear the trade war will hit them hard, while Canadians are cutting back on travel.

A new suspension bridge connecting the United States to Canada recently opened after more than two decades of planning, but only the Canadians showed up to celebrate.

The Gordie Howe International Bridge spans the Detroit River, connecting Detroit, Michigan with Windsor, Ontario. It is named after a Canadian hockey player who starred for a US team.

"In normal times, that would be a very, very big celebration, a grand event, with leaders of both countries present," Michigan auto industry spokesperson Glenn Stevens Junior told DW.

But these are hardly normal times in US-Canada relations.

'Escalating tariffs will harm workers'

In July, US President Donald Trump announced a 50% tariff on a wide range of goods from Canada. A second Trump announcement days later of the doubling of tariffs on Canadian automobiles and auto parts to 50%triggered even more concern for businesses on both sides of the new bridge.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney countered with tariffs between 15% and 50% on $20 billion (€17.2 billion) worth of goods imported from the US.

US-Canada trade war: The cost of fighting back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The retaliatory measures took effect at 12.01 Eastern Standard Time (05:01 GMT/UST) on Tuesday September 8. Polls by the Canadian non-profit Angus Reid suggested that the majority of Canadians were in favor of a tougher stance in tariffs.

At the same time, Canadian workers feared for their jobs, the polls found.

Business leaders, too, have warned of the harmful effects of the tariffs on the economies of both countries.

"An escalating cycle of tariffs and retaliation will ultimately harm businesses, workers, and consumers on both sides of the border," the Detroit-based Canada and US Business Association (CUSBA) said in a statement in response to the tit-for-tat tariff hikes. "Each new tariff compounds costs, disrupts production, delays investment, and weakens the competitiveness of US and Canadian businesses."

Jobs at stake on both sides of the border

Further north, the Financial Accountability Office of Ontario estimated the new tariff regime will cost 119,000 local jobs in 2026.

Many of these are predicted to be in the auto industry, with Ontario's auto manufacturing output estimated to shrink by 8% in 2026 compared with a no-tariff scenario.

This contraction is expected to be felt on the US side too, especially in Michigan, where more than a fifth of all vehicles produced in the US in 2022 were built, including several well-known household brand names.

The economies of Michigan and Ontario are deeply interconnected, the Detroit Regional Chamber stressed in August.

"Engines that are built in Michigan go into trucks that are built in Ontario, engines that are built in Ontario go into trucks that are built into Michigan," said Glenn Stevens Jr, who is also the chamber's Chief Automotive and Innovation Officer.

Figures show that by 2023, Detroit automakers supported 815,000 indirect jobs through supply chains, as well as 147,000 direct workers across the US.

Detroit's chamber has called for a restoration of "normalcy," defined as a focus on the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, (USMCA, or CUSMA in Canada), due for an annual review.

Tariffs, EV attacks and AI blamed for job cuts

Even before the announcement of Trump's tariffs and Canada's counter-tariffs, Detroit's famous car industry had stalled.

The volume of production for companies was relatively stable as were jobs on and around auto factory lines, Stevens Jr said.

Although this meant there wasn't a significant loss in employment, new job opportunities weren't being created.

Analyzing the number of US car dealership franchise listings for new vehicles is a standard way of tracking auto production.

These listings show vehicle production has generally increased in the past 12 months, but the past 30 days show a significant slowdown.

Data from industry weekly Automotive News has around 33,000 more listed vehicles compared to this time last year, but 70,000 fewer vehicles were listed in the past month.

Can North America launch its own EV revolution? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Beyond the car showrooms, the US auto industry's cautionary approach is apparent.

US auto companies were adjusting business plans even before the latest round of tariff announcements, with business leaders warning of increased US manufacturing costs.

These costs have now been handed down to the consumers, with US shoppers seeing record sales prices of more than $52,000 for new cars in September.

Companies had resisted hiring people or expanding over the past 18 months since tariff talks between Canada and the US had started to intensify, Stevens Jr said, adding to a lack of investment in new designs owing to withdrawn US federal support for electric vehicles.

Is cross-border friendship fraying?

Apart from the auto industry, the tariffs are impacting other sectors.

Across the US, real estate market media in June described a "cooling relationship between the two countries," affecting property transactions, tourism revenue and the local economy.

"Most Canadians think it's unpatriotic ... to visit the United States," Claude Molineri, CEO of Visit Detroit said of the cooling friendship and downturn in tourism.

Earlier this year, Detroit's official visitor site reported that the city had seen an 11% decrease in Canadian guests compared to 2025.

Meanwhile, several "buy Canadian first" online campaigns have been referring users to local businesses and Canadian ingredients in everyday grocery items in response to the tariff enouncements.

The cities of Detroit and Ontario's Windsor/Essex normally facilitate trade worth more than $100 billion each year, which is almost a third of all annual trade between the US and Canada, according to Downtown Detroit Partnership, a group of business and community leaders.

The cooling ties between the two countries could come at a heavy price.

Why Canada rejected Trump's terms despite economic risks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: R. Casey, M. Sass

World.title: Kenya: Crackdown on foreign traders prompts xenophobia fears
World.content:
Fears of xenophobia are rising in Kenya after President William Ruto ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as hawkers. The government insists however that legally documented foreign traders remain protected.

Kenyan authorities are moving in on some foreign nationals working in the country's informal economy after President William Ruto called for small-scale businesses focused on hawking and petty retail to be primarily reserved for Kenyan citizens.

"We have a bill in parliament [requiring] that there are some trading activities that foreigners can't do in Kenya," he explained, adding that foreign nationals should not come to Kenya to compete with citizens in business settings which need little capital.

The government had announced that the enforcement of this law would begin on Monday, September 7 — and appears to have made good on its pledge.

Ruto framed the latest move as a protection measure for Kenya's economy, highlighting that the focus in the country's economic development should shift to foreign investors who bring capital, create jobs and contribute to local production.

"The investor confidence we have built is for investors, not traders and hawkers. From next week, all traders doing those small businesses should close them," Ruto emphasized, highlighting also that there has been a step increase in informal traders from China in the country.

For many young Africans, running a small, informal business remains one of the few options to make a living Image: AP

Mixed reactions to a complex situation

Reactions among Kenyans to these developments have been mixed; some welcomed the crackdown, arguing that foreign traders have been taking away job opportunities in a struggling economy.

"We have been suffering for long. Our jobs are taken," said Nairobi resident James Mwaurah, adding that many Kenyans are unemployed, competing with foreign workers who often are willing to work for lower wages.

"We say thanks to the president for what he has done," Mwaurah added.

Others meanwhile have expressed support for the government's initiative to enforce immigration laws and business regulations, but reject the idea of simply sending foreigners home.

"We accept to have foreigners in our country. Legally, we live with them very peacefully," another local resident, Babu Claudius, told DW on the streets of Nairobi.

In his view, Kenya continues to need foreign workers as well as international business, warning that "chasing them away might scare investors."

Many Kenyans — including Claudius — however seem to agree on one thing: Foreign nationals "have to be here legally."

China, US and EU all want to do business in Africa To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There are some 17.4 million people who work in Kenya's informal sector, according to official numbers published in 2024; eight in ten of those workers engage in registered business dealings.

For many people, hawking or running a small shop in the informal economy — with or without papers — remains one of the few accessible ways to make a living — including foreigners in the country.

Kenya's mood ahead of elections

Political economist Sheila Owigo Olang says that there is little evidence suggesting "that if you were to kick out the traders, that would immediately result in Kenyan nationals having more opportunities."

According to Olang, there may be other motivations at play, as the new policy appears to come at a "convenient" moment ahead of elections.

In her view, "a lot of it is also just populist," describing the current crackdown on foreign traders as a "feel good policy" ahead of the polls; she highlights that the policy could also serve as a message to external players at this moment: "Foreign investors coil back or they freeze or they wait until the election is finished."

Olang argues that since Kenya wants to keep making itself more attractive to serious foreign investment, it should rather concentrate on tackling broader structural problems instead of focusing on smalltime foreign traders.

"We need to work on corruption. We need to work on our Ease of Doing Business Index so that it's easy to invest within Kenya," she told DW.

The East African country meanwhile attracted a record $3.2 billion (€2.75 billion) in foreign direct investment in 2025 — an increase of almost 38% compared the previous year, according to UNCTAD.

Ruto remains keen to expand on this success story.

Youth unemployment remains a major issue across the African continent; in South Africa, these disparities have led to repeated attacks on foreigners Image: Nic Bothma/EPA-EFE

A wider push for local opportunities

One approach in Ruto's arsenal is the proposed Local Content Bill 2025, which is currently before parliament. The draft law would require foreign companies covered by the legislation to source at least 60% of certain goods and services locally.

Among other things, it would require at least 80% of their workforce to be Kenyan citizens.

But according to Olang, the measure would not address the roots of Kenya's unemployment crisis, in particular among the country's discontent youth:

The World Bank estimates the unemployment rate among Kenyans aged between 15 and 24 to stand at 15.25%, though local and regional organizations like the Federation of Kenya Employers often cite a much higher figure of roughly two-thirds of all young Kenyans being affected by unemployed and underemployment.

There are an estimated 7.41 million micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) operating in Kenya Image: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty Images

Who is actually affected by the policy?

The government has not published a comprehensive list of businesses that will be affected by the crackdown, as it remains unclear how many foreign nationals could be impacted by the move.

Meanwhile, Kenya's Foreign Affairs Principal Secretary Abraham Korir Sing'oei emphasized that foreign nationals who meet all existing legal requirements, including holding the necessary work permits and licences, will remain legally protected to operate their businesses in the country.

He said that Ruto's current initiative was direcly linked to the introduction of the Local Content Bill, and should not be regarded as a push to get rid of foreigners in the country.

Questions remain over the broader legality of the developments: Under the East African Community's Common Market rules, citizens of member states have the right to move and provide services across the region — though they have to comply with national licensing and other legal requirements.

The debate has also resulted in comparisons being drawn to recent developments in South Africa, where widespread frustration over a sluggish economy has led to foreign-owned businesses and migrants repeatedly being targeted by anti-immigration campaigns this year.

Kenya has not experienced anti-migrant violence on the scale seen in South Africa — yet.

Immigrants in South Africa pushed out of their own shops To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Australia targets big tech with algorithm opt-out bill
World.content:
The "My Feed, My Way," legislation would require the likes of Facebook, TikTok and Instagram to let users opt out of algorithms or risk heavy fines.

The Australian government announced planned new rules for social media platforms on Tuesday that would give users greater control over their social media algorithms.

Under the "My Feed, My Way" initiative, social media platforms would have to allow users to opt out of content recommended by an algorithm in their feeds.

What is in Australia's social media algorithm bill?

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese unveiled draft legislation that would impose a "duty of care" on major social media platforms, including Facebook, TikTok, and Instagram.

Users would only see content from accounts they choose to follow.

"It's not about giving government control. It's about giving people control," Albanese said.

The bill is expected to be approved by the Australian Parliament and introduced later this year.

Companies that do not comply could be fined up to AU$100 million ($72 million, €62 million).

Social media bans: What it means for you To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Social media bans for children

Anika Wells, Australia's Minister for Communications, said the measure would help ensure children's safety on social media. Australia became the first country to restrict social media access for under-16s in 2025.

Several countries, including Germany, Spain, France, Denmark, and New Zealand, followed Australia's lead and drafted plans to introduce similar age restrictions.

Some big tech companies have opposed such new regulations. They argue it could encourage young users to move to unregulated online spaces.

Edited by: Rob Turner
