World.title: Consistency in illusions and inaction out of fear: barriers to Georgian-Abkhaz dialogue. An opinion from Tbilisi
World.content:
Georgian-Abkhaz dialogue

Numerous criticisms are heard regarding the foreign or domestic policy of the Georgian government. One of the main accusations is inattention and inaction toward the topic of conflicts. In an interview with conflict researcher Vano Abramashvili, we attempted to assess the reality in which peace policy finds itself today, to understand the reasons behind this reality, and, most importantly, to discuss future prospects.

Vano Abramashvili

Question: How would you evaluate the currently existing peace policy? Where are we now, and what processes are taking place on both the Georgian and Abkhaz sides?

Vano Abramashvili: Currently, we find ourselves in a paradigm-less peace. Georgian Dream has utilized “peace policy” in an entirely different sense. Issues regarding Georgian-Abkhaz relations are completely sidelined. As a result, the process has been left entirely to drift. There is also a total lack of trust toward this policy.

On the one hand, everyone realizes that the end of the war in Ukraine will have a major impact on what the situation will be in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region. It will also have a major impact on our policy. We have no guarantee whatsoever that this war will end favorably. Therefore, the Georgian side has entered a spiral of mistrust.

In domestic political discourse, the leading narrative is that we must fortify ourselves like a fortress, that we have no friends, and that everyone has their own interests. This approach has also affected the topic of conflicts.

Every policy and movement related to Abkhazia is perceived as a source of potential destabilization. The attitude is that no way out exists to resolve these problems. There is a feeling that even internal resources do not exist to take these steps.

It is a state of despair and hopelessness.

For our society, this is also an unfamiliar state, because today it seems there are not even alternative visions and ideas. Until now, there existed the idea of Euro-Atlantic integration and, against this backdrop, a vision for conducting peace policy. However, today this Western policy has been suspended. We do not even know how much time and what scale of work will be required of us to restore these damaged relations.

Added to all this is the altered geopolitical situation in the region and globally.

That is why I would call the current state a paradigm-less peace.

Question: Is this paradigm-less state artificially created, or does it simply reflect the reality that took shape after the August 2008 war?

Vano Abramashvili: I think that such a choice was made, and this reality did not create itself.

Any state, no matter what blow it receives, decides for itself what position to place itself in. Back then, the war ended with an undesirable outcome for Tbilisi. The idea of returning the regions through military force became unpopular, and conflict issues shifted entirely into the dimension of Russian-Georgian relations.

Georgian Dream inherited the peace policy of the United National Movement and, in its own way, tailored this policy to its own comfort. It is through this comfort based on nothing that we have arrived at today’s state.

Question: When describing this modern reality, the main attention and responsibility shift to the Georgian side. But if the conflict also has a second side—we must also evaluate the Abkhaz side and its steps. What is their approach and paradigm? What are they doing or not doing that serves to create this lack of perspective?

Vano Abramashvili: The main difference between the Georgian and Abkhaz sides is consistency. The Abkhaz know what they want. Whether it works out for them or not—that does not matter. Their consistent steps obey a logic.

On the Georgian side, it is not like that. Here, policies changed, and individuals changed.

Over the last thirty years, we have clearly seen who is consistent. We must also understand this issue correctly. You can be consistent even in your illusions. The Abkhaz do not have the resources and means to achieve their goals. Creating an independent state is impossible. It is a fact that they are trying to do this, although it is also clear that it is not working out for them.

The Russians also have a consistent vision and plan. There must be an alienation of Georgians and Abkhaz from one another, and Abkhazia must be turned into merely a territory. This territory will ultimately have no ethnic content or purpose.

When the Georgian political class does nothing on a large scale against this and refrains from taking potential political steps due to security risks and fears—this makes it easier for Russia to achieve this long-term goal.

Question: Peace policy must be mutual. Do you notice in Abkhaz political circles or civil society any kind of interest, change, or reflection regarding the policy they themselves carry out toward Georgia? Are there any signs visible that, given a desirable political environment and willingness, peace policy would become mutual?

Vano Abramashvili: A situational alliance with them is possible on many things. We say that peace policy requires two sides, but my argument is that currently not even one side exists.

Both sides today live our own lives; we are in parallel realities.

Let us take even the population of Gali, which is our and the Abkhazians’ natural point of intersection, and assess what special attention they feel from our side.

Neither side is actually interested in a positive peace policy. What we have is a negative peace. And this is merely the absence of war. Real peace requires clarifying where we are, what speaking positions we have, who is ready to concede what, and so forth.

Abkhaz society is even smaller than ours, and they have far fewer resources. Given the established political logic, it does not even surprise me that the first steps do not originate from there.

To evaluate peace steps, those steps must first exist. We cannot evaluate what simply does not exist. And this non-existence has its own understandable reasons.

Question: The architects of the current stagnation are the political forces on all three sides. If political will exists, what topics do you think are practical and future-oriented that would interest the Georgian and Abkhaz sides and “force” them to talk to each other?

Vano Abramashvili: These topics must relate to development – socio-economic and rights-based development, and the improvement of the standard of living.

Everything except status.

I think that even under the conditions of occupation with the Abkhaz, we can talk. It simply requires political will and the correct formats.

On our side, we do not see the ruling party demonstrating political courage, committing to a revolutionary change in a good sense, and taking any step.

Topics with which dialogue can be initiated and which are in the interest of both sides could be a shared living space. For example, energy, climate. Everyone wants to live in a predictable natural environment.

If we explicitly state that in the long-term perspective we aim for cohabitation in a unified state, it is important that democracy, as a political system and a political culture, exists on the ground. Accordingly, this too could be a matter of common touch.

“Georgian Dream” failed to draw the line between strengthening the de facto regime on the ground and protecting human rights, choosing instead to avoid touching this topic altogether in public policy. This, however, is a flawed approach.

Question: Considering the ongoing political processes, do you expect any kind of changes in the direction of peace policy? The war in Ukraine also breeds uncertainty. It is not clear where the processes are ultimately heading.

Vano Abramashvili: We see that conducting the war is costing Russia more and more. This cost is human, political, and economic as well. Accordingly, Russia should likely steer this conflict toward an end; it must end it in some form.

It is natural that the end of the war in Ukraine will exert a major influence on our region—whether it be a temporary freezing of the conflict, a pause, or its final end. But if political initiative is not demonstrated and a vision or formats for a renewed peace policy are not proposed, we may again fail to utilize this new geopolitical reality to strengthen the process of restoring trust.

In peace policy, the human dimension is important – how this policy translates into people’s lives. We are talking about living human beings, about the future. If our policy is not reflected in the lives of the people living there—first and foremost, the population of Gali – then it was never a real and sincere peace policy. It is more indicative of political messaging.

If you speak about poverty reduction, this requires concrete steps and instruments. Peace too is achieved and felt through concrete mechanisms at the human level: through security, social attention, and culture. When this is not present on the ground, a person cannot develop a feeling of peace merely through talks on television.

World.title: “Georgia against Ivanishvili!” – 38th Saturday march in Tbilisi | Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Protests in Georgia against Ivanishvili

The traditional “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on September 5 was held under the main slogan “Georgia against Ivanishvili”. Speakers said democracy was declining in Georgia, relations with the EU and Western partners had sharply deteriorated, and the country’s EU integration process had been suspended despite Georgia already having candidate status.

Participants blamed the situation on Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party and an oligarch widely seen as the country’s de facto ruler.

“Protests will continue until the Ivanishvili government leaves office,” march participants said.

The traditional Saturday march was held in Tbilisi for the 38th time. The demands remain unchanged: the release of detained protesters, new parliamentary elections and a return to the path of European integration.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: ADB to prepare new report on ports, shipping, and logistics in CAREC region
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. The Asian Development Bank will prepare a new report on ports, shipping, and logistics in the Central Asian Regional Economic Cooperation (CAREC) region, ADB’s Senior Transport Specialist (Maritime Transport and Ports), Adrian Sammons, said, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

Sammons made the announcement during the 5th International Conference and Exhibition, Black and Caspian Freight Forum 2026 in Baku.

According to him, there is a difference between a project that is strategically desirable and one that is truly ready for investment.

“First, demand must be demonstrated. Freight volume forecasts must be realistic and supported by market data. The infrastructure must meet actual trade flows, not just projected figures,” he said.

The expert noted that the project must also address critical issues in the transport corridor, particularly by eliminating identified bottlenecks.

“The greatest value often lies in removing constraints such as inefficient border crossings, capacity constraints on railways, roads, or ports, weak intermodal connections, or underdeveloped digital systems,” he said.

According to him, another important component is the institutional environment: “Investors look for transparent governance, predictable regulation, efficient customs procedures, and a clear division of responsibilities among government agencies.”

He also emphasized the need for projects to be economically viable and ready for implementation: “This means demonstrating measurable benefits for trade connectivity, as well as having environmental permits, project documentation, procurement mechanisms, and institutional capacity.” The ADB is expanding its focus on ports, shipping, and multimodal logistics as part of a new initiative to enhance the climate resilience of ports, logistics, and shipping connectivity in the CAREC region.

According to him, the ADB will prepare a new report on ports, shipping, and logistics in the CAREC region.

“The new report will help identify future investments in ports, the decarbonization of shipping, digitalization, and sustainable trade corridors in the Caspian, Black Sea, and broader CAREC regions,” he said.

The expert added that the ADB has long been a partner to Central Asian countries in providing financing and advisory services for major transportation, energy, water, and trade projects, including roads, railways, logistics facilities, improvements to border crossings, and the development of regional economic corridors under the CAREC program.

“Funding will follow well-prepared projects, not just good ideas. A project becomes investment-ready when it solves real problems, creates measurable benefits, and can be successfully implemented,” he said.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Armenia target stronger cooperation across key sectors
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. Uzbekistan and Armenia discussed expanding bilateral cooperation in industry, transportation, agriculture and digital technologies during a new round of political consultations between their foreign ministries.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbek MFA, following consultations between Uzbek Deputy Foreign Minister Bobur Usmanov and Armenian Deputy Foreign Minister Mnatsakan Safaryan held in Yerevan on September 7.

The sides reviewed the current state of bilateral relations and prospects for developing cooperation across political, trade and economic, cultural and humanitarian areas. They also discussed progress in implementing priorities established during contacts between the countries’ leaders and senior officials.

The sides reaffirmed their commitment to expanding the legal framework governing bilateral cooperation and strengthening coordination at international organizations and other multilateral platforms.

Particular attention was given to sectors where the two countries see potential for greater practical cooperation, including industrial cooperation, transportation and logistics, agriculture, digital technologies, tourism and education.

“The sides confirmed their shared commitment to further developing bilateral cooperation and strengthening coordination on a broad range of issues on the bilateral agenda,” the Uzbek Foreign Ministry said.

The discussion of transportation and logistics comes amid efforts by Uzbekistan and Armenia to expand connectivity and identify new opportunities for economic cooperation. Industrial cooperation and agriculture were also highlighted as areas with potential for closer engagement between businesses and relevant institutions.

Digital technologies, tourism and education were included in the discussions, reflecting the broadening scope of the bilateral agenda beyond political dialogue and traditional economic sectors.

The two countries also agreed to continue close coordination between their foreign ministries to strengthen practical cooperation across the bilateral agenda.

The latest round underscored the two sides’ intention to maintain active diplomatic engagement while translating high-level agreements into practical cooperation across economic and humanitarian sectors.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Serbia push for free trade agreement to deepen trade ties
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. Uzbekistan and Serbia are moving toward developing a free trade agreement aimed at increasing bilateral trade by expanding supplies of in-demand goods, as the two countries seek to deepen economic cooperation.

This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Uzbek president, following talks between Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić in Belgrade, where the sides emphasized the need to increase mutual trade and create conditions for broader access to each other’s markets.

The leaders highlighted the importance of developing and adopting a free trade agreement as part of efforts to expand trade between Uzbekistan and Serbia. They also stressed the need to establish cooperation in the field of standardization and organize reciprocal trade exhibitions.

The proposed agreement is expected to become part of the broader economic agenda between the two countries, alongside efforts to strengthen direct contacts between businesses and promote goods that are in demand in their respective markets.

“Particular attention was paid to increasing mutual trade, primarily through expanding supplies of goods in demand in the markets of the two countries,” the Uzbek presidential administration said.

The sides also emphasized the importance of cooperation in standardization, which was identified as another area requiring closer coordination as bilateral trade develops.

Reciprocal exhibitions were also highlighted as a practical tool for promoting products and strengthening business contacts between Uzbekistan and Serbia.

The trade discussions took place as the two countries seek to translate growing political relations into broader economic cooperation. Earlier during the visit, Uzbekistan and Serbia also discussed new joint projects in transportation and logistics, light and food industries, agriculture, pharmaceuticals, medicine and the digital economy.

The two sides have also identified industrial cooperation in areas including auto components, equipment, electrical engineering and electronics as having significant potential.

The development of a free trade agreement would add another dimension to these efforts, with the immediate focus placed on increasing mutual trade and expanding the range of goods supplied between the two countries.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Georgia discuss Middle Corridor infrastructure development
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ) and Georgian partners discussed the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR or Middle Corridor) and logistics infrastructure during a working visit by a KTZ delegation to Batumi, KTZ’s press service said.

The delegation was headed by KTZ Deputy Chairman Yerlan Koishibayev and held a series of meetings with key Georgian partners.

During a meeting with Georgian Deputy Minister of Economy and Sustainable Development Tamar Ioseliani and Director at the Anaklia Deep Sea Port Development Agency David Javakhadze, the parties discussed strategic cooperation, including the joint development of terminal capacities and key projects such as the launch of the Anaklia deep-sea port.

KTZ representatives also met with the management of International Container Terminal Services Inc. (ICTSI) to discuss the joint development of infrastructure at the Batumi International Container Terminal.

The sides paid particular attention to increasing transit cargo volumes along the joint logistics routes. KTZ noted that it continues to develop a terminal network along the entire route, covering the corridor from China and Kazakhstan across the Caspian Sea to the Black Sea and further to Europe.

“KTZ is consistently continuing to build the terminal framework along the entire route, which will increase transit potential and strengthen the connectivity of the regions,” the company said.

During talks with Georgian Railway CEO Lasha Abashidze, the sides noted growing transportation volumes along the TITR.

The parties also discussed practical steps to eliminate bottlenecks and optimize logistics to ensure the uninterrupted movement of container flows along the Trans-Caspian route.

Following the meetings, the sides confirmed their readiness to further strengthen bilateral cooperation aimed at attracting additional cargo flows and developing transport corridors between Kazakhstan and Georgia.

According to KTZ, transit transportation volumes along the TITR amounted to 36,000 TEUs, or 350 container trains, in the first seven months of 2026. Container transportation increased by 50% year-on-year, while the number of container trains rose by 82%. For comparison, 24,000 TEUs and 192 container trains were transported along the route in the same period of 2025.

World.title: UK announces import ban, sanctions on Israeli settlements
World.content:
Britain will ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and sanction Israeli individuals and businesses which work to expand them, in a symbolic move that could reshape Western foreign policy in the region.

Speaking in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon, local time, the United Kingdom's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said his announcement "marked the start of a new approach" for his country.

The move by Britain's Labour government is not expected to have a significant effect on either country's economy.

However, it does represent a G7 nation toughening its stance against Israel, which has historically been considered one of the UK's closest allies.

The specifics of Britain's plan have not been announced, although Mr Miliband told the Commons his country would ban imports from Israeli settlements and "take action" against companies and individuals that provide services, such as construction or finance, for settlement expansion.

"You will face the full force of UK sanctions," he said.

The UK's announcement was widely telegraphed ahead of Mr Miliband's speech, and drew condemnation from right-wing politicians in Israel, the country's president Isaac Herzog and US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee earlier in the day.

World.title: Legendary horseman Paddy Payne Sr dies aged 90
World.content:
Legendary horseman and patriarch of the famous Australian racing family, Paddy Payne Sr, has died aged 90.

He was father of Michelle Payne, the first woman to win the Melbourne Cup, and husband to late Mary Payne, whom he had 10 children with.

Daughter Michelle took to social media to pay a tribute to her father, saying "RIP Dad. You finally get to go and see Mum again".

Paddy Payne (left) with daughter Michelle (centre) and son Stevie (right). (ABC Ballarat: Dominic Cansdale)

Racing Victoria issued a statement acknowledging the passing of the "legendary Ballarat horseman".

"Paddy was the patriarch of the Payne family as they established themselves as one of the most famous surnames in Australian racing," the statement continued.

Racing Victoria Chief Executive Aaron Morrison said "Paddy was the doyen of a family that has greatly enriched Australian racing and provided us with so many great memories".

" Whilst Paddy has passed, his contribution to the sport will not be forgotten and his legacy will live on. "

Eight of Payne's 10 children became professional jockeys.

Daughter Michelle enjoyed multiple Group One triumphs, including her trailblazing 2015 Melbourne Cup win.

Michelle Payne's father never doubted her Paddy Payne said unlike many punters he thought Prince Of Penzance had a good chance of winning Australian racing's biggest prize.

Son Patrick also achieved great success in Group One racing, both as a jockey and a trainer.

Paddy Payne was immortalised in a film about Michelle's Melbourne Cup victory titled Ride Like a Girl, where he was played by the late Sam Neill.

Payne's wife Mary died in a car accident in 1986, leaving him to raise their children when Michelle was just six months old.

Later in life, two of his daughters died — Brigid in 2007 and Bernadette in 2025 — both were jockeys.

In an interview with the ABC in 2015, Payne said: "We've had some good success and some bad luck as well."

World.title: Three attacks in Tehran could 'amount to war crimes', report finds
World.content:
Amnesty International is demanding formal investigations into three American and Israeli attacks on densely packed suburbs in Tehran that killed at least 41 civilians, arguing the devastating impact and choice of weapons may amount to war crimes.

The advocacy group examined the March incidents, analysing photos and videos of the attacks available on social media as well as eyewitness accounts and official reports in Iranian state media to question the legitimacy of the strikes.

It found that the targets of the strikes, namely police stations and paramilitary compounds, may have been justified under international law.

But Amnesty said the damage to the surrounding areas, specifically civilian apartment blocks and businesses in congested neighbourhoods, should have been cause to rethink the attacks because of "entirely predictable consequences for civilians".

"Military combatants have to take feasible precautions to avoid civilian casualties," Andrew Witheford, a spokesperson for Amnesty International Australia, told the ABC.

"If it's possible, they need to give warning, and the strike itself and the action taken need to be proportionate to the military objectives that are being sought.

" Our analysis of these three attacks indicate that this bar wasn't cleared. "

Amnesty, which describes the US and Israel's war with Iran as unlawful, said the two countries must allow independent investigations of their conduct relating to the three attacks, as well as the widely criticised strike on the Minab school on the very first day of the war which killed 150 people, including 120 children.

When asked whether those countries would launch independent investigations, Mr Witheford said: "It saddens me to say that it's not looking good so far."

Loading...

'Horrific' scenes after early air strikes

One of the attacks investigated by Amnesty was on Niloufar Square in central Tehran on the evening of March 1, the second day of the war.

A police station appeared to be the target, but significant damage was reported to nearby apartment buildings and shops in the area.

Iranian officials said at least 20 civilians were killed in the strikes.

Amnesty said it had spoken to a local journalist, whom the organisation named "Kiana", who said that the scene was "horrific" and that between 15 and 20 apartment buildings had been damaged in the blasts.

Residential buildings were reduced to rubble near Niloufar Square. (AFP)

She told the organisation that a father and son working in a bakery were believed to be among the dead.

The second strike was on the Resalat neighbourhood in eastern Tehran, where Iranian officials said at least 16 people were killed, including 12 members of the same family, on the afternoon of March 9.

The strike there appeared to target a building belonging to the Basij, the Iranian regime's notorious paramilitary branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Amnesty's investigation revealed another three buildings were badly damaged, but the organisation could only verify one as being a residential block.

One source it spoke to insisted the residents of the building, known as Number 12, were all civilians, and said he had seen horrific injuries and bodies blown to pieces.

Despite threats from Trump, Iran's regime is 'at war with its own people' Three Iranians share their insights on life under the regime, as the war passes its fifth month.

At the time, the Israeli military had announced it was hitting Basij targets across the Iranian capital.

The third attack scrutinised by Amnesty occurred on March 13 in Javadieh, southern Tehran, where at least five people were killed.

The group described it as a "low-income neighbourhood characterised by aging infrastructure and small, closely packed homes and other civilian structures".

Again, a police station appeared to be the target. But Iranian state media reported a number of other buildings were either destroyed or seriously damaged, including an apartment block and nearby businesses.

Amnesty said it had reviewed a photograph published by state media and believed it showed components of an American guided missile system used by the US and Israeli militaries.

Effects extend 'well beyond' targets

The United States and Israel are yet to respond to Amnesty's report but have previously defended their military actions as lawful.

Both countries have said they do not target civilians.

Amnesty said the control the Iranian regime has over the country's police force may have made the police stations lawful military targets — despite police generally being considered civilian in many circumstances.

It also said the Basij, being paramilitary, may also have qualified "as a military objective under international humanitarian law".

But it argued its analysis of the three strikes raised "serious concerns" about breaches of international law, "particularly the principles of distinction and precautions in attack."

Loading...

In Niloufar, Amnesty argued the presence of civilians was predictable.

"Even if the police station could qualify as a military objective … the timing and location, the presence of civilians in surrounding residential buildings, restaurants and public spaces required the attacking forces to take all feasible precautions to avoid or minimise incidental death of or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects," it said.

"The extensive blast damage affecting numerous apartment blocks, a school, and commercial premises, coupled with reports of significant civilian casualties, suggests the use of explosive weapons with wide area effects.

" The use in a densely populated area of a weapon whose effects extend well beyond the targeted object raises serious concerns regarding the respect of the principles of distinction and precaution. "

Israel undertaking genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, Amnesty International claims A new 300-page report alleges Israel has and continues to undertake acts of genocide against Palestinian people in Gaza.

In Javadieh, Amnesty said the concerns around harm to civilians should have been considered.

"The reported blast radius, extending up to 50 metres, and the scale of damage to homes and commercial properties indicate that the effects of the attack were not limited to the intended target," it said.

In Resalat, the organisation said it was likely a building other than the Basij compound was hit in a separate strike.

"Investigations should clarify whether any residential buildings that were struck were intentionally targeted, or whether they were struck recklessly despite indications that they were civilian objects," Amnesty said.

"If so, those attacks may amount to war crimes."

Hundreds of civilians have been killed since the Iran war began on February 28, with estimates ranging from 1,700 to more than 3,400.

Mr Witheford said Iran had also contributed to civilian deaths during the war, both through attacking other countries and executing its own people.

"The laws of war apply to the Iranian military as well, and they have dropped the ball in this case as well," he said.

Mr Witheford said Amnesty approached both the Israeli and United States militaries for input on its report and did not receive a response.

World.title: Football league says Swans scandal comments 'clearly insensitive'
World.content:
A country football league has distanced itself from "insensitive" and "unacceptable" comments made at a recent awards event at which the master of ceremonies joked about the Sydney Swans scandal.

But the league also said that, "in his defence", the man was attempting "to show how certain events can galvanise a team's resolve".

In video posted online, the MC at the Whyalla Football League's event made light-hearted reference to the Swans scandal, citing it in the context of local club South Whyalla's upcoming match.

The man, Jock Sleep, suggested the local club draw inspiration from Sydney's win over Brisbane in Saturday's AFL qualifying final, linking that performance to the scandal engulfing the Swans.

"My advice to the Souths' coach … [is] maybe we can manufacture a good old-fashioned scandal just to get that team going," the MC said.

"It worked for the Sydney Swans. I'm just talking a scandal — not a real big one."

Last week, Victoria Police detectives spoke with four Sydney Swans players as part of their sexual assault investigation linked to the club.

A still from the video shared online. (Facebook)

The man's remarks at the Whyalla awards night were strongly condemned by Australian Femicide Watch's Sherele Moody, who shared video on her social media pages and described the comments as "terrible".

"The crowd at the awards night laughed along with him. There was no attempt to shut down the conversation by the organisers," she wrote.

In a statement, Whyalla Football League president Keith Sichler said Mr Sleep was a "well-known local identity" and local football historian.

"His comments and joke were clearly insensitive and not indicative of current attitudes. In his defence, it was merely an attempt to show how certain events can galvanise a team's resolve with the intent of improving their performance. Nothing more," Mr Sichler said.

"Nonetheless, references of this nature are unacceptable and inconsistent with the inclusive and respectful environment we expect across our League.

"The WFL has spoken with him, and he understands the impact of his remarks and has expressed regret for any harm caused."

The ABC has reached out directly to Mr Sleep for comment.

Last week, the Swans said five players would remain stood down for the remainder of the season for breaching the club's behavioural standards in a post-AFL match hotel party in August, regardless of how an ongoing police investigation unfolded.

Victoria Police has interviewed four Sydney men as part of an investigation into sexual assault allegations during a post-AFL match party at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel.

World.title: Thieves steal two paintings from Renoir Museum worth 9 million euros
World.content:
Thieves have stolen two paintings from the Renoir Museum in France via a hole made in a garden fence.

The town's mayor, Bryan Masson, said a group of “well-equipped” and “well-informed” thieves broke into the museum dedicated to French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, early Tuesday, local time.

They sliced through a fence and entered the museum through the ground floor, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames, Mr Masson said.

Coco Lisant (1905) by Renoir, one of the paintings reportedly stolen. (Wikimedia Commons: Pierre-Auguste Renoir)

The museum had 12 works by Renoir in total, four were stolen, but two canvases were dropped during the police chase and found in the museum garden.

Local French newspaper Nice-Matin reported the stolen paintings as Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895), Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910), Coco Lisant (1905) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

The mayor confirmed Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Jeune fille au puits were the two artworks still missing.

Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (left) and Portrait of Madame Pichon (right) by Renoir. (Wikimedia Commons: Pierre-Auguste Renoir)

Mr Masson's office estimated the value of the stolen works at 9 million euros ($14.5 million).

"Spotted thanks to the town's video surveillance cameras, the two individuals fled, abandoning one of the stolen paintings as they ran," Mr Masson said.

Mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer Bryan Masson makes a statement outside the Musee Renoir after four paintings were stolen. (AFP: Valery Hache)

"The museum alarm went off at 5:48am. At 5:53am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene.

"Since this morning, both the municipal and national police have been deployed to the site.

" The perpetrators are being actively sought, and the investigation is ongoing. "

The museum was closed Tuesday while the investigation unfolded.

The mayor said it took five minutes for authorities to respond. (AFP: Valery Hache)

The Renoir Museum was opened in 1960 in the painter's last home before his death in 1919.

Its collection includes objects and furniture that belonged to Renoir, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as portraits, landscapes, and nudes painted by the artist.

Spate of art heists in Europe

The theft comes less than a year after jewels valued at around 88 million euros ($141 million) were stolen during a daylight robbery from the Louvre in Paris.

The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the stolen items still have not been found despite extensive searches by French investigators in the Paris region and exchanges with police in Belgium, Italy and beyond.

How the Louvre jewellery heist was pulled off Here are the details on the items stolen in the Louvre heist that unfolded in broad daylight in Paris.

In August, three century-old paintings, including a Renoir, stolen by an organised gang from an Italian museum during a three-minute heist were recovered.

The artworks included Fish by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cézanne's Still Life with Cherries, and Odalisque on the Terrace by Henri Matisse.

Days after their recovery, another four paintings were stolen from another Italian museum.

Artworks by 15th century painter Antonello da Messina were taken from the Museo Regionale di Messina — the pieces some of the only surviving work by the Renaissance painter to have remained in his native city.

ABC/AFP/AP

World.title: Gun law reform in Tasmania on knife's edge with independent holding casting vote
World.content:
Independent MP George Razay has emerged as holding the deciding vote on whether ownership firearm limits will be included in the Tasmanian government's firearms reform legislation.

Debate on the highly contentious legislation, tabled by Police Minister Felix Ellis, began Tuesday with the lower house members outlining their positions on the bill, and several amendments being flagged.

While the bill does not include an ownership cap, Labor will move amendments to include an ownership cap of five guns for individuals.

The proposed legislation was tabled by Police Minister Felix Ellis. (Facebook: Felix Ellis)

Under the opposition's plan, primary producers and sporting shooters would be eligible to own up to 10 guns, while exemptions would also be available from the police commissioner.

While debate on the amendments is not expected to take place until Thursday, numbers in the House of Assembly on the issue of caps appear to be locked at 17–17.

The Greens are expected to support the caps, as are independents Kristie Johnston, Helen Burnet and Peter George.

But the caps are not supported by the Liberal government; Shooters, Fishers and Farmers MP Carlo Di Falco; or independents David O'Byrne and Craig Garland.

About 20 amendments have been flagged for Thursday's debate by the opposition and cross-bench. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

It leaves independent Bass MP George Razay as the deciding vote, however, he did not reveal his position in his second reading speech.

Dr Razay told the house that he understood the issue would be up for consideration during the committee phase of the debate, where amendments are discussed.

The bill, a response to the Bondi terror attacks of 2025, is expected to pass the lower house in some form.

Among other reforms, the bill introduces mandatory minimum jail terms for firearms offences and for setting up Tasmanian requirements for a National Firearms Register.

Community safety at forefront

Mr Ellis told the house that the tabled bill represented the "most comprehensive legislative reform" to the Firearms Act since it was introduced in 1996.

Labor's Police spokesperson Jen Butler told parliament on Tuesday that MPs had "a responsibility" to question its strength.

"Do we want to reflect on this decision with regret, when there is another incident where a gun is used to maim, kill or bring terror to a community?" she said.

Ms Butler said there was evidence that owners with a high number of guns were targeted by thieves. Relatively few guns were also recovered after being stolen, she said.

The state government has said caps would unfairly target law-abiding firearms owners, and there was no evidence the caps would improve public safety.

Some firearms will be put into a more restrictive licence category under the proposed reforms. (ABC News)

The opposition has claimed this equates to support for "unlimited guns" — something Premier Jeremy Rockliff hit back at during the debate.

"Tasmania does not have unlimited gun ownership today, and this bill does not create it tomorrow," he said, pointing to significant regulations on gun ownership.

Independent MP David O'Byrne said compelling evidence that gun caps would improve community safety was needed, and that it would mean the same number of people owned guns, even if they each had fewer.

Police Commissioner Donna Adams is supportive of ownership caps. Earlier this year, she wrote to Mr Ellis, saying "public safety must take precedence over the privilege of firearms ownership".

More than 11,000 Tasmanians have signed a parliamentary petition opposing ownership caps.

Proposed grandfathering to be removed

The government's bill reclassifies straight pull rifles and shotguns to the more restrictive category C licence, available to approved collectors and primary producers.

'Weaker' Tasmanian gun reforms criticised Tasmania's government says its proposed gun reform legislation strikes the right balance and will result in a significant uplift in community safety — but critics say the laws are a "betrayal" and won't make Tasmania safer.

However, those arrangements would be grandfathered, meaning that current owners of those guns could retain ownership without an upgraded licence.

Instead, transition arrangements would be included, so people could keep the guns while they applied for a category C licence.

"There may be sound reasons for this transition, but parliament should ask whether the sound reason for reclassification is fully achieved if the firearms already in circulation remain unaffected," Greens Police spokesperson Tabatha Badger said.

The government's bill also makes Australian citizenship a requirement for holding a firearms licence — with exceptions for New Zealanders or those with a genuine work-related reason.

While Labor has said it wanted to amend the bill to remove grandfathering provisions, that proposal is expected to fail.

The Greens indicated that it may put non-citizens "at risk of unreasonable outcomes".

Raft of amendments flagged

The 87-page bill makes other changes to firearms laws in Tasmania, including the introduction of mandatory minimum jail terms for those who commit serious firearms offences, along with increases to penalties.

The bill would also allow the set up of the National Firearms Register, a buyback scheme, and looks to increase intelligence-sharing capabilities between law enforcement agencies.

There are also new rules for antique firearms, which Mr Ellis said would simplify the process for possessing, displaying and storing antique firearms.

Owners would need to provide contact details, information about the type of firearm, and where and how it is stored, while display requirements have been updated.

Loading...

About 20 amendments have been flagged for Thursday's debate by the opposition and cross-bench.

These include attempting to reduce the licence renewal period from five years to two, to remove the mandatory jail terms, and expand the 'fit and proper persons' test.

Ms Johnston will seek an amendment to allow police to consider a person's history of family violence or coercive control behaviour, even if no offence or protection order has been recorded.

She recounted the story of one constituent, which she said still haunted her.

"She confided in me that her law-abiding, firearms-owning husband — a licensed owner — would simply play with his gun safe keys whenever she displeased him," she said.

"No shot was fired, but she could see what was intended with that act."

World.title: 'People are furious': RBA deputy governor says more needs to be done on inflation
World.content:
The Reserve Bank's Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser knows Australians are "furious" about inflation and while he is determined to bring it down, he says the RBA is not at the point where it has to take more drastic action.

In a wide-ranging interview, Mr Hauser told 7.30 that inflation is the major problem for Australia's central bank, as he acknowledged Australians are struggling with the continued high cost of living and rising interest rates.

He indicated those rates could rise higher in the coming months.

While Mr Hauser defended the Australian economy as "doing quite well" on issues of unemployment and real household incomes, he signalled out the continuing scourge of inflation as the nation's biggest problem.

Headline inflation rose to 3.5 per cent in the year to July, despite the continued efforts of the RBA and government to bring it down.

The four major banks are all forecasting the RBA will lift interest rates by the end of the year. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Hauser acknowledged the anger and frustration in the community.

"People are furious about inflation," he said, calling it the RBA's "one big problem".

"I understand why. It's unfair. It hits people on low incomes, it damages price signals, it makes the job of companies difficult.

"What [people] want us to do is our job and bring inflation down.

"Everywhere I go, I hear cost, cost, cost, inflation, inflation, inflation, and that's our responsibility. We have to put that right.

"When people go to the supermarket every week, they look at the price of the goods they're buying, they compare them to where they were a few years ago and they say, 'Hell, what's going on here?'.

"That is a very lasting and pervasive issue that is a function of the pick-up in inflation after COVID and will take years for us to fully resolve."

As to why Australia is still struggling with inflation, Mr Hauser says it is a three-headed monster.

"One is the Middle East and the ongoing crisis there, one is a really unexpected global boom driven by AI, and one is the weakness of the supply potential of the Australian economy."

Rate hike not 'inevitable' but likely

One solution to fixing inflation could be hiking interest rates dramatically, but Mr Hauser said the RBA was unlikely to do that just yet.

"We could raise interest rates sharply [and] we could do it tomorrow," he said.

"We could decide, 'You know what? We no longer take seriously the full employment part of our objective. We're going to bring inflation down come hell or high water.'"

Mr Hauser said Australia was not at that point just yet but gave a strong indication that the central bank is contemplating hiking interest rates this month as the economy continues to grow — albeit slowly — and the labour market remains tight.

He denied a rate hike was "inevitable" but said the bank was very focused on bringing inflation down.

"Inflation is too high and that's why we raised interest rates three times at the beginning of this year," Mr Hauser said.

" The question now, frankly, for us is have we done enough or is more needed? "

Australia's four major banks are all forecasting the central bank will lift interest rates by 0.25 percentage points to 4.6 per cent by the end of the year.

Mr Hauser's comments came hours after his RBA colleague, assistant governor Sarah Hunter, said the central bank "may well have to raise interest rates" if it senses inflation is stronger than its forecasts."

The RBA board will meet at the end of September to decide whether to move or hold the cash rate — currently sitting at 4.35 per cent.

New inflation figures, however, will only become public a day after that crucial decision — on September 30.

Mr Hauser says he expects house prices to fall "a little bit more". (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Asked about the current downturn in the housing market, Mr Hauser said the bank was watching it closely as the price adjustment will have an impact on consumption growth.

He expected prices to fall "a little bit more" but said current conditions in the housing market are not a key factor in the bank's forecasts.

"While house prices play a role in the economy, they're not really as big as some of the things we talked about earlier in the conversation, global growth trends, productivity, the risk environment globally, in the Middle East and so on and so forth," he said.

Persistent inflation eroding trust in central banks

Compared to nations including the UK, Canada and the US, Australia has been slow to bring inflation down.

The RBA projects inflation will return to its target by early 2028.

Last year, the central bank began cutting interest rates before being forced to change course this year just before the war in Iran started.

Mr Hauser said that at the time it looked like a "sweet spot" but that the RBA had consistently updated its position when needed.

Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"When the facts change, we change our position," he said.

" We raised interest rates earlier than other central banks and ... we stand ready to do so again if we need to do. "

Mr Hauser rejected the notion that the RBA was not prepared to answer a question on the role of government spending in the economy.

“We are an equal opportunity monetary policymaker. A dollar of demand, whether it comes from the government or it comes from the private sector or it comes from overseas, has roughly the same effect on the outlook for inflation as a dollar for demand from anywhere else," he said.

“We take government policy as given. It's part of our judgement about the outlook for inflation, but it doesn't have a special status."

Could AI boom be a bust?

Mr Hauser said a recent trip to the US made him more concerned about the global economic outlook as he defended the RBA's longer-term move on inflation.

"We are doing it over a longer period than some other central banks have done. And we're doing it in order to try to protect the jobs gains that happened during COVID," he said.

"We will raise interest rates further than otherwise we would need to do so. We're not at that point yet, but some of these upside risks to inflation are certainly on our mind, and I come back from the US a bit more worried about them than I did when I went."

The Deputy Governor's recent trip to the US saw him look firsthand at a productivity bonanza and an investment boom in artificial intelligence.

Mr Hauser says only time will tell if investments in data centres will pay off. (ABC News: Daniel Irving)

While he said he could see the adoption of the technology, he warned the jury was still out on whether AI companies would all make a fortune — and said the million-dollar question on AI was how to value a future income stream deriving from it.

"Much of it may be a failure," he said.

"Much of it may turn out to be a wrongful allocation of technology to tasks that won't actually solve its purpose, but there is an enormous vibrancy to that process."

" Most of the valuations assume that these companies are going to make a fortune. In practise, several of them won't. "

World.title: Child dead, six others injured in rollover west of Melbourne
World.content:
A school-aged child has died and six others have been taken to hospital with injuries after a single-vehicle rollover on a regional road in Parwan, west of Melbourne, this afternoon.

One child was flown to the Royal Children's Hospital in a critical condition.

Emergency services received reports of a crash near the Nerowie and Parwan-Exford road intersections, south-west of Melton, just before 4pm.

Victorian Police said one child died at the scene while six others were injured.

"Despite CPR being performed, one school-aged child died at the scene," a spokesperson said.

"A second child was airlifted with critical injuries. Five more children were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

"One woman was taken to hospital for observation."

Ambulance Victoria said several children had been taken to the Royal Children's Hospital, including the one who was flown by helicopter.

A Western Health spokesperson said three children were being treated at Sunshine Hospital and all were in a stable condition.

An adult was taken to the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

Ambulance Victoria said many of its specialist crews responded to the incident.

A child has been flown to hospital with critical injuries after a fatal car crash west of Melbourne. (ABC News)

"Two specialist Air Ambulance Victoria helicopter crews, two Mobile Intensive Care Ambulance paramedic crews and seven Advanced Life Support paramedic crews assessed eight people at the scene," an ambulance spokesperson said.

An investigation into the crash is ongoing.

World.title: The loving memory of Michelle Payne’s father that almost made her cry at school
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing The loving memory of Michelle Payne’s father that almost made her cry at school Danny Russell Updated September 8, 2026 — 10:34pm ,first published 6:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of all the stories told about racing patriarch Paddy Payne, few better encapsulated the loving, chaotic nature of his life than the day he dropped off youngest daughter Michelle for her first day of secondary school. It was one of his forgetful moments – a memory lapse that could be brought on by running farms, training horses and raising 10 rowdy kids. A moment that would happen almost 30 years before his peaceful death at home on Tuesday at the age of 90. Paddy Payne, father of 2015 Melbourne Cup winning jockey Michelle Payne, at his family home where he raised his 10 children in Miners Rest. Jesse Marlow The year was 1998, and Michelle, not long turned 13, was following in her sisters’ footsteps. They, too, had gone to Ballarat’s Loreto College. But soon after her father drove in from Miners Rest and dropped her at the school gates, Michelle was hit by a confronting reality: no one could find her name on the classroom lists.



Related Article CBD The next big change coming for pregnant Michelle Payne Confused, she went to the front office with a friend. There she was told she hadn’t been enrolled. “I started to get a bit sad and was nearly crying, and they’re like, ‘don’t cry, it’s okay. We’ll call your dad’,” Michelle told The Age last year. “And they ring dad, who is home by this stage after dropping us off, and they said, ‘Oh, we’re just here with your daughter, Mr Payne, we just have a problem: You haven’t enrolled her’. “And he was like, ‘Ah, haven’t I?’ Because I could hear him. He’s always louder over the phone speaker. And he goes, ‘Oh, sorry about that’.



“They’re like, ‘Oh, that’s alright. We’ll try and find her a spot’. So they found me a classroom. Thank God they understood, you know, because he was doing his best – a single parent raising 10 kids.” Born in Hawera in South Taranaki, New Zealand, Payne’s best turned out to be pretty good. His life was upended in 1986 when his wife, Mary, was killed in a car accident near Ballarat. Initially, there was talk of farming out the youngest children to other families to help ease the burden. Michelle was just six months old. But the patriarch wanted to keep the family together and decided to raise the children on his own. “My dad always talked about her to me, always told me what a beautiful lady she was,” Michelle recalled in an interview when she was 24.



“It was probably hard for the older kids who remembered her to talk about her. They had their memories they kept to themselves. Dad used to tell me every day how lucky he was. I think it was good for him to get it out, but it was good for me too.” Under Payne’s guidance, the family would go on to leave an indelible mark on the sport of racing. Maree, Cathy and Bernadette Payne at Flemington. Neil Newitt Eight of the 10 kids would become jockeys – Brigid, Bernadette, Therese, Patrick, Andrew, Maree, Cathy and Michelle. Only Margaret and Stevie would not ride in a race. Patrick, Andrew and Michelle would later become trainers like their father.



“He passed away peacefully in his sleep, early this morning at home, he got to have his dying wish,” daughter Therese said in a family statement on Thursday. “We feel he had a great life, and we were happy he was comfortable. We hope he’s joined our mum and brother and sisters.” The Paynes lost son Michael in 1985, three days after he was born. Eldest sister Brigid died in 2007 from a heart attack, six months after a bad track work fall, while the family lost second-eldest daughter Bernadette in March last year. Mercifully, there were high points in between. Patrick Jr won the 2002 Cox Plate on Northerly and Michelle would create history by becoming the first woman to ride the winner of the Melbourne Cup in 2015.



Michelle’s trailblazing exploits would be captured in the film Ride Like a Girl. Her father was portrayed by the late, great Kiwi actor Sam Neill, while his youngest son Stevie would play himself, the strapper of Prince Of Penzance. Michelle rode her first winner as a 15-year-old on her father’s horse Reigning in front of her cheering schoolmates at Ballarat. Soon after the victory, her father suggested she chuck it in and go back to school. Michelle Payne with brother Stevie and 2015 Melbourne Cup winner Prince Of Penzance. Getty Images “For the first six months, Dad was saying, ‘You just don’t seem to have it. All the other kids showed a little bit of potential...’,” Michelle said. “I remembered him telling the other kids that they weren’t any good either, telling Maree she could only sit one leg either side and move her little fingers, that was all she could do.



“I knew it wasn’t just me, but it made me so angry. It made me more determined to try harder and prove him wrong.” In some ways, she did prove him wrong. Payne was always a big supporter of female jockeys and knew they would one day win the Melbourne Cup. He just didn’t dream it would be one of his daughters. Patrick and Michelle Payne. Getty Images Apart from his lifelong love of horses, Payne was also a dairy farmer. He spent his final years at the family property at Miners Rest near Ballarat. Michelle and Stevie lived nearby. His last runner was Nip at Kilmore on March 6 this year, 10 days before his 90th birthday, while his final winner was Rosalia at Ballarat in August 2024 when he was 88.



His filly Miner’s Miss, ridden by Michelle, finished third in the 2018 VRC Oaks. It gave the entire family a thrill. “I worked my whole life with him and started my apprenticeship with him and I can’t remember him having a runner in a group 1, let alone riding for him in one,” Payne told The Age before the race. “Riding for him in a group 1 is so special.” While Payne won races over the jumps in New Zealand, the galloper that would help set him up for life was Our Paddy Boy, a horse he bought in New Zealand for $1300 in the late 1970s who would go on to win the 1980 group 1 Ellerslie Sires’ Produce Stakes (1400m). Payne sold Our Paddy Boy to Robert Sangster for $300,000, a transaction that would bankroll the family’s movie to Australia. They intended to come for two years and never left. As the Payne family mourned the loss of their father on Thursday, the tributes poured in from the racing world.



Racing Victoria chief executive Aaron Morrison called him “the doyen of a family that has greatly enriched Australian racing”. “Paddy will be remembered as a great horseman and a loving father,” Morrison said. “His positive influence on female jockey participation cannot be undersold, having encouraged his daughters to ride at a time when female jockeys were fighting for acceptance.” Victorian Jockeys’ Association chief executive Matt Hyland said the state’s riding ranks were richer for the Payne family’s contributions, and “for that we must say thank you to Paddy”. Australian Trainers’ Association chief executive Stephen Bell said Payne held a trainer’s licence in Victoria for more than 40 years after earlier success in New Zealand. “His role in nurturing a family that has contributed so much to racing is legendary and something that we all respect and are thankful for,” Bell said.



Ballarat Turf Club chairman Bill Gribble said Payne’s contribution to racing extended well beyond the racetrack. “Paddy was the patriarch one of Australian racing’s most remarkable families, and his influence, horsemanship and dedication to the industry will leave a lasting legacy,” Gribble said. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Super-sized political battle: Chalmers issues warning on ‘existential threat’
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSuperannuation Super-sized political battle: Chalmers issues warning on ‘existential threat’ Shane Wright September 8, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The cost of the age pension to taxpayers will fall even as more than 9 million people reach retirement age over the next 40 years, Treasurer Jim Chalmers will reveal on Wednesday amid accusations that the next election will be an existential fight for the future of superannuation. As the Liberal Party signalled it was looking at allowing young people to access their super to get out of the rental market, Chalmers will argue Australia is defying a global trend in age pension cost blowouts because of the superannuation system. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will release data showing the cost to the budget of the age pension is falling – due to superannuation. Alex Ellinghausen One Nation this week revealed that if it formed government, renters and people with a mortgage could take a quarter of their 12 per cent super guarantee as income for up to three years in a move it said would deliver $44 a week to someone on the median wage. It has since struggled to explain how the policy would work, denied it would add to inflation while reducing retirement incomes, and prompted One Nation’s treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce to declare he was “not Jesus Christ” when pressed by ABC’s 7.30 to outline key elements of his party’s plan.



Chalmers, in a speech to the Super Members Council on Wednesday, will reveal findings of the upcoming intergenerational report that is due to be delivered on September 21. The report, instigated by Peter Costello in 2002, outlines key pressures on the budget over the coming four decades. Related Article Analysis

Superannuation One Nation’s super raid: inflationary today, impoverishing tomorrow According to Chalmers, the latest intergenerational report will show that by 2066, there will be about 9 million people over the age pension age of 67. But the number of people on the pension is expected to fall from 66 per cent last year to 52 per cent. Budget spending on the pension is expected to fall from 2.3 per cent of GDP last year to 1.8 per cent by the mid-2060s. By contrast, pension spending is expected to reach 10 per cent by 2060 in the UK, 8 per cent in Canada, 7 per cent in New Zealand and 6 per cent in the US.



“That is phenomenal in an ageing society, and it’s essential,” Chalmers will say. “Super takes serious pressure off social security outlays and makes the budget much more sustainable as a consequence. “Having super at the core of the best retirement incomes system in the world means pension spending as a share of the economy will be the lowest in the OECD, but even as those costs moderate, retirees will have more economic security, not less.” Chalmers will reveal that the median retirement age super balance will approach $450,000 by the mid-2030s. That would be more than double the current estimated $200,000 and well up on the $115,000 of 2015. In Costello’s first intergenerational report, the age pension was forecast to climb to 4.6 per cent of GDP by 2046-47 and continue to increase. At the time, the superannuation guarantee levy was legislated to rise to 9 per cent.



The guarantee reached 12 per cent last financial year. In Chalmers’ 2023 intergenerational report, Treasury expected the age pension to cost 2 per cent of GDP by the early 2060s. On Tuesday, the Australian Financial Review revealed that the Liberal Party under Sussan Ley costed a policy almost identical to that unveiled by Hanson. Under the Liberal proposal, while a worker could withdraw three percentage points of their super, there was no time limit. And rather than coming through a person’s super fund as proposed by One Nation, payments would come directly from a person’s employer. The extra pay would be taxed at a person’s marginal rate. This would deliver an extra $1 billion in personal income tax to the government every year as superannuation is taxed at a concessional rate.



Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg said the Coalition was concerned that more people would enter retirement as renters. Related Article Superannuation Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy “If we are going to become almost a majority nation of retired renters, then we need to look very carefully at how these things are calibrated,” he said. But Chalmers will argue both the Coalition and One Nation were intent on dismantling superannuation in a move that would hurt the budget and the retirement incomes of older Australians. “We’re witnessing now the biggest threat to compulsory super, with preservation at its core, in the four decades since it began.



“The next election will be super’s existential moment. It will help determine whether we make the most of our intergenerational advantages or trash them.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Stayin’ alive on that big dipper
World.content:
The Brothers Gibb (C8) sure got around back in the day, going by this latest encounter. Les Herbert of Concord recalls that “in 1963, my brother Paul, then aged 14 was a friend of Bandstand regular Trevor Gordon who invited him to Luna Park where they spent the day with a couple of other 14-year-olds, Gibb twins, Maurice and Robin. He reminisced on that story over many years. On a sad note, not one of the four from that day made the age of 65.”

“Robyn Cashman suggests a Cathy Wilcox book would make a great addition to every school’s modern history reading list,” notes Maralyn Lawson of Greenwich. ” A wonderful idea. Europe Since Versailles : A History in One Hundred Cartoons with a Narrative Text (1940) by the New Zealand-born political cartoonist David Low was brilliant teaching resource. Like Wilcox, Low encapsulated dire circumstances with honesty, wit and a depth of understanding which clarified complexity and human failing without rancour.”

“Don’t know about a book,” says Barry Riley of Woy Woy. “But surely, there’s an art gallery somewhere dedicated to Cathy Wilcox’s work.”

Merilyn McClung of Forestville rejoins the name (change) game: “I suggest that north of the 40th parallel in the US be renamed (C8) Canada South and the remainder North Mexico. That will rid the world of this troublesome president.” Grand idea. Now you just have to talk those two nations into taking on a $US40 trillion ($55.3 trillion) debt.

“Being retired and having time on my hands and needing a good laugh, I thought I might attend the ICAC inquiry (C8),” says Paul Duncan of Leura. “But then I realised I’d better not in case I contracted the memory loss, which seems to be contagious, and could not find my way home.” Jeff McNamara of Ulverstone (Tas) adds: “Seems Ray Hadley (as a witness in the Alan Jones trial) has also been infected with Amnesia testium following outbreaks in the ICAC inquiries. Better get the N95 face masks out if you’re in Sydney at the moment.”

World.title: Some designer clothing attracts a collector’s premium. But which?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingCollectables Opinion Some designer clothing attracts a collector’s premium. But which? Stephen Crafti Money contributor September 8, 2026 — 8:00pm

September 8, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fashion museums around the world include a feast of designers from Chanel through to Jean Paul Gaultier. While there are a few Australian designers in the mix, it’s still fairly early days when it comes to collecting the more recent talent from Down Under. The National Gallery of Victoria (NGV) was recently donated a substantial collection by Australian designer Martin Grant, now based in Paris, along with others, such as Akira Isogawa and Toni Maticevski. Several more are being closely watched. A collection of looks by Toni Maticevski. Steven Siewert Shapiro Auctioneers is regularly finding Australian designers appearing at auction, including Collette Dinnigan, who first presented her collection in Paris in 1995. It’s surprising then, given her presence on the fashion scene well into the ’90s, that her clothing, such as a laced embossed camisole, can be purchased on the secondary auction market for only $40. Buy what you love rather than banking on a financial return. Ida Combley, co-ordinator of design at Shapiro Auctioneers



Others, such as Zimmermann, who also cut through to a European audience and still does, fares considerably better at Shapiros. “Zimmerman’s ‘Amalfi Coast’ collection with its lace and floral prints, is still popular, as well its evening dresses, reaching several hundred dollars,” says Ida Combley, co-ordinator of design at Shapiro Auctioneers in Sydney. It takes a few more decades back into this fashion industry before the big bucks ‘kick in’. Comley refers to a late 1980s dress designed by Linda Jackson in collaboration with Jenny Kee and sold through their store, Flamingo Park in Sydney’s Strand Arcade, as getting more traction, selling at Shapiros for $480 plus buyer’s premium. Designers from the more recent past, such as Bianca Spender, are also attracting an audience on the secondary market – with one of her dresses selling for $945 plus buyer’s premium. Some Australian designers attracting attention are less well known to the broader Australian audience, with Combley noting the recent collections of Nicol & Ford, recognised for their silhouettes and garment construction.



“They’re continually experimenting with fabrics,” she adds. Other designers such as Song for the Mute are drawing attention, not only for their designs but the use of poetry on many of the garments. Songs for the Mute “Most of the people collecting Song for the Mute are in their mid-20s and it’s often difficult to predict if the prices on the secondary market will head north,” says Combley, who certainly sees a designer’s representation on the catwalks of Paris as being one factor to increase the value of a designer’s work long term. “Sometimes, you need a 20-year gap between when something’s first released and how valuable it is now. There’s a considerably longer time period when you’re valuing European fashion,” adds Combley, who suggests “buy what you love rather than banking on a financial return”. Patty Huntington, Features & Fashion News Director at Harper’s BAZAAR Australia, has been following the rise of Australian fashion designers since the mid-1980s.



She singles out designers such as Toni Maticevski, who certainly made an impact with his recent collection at Australian Fashion Week, held in May. His two brides, one wearing black lace, the other white, were donned with headdresses akin to bird cages. “Designers like Toni, who have an artisanal approach will certainly be highly collectable in the future, together with others such as Romance was Born,” says Huntington, who also points out the designs of Grace Lillian Lee, a First Nations fashion designer, who has also collaborated with the likes of Jean Paul Gaultier. “I would say that the value is in the craftsmanship, with some of Lee’s designs conceived like sculpture.” While museums and galleries such as the NGV and Sydney’s Powerhouse Museum have been collecting contemporary Australia fashion for many years, there are also smaller institutions, such as The Australian Museum of Clothing and Textiles in Maitland in the Hunter Valley, that include fashion designers from the more recent past. Here, one can find a blouse from the 1980s, designed by Prue Acton along with a pewter coloured shirt-style dress from the late 1970s, designed by Anthea Crawford.



“We have over 10,000 items up to the year 2000, from ball gowns to clothes people wore every day. World.title: Essendon asked the AFL for help. It won’t be in the form of early draft picks
World.content:
Photo: Artists Essendon’s draft assistance package is unlikely to include extra first- or second-round picks because of new rules introduced by the AFL this year. The AFL Commission is due to make a decision on the Bombers’ application on the Monday before the grand final, but it is more likely the league will grant the club extra rookie spots to add depth to its list, rather than extra picks. New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh is keen to add talent to the Bombers’ list. Getty Images The assistance package awarded to West Coast at the end of 2025 included one end-of-first-round draft selection and four extra rookie spots for three seasons, while the Kangaroos were awarded extra end-of-first-round draft picks (some of which had to be traded) and extra rookie spots.



But Essendon are set to miss out on such a haul thanks to new AFL rules, which have built additional compensation picks into the system for bottom-five teams if their first-round pick slides back due to a matched bid for a father-son or academy player. The compensation will come in the form of an additional second-round pick, but the Bombers won’t be the only beneficiaries if they trigger it. McVeigh left his job as Sydney assistant coach to take the senior job at Essendon, the club he played for. Getty Images Though they have applied for extra assistance, the new rules mean Richmond, West Coast, potentially Port Adelaide and the Kangaroos would also receive compensation if a bid by the Bombers is matched by a rival. Essendon only need to bid on Carlton’s Cody Walker or Port Adelaide’s Dougie Cochrane with pick No.1 and those clubs, as expected, to match the bid to activate compensation.



Related Article Money Talks

AFL 2026 Buttering up the Power: The Cat-and-Dog fight to land an AFL superstar The Bombers are interested in Melbourne’s Jack Viney, who was among a number of players who entered the trade market in a busy start to the week, with St Kilda’s Rowan Marshall and North Melbourne’s Zane Duursma both requesting a trade, while Lions’ premiership forward Zac Bailey signed a whopping eight-year contract to remain in Brisbane. Based on ladder order, Essendon, who appointed new coach Mark McVeigh last month, have picks No.1 and No.19, as well as No.55 already in this year’s national draft after finishing on the bottom with just two wins. They could also add draft capital if they trade out former skipper Zach Merrett, as expected, to Hawthorn with defender Jordan Ridley also potentially on the move. Essendon fell just short of beating Port Adelaide in the final round of the season. Getty Images



They have added five players inside No.14 in the past three national drafts with Sullivan Robey, Jacob Farrow, Dyson Sharp, Isaac Kako and Nate Caddy all showing promise. Koby Bewick, the son of dual premiership forward Darren, is also a strong prospect in the 2027 national draft, which will include Tasmania in a draft for the first time. Zane Duursma is keen to join the Demons After a year spent contemplating his future, Zane Duursma has decided he can instead flourish at Melbourne after three seasons at the Kangaroos yielded just 38 matches. The forward, who was taken with pick No.4 in the 2023 national draft, one spot ahead of Hawthorn star Nick Watson, is keen to make a fresh start under Steven King, however finalising a trade is likely to take some work.



The Demons have no intention of handing over one of their first round picks while the Kangaroos are expected to value Duursma, who had an offer from North Melbourne, highly given he has just turned 21. Essendon also shape as a stalking horse for the forward (whose brother Xavier plays for the club), having shown some interest in him at the end of last season. Zane Duursma has shown talent in glimpses at the Kangaroos AFL Photos Melbourne have picks six and 10, which could lob a player such as key defender Tyson Bradley with one of those selections. They are keen to use their picks to add to their pool of emerging talent. The Demons have offered Christian Salem a one-year deal as he enters the twilight of his career while they are one of several clubs interested in Brisbane Lions’ forward Will McLachlan. Carlton not resting on their laurels



Having missed out on Bulldogs defender Buku Khamis who will accept a five-year deal to remain at the kennel, the Blues remain in the race for Swans’ forward Joel Amartey, who missed the qualifying final through injury. Carlton are also likely to extend out-of-contract wingman/defender Ollie Hollands, who had an exceptional finals series after a patchy 2026. North Melbourne showed some interest in Hollands but the first-round draft pick is keen to remain with the Blues and discussions are likely to ramp up. Carlton’s Ollie Hollands celebrates a goal against Fremantle. Getty Images The Blues major priority is ensuring they do not upend their list management strategy as they collect enough draft points to match any bid for Cody Walker, the son of 200-gamer, Andrew. Rowan Marshall hollers for a trade



Veteran ruckman Rowan Marshall has declared his desire to leave St Kilda in this year’s trade period after a failed bid to join the Cats last season. Marshall, who still has a year remaining on his contract, wants to get to Geelong, but he has not nominated a preferred destination as he is aware their priority is Zak Butters. Rowan Marshall showed class in his time at the Saints AFL Photos The 30-year-old played well in 2026 after being forced to share ruck duties with highly paid recruit Tom De Koning. Marshall’s cause may be helped if St Kilda can convince Geelong premiership player Sam De Koning to join his brother at the Saints, however there is no indication the Cats’ defender-ruck wants to leave.
